Tab 01 · The machine underneath

What actually happens when you run a query

Most SQL tutorials teach syntax. This one teaches the machine: how a row becomes bytes on a page, why a B+ tree turns a 40-million-row scan into four disk reads, how the planner chooses a join, and what the database is really doing when 8,000 people book the last seat at the same instant. Every chapter is anchored to a real production incident — with the numbers.

15Chapters, basics → internals
26Detailed diagrams
10Production case studies
PostgresReference engine, MySQL noted

01 Why a database at all?

The problem is never "where do I put the data". It's what happens when two people touch it at the same millisecond, and the power dies halfway through.

Production caseFlipkart Big Billion Day — the order that charged but never shipped

A checkout service wrote orders to a log file, called the payment gateway, then decremented stock in a second file. During peak load a pod was OOM-killed between step 2 and step 3.

What broke

Card charged. Order recorded. Stock never decremented, so the item kept selling.

Blast radius
1,840

oversold units before anyone noticed, all needing manual refunds.

Why nothing caught it

No component knew the sequence was incomplete. Each step succeeded on its own.

The fix

One transaction. On restart the engine reads its log, sees no COMMIT, and undoes everything.

The same checkout, with and without a transaction

The five guarantees you're buying

  • Durability — once it says saved, a power cut can't unsay it.
  • Atomicity — a group of changes happens whole, or not at all.
  • Isolation — concurrent users don't corrupt each other's view.
  • Indexed access — find one row in a billion without reading a billion.
  • A query language — ask new questions without rewriting storage.

What it costs

Every one of those is paid for in the pages that follow: durability costs an fsync, isolation costs snapshots and vacuum, indexes cost write amplification.

Understanding which guarantee you're paying for is the difference between tuning a database and guessing at it.

02 Schema, keys and constraints Foundations

Constraints aren't bureaucracy. Each one is a specific production incident that can no longer happen.

Amazon order schema · and the incident each constraint prevents
schema.sqlpostgres
CREATE TYPE order_status AS ENUM ('PENDING','PAID','SHIPPED','CANCELLED');

CREATE TABLE customers (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email       TEXT        NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name        TEXT        NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id              BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id     BIGINT       NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  status          order_status NOT NULL DEFAULT 'PENDING',
  total_paise     BIGINT       NOT NULL CHECK (total_paise >= 0),
  idempotency_key TEXT         UNIQUE,          -- kills duplicate checkouts
  placed_at       TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

-- Money is BIGINT paise. Never FLOAT: 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3 in binary floating point,
-- and that rounding error becomes a finance reconciliation ticket at scale.
Normalisation, compressed1NF no repeating groups — don't store "sku1,sku2" in a column. 2NF every non-key column depends on the whole key. 3NF no column depends on another non-key column — don't keep customer_email on orders. Then denormalise deliberately where reads demand it: a maintained order_count on customers is a legitimate, documented violation, not an accident.

03 How a row becomes bytes Storage engine

Everything above this layer is an abstraction over one fact: disks are read in fixed-size pages, never in rows.

Production caseZomato — the SELECT * that tripled the bill

A restaurant listing endpoint did SELECT * FROM restaurants and used 4 of the 38 columns. The table had a description TEXT and a menu_json JSONB averaging 14 KB per row.

Rows per 8 KB page
0.5

Wide rows meant one row spanned two pages plus TOAST lookups.

After selecting 4 columns
96

rows per page — a covering index made it an index-only scan.

Page reads for 50 results

~100 → 1. Buffer-pool churn stopped evicting other hot tables.

Lesson

SELECT * isn't a style issue. It's a page-count issue.

An 8 KB heap page, and the buffer pool in front of it
within its page and only the line pointer updates — indexes stay valid. Why row width is a performance knob 8192 bytes ÷ 80-byte row = ~100 rows/page 8192 bytes ÷ 900-byte row = ~9 rows/page Same query, 11× the page reads, 11× the cache pressure. THE BUFFER POOL — WHY THE SECOND RUN OF A QUERY IS 1,000× FASTER RAM · shared_buffers page 0 clean page 7 clean page 3 DIRTY page 12 clean hit ≈ 100 nanoseconds EVICTION: CLOCK-SWEEP, DIRTY PAGES FLUSHED FIRST Disk · the heap file base/16384/24576, 24576.1, … SSD miss ≈ 100 microseconds HDD miss ≈ 10 milliseconds RAM IS ~1,000× FASTER THAN SSD AND ~100,000× FASTER THAN A SPINNING DISK READ FLUSH The one metric to watch heap_blks_hit ─────────────── > 0.99 hit + read Below that on a hot table means you are disk-bound, not CPU-bound.
inspect.sqlsee all of this on your own database
-- physical location of each row
SELECT ctid, id, customer_id FROM orders LIMIT 3;
--  (0,1) | 1 | 4821     ← page 0, slot 1

-- pages, rows, and average row width
SELECT relname, relpages AS pages, reltuples::bigint AS rows,
       pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(oid)) AS size,
       (pg_relation_size(oid) / nullif(reltuples,0))::int AS bytes_per_row
FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders';

-- cache hit ratio — under 0.99 on a hot table means you are disk-bound
SELECT relname,
       round(100.0*heap_blks_hit/nullif(heap_blks_hit+heap_blks_read,0),2) AS hit_pct
FROM pg_statio_user_tables ORDER BY heap_blks_read DESC LIMIT 5;
The question to always askNot "how fast is this query" but "how many pages must it touch, and are they already in RAM?" Indexes, covering indexes, narrow rows, partitioning and clustering are all different answers to that one question.

04 The B+ tree The idea that makes databases fast

40 million rows, 4 page reads. Here is exactly how — and why it's a B+ tree rather than a binary tree or a hash map.

Walking the tree for customer_id = 4821 · every read counted
is a page, so it holds ~400 keys — hence 4 levels, not 25.
path takenleaf hitheap fetchthe alternative
Production caseShopify — the UUID primary key that halved write throughput

A high-volume events table used UUIDv4 as its primary key. Because values are random, every insert landed in a different leaf page of the index.

With UUIDv4

Each insert dirties a random page. The working set becomes the whole index — it stops fitting in RAM.

Page splits
everywhere

Leaves split across the entire tree, fragmenting it and inflating WAL with full-page images.

With BIGSERIAL / ULID
1 page

Inserts append to the rightmost leaf, which is permanently hot in cache.

Rule

Need generated IDs? Use ULID or Snowflake — random-looking but time-ordered.

Sequential vs random key inserts · what the tree does differently

05 Indexes in practice Highest-leverage skill

Composite column order, covering indexes, partial indexes — and the reasons an index quietly gets ignored.

Composite index column order · the leftmost-prefix rule as a phone book
Production caseSwiggy — a 40 GB index replaced by a 6 MB one

The order-dispatch service polls for orders awaiting a delivery partner: WHERE status = 'PENDING' ORDER BY placed_at. The table holds 900 million historical orders; at any instant roughly 40,000 are actually PENDING.

Full index on (status, placed_at)
40 GB

Indexes all 900M rows, 99.99% of which will never match. Never fully cached.

Partial index
6 MB

WHERE status='PENDING' — indexes only live rows. Permanently in RAM.

Query latency

p99 210 ms → 3 ms, and the index self-shrinks as orders complete.

Bonus

Writes to non-PENDING rows stop touching this index entirely.

indexes.sqlthe five that earn their keep
-- 1 · COMPOSITE — equality first, then range, then sort
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_status_time
  ON orders (customer_id, status, placed_at DESC);

-- 2 · COVERING — INCLUDE the columns you SELECT so the heap is never touched.
--     Turns "Index Scan + heap fetch" into "Index Only Scan".
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cover
  ON orders (customer_id, placed_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_paise, status);

-- 3 · PARTIAL — the Swiggy case above. 40 GB → 6 MB.
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_pending
  ON orders (placed_at) WHERE status = 'PENDING';

-- 4 · EXPRESSION — the query must match the expression exactly
CREATE INDEX idx_customers_lower_email ON customers (lower(email));
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE lower(email) = 'a@b.com';   -- ✓ uses it
SELECT * FROM customers WHERE email       = 'a@b.com';    -- ✗ does not

-- 5 · Build on a live table without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_orders_status ON orders (status);
Index-only scan · why INCLUDE eliminates half the work
Why your index is being ignoredFix
Function wrapping the column — WHERE lower(email)=… on a plain indexExpression index, or stop wrapping the column
Implicit cast — WHERE id = '4821', or varchar vs text mismatchCast the literal, never the column
Leading wildcard — LIKE '%phone'pg_trgm GIN index, or a real search engine
Low selectivity — the value matches 80% of rowsNothing. A scan genuinely is cheaper; the planner is right
Stale statistics after a bulk loadANALYZE orders;
OR across different columnsRewrite as UNION ALL, or add a composite index
The cost nobody budgets forEvery index makes writes slower — an INSERT into a table with 8 indexes performs 9 tree modifications, all WAL-logged. Audit ruthlessly: SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0; — anything at zero after a month of production traffic is pure write tax.

06 How a query executes Text → rows

Five stages between the string you send and the rows you get back. Knowing them tells you exactly where to look when something is slow.

The full path of one SELECT
Where to look when it's slowParser — never. Rewriter — rarely (a nested view of views). Planner — a bad row estimate picked the wrong join. Executor — the plan is right but the data volume is genuinely large. In practice, 9 times out of 10 it's a planner row-estimate problem, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows it instantly as estimated-vs-actual divergence.

07 Join algorithms Three strategies

SQL has one JOIN keyword and the engine has three completely different ways to execute it. Which one it picks is usually the whole story.

Production caseAirbnb — the plan flip that took search down for 40 minutes

A search query joining listings to availability ran in 30 ms for eight months. After a bulk import of 12 million availability rows, statistics went stale and the planner estimated rows=1 for the outer side.

Plan before

Hash Join — both sides scanned once. 30 ms.

Plan after
Nested Loop

2.1M outer rows × 4 index reads = 8.4M page reads per query.

The tell in EXPLAIN

rows=1 … actual rows=2114882 — a 2-million-fold estimate error.

Fix
ANALYZE

One command. Then autovacuum thresholds tuned so it can't recur.

Nested loop vs hash join vs merge join — same query, three machines
AlgorithmCost modelChosen whenWarning sign in EXPLAIN
Nested LoopNouter × lookupOuter side is tiny; inner has an indexNested Loop with rows=1 estimated but millions actual
Hash JoinN + M, once eachBig × big, no useful sort orderBatches: 8 — it spilled to disk, raise work_mem
Merge Joinsort + N + MBoth inputs already ordered on the keyAn explicit Sort beneath it on a huge input
The classic production incidentA query is fast for months, then falls off a cliff after a data load. Cause: statistics went stale, the planner estimated rows=1 for the outer side and chose a nested loop. Reality was 2 million rows, so it did 2 million index lookups. Fix is usually just ANALYZE — and the tell in EXPLAIN ANALYZE is rows=1 … actual rows=2000000.

08 Reading EXPLAIN The debugging skill

One command separates guessing from knowing. Here's how to read it in the order that matters.

explain.sqlalways use ANALYZE, BUFFERS
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, FORMAT TEXT)
SELECT c.name, sum(o.total_paise) AS spend
FROM orders o
JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id
WHERE o.placed_at > now() - interval '30 days'
GROUP BY c.name
ORDER BY spend DESC
LIMIT 10;
Annotated output · what each number is telling you
find-the-problem.sqlstart here on any slow database
-- 1. Which queries actually cost the most total time? (not the slowest single run)
SELECT calls, round(mean_exec_time::numeric,2) AS avg_ms,
       round(total_exec_time::numeric/1000,1)  AS total_s, query
FROM pg_stat_statements ORDER BY total_exec_time DESC LIMIT 10;
-- A 5ms query run 2M times beats a 3s query run twice. Optimise by TOTAL.

-- 2. Tables being sequentially scanned in production
SELECT relname, seq_scan, seq_tup_read, idx_scan
FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE seq_scan > idx_scan ORDER BY seq_tup_read DESC;

-- 3. Indexes that have never been used — pure write cost
SELECT relname, indexrelname, idx_scan, pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(indexrelid))
FROM pg_stat_user_indexes WHERE idx_scan = 0 ORDER BY pg_relation_size(indexrelid) DESC;

-- 4. Is the table bloated with dead tuples? (see Chapter 12)
SELECT relname, n_live_tup, n_dead_tup,
       round(100.0*n_dead_tup/nullif(n_live_tup+n_dead_tup,0),1) AS dead_pct
FROM pg_stat_user_tables ORDER BY n_dead_tup DESC LIMIT 10;

09 Transactions and ACID The contract

Four letters everyone recites and few can explain mechanically. Here's what each one actually costs to implement.

A — Atomicity

All or nothing. If the transaction touches five tables and dies on the fourth, the first three are undone as if they never happened.

Mechanism: the undo log / WAL. Postgres marks tuples with the transaction id that created and deleted them; on abort those tuples simply become invisible. InnoDB replays undo records backwards.

C — Consistency

The database never violates its own declared rules. Foreign keys, checks, unique constraints and triggers all hold at commit time.

Mechanism: constraint validation before commit. Note this is the weakest letter — it's mostly a consequence of the other three plus your schema. It is not the "C" in CAP.

I — Isolation

Concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-finished work. How strictly is a dial you set (Chapter 13).

Mechanism: MVCC snapshots plus locks. This is the expensive letter, and the one people trade away for throughput.

D — Durability

Once COMMIT returns, the data survives a power cut — even if it's not yet in the table file.

Mechanism: write-ahead log, flushed with fsync before commit is acknowledged. The whole trick is that the log is sequential and the table file is random.

PayPal transfer · atomicity under a crash
The rule that followsA commit record in the log is the commit. If the log says "committed", recovery rolls the change forward even if the table page never made it to disk. If the log doesn't, recovery rolls it back even if the table page did. The log is the truth; the table file is a cache of it.

10 Write-ahead logging How durability is affordable

The counter-intuitive trick: writing your data twice makes the database faster, not slower.

Why sequential log + lazy pages beats writing pages directly

11 MVCC Readers never block writers

How Instagram serves a million concurrent readers while writes are happening: don't overwrite rows, version them.

Production caseGitLab — one idle transaction, 400 GB of bloat

A metrics dashboard opened a transaction and never closed it. Autovacuum cannot reclaim any row version newer than the oldest open snapshot, so dead tuples accumulated for days.

Table size
18 GB → 400 GB

Almost entirely dead tuples that vacuum was forbidden to touch.

Why queries slowed

Sequential scans had to read 22× more pages to find the same live rows.

Detection

state = 'idle in transaction' with an xact_start hours old.

Prevention
1 setting

idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '5min'.

The idea

An UPDATE does not modify the row in place. It writes a new version and marks the old one as expired at transaction N.

Every transaction gets a snapshot — a definition of which versions it may see. Two transactions can therefore read totally different, both-correct versions of the same row at the same instant, with no locks between them.

The hidden columns

  • xmin — transaction id that created this version.
  • xmax — transaction id that deleted / superseded it (0 if live).
  • A version is visible to you if xmin is committed and ≤ your snapshot, and xmax is unset or not yet committed in your snapshot.

Try it: SELECT xmin, xmax, * FROM orders LIMIT 5;

Two transactions, one row, two truths — and where dead tuples come from
The production incident this causesAn analyst opens a session, runs one query, and leaves the transaction open all afternoon. autovacuum can't clean anything newer than that snapshot. A hot table grows from 2 GB to 40 GB of mostly-dead tuples, and every query slows down. Monitor it: SELECT pid, state, now()-xact_start AS age FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE state='idle in transaction' ORDER BY age DESC; — and set idle_in_transaction_session_timeout.
MVCC vs lock-based reads · why the throughput difference is enormous

12 Isolation levels The most-asked interview topic

Four levels, four anomalies. Learn the anomalies first — the levels are just "which of these am I willing to tolerate".

Production caseBookMyShow — 8,000 requests for one seat in 50 ms

A blockbuster release opens booking at 10:00:00. Thousands of clients hit the same seat rows in the same instant. The original code did SELECT available, checked it in Java, then UPDATE.

The race

Two transactions both read available = 1, both write 0. Two tickets, one seat.

Double bookings
312

in the first 90 seconds — every one a manual refund plus support cost.

Fix
1 statement

UPDATE … SET available=available-1 WHERE id=? AND available>0, then check rows affected.

Why it works

The row lock is held by the engine for the duration of one statement. No read-then-write gap exists.

The four anomalies, each as a two-transaction timeline
Isolation levelDirty readNon-repeatablePhantomLost updateCost
READ UNCOMMITTEDpossiblepossiblepossiblepossibleNone — and Postgres doesn't even implement it
READ COMMITTED PG defaultsafepossiblepossiblepossibleVery low. New snapshot per statement.
REPEATABLE READ MySQL defaultsafesafePG: safe · MySQL: possibleneeds explicit lockingLow. One snapshot per transaction.
SERIALIZABLEsafesafesafesafeHighest — expect serialization failures and retries
BookMyShow · four ways to sell the last seat, only three of them correct
isolation.sqland the retry it forces
-- Per-transaction, not global
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
  SELECT sum(total_paise) FROM orders WHERE placed_at::date = CURRENT_DATE;
  -- …other work…  every read sees the SAME snapshot as the first
COMMIT;

-- SERIALIZABLE can and WILL fail — the app must retry
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
  UPDATE seats SET available = available - 1 WHERE id = 'A14';
COMMIT;
-- ERROR: could not serialize access due to read/write dependencies
-- SQLSTATE 40001 → catch it and retry the whole transaction

-- The job-queue pattern: N workers, no contention, no double processing
BEGIN;
  SELECT id, payload FROM jobs
   WHERE status = 'PENDING'
   ORDER BY created_at
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED          -- skip rows another worker already holds
   LIMIT 10;
  UPDATE jobs SET status = 'RUNNING' WHERE id = ANY($1);
COMMIT;
RetryableBooking.javaspring boot · serialization failures are normal
@Service
public class BookingService {

    /** 40001 is not a bug — at SERIALIZABLE it is the engine doing its job. */
    @Retryable(retryFor = CannotSerializeTransactionException.class,
               maxAttempts = 4, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 40, multiplier = 2))
    @Transactional(isolation = Isolation.SERIALIZABLE)
    public Ticket book(String seatId, long userId) {
        int rows = seatRepo.reserveIfAvailable(seatId);   // atomic conditional UPDATE
        if (rows == 0) throw new SeatUnavailableException(seatId);
        return ticketRepo.save(Ticket.of(seatId, userId));
    }
}

interface SeatRepo extends JpaRepository<Seat, String> {
    @Modifying
    @Query(value = """
        UPDATE seats SET available = available - 1
        WHERE id = :id AND available > 0
        """, nativeQuery = true)
    int reserveIfAvailable(@Param("id") String id);
}
The nuance that impressesPostgres's REPEATABLE READ is implemented with snapshots, so it also prevents phantoms — stricter than the SQL standard requires. MySQL's REPEATABLE READ permits phantoms in some cases but uses gap locks to block many of them. So "REPEATABLE READ" means measurably different things on the two engines, and code ported between them can break silently.

13 Locks and deadlocks Production pathologies

MVCC means readers don't lock. Writers still do — and that's where the 3 a.m. pages come from.

Production caseThe ALTER TABLE that took an entire site down

A migration ran ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN … during business hours. The ALTER itself is instant in modern Postgres — but it needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE, and one analytics SELECT had been running for 6 minutes.

Step 1

ALTER waits behind the long SELECT. Harmless so far.

Step 2
queue forms

Lock requests are ordered. Every new query now queues behind the waiting ALTER — including plain SELECTs.

Step 3

Connection pool exhausts. Health checks fail. Full outage in ~30 s.

Fix
lock_timeout

SET lock_timeout='3s' before DDL — it fails fast instead of forming a queue. Retry later.

A deadlock, and the one-line discipline that prevents it
LockTaken byBlocksWatch out
ACCESS SHAREPlain SELECTOnly ACCESS EXCLUSIVEHarmless — but it does block a DDL migration
ROW EXCLUSIVEINSERT/UPDATE/DELETEDDL, not other DMLNormal write traffic
FOR UPDATEExplicit row lockOther writers of that rowHeld until commit — keep the transaction tiny
SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVECREATE INDEX (non-concurrent)All writes to the tableUse CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY in production
ACCESS EXCLUSIVEALTER TABLE, DROP, VACUUM FULLEverything, including SELECTThe classic outage — see below
The migration outage, step by stepALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN … needs ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. It waits behind one long-running SELECT — and while it waits, every new query queues behind it, because lock requests are ordered. Thirty seconds later the whole site is down, and the culprit looks like an innocent ALTER. Fix: SET lock_timeout = '3s'; before the DDL so it fails fast instead of forming a queue, and retry.
who-is-blocking-whom.sqlrun this during an incident
SELECT blocked.pid          AS blocked_pid,
       blocked.query        AS blocked_query,
       blocking.pid         AS blocking_pid,
       blocking.query       AS blocking_query,
       now() - blocking.xact_start AS blocking_age
FROM pg_stat_activity blocked
JOIN pg_stat_activity blocking
  ON blocking.pid = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid))
WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(blocked.pid)) > 0;

-- then, deliberately:
SELECT pg_cancel_backend(12345);     -- polite: cancel the query
SELECT pg_terminate_backend(12345);  -- forceful: kill the connection

14 Advanced SQL that replaces application code Leverage

Window functions, CTEs and upserts routinely turn 60 lines of Java plus three round trips into one query.

GROUP BY vs window function · the difference in one picture
windows.sqltop-N per group — the classic
-- "3 most recent orders per customer" — one pass, no correlated subquery
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT o.*,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY placed_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM orders o
) t WHERE rn <= 3;

-- Running total of daily revenue, plus day-over-day delta
SELECT day,
       revenue,
       SUM(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day)                    AS running_total,
       revenue - LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day)          AS vs_yesterday,
       ROUND(AVG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY day
             ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW), 0) AS rolling_7d
FROM daily_revenue ORDER BY day;

-- Percentile bucketing for a cohort analysis
SELECT customer_id, total_spend,
       NTILE(10) OVER (ORDER BY total_spend DESC) AS decile
FROM customer_totals;
cte-upsert.sqlrecursive CTE + idempotent write
-- RECURSIVE CTE: walk a category tree of unknown depth in ONE query
WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, name, parent_id, 1 AS depth, name::text AS path
  FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL          -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.name, c.parent_id, t.depth + 1, t.path || ' > ' || c.name
  FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id   -- recursive step
)
SELECT depth, path FROM tree ORDER BY path;
-- The alternative is N round trips from Java, one per level.

-- UPSERT: safe under concurrency, no read-then-write race
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, qty) VALUES ('IPH15-256', 10)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE
  SET qty = inventory.qty + EXCLUDED.qty,
      updated_at = now()
RETURNING sku, qty;      -- RETURNING avoids a second SELECT round trip

-- Idempotency key: the cleanest defence against a double-submitted checkout
INSERT INTO orders (idempotency_key, customer_id, total_paise)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
RETURNING id;            -- no row returned ⇒ it was a retry, fetch the original
The round-trip argumentA join done in the database costs one network hop. The same join done in Java costs N+1 hops, each with latency, serialization and connection-pool pressure. For a 500-row result at 1 ms RTT that's 0.5 s of pure waiting. Push set-based work into SQL; keep business rules in the application.

15 The interview checklist

If you can answer these from the mental model rather than memory, you're done.

QuestionThe answer that shows understanding
Why is an index fast?A B+ tree node is one page, so fan-out is ~400 and depth is 3–4 for tens of millions of rows. Lookup is 4 page reads instead of 500,000, and the top levels stay cached.
Why does column order matter in a composite index?It's sorted left to right, like a phone book. You can seek on a leftmost prefix only — (a,b,c) serves a, a,b, a,b,c, but never b alone.
What actually happens at COMMIT?The WAL record is flushed with fsync. That's it — the table page can stay dirty in RAM. The log is the durability boundary, not the heap.
How do readers avoid blocking on writers?MVCC. Updates write a new row version with xmin/xmax; each transaction reads through a snapshot. Cost is dead tuples, paid off by vacuum.
READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ?New snapshot per statement vs one snapshot per transaction. The second prevents non-repeatable reads — and in Postgres, phantoms too.
How do you stop a double booking?Atomic conditional UPDATE … WHERE available > 0, or SELECT FOR UPDATE, or an optimistic version column. Never read-check-write in application code.
Why did a fast query suddenly get slow?Usually stale statistics flipped the plan to a nested loop. EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows rows=1 … actual rows=2000000. Fix with ANALYZE.
When do you shard?After indexing, pooling, caching, a bigger box, read replicas and partitioning. Sharding costs you cross-shard joins and transactions permanently.
Why not store money as FLOAT?Binary floating point can't represent 0.1 exactly. Use BIGINT in the smallest unit, or NUMERIC.
What makes a UUID primary key expensive?Random inserts split leaves all over the tree and, in InnoDB where the PK is the table, fragment the data itself. Use ULID/snowflake if you need generated ids.
The one sentence to carry awayEvery performance question in SQL reduces to "how many pages must the engine touch, and are they in RAM?" Indexes, covering indexes, partitioning, clustering, caching and narrow rows are all the same answer to that one question.
Tab 02 · Where the internals meet your code

The eight things that actually matter in JPA

Not a Hibernate tutorial. These are the eight places where the internals from Tab 1 leak into your application code — and where nearly every real Spring Boot performance incident originates. Each one maps directly back to a chapter: N+1 is page reads, @Version is lost updates, batch size is WAL round trips.

8Concepts, chosen by production impact
Boot 3.xJava 21 · Hibernate 6
PostgresHikariCP · Spring Data JPA
Why only eightJPA has hundreds of features. In production, the same handful of mistakes cause the overwhelming majority of database incidents: N+1 queries, missing indexes, long transactions, lost updates, unbatched writes, OFFSET pagination, oversized pools, and open-session-in-view. Fix those and the rest is detail.

01 The N+1 problem The #1 JPA incident

One innocent loop turns 1 query into 201. It never shows up in local testing, because your dev database has 20 rows.

Production caseAn order-history page that issued 1,001 queries

"Show my last 100 orders with their items." One query loaded 100 orders; iterating order.getItems() lazily fired one more query per order. Then item.getProduct() fired one per item.

Queries issued
1,001

1 + 100 (items) + 900 (products), each a full network round trip.

Latency

1,001 × 0.8 ms RTT = ~800 ms of pure waiting, before any real work.

After JOIN FETCH
1

~12 ms. Same data, same entities, one round trip.

Why QA missed it

The test database had 3 orders. 4 queries feels identical to 1.

N+1 vs JOIN FETCH · what leaves the JVM
waiting, not compute.
N+1 — the default trap
@Entity
public class Order {
    @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order")      // LAZY by default — good
    private List<OrderItem> items;
}

// 1 query for orders …
List<Order> orders = orderRepo.findByCustomerId(id);

for (Order o : orders) {
    // … + 1 query EVERY iteration
    total += o.getItems().stream()
              .mapToLong(OrderItem::getSubtotal).sum();
}
JOIN FETCH — one query
public interface OrderRepo extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    @Query("""
        SELECT DISTINCT o FROM Order o
        LEFT JOIN FETCH o.items i
        LEFT JOIN FETCH i.product
        WHERE o.customerId = :cid
        """)
    List<Order> findWithItems(@Param("cid") Long cid);

    // or declaratively:
    @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"items", "items.product"})
    List<Order> findByCustomerId(Long customerId);
}
The trap inside the fixJOIN FETCH plus Pageable makes Hibernate log HHH90003004: firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory — it loads every matching row into RAM and paginates there. On a large table that is an OOM waiting to happen. Fix: fetch the page of IDs first, then fetch the collections for those IDs in a second query (WHERE id IN :ids).
detect-n-plus-1.ymlmake it impossible to ship
spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        # log every statement with its parameters
        format_sql: true
        # batch lazy collection loads: 100 queries become 1 with IN (…)
        default_batch_fetch_size: 100
logging:
  level:
    org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG
    org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind: TRACE

# Better: fail the build. datasource-proxy or Hypersistence Utils can assert
# "this endpoint must issue <= 3 queries" in an integration test.
One line that saves you anywaydefault_batch_fetch_size: 100 converts N+1 into 1 + ceil(N/100) by rewriting the lazy loads as WHERE order_id IN (1,2,…,100). It doesn't excuse bad queries, but it turns a 1,001-query page into an 11-query page with zero code changes. Set it on every project.

02 @Transactional, precisely Ch. 10 in code

Three rules cover almost every bug: it's a proxy, it only rolls back on unchecked exceptions, and its scope is a held connection.

Why @Transactional silently does nothing sometimes
three silent failures
@Service
public class OrderService {

    // ✕ 1. self-invocation — proxy bypassed, NO transaction
    public void process(Order o) { this.save(o); }
    @Transactional public void save(Order o) { … }

    // ✕ 2. checked exception — Spring COMMITS by default
    @Transactional
    public void charge() throws PaymentException {
        repo.save(order);
        throw new PaymentException();   // order stays saved!
    }

    // ✕ 3. transaction held across a network call
    @Transactional
    public void checkout(Order o) {
        repo.save(o);
        paymentGateway.charge(o);   // 800 ms holding a DB connection
        repo.markPaid(o);           // + row locks the whole time
    }
}
corrected
@Service
public class OrderService {

    // ✓ 1. boundary at the entry point, called from outside
    @Transactional
    public void process(Order o) { save(o); }

    // ✓ 2. tell Spring to roll back on checked exceptions
    @Transactional(rollbackFor = PaymentException.class)
    public void charge() throws PaymentException { … }

    // ✓ 3. keep the network call OUTSIDE the transaction
    public void checkout(Order o) {
        Long id = persistPending(o);            // tx 1, short
        var res = paymentGateway.charge(o);     // no tx held
        markPaid(id, res);                      // tx 2, short
    }

    @Transactional Long persistPending(Order o) { … }
    @Transactional void markPaid(Long id, Result r) { … }
}
SettingWhat it doesUse it for
readOnly = trueSkips dirty-checking, hints the driver, can route to a replicaEvery query-only service method — real CPU saving on large result sets
REQUIRES_NEWSuspends the outer transaction, opens a second connectionAudit rows that must survive an outer rollback. Costs a second pool connection — deadlock risk if the pool is small
rollbackForRolls back on checked exceptions tooAny method that throws checked exceptions
timeout = 5Aborts a transaction exceeding N secondsAnything user-facing — stops one stuck transaction pinning vacuum (Ch. 12)
Turn this offspring.jpa.open-in-view defaults to true, which holds a database connection for the entire HTTP request — including JSON serialisation and view rendering. Under load your pool exhausts while the database sits idle. Set spring.jpa.open-in-view: false on day one; you'll get honest LazyInitializationExceptions that point at real N+1 problems instead.

03 Optimistic vs pessimistic locking Ch. 13 in code

The BookMyShow problem, implemented three ways. Pick by contention level, not by preference.

@Version in flight · how the lost update is detected
Seat.java + BookingService.javaall three strategies
@Entity
public class Seat {
    @Id private String id;
    private int available;

    @Version                       // Hibernate adds "AND version = ?" to every UPDATE
    private long version;
}

public interface SeatRepo extends JpaRepository<Seat, String> {

    // ── Strategy A: atomic conditional UPDATE — best for a hot single row
    @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true)
    @Query(value = """
        UPDATE seats SET available = available - 1
        WHERE id = :id AND available > 0
        """, nativeQuery = true)
    int reserveIfAvailable(@Param("id") String id);   // returns 0 or 1

    // ── Strategy B: pessimistic — SELECT … FOR UPDATE
    @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
    @QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "3000"))
    Optional<Seat> findById(String id);
}

@Service
public class BookingService {

    // ── Strategy C: optimistic, with retry (uses @Version above)
    @Retryable(retryFor = {ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class,
                           CannotAcquireLockException.class},
               maxAttempts = 4, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 30, multiplier = 2, random = true))
    @Transactional
    public Ticket book(String seatId, long userId) {
        int rows = seatRepo.reserveIfAvailable(seatId);   // strategy A inside
        if (rows == 0) throw new SeatUnavailableException(seatId);
        return ticketRepo.save(Ticket.of(seatId, userId));
    }

    @Recover
    Ticket exhausted(Exception e, String seatId, long userId) {
        throw new SeatUnavailableException(seatId);       // stop retrying, fail cleanly
    }
}
StrategyBest whenFails badly whenReal use
Atomic UPDATEOne hot row, high contentionYou need to read-decide-write across statementsSeat/stock decrement, counters
Optimistic @VersionLow contention, long think-time (edit forms)Everyone hits the same row — retries livelockProfile edits, admin CRUD
Pessimistic FOR UPDATEMust read, compute, then write atomicallyHeld across a slow call — blocks everyoneWallet balance, ledger posting
SKIP LOCKEDMany workers draining a queue tableYou need strict FIFO orderingJob runners, outbox relays
JobRepo.javathe queue pattern — workers never block each other
public interface JobRepo extends JpaRepository<Job, Long> {

    @Query(value = """
        SELECT * FROM jobs
        WHERE status = 'PENDING'
        ORDER BY created_at
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED        -- skip rows another worker already holds
        LIMIT :n
        """, nativeQuery = true)
    List<Job> claimBatch(@Param("n") int n);
}

@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
@Transactional
public void drain() {
    List<Job> batch = jobRepo.claimBatch(20);   // 10 pods, zero contention
    batch.forEach(this::execute);              // no double processing, no waiting
}

04 Batch writes Ch. 11 in code

Saving 10,000 rows one at a time is 10,000 network round trips. Three config lines make it 200.

Production caseA nightly import that took 4 hours and now takes 6 minutes

A catalogue sync called repository.save() inside a loop for 1.2 million products. Each call issued its own INSERT, its own round trip, and its own WAL flush.

Before
1,200,000

round trips × ~0.7 ms = ~14 min of pure latency, plus per-statement overhead.

Root cause 2

GenerationType.IDENTITY — Hibernate cannot batch with it, because it needs the id back after every insert.

After SEQUENCE + batch 50
24,000

statements instead of 1.2M. 4 h → 6 min.

Third fix

flush() + clear() every batch, or the persistence context OOMs.

Unbatched vs batched inserts on the wire
application.yml + BulkImporter.javaall three fixes together
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/shop?reWriteBatchedInserts=true   # ← Postgres driver
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        jdbc.batch_size: 50
        order_inserts: true      # group by table so batches are contiguous
        order_updates: true      # also gives consistent lock order → fewer deadlocks
        batch_versioned_data: true
BulkImporter.java
@Entity
public class Product {
    @Id
    // ✕ IDENTITY disables batching entirely — Hibernate must read the id back per row
    // ✓ SEQUENCE with an allocationSize matching batch_size
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "product_seq")
    @SequenceGenerator(name = "product_seq", sequenceName = "product_seq",
                       allocationSize = 50)
    private Long id;
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class BulkImporter {

    private final EntityManager em;

    @Transactional
    public void importAll(List<Product> products) {
        for (int i = 0; i < products.size(); i++) {
            em.persist(products.get(i));
            if (i % 50 == 0) {          // must match jdbc.batch_size
                em.flush();             // push the batch to the database
                em.clear();             // ← without this the context grows until OOM
            }
        }
    }
}
Verify it actually batchedTurn on logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL: DEBUG and count statements — but the reliable check is datasource-proxy or pg_stat_statements: look for calls dropping by ~50×. Batching silently doesn't happen if you left IDENTITY in place, and nothing warns you.

05 Pagination that doesn't degrade Ch. 05 in code

OFFSET 500000 makes the database read and discard 500,000 rows. Page 1 is fast; page 10,000 times out.

OFFSET vs keyset · cost as the user pages deeper
skips or repeats rows if data changes between pages. KEYSET / SEEK — REMEMBER WHERE YOU STOPPED AND SEEK STRAIGHT THERE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE (placed_at, id) < (:lastTime, :lastId) ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20; B+ TREE SEEK STRAIGHT TO THE LEAF, THEN WALK 20 SIDEWAYS Page 1: 2 ms · Page 100: 2 ms · Page 25,000: 2 ms — constant, because it never reads what it skips. This is exactly the linked-leaf property from Chapter 5. It is also stable under concurrent inserts.
KeysetPagination.javatie-break on id or you will lose rows
public interface OrderRepo extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    // Row-value comparison — needs a matching index on (placed_at DESC, id DESC)
    @Query(value = """
        SELECT * FROM orders
        WHERE customer_id = :cid
          AND (placed_at, id) < (:lastTime, :lastId)
        ORDER BY placed_at DESC, id DESC
        LIMIT :size
        """, nativeQuery = true)
    List<Order> nextPage(@Param("cid") Long cid,
                         @Param("lastTime") Instant lastTime,
                         @Param("lastId") Long lastId,
                         @Param("size") int size);
}

// The client sends back an opaque cursor instead of a page number:
//   { "items": [...], "nextCursor": "MjAyNi0wOC0wOVQxMDoxMnw0ODIx" }
// base64 of "placedAt|id" — stable, cheap, and impossible to skip rows with.

// Still need a total count? Don't. Use "load more", or an approximate count:
//   SELECT reltuples::bigint FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'orders';
Why the tie-break mattersOrdering by placed_at alone breaks when two orders share a timestamp — the boundary row can appear on both pages or neither. Always include a unique tie-break column (id) in both the ORDER BY and the cursor comparison, and index them together in that exact order.

06 Projections & read-only queries Ch. 04 in code

Loading a full entity to read two fields costs you the wide-row penalty from Chapter 4, plus dirty-check overhead.

full entity for 2 fields
// Loads all 38 columns including a 14 KB menu_json,
// puts every row into the persistence context,
// and dirty-checks all of it at flush time.
List<Restaurant> all = repo.findByCity("Pune");
return all.stream()
          .map(r -> new Card(r.getName(), r.getRating()))
          .toList();
projection — 2 columns
// SELECT name, rating FROM restaurants WHERE city = ?
// No entity, no persistence context, no dirty checking.
public interface CardView {          // interface projection
    String getName();
    Double getRating();
}
List<CardView> cards = repo.findByCity("Pune");

// or a record (DTO projection):
@Query("SELECT new com.x.Card(r.name, r.rating) FROM Restaurant r WHERE r.city = :c")
List<Card> findCards(@Param("c") String city);
TechniqueWhat it savesWhen
Interface / DTO projectionColumns fetched, network bytes, persistence-context memory, dirty-check CPUEvery list/read endpoint — the default for read paths
@Transactional(readOnly=true)Dirty-check pass and snapshot copies of every loaded entityAll query-only service methods
@QueryHints(HINT_READ_ONLY)Same, at the individual query levelOne hot query inside a read-write service
Covering index matching the projectionThe heap fetch entirely — Index Only Scan (Ch. 6)When the projection's columns are stable and the query is hot
The pairing that compoundsA DTO projection selecting (customer_id, placed_at, total_paise) combined with CREATE INDEX … (customer_id, placed_at DESC) INCLUDE (total_paise) becomes an Index Only Scan: the heap is never touched, the entity is never built, and the persistence context stays empty. That's Chapters 4 and 6 cashing out in one endpoint.

07 Connection pool sizing Little's Law

A bigger pool never makes a slow database faster. It just moves the queue somewhere worse.

Where the queue forms · pool too large vs correctly sized
falls. POOL = 20 — THE QUEUE STAYS IN THE APP, WHERE IT IS CHEAP AND VISIBLE 200 threads 20 connections 180 THREADS WAIT IN HIKARI Database runs at full speed with no contention. Waiting is measurable (hikaricp.connections.pending) and fails fast.
application.ymlsize it with arithmetic, not vibes
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      # Little's Law:  connections = throughput × latency
      #   500 rps × 0.040 s  =  20 concurrent  →  pool ≈ 20-25
      maximum-pool-size: 20
      minimum-idle: 20                # keep it flat; avoids cold-start latency spikes
      connection-timeout: 3000        # fail fast instead of piling up threads
      max-lifetime: 1800000           # recycle before the LB or DB reaps them
      leak-detection-threshold: 60000 # logs a stack trace for connections held > 60s
      validation-timeout: 2000
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false               # ← stop holding a connection for the whole request

# Watch these three, in this order:
#   hikaricp.connections.pending  > 0 for long  → pool too small OR queries too slow
#   hikaricp.connections.usage    p99 near max  → saturated
#   hikaricp.connections.acquire  rising        → the database is the bottleneck, not the pool
The multiplication people forgetPool size is per pod. 20 connections × 30 pods = 600 backends, against a Postgres max_connections of 200. Either size for the fleet, or put PgBouncer in transaction mode in front — which is what everyone eventually does.

08 Idempotent writes & the outbox Correctness under retry

Every client retries. Every network times out. The database is the only place you can enforce "exactly once".

CheckoutService.javaupsert + outbox in one transaction
public interface OrderRepo extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {

    /** Retry-safe insert. A duplicate key returns 0 rows instead of throwing. */
    @Modifying
    @Query(value = """
        INSERT INTO orders (idempotency_key, customer_id, total_paise, status)
        VALUES (:key, :cid, :total, 'PENDING')
        ON CONFLICT (idempotency_key) DO NOTHING
        """, nativeQuery = true)
    int insertIfNew(@Param("key") String key, @Param("cid") Long cid,
                    @Param("total") long total);

    Optional<Order> findByIdempotencyKey(String key);
}

@Service
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class CheckoutService {

    private final OrderRepo orders;
    private final OutboxRepo outbox;

    @Transactional
    public Order checkout(CheckoutRequest req) {
        int inserted = orders.insertIfNew(req.idempotencyKey(),
                                          req.customerId(), req.totalPaise());
        if (inserted == 0) {
            return orders.findByIdempotencyKey(req.idempotencyKey()).orElseThrow();
        }
        Order order = orders.findByIdempotencyKey(req.idempotencyKey()).orElseThrow();

        // Same transaction as the order ⇒ no dual-write problem.
        // If the transaction rolls back, the event disappears with it.
        outbox.save(new OutboxEvent("order.placed", order.getId(), toJson(order)));
        return order;
    }
}
The dual-write problem, and why the outbox is the standard answer
The closing thoughtEvery technique in this tab traces back to Tab 1. N+1 is page reads and round trips. @Version is the lost-update anomaly. Batch size is WAL flushes. Keyset pagination is the linked leaves of a B+ tree. The outbox is atomicity. Learn the engine and the framework stops being magic.
