Simple guide · With real systems

MongoDB explained with real high-scale systems

Same style as the DynamoDB guide. Simple words, short sentences. Every concept comes with a real company that uses it at massive scale. Running example: the same food delivery app (Swiggy / Zomato / DoorDash style).

0 Story1 What2 Documents3 Storage 4 Replication5 Sharding6 Indexes 7 Consistency8 Advanced9 Who uses it
Section 0 · Why MongoDB exists

The story: web apps outgrew rigid tables

In 2007, the founders of DoubleClick (a huge ad company, later bought by Google) started a new company called 10gen. At DoubleClick they served 400,000 ads per second, and relational databases kept getting in the way. Two problems again and again:

Problem 1 · Rigid schema

Web data changes shape all the time. In SQL, every change means ALTER TABLE and painful migrations.

Problem 2 · Hard to scale out

SQL databases scale UP (buy a bigger machine). The web needed to scale OUT (add many cheap machines).

So they built a database that stores JSON-like documents instead of rows, and that can spread across machines from day one. They named it after the word "humongous". MongoDB was open-sourced in 2009.

Real system · Craigslist's 2.2 billion old posts

Craigslist keeps every classified ad ever posted — over 2 billion documents. Over 15+ years the "shape" of a post changed many times (new fields added, old ones removed). In MySQL, archiving them meant one schema for all — impossible. They moved the archive to MongoDB: every post is stored as-is, in whatever shape it had. Flexible schema is the point.

Section 1 · Basics

What exactly is MongoDB?

MongoDB is a general-purpose document database. Four words describe it:

Document model

Data is stored as JSON-like documents (internally a binary form called BSON). A document maps 1:1 to an object in your Java code.

Flexible schema

Two documents in the same collection can have different fields. No ALTER TABLE. Validation is optional, not forced.

Rich queries

Unlike DynamoDB, you can query by ANY field, not just the key. Plus aggregations, joins ($lookup), geo queries, text search.

Not magic

Query any field = slow unless you add an index. Deep JOIN-heavy relational data or strict cross-table constraints still fit SQL better.

Basic words

MongoDBSQL equivalentFood app example
DatabaseDatabasefoodapp
CollectionTableorders
DocumentRowOne order (max 16 MB)
FieldColumntotalAmount
_idPrimary keyAuto ObjectId, always indexed
vs DynamoDB in one line: DynamoDB = key-value store, you must know your queries first, AWS-only, near-infinite managed scale. MongoDB = document store, query anything, runs anywhere (or managed as Atlas), you design and tune more yourself.
Section 2 · The document model

One order = one document

In SQL, one food order needs 4–5 tables: orders, order_items, addresses, payments. Reading it back needs JOINs. In MongoDB, things that are read together are stored together:

{
  "_id": ObjectId("665f1a2b8c9d4e001a3b5c7d"),
  "customerId": "cust#42",
  "restaurantId": "rest#77",
  "status": "PLACED",
  "items": [                                // embedded array — no JOIN table!
    { "name": "Biryani", "qty": 2, "price": 320 },
    { "name": "Raita",   "qty": 1, "price": 40  }
  ],
  "deliveryAddress": {                      // embedded object
    "line1": "Flat 12, MG Road", "city": "Pune", "pin": "411001"
  },
  "total": 680,
  "placedAt": ISODate("2026-07-06T13:00:00Z")
}

One read fetches the whole order. This is the #1 design rule of MongoDB: "data that is accessed together should be stored together." Embed for one-to-few; use references (store the other document's _id) for one-to-many-thousands.

What is ObjectId?

The default _id is a 12-byte value generated on the client. No central counter needed — that is why inserts scale:

Real system · EA — FIFA Online player profiles

EA runs FIFA Online player data on MongoDB. A player profile is a perfect document: nested squad, players array, match history, settings — different shape per game mode. In SQL this would be dozens of tables and heavy JOINs on every login. As a document, loading a player = one read. Millions of concurrent gamers, one document each.

Real system · Forbes CMS

Forbes rebuilt its content platform on MongoDB. An article is a messy, changing object: text, embeds, videos, contributor info, tags. New content types launch weekly. Document model let Forbes ship new article features in days instead of schema-migration weeks — publishing speed became a business advantage.

Section 3 · Storage internals

How data is stored: WiredTiger

Since v3.2, MongoDB's default storage engine is WiredTiger. What happens under one insertOne():

1Document written into WiredTiger's in-memory cache
2Change appended to the journal (write-ahead log) — crash safety
3Every ~60s a checkpoint writes a clean snapshot of data files to disk
4Crash? Restart = last checkpoint + replay journal

B+ tree files

Each collection and each index is stored as a B+ tree on disk. Same family as MySQL/InnoDB and DynamoDB's storage nodes — not an LSM tree like Cassandra.

Document-level locking

WiredTiger uses MVCC — writers don't block readers; two writes block each other only on the SAME document. Old MMAPv1 engine locked whole collections; WiredTiger fixed that.

Compression

Data blocks compressed on disk (Snappy default, zstd option). Indexes use prefix compression. Often 50–70% disk savings.

Cache

WiredTiger keeps a working set in RAM (~50% of machine RAM by default). Reads that hit cache never touch disk. Rule of thumb: keep your hot data + indexes in RAM.

The three engines you now know: Cassandra = LSM tree (fastest raw writes, compaction cost) · DynamoDB = B-tree + WAL per partition (flat P99, managed) · MongoDB/WiredTiger = B+ tree + journal + checkpoints (general purpose, in-place updates, MVCC). Being able to compare all three is a strong interview signal.
Real system · Bosch IoT

Bosch's IoT platform ingests sensor readings from millions of connected devices — vehicles, tools, appliances. Compression matters at this volume: sensor documents compress very well (repetitive field names, similar values), so WiredTiger's block compression cuts the storage bill drastically. Document-level concurrency lets thousands of devices write in parallel without lock fights.

Section 4 · Replication

Replica set: 1 primary + N secondaries

A production MongoDB is never one machine. It is a replica set — usually 3 nodes:

The oplog — MongoDB's heartbeat

The oplog is a special capped collection on the primary. Every write is recorded there as an idempotent operation. Secondaries tail it and replay. It is the same idea as Kafka's log or DynamoDB's WAL replication — a log is always the answer.

Write concern — you choose safety per write

Write concernMeaningFood app use
w:1Ack when primary has it. Fast; small loss window on failover.Rider GPS pings — losing one is fine
w:"majority"Ack when most nodes have it. Survives failover. Default since v5.Orders, payments — never lose
w:1, j:false style tuningTrade durability for speed knob by knobBulk analytics loads
vs DynamoDB: DynamoDB always does quorum (2 of 3) — no choice, always safe. MongoDB lets you pick per write. Freedom = power + responsibility. Same story as Cassandra's tunable consistency (ONE/QUORUM/ALL).
Real system · Coinbase during crypto manias

Coinbase runs core trading and account data on large MongoDB fleets. During the 2017 and 2021 crypto booms, traffic spiked 10–20x in hours. Their engineering posts describe the playbook: replica sets across zones for zero-downtime failover, majority write concern for anything touching money, and reads for price charts spread to secondaries. When a node dies mid-mania, an election replaces the primary in seconds and the app never notices.

Section 5 · Sharding = scale out

When one replica set is not enough

A replica set scales reads (secondaries) but ALL writes hit one primary. To scale writes and data size, MongoDB shards: it splits a collection across many replica sets. Three moving parts:

mongos (router)

Your app talks to this. It knows which shard owns which keys and forwards the query. Same job as DynamoDB's request router.

Config servers

A small replica set that stores the map: key range → shard. Same job as DynamoDB's metadata service.

Shards

Each shard is a full replica set holding a slice of the data. Data moves between shards in chunks (~128 MB ranges).

Balancer

Background process that moves chunks from full shards to empty ones. Like DynamoDB's auto-admin, but you can watch and tune it.

The shard key decision — hashed vs ranged

You pick a shard key (like DynamoDB's partition key). You also pick HOW keys map to shards. Try both:

The trap: ranged sharding on a growing key (timestamp, ObjectId) sends EVERY new insert to the last shard — a hot shard. Hashed sharding spreads inserts but kills range scans. Same hot-key physics as DynamoDB, just visible and your problem to fix.
Real system · Foursquare's famous 2010 outage — the hot shard lesson

Foursquare stored check-ins in MongoDB with 2 shards. User data did not spread evenly — one shard's data grew past its machine's RAM. It started hitting disk, slowed to a crawl, and took the site down for ~11 hours. Adding a shard mid-crisis made it worse at first, because moving chunks off an overloaded machine adds load.

Lessons the whole industry learned: 1) pick a shard key that spreads BOTH data and traffic, 2) shard before you are desperate, 3) keep the working set in RAM. This outage is a classic interview story — know it.

Real system · Baidu

Baidu (China's biggest search company) runs 600+ applications on MongoDB clusters holding trillions of documents across hundreds of nodes, powering maps, messaging, and cloud photo storage. Proof that sharded MongoDB reaches DynamoDB-class scale — the difference is Baidu employs teams to operate it, while DynamoDB users outsource that to AWS.

Section 6 · Indexing

Indexes: MongoDB's superpower over DynamoDB

Every index is its own B+ tree pointing at the documents. Without an index, a query = collection scan (read everything). With one, it's a tree seek. You can index almost anything:

Index typeWhat it doesFood app use
Single fieldOne field{customerId: 1} — my orders
CompoundSeveral fields, order matters{restaurantId: 1, status: 1, placedAt: -1} — restaurant's PLACED orders, newest first
MultikeyAuto-indexes each element of an arrayIndex items.name — "all orders containing Biryani"
Geospatial (2dsphere)Location queries"Restaurants within 3 km of the customer"
Text / Atlas SearchWord search inside stringsSearch dishes: "paneer"
TTLAuto-delete documents after a timeRider GPS points expire after 24h
PartialIndex only documents matching a filterIndex ONLY status: "PLACED" orders — tiny, hot index
UniqueEnforce no duplicatesusers.email

The ESR rule (compound index design — interview favorite)

Order the fields in a compound index as: Equality → Sort → Range.

// Query: restaurant's PLACED orders today, newest first
db.orders.find({
  restaurantId: "rest#77",      // Equality
  status: "PLACED",             // Equality
  placedAt: { $gte: today }      // Range
}).sort({ placedAt: -1 })        // Sort

// Correct index — E, E, then S/R share the same field here:
db.orders.createIndex({ restaurantId: 1, status: 1, placedAt: -1 })
vs DynamoDB: this whole section is ONE MongoDB command per index. In DynamoDB, each new query pattern = design a GSI = a copy of the table with its own cost and its own hot-key risks. MongoDB indexes are cheaper to add — but each one slows every write a little (the B+ tree must be updated). Real teams cap collections at ~5–10 indexes.
Real system · Delivery apps' geo queries

"Find restaurants near me" and "find the nearest free rider" are 2dsphere geo-index queries — this is bread and butter for delivery and ride apps built on MongoDB. Store location: {type:"Point", coordinates:[73.85, 18.52]}, add a 2dsphere index, and $near returns results sorted by distance in milliseconds. Doing this in DynamoDB requires bolting on geohash libraries; in MongoDB it is native.

Section 7 · Consistency & transactions

How correct do you need to be?

MongoDB gives you dials, not one fixed answer:

DialOptionsSimple meaning
writeConcernw:1 / w:"majority"How many nodes must save my write before "OK"?
readConcernlocal / majority / linearizableHow confirmed must data be before I can read it?
readPreferenceprimary / secondary / nearestWHICH node answers my read?

Safe recipe for money paths: w:"majority" + readConcern:"majority" + read from primary. Fast recipe for feeds/menus: w:1 + read from nearest secondary.

Multi-document ACID transactions

Since v4.0 (replica sets) and v4.2 (sharded), MongoDB supports real transactions across many documents:

session.startTransaction();
db.wallets.updateOne({ _id: "cust#42", balance: { $gte: 680 } },
                     { $inc: { balance: -680 } });
db.orders.insertOne({ ...order });
session.commitTransaction();   // both happen, or neither

But note the culture: good document design (order + items in ONE document) makes most writes single-document, which are always atomic anyway. Transactions are the exception, not the default — they cost speed.

Real system · A payment wallet done right

Every wallet system (think Paytm-style) faces the same two ops: deduct balance + record the order. The pattern above — a conditional $gte check inside the update plus a transaction — prevents both overdrafts and the "money deducted but no order" bug. It is the exact same idea as your DynamoDB conditional-write + TransactWriteItems flow, and your SQL UPDATE ... WHERE stock > 0 inventory trick. One pattern, three databases — say that in an interview.

Section 8 · Advanced tools

The rest of the toolbox — each with a real use

FeatureSimple meaningReal use
Aggregation pipelineData flows through stages: $match → $group → $sort... Like Java Streams for the database."Top 10 restaurants by revenue this week" computed inside the DB — no data shipped to the app
Change streamsSubscribe to live changes on a collection (built on the oplog)Order status changes → push to the customer's app in real time. Same role as DynamoDB Streams.
$lookupA left JOIN between collectionsJoin orders with restaurant details for a report — use sparingly, not in hot paths
Capped collectionsFixed-size collection, old data falls off automaticallyRecent activity logs; the oplog itself is one
Time series collectionsOptimized storage for metric/sensor data (v5+)Rider GPS history, order-volume metrics
GridFSStore files bigger than 16 MB in chunksMenu images (though S3 + CDN is usually better — your CDN design)
AtlasMongoDB's managed cloud service — the "DynamoDB experience" for MongoDBServerless/auto-scaling clusters, built-in search, global distribution
explain()Shows the query plan — index used or collection scan?Your #1 debugging tool. COLLSCAN in production = bug.
// Aggregation: top restaurants by revenue this week
db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { placedAt: { $gte: weekStart }, status: "DELIVERED" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$restaurantId", revenue: { $sum: "$total" } } },
  { $sort:  { revenue: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
])
Real system · The food app's order flow, MongoDB edition

1. Transaction + conditional update: deduct wallet only if balance ≥ total, insert the order — atomic.

2. Change stream: a Spring Boot service watches orders; on insert it notifies the restaurant. No dual-write.

3. Compound index (ESR): restaurant dashboard reads {restaurantId, status, placedAt}.

4. Geo index: assign the nearest free rider with $near.

5. TTL index: rider GPS trail expires after 24 h.

Same story as the DynamoDB version of this app — different tools, same patterns.

Section 9 · Quick recall

Who runs what on MongoDB — memory hooks

CompanyWhat they storeConcept it proves
Craigslist2.2B archived posts, 15 years of changing shapesFlexible schema
EA (FIFA Online)Player profiles as rich nested documentsDocument model = 1 read, no JOINs
ForbesCMS / articlesShip new fields fast, no migrations
CoinbaseTrading & account data through crypto maniasReplica sets, majority writes, failover
Foursquare (2010)Check-ins — the famous 11h outageBad shard key = hot shard. Know this story.
BaiduTrillions of docs, 600+ apps, hundreds of nodesSharding reaches hyper-scale (if you operate it)
Bosch IoTMillions of device sensor streamsCompression + document-level concurrency

MongoDB vs DynamoDB vs Cassandra — the 30-second answer

MongoDBDynamoDBCassandra
ModelDocuments (BSON)Key-value / wide-columnWide-column
Query powerRichest: any field, aggregations, geo, textKey-based only (+GSIs)Key-based only (+denormalized tables)
Storage engineB+ tree (WiredTiger)B-tree + WALLSM tree
Writes topologySingle primary per shardPaxos leader per partitionLeaderless, any node
ScalingManual-ish sharding (or Atlas)Fully automaticAdd nodes, ring rebalances
ConsistencyTunable (write/read concern)Choose per read; writes always quorumTunable (ONE/QUORUM/ALL)
Best whenRich queries, evolving schema, general app dataKnown access patterns, AWS, zero ops, extreme scaleExtreme write throughput, multi-DC, self-managed

One-line summaries to say in an interview

What is it

"A document database — JSON-like documents in collections, stored in WiredTiger B+ trees, replicated via an oplog in replica sets, scaled out by sharding."

Design rule

"Data accessed together is stored together — embed one-to-few, reference one-to-many. Most writes become single-document, which is atomic for free."

Why teams pick it

"Query flexibility plus schema flexibility — you don't need to know all your access patterns on day one, unlike DynamoDB."

Its weakness

"You own more decisions: shard key, indexes, RAM sizing, write concern. A bad shard key is a Foursquare-style outage."

Section 10 · Hands-on, one story, eleven chapters

Spring Boot 4 + Java 25 Implementation

This section follows one company — QuickBite — from day one to a 50-million-order-a-month business. Every chapter is a real production incident: something breaks, we find out why it broke, and then we fix it with Spring Boot code. Same characters throughout: Aisha (a customer), Spice Garden (a restaurant), Rahul (a delivery rider).

How to read each chapter: first the incident (what actually went wrong in production), then why it happened (the root cause, in plain words), then how Spring Boot + MongoDB fix it, step by step, then the code, then a walkthrough of that code, and — where settings are involved — a table showing what each setting really controls, and what changes if you change it.

10.1 Setup 10.2 Documents & CRUD 10.3 Storage & Write Safety 10.4 Replication 10.5 Sharding 10.6 Indexes 10.7 Transactions 10.8 Aggregation, Streams, GridFS 10.9 Repository vs Template 10.10 War Stories 10.11 Capstone ★
10.1

Project setup & connection

📖 Launch night · The 9 PM crash
🔴 The incident

QuickBite goes live on a Friday evening. On the developer's laptop, everything worked perfectly for weeks. In production, the app crashes within seconds of starting: MongoTimeoutException: connection refused — localhost:27017. While fixing that under pressure, a second, quieter problem is discovered: the database password is written directly inside a Java file — and that file has been sitting in the company's Git repository for a month, visible to everyone with repo access, including two contractors who already left.

Why this happens: on a laptop, the database really is at localhost. In production it is a separate cluster on a different machine — a hardcoded address that was never meant to leave the laptop, did. And passwords end up in Git for the simplest reason: putting them in the code is the easiest thing to type on day one. Both are among the most common real production mistakes in the industry — not beginner mistakes, everyone's mistakes.
💡 How Spring Boot solves it, step by step
  1. Add one dependency (spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb). Spring Boot now builds and manages the actual database connection object (MongoClient) for you — you never write connection code by hand.
  2. Move the address out of Java code and into application.yml. Now the same code runs on a laptop AND in production — only the config file differs per environment.
  3. Move the password out of the config file too, into an environment variable (${DB_PASSWORD}). The real password now lives only on the server, never in Git.
  4. Turn on the safety flags (retryWrites, w=majority) in the connection string, so every write in the whole app is protected by default — nobody has to remember to be careful in every service class.
// pom.xml — Spring Boot 4, Java 25
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb</artifactId>
</dependency>

<properties>
    <java.version>25</java.version>
</properties>
# application.yml
spring:
  data:
    mongodb:
      uri: mongodb+srv://quickbite_user:${DB_PASSWORD}@cluster0.mongodb.net/quickbite?retryWrites=true&w=majority
      auto-index-creation: true   # dev only — see the table below for why
⚙️ What each setting actually decides
SettingWhat it controls behind the scenesIf you change it
cluster0.mongodb.netWHICH database cluster every query in the app goes toPoint it at a staging cluster → same code, different data. This one line is the difference between laptop, staging, and production.
${DB_PASSWORD}Reads the password from the server's environment at startupIf the variable is missing, the app fails immediately at startup with a clear error — much better than starting "successfully" and failing on the first query at 9 PM.
retryWrites=trueIf a write fails because the primary node just died, the driver silently retries it once against the new primarySet it to false and every failover (a normal event, happens monthly) turns into visible errors for whoever clicked "Place Order" at that exact second.
w=majorityThe default safety level for every write: "don't say 'saved' until most replicas really have it"Change to w=1 and writes get faster — but a write acknowledged just before a crash can silently vanish. Chapter 10.3 shows when that trade is actually okay.
auto-index-creationWhether @Indexed annotations automatically build real indexes when the app startsGreat in dev. In production, leaving it on means a fresh deployment can start building a huge index on a live cluster at peak hour — teams turn it off and build indexes in planned migrations instead.
🔍 Code walkthrough
  1. The dependency is the whole "installation" — it brings in MongoRepository, MongoTemplate, and the auto-configured connection.
  2. The uri line holds everything about "where and how to connect" in one place — no Java class in the entire codebase mentions a hostname or password.
  3. After this chapter, QuickBite's launch-night crash is structurally impossible: production config points at production, laptop config points at localhost, and no password exists in Git at all.
10.2

Document model → Entity classes + CRUD

📖 Week 3 · The slow order page
🔴 The incident

Users start complaining that opening an order takes noticeably long. The team checks their monitoring: the "order details" page has a p99 latency of 900 milliseconds — nearly a full second. Tracing one page load shows the real story: it fires five separate database queries — one for the order, one for its items, one for the delivery address, one for the customer's name, one for the payment status — and then stitches the results together in Java.

Why this happens: the team modeled the data the SQL way, out of habit: orders in one place, items in another, addresses in a third, connected by IDs. That style exists because relational databases are built around it. But every extra query is a full network round trip (a few milliseconds each), and they run one after another. Five round trips, plus stitching, on the single most-viewed page in the app — the latency was designed in, not a bug.
💡 How MongoDB + Spring Boot solve it, step by step
  1. Apply MongoDB's #1 design rule: data that is always read together should be stored together. An order's items, address, and totals are never shown without the order — so they belong inside the order document, not in separate collections.
  2. Map that document to exactly one Java record. The nested JSON becomes nested Java types — no mapping layer, no joins.
  3. Let Spring write the queries. Declare a method like findByCustomerIdOrderByPlacedAtDesc on a MongoRepository interface — Spring reads the method name and generates the query. Five queries become one.
📄 What Aisha's order actually looks like, stored in MongoDB
 quickbite.orders — one document
{
  "_id": ObjectId("665f1a2b8c9d4e001a3b5c7d"),
  "customerId": "cust#42",          // Aisha
  "restaurantId": "rest#77",       // Spice Garden
  "status": "PLACED",
  "items": [                              // embedded — was its own table before
    { "name": "Biryani", "qty": 2, "price": 320 },
    { "name": "Raita",   "qty": 1, "price": 40  }
  ],
  "deliveryAddress": {                    // embedded — was its own table before
    "line1": "Flat 12, MG Road", "city": "Pune", "pin": "411001"
  },
  "total": 680,
  "placedAt": ISODate("2026-07-06T13:00:00Z")
}

The page that needed 5 queries now needs 1. Measured after the change: p99 dropped from 900ms to under 15ms.

// Order.java — the document above, field for field
@Document(collection = "orders")
public record Order(
    @Id String id,                       // maps to _id — Mongo generates it if you leave it null
    String customerId,
    String restaurantId,
    OrderStatus status,
    List<OrderItem> items,               // the embedded array, unchanged
    Address deliveryAddress,              // the embedded object, unchanged
    BigDecimal total,
    Instant placedAt
) {}

public record OrderItem(String name, int qty, BigDecimal price) {}
public record Address(String line1, String city, String pin) {}
public enum OrderStatus { PLACED, PREPARING, OUT_FOR_DELIVERY, DELIVERED, CANCELLED }
// OrderRepository.java — method name IS the query, Spring writes the rest
public interface OrderRepository extends MongoRepository<Order, String> {

    List<Order> findByCustomerIdOrderByPlacedAtDesc(String customerId);   // "my orders" screen

    List<Order> findByRestaurantIdAndStatus(String restaurantId, OrderStatus status);  // restaurant dashboard
}
// OrderService.java — placing Aisha's real order
@Service
public class OrderService {
    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;

    public Order placeOrder(Order order) {
        return orderRepository.save(order);          // INSERT — Mongo assigns _id
    }

    public List<Order> myOrders(String customerId) {
        return orderRepository.findByCustomerIdOrderByPlacedAtDesc(customerId);
    }
}
MongoRepository
⚙️ What each annotation actually decides
AnnotationWhat it controls behind the scenesIf you change / remove it
@Document(collection="orders")Which collection this class reads from and writes toRemove the name and Spring guesses from the class name ("order") — fine until someone renames the class and silently starts writing to a new, empty collection.
@IdMarks the field that maps to MongoDB's _idLeave the field null on insert → Mongo generates an ObjectId. Set it yourself → you control the ID (used later for idempotency).
record (vs class)Java 25 records are immutable, compact data holdersA plain class with setters also works — records just remove ~40 lines of boilerplate per entity and prevent accidental mutation.
🔍 Code walkthrough
  1. The record's shape mirrors the JSON exactly — items is a List, deliveryAddress is a nested record. Spring Data converts between them automatically in both directions.
  2. findByCustomerIdOrderByPlacedAtDesc — Spring parses this name at startup into "filter by customerId, sort by placedAt, newest first." Misspell a field name and the app fails at startup, not at runtime in front of a customer.
  3. save(order) is the whole insert. One call, one document, one network round trip.
Performance note: this stays fast only if customerId is indexed. It isn't yet — and that exact gap becomes the production incident in chapter 10.6.
10.3

Connection pool & write concern

📖 Month 2 · The Diwali flash sale
🔴 The incident

QuickBite runs a 50%-off Diwali promotion. Normal traffic is ~50 orders/second; Diwali morning hits 1,000 orders/second. Two things break at once. First, the logs fill with Timeout waiting for connection from pool — thousands of requests fail. Second, and scarier: during a brief 8-second primary failover that morning, an engineer later proves that a small batch of "successful" orders never actually got saved. Customers were charged; the orders don't exist.

Why this happens: two separate root causes. (1) The pool: every request to the database borrows one connection from a shared pool and returns it when done. The default pool holds ~100 connections. At 1,000 requests/second, all 100 are busy, and new requests wait in a line that grows faster than it shrinks — until they time out. (2) The lost writes: a write acknowledged by only the primary ("w:1") can vanish if the primary dies in the split second before copying it to the secondaries. It's rare — which is exactly why it only showed up during a failover under peak load, the worst possible time.
💡 How Spring Boot + MongoDB solve it, step by step
  1. Size the pool deliberately — raise maxSize so one instance can handle a burst, and set maxWaitTime so that when the pool IS full, requests fail fast with a clear error instead of hanging.
  2. Make the safe write setting the default — WriteConcern.MAJORITY app-wide, so orders and payments are protected without anyone remembering to ask.
  3. Deliberately relax it only where it's truly safe — Rahul's GPS pings arrive every few seconds; losing one in a thousand is invisible. Those writes get the cheaper W1 setting, and get batched: many pings in one network call instead of one call each.
// MongoConfig.java — connection pool tuned for burst traffic
@Configuration
public class MongoConfig {

    @Bean
    public MongoClientSettings mongoClientSettings() {
        return MongoClientSettings.builder()
            .applyToConnectionPoolSettings(builder -> builder
                .maxSize(200)                         // max parallel connections per app instance
                .minSize(10)                           // keep some warm even when idle
                .maxWaitTime(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS))     // fail fast, don't queue requests forever
            .writeConcern(WriteConcern.MAJORITY)       // safe DEFAULT for the whole app
            .build();
    }
}
// RiderLocationService.java — GPS pings, batched, deliberately cheaper write concern
@Service
public class RiderLocationService {
    private final MongoTemplate mongoTemplate;

    public void saveGpsPingsBulk(List<RiderLocation> pings) {
        BulkOperations bulkOps = mongoTemplate.bulkOps(BulkMode.UNORDERED, RiderLocation.class);
        pings.forEach(bulkOps::insert);
        bulkOps.withWriteConcern(WriteConcern.W1).execute();   // fast: only the primary needs to have it
    }
}
MongoTemplate
⚙️ What each setting actually decides
SettingWhat it controls behind the scenesIf you change it
maxSize(200)How many database conversations ONE app instance can hold at the same timeToo low → requests queue and time out under load (the Diwali bug). Too high → 10 instances × 500 connections = 5,000 connections, which can overwhelm MongoDB itself. Rule: (Mongo's connection limit) ÷ (number of app instances), with headroom.
minSize(10)Connections kept open and ready even when traffic is quietSet to 0 and the first requests after a quiet period each pay the cost of opening a fresh connection — a small but visible latency spike every morning.
maxWaitTime(2s)How long a request waits for a free connection before giving upSet to 30s and an overloaded app doesn't fail — it just gets slower and slower while requests pile up invisibly. 2s makes overload loud, obvious, and quick to alarm on.
WriteConcern.MAJORITYA write is only "done" when most replicas have it — it survives a primary crashThis is the setting whose absence lost real orders on Diwali morning. Changing the app default to W1 makes every write in the company gamble on failover timing.
W1 (per-call, GPS only)A write is "done" when the primary alone has it — faster, tiny loss windowFine for GPS pings. Copy-paste this line into the payment service and you've quietly re-created the Diwali data-loss bug for money.
🔍 Code walkthrough
  1. bulkOps(BulkMode.UNORDERED, ...) collects many inserts into ONE network round trip. UNORDERED means Mongo may write them in any order and one failure doesn't stop the rest — perfect for independent GPS points.
  2. .withWriteConcern(WriteConcern.W1) overrides the safe app default for this one call only — a visible, deliberate, commented decision, exactly where it belongs.
  3. After this chapter: the pool survives 20x bursts, important writes survive failovers, and cheap writes are cheap on purpose.
10.4

Replica set → Read preference in code

📖 Month 3 · The 2 AM page
🔴 The incident

2:14 AM: a disk fails on the primary MongoDB node. The on-call engineer is paged. By the time she logs in, MongoDB has already elected a new primary and the app recovered on its own. But while reading the dashboards, she notices something wasteful: QuickBite pays for three database nodes, yet the two secondaries sit at 3% CPU while the primary runs at 85% — every single read in the app, even a restaurant menu that changes once a week, goes to the primary.

Why this happens: the driver's default read preference is primary — the safest possible choice, so it's the default. Nobody on the team ever made a decision about reads; the default made it for them. The result: one node does all the work, two nodes are expensive spectators, and during any primary trouble, ALL reads suffer together.
💡 How MongoDB + Spring Boot solve it, step by step
  1. Sort every read in the app into two buckets. Bucket A: "a few milliseconds of staleness is invisible" (menus, restaurant lists, old order history). Bucket B: "must be the absolute latest value" (wallet balance right before payment, order status right after placing).
  2. Send bucket A to the secondaries with ReadPreference.secondaryPreferred() — the idle nodes start earning their cost, and the primary's load drops.
  3. Keep bucket B on the primary with ReadPreference.primary() — correctness where correctness matters.
📄 Same database, two very different reads
Menu screen (bucket A)Read from ANY replica. A few ms of staleness is invisible — spreads load, faster for the user.
Wallet balance before payment (bucket B)Must read the PRIMARY. Reading a stale, slightly-higher balance could let a customer overspend.
// MenuService.java — fast path: spread the load across secondaries
@Service
public class MenuService {
    private final MongoTemplate mongoTemplate;

    public List<MenuItem> getMenu(String restaurantId) {
        Query query = new Query(Criteria.where("restaurantId").is(restaurantId));
        mongoTemplate.setReadPreference(ReadPreference.secondaryPreferred());
        return mongoTemplate.find(query, MenuItem.class);
    }
}

// WalletService.java — safe path: always the freshest value
@Service
public class WalletService {
    private final MongoTemplate mongoTemplate;

    public Wallet getBalanceForPayment(String customerId) {
        mongoTemplate.setReadPreference(ReadPreference.primary());
        return mongoTemplate.findById(customerId, Wallet.class);
    }
}
MongoTemplate
⚙️ What each read preference actually decides
ValueWhat it controls behind the scenesIf you use it
primary (default)Every read goes to the one node that accepted the writesAlways correct, but one node does 100% of read work — the exact waste from this chapter's story.
secondaryPreferredReads go to a secondary if one is healthy, else fall back to the primarySpreads load with a safety net. Data can lag by milliseconds — fine for bucket A, dangerous for money.
nearestReads go to whichever node answers fastest (lowest network delay)Best latency for read-heavy, geo-distributed apps; same staleness caveat as secondaries.
🔍 Code walkthrough
  1. Both services query the same data — the only difference is one line choosing WHICH copy of the data to trust for that call.
  2. After the change, QuickBite's dashboards showed the primary dropping to ~40% CPU and menus loading measurably faster during peak hours — the two "spectator" nodes finally doing real work.
Real-world parallel: this split — cheap reads to secondaries, money reads to the primary — is the standard pattern at every large company running MongoDB; the theory tab's Coinbase example is exactly this.
10.5

Sharding → choosing and applying the shard key

📖 Month 6 · Outgrowing one machine
🔴 The incident

QuickBite crosses 50 million orders. Monitoring shows the primary's memory usage climbing week after week — the "working set" (the data touched often, plus indexes) no longer fits in RAM, so more and more reads go to disk, and disk is thousands of times slower than memory. Latency graphs develop an ugly upward slope. Buying a bigger machine buys a few months, at double the cost — then the same wall again.

Why this happens: a replica set has copies for safety, but every copy holds ALL the data, and all writes still go through ONE primary. Past a certain size, no single machine — at any price — can hold the working set in RAM and absorb all the writes. This is the wall every successful product hits; the only durable answer is to split the data across machines: sharding.
💡 How MongoDB + Spring Boot solve it, step by step
  1. Choose the shard key first, calmly, before the crisis. The team studies its queries: almost everything filters by customerId. That's the natural key.
  2. Choose HOW keys map to shards. Hashed — because customerIds must spread evenly. (A time-based key would pile all of today's orders onto one shard — the exact mistake behind Foursquare's famous 11-hour outage in the theory tab.)
  3. Apply it with a one-time admin command, run by an engineer via a migration script — sharding is a structural decision, not runtime application logic.
  4. Change zero lines of service code. The mongos router transparently sends each query to the right shard. Repositories, services, controllers — untouched.
📄 Before vs after, in one picture
Before1 replica set. ALL 50M orders' data and writes funnel through 1 primary. RAM wall approaching.
After4 shards. Each holds ~12.5M orders — each shard's working set fits comfortably in its own RAM. 4x total write capacity.
// ShardSetup.java — an ADMIN action, run ONCE at collection creation time, never per-request
@Component
public class ShardSetup {
    private final MongoTemplate mongoTemplate;

    public void enableShardingForOrders() {
        mongoTemplate.executeCommand(
            new Document("enableSharding", "quickbite"));

        mongoTemplate.executeCommand(new Document("shardCollection", "quickbite.orders")
            .append("key", new Document("customerId", "hashed")));  // spreads inserts evenly
    }
}
⚙️ What the shard key choice actually decides
ChoiceWhat it controls behind the scenesIf you choose differently
customerId as the keyAll of one customer's orders live on the same shard — "my orders" stays a single-shard queryKey on something you don't query by, and every "my orders" query must ask ALL shards and merge — slower and more expensive with every shard you add.
"hashed"MongoDB hashes the value before placing it, spreading even similar values evenlyRanged instead: great for range scans, but an ever-growing value (dates, ObjectIds) piles ALL new inserts onto the last shard — a hot shard, the Foursquare failure.
When it runs (once, by hand)Sharding physically reorganizes data placementWire it to app startup and every deployment re-attempts a structural change — at best noisy errors, at worst a surprise during peak traffic.
🔍 Code walkthrough
  1. enableSharding flips the database into sharded mode; shardCollection names the collection and the key. Two commands, run once — that's the entire application-side footprint of sharding.
  2. The genuinely hard part was the meeting, not the code: agreeing on customerId + hashed after studying real query patterns. The best engineering here is the decision.
10.6

Indexes → fixing the slow screens

📖 Month 6, continued · The 8-second screen
🔴 The incident

A support ticket: "My Orders takes 8 seconds to load." The engineer runs the query with .explain() and sees the dreaded word: COLLSCAN. MongoDB is reading through all 50 million order documents to find Aisha's twelve. The same week: Spice Garden's dashboard crawls, and the job that assigns the nearest rider to an order starts timing out.

Why this happens: without an index, a database has only one way to find matching documents — check every single one. In development this was invisible: the dev database had 300 orders, and scanning 300 of anything is instant. The bug didn't appear at 50 million orders — it was there from day one, hidden by small data. This is the single most common performance bug in real production systems, in every database.
💡 How MongoDB + Spring Boot solve it, step by step
  1. Find the guilty queries with .explain() — it shows whether a query used an index (IXSCAN) or scanned everything (COLLSCAN), and how many documents it touched.
  2. Add a single-field index on customerId — one annotation — to fix "My Orders."
  3. Add a compound index for the dashboard, ordered by the ESR rule (Equality fields first, then Sort, then Range): restaurantId, status, placedAt — matching exactly how the dashboard asks its question.
  4. Add a geospatial index for "nearest rider," and a TTL index so old GPS points delete themselves — two more annotations.
📄 What .explain() showed, before and after
Before — COLLSCAN"examined": 50,000,000 documents to return 12. ~8 seconds.
After — IXSCAN"examined": 12 documents to return 12. ~4 milliseconds.
// Order.java — indexes added right on the fields they protect
@Document(collection = "orders")
@CompoundIndex(name = "restaurant_status_time",
               def = "{'restaurantId': 1, 'status': 1, 'placedAt': -1}")  // ESR: Equality, Equality, Sort/Range
public record Order(
    @Id String id,
    @Indexed String customerId,          // fixes the "My Orders" screen
    String restaurantId,
    OrderStatus status,
    List<OrderItem> items,
    Address deliveryAddress,
    BigDecimal total,
    Instant placedAt
) {}
// RiderLocation.java — geospatial index (nearest rider) + TTL index (auto-cleanup)
@Document(collection = "rider_locations")
public record RiderLocation(
    @Id String id,
    @Indexed(name = "2dsphere") GeoJsonPoint location,       // powers "find nearby riders"
    String riderId,
    @Indexed(expireAfterSeconds = 86400) Instant recordedAt   // self-deletes after 24h
) {}

public interface RiderLocationRepository extends MongoRepository<RiderLocation, String> {
    List<RiderLocation> findByLocationNear(Point point, Distance distance);   // "riders within 3 km"
}
// Assigning Rahul: find riders within 3 km of Spice Garden
Point restaurantPoint = new Point(73.85, 18.52);
List<RiderLocation> nearbyRiders =
    riderLocationRepository.findByLocationNear(restaurantPoint, new Distance(3, Metrics.KILOMETERS));
MongoRepository
⚙️ What each index setting actually decides
SettingWhat it controls behind the scenesIf you change it
@Indexed on customerIdBuilds a sorted lookup structure so "customerId = X" jumps straight to matchesRemove it and the query silently degrades back to a full scan — no error, just slowness that grows with your success.
Field order in @CompoundIndexThe index sorts by field 1, then 2, then 3 — like a phone book sorted by city, then surname, then first namePut placedAt first and the dashboard query can't use the index efficiently — order matters, that's the whole ESR rule.
expireAfterSeconds = 86400A background process deletes each document that many seconds after its timestamp86400 = keep 24h of GPS trail. Raise it and storage grows; set 0-with-explicit-dates for per-document custom expiry.
Every index you addEach write must also update every index on the collection10+ indexes on a hot collection = visibly slower writes. Indexes are bought with write speed — add the ones your real queries need, not "just in case."
🔍 Code walkthrough
  1. @Indexed / @CompoundIndex keep the index definitions right next to the fields they protect — future readers see the query contract in the entity itself.
  2. findByLocationNear — Spring recognizes the Near keyword and builds a geo query against the 2dsphere index, returning riders already sorted by distance.
  3. Three screens, three index types, ~5 added lines total — and the 8-second screen now answers in 4ms.
Process change after this incident: QuickBite added a rule to code review — any new repository query must include its .explain() output in the pull request. Cheap rule, has caught every COLLSCAN since.
10.7

Consistency & multi-document transactions

📖 Month 7 · The vanishing ₹680
🔴 The incident

The worst kind of ticket: Aisha was charged ₹680 — her wallet history clearly shows the deduction — but no order exists. No food arrived. Support refunds her manually and apologizes. Then it happens again to someone else. And again: 12 cases in one week, always during deploys or brief crashes.

Why this happens: "place an order" is really TWO writes — (1) deduct the wallet, (2) create the order document. Each write on its own is atomic. But between them there is a gap of a few milliseconds — and if the app crashes, restarts, or gets redeployed inside that gap, write 1 survives and write 2 never happens. Rare per-request, but at millions of requests, "rare" becomes "12 times a week." This exact bug shape exists in every payment system ever built; it's why transactions were invented.
💡 How MongoDB + Spring Boot solve it, step by step
  1. Register one bean — MongoTransactionManager — which teaches Spring's standard @Transactional annotation how to drive MongoDB transactions.
  2. Put @Transactional on the method that does both writes. Now they commit together or roll back together — the gap between them can no longer exist half-done.
  3. Bake the balance check into the update itself (balance >= total inside the query) — so checking and deducting happen as one step, and two simultaneous orders can't both spend the same money.
📄 The sequence, with and without a transaction
Without a transaction1) Deduct ₹680 ✅  2) App crashes 💥  3) Order never created. Money gone, nothing to show for it.
With a transaction1) Deduct ₹680 (pending)  2) App crashes 💥  3) MongoDB auto-rolls back the deduction. Aisha's balance untouched — she simply retries.
// MongoConfig.java — enables @Transactional (requires a replica set, even a local single-node one)
@Bean
MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(MongoDatabaseFactory dbFactory) {
    return new MongoTransactionManager(dbFactory);
}
// PaymentService.java — Aisha's ₹680 order, done safely
@Service
public class PaymentService {
    private final MongoTemplate mongoTemplate;

    @Transactional   // both writes commit together, or both roll back
    public Order placeOrderWithPayment(String customerId, Order order) {

        Query walletQuery = new Query(Criteria.where("_id").is(customerId)
                                .and("balance").gte(order.total()));      // must have enough money
        Update deduct = new Update().inc("balance", order.total().negate());

        var result = mongoTemplate.updateFirst(walletQuery, deduct, Wallet.class);
        if (result.getModifiedCount() == 0) {
            throw new InsufficientBalanceException(customerId);   // triggers a full rollback
        }
        return mongoTemplate.insert(order);
    }
}
MongoTemplate
⚙️ What each piece actually decides
PieceWhat it controls behind the scenesIf you change / remove it
MongoTransactionManager beanConnects Spring's @Transactional machinery to MongoDB sessionsWithout it, @Transactional on a Mongo method silently does nothing — the writes run un-grouped and the ₹680 bug quietly returns.
@TransactionalStarts a session before the method, commits after it, rolls back on any exceptionIts scope is the method — put only the two money writes inside. Adding slow work (an API call, an email) inside the method holds database locks for the whole duration.
balance ≥ total inside the queryCheck-and-deduct as ONE atomic step on one documentCheck first in Java, deduct second, and two simultaneous requests can both pass the check — the classic double-spend race.
🔍 Code walkthrough
  1. updateFirst returns a count. Zero modified = the balance condition didn't match = insufficient funds. Throwing here makes Spring roll back the whole unit.
  2. insert(order) only runs after a successful deduction — and if THIS write fails, the deduction above is rolled back too. That is the entire fix: the two writes now share one fate.
  3. After shipping: zero "charged but no order" tickets in the following months.
10.8

Aggregation, Change Streams, $lookup, GridFS

📖 Month 8 · Growing pains of success

Four real problems landed in the same sprint. Each has a one-paragraph story, a why, and a fix.

A) The Monday Excel ritual → Aggregation pipeline

🔴 The incident

Every Monday an analyst exports last week's orders to Excel and hand-builds "top restaurants by revenue." It takes half a day, and one week a copy-paste error paid the wrong restaurant a bonus.

Why this happens: pulling millions of rows OUT of the database to add them up elsewhere is slow, manual, and error-prone. The database can do the math where the data already lives.
💡 The fix

An aggregation pipeline: filter → group → sum → sort → top 10, all inside MongoDB. The app receives 10 small rows, not 2 million.

// AnalyticsRepository.java
public List<RestaurantRevenue> topRestaurantsThisWeek(Instant weekStart) {
    MatchOperation match = Aggregation.match(
        Criteria.where("placedAt").gte(weekStart).and("status").is("DELIVERED"));
    GroupOperation group = Aggregation.group("restaurantId").sum("total").as("revenue");
    SortOperation sort = Aggregation.sort(Sort.Direction.DESC, "revenue");
    LimitOperation limit = Aggregation.limit(10);

    Aggregation pipeline = Aggregation.newAggregation(match, group, sort, limit);
    return mongoTemplate.aggregate(pipeline, "orders", RestaurantRevenue.class).getMappedResults();
}
public record RestaurantRevenue(@Id String restaurantId, BigDecimal revenue) {}
MongoTemplate
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. match = filter (like WHERE) — always first, so later stages handle less data.
  2. group + sum = the Excel formula, but computed next to the data.
  3. sort + limit = only the top 10 ever leave the database. The Monday ritual became a dashboard that's always current.

B) Restaurants refreshing the page all day → Change Streams

🔴 The incident

Spice Garden's staff hit refresh constantly, waiting for new orders. During rush hour they miss some for minutes — food starts late, customers wait longer, ratings drop.

Why this happens: refresh-based (polling) designs always trade delay for load: poll rarely and you're late; poll constantly and you hammer the database. Neither is right. The database already KNOWS the moment an order arrives — the app just needs to be told.
💡 The fix

A change stream: the app subscribes to the orders collection, and MongoDB pushes each insert to it the moment it happens — built on the same oplog that replication uses.

// OrderChangeListener.java — fires the moment a new order document is inserted
@Component
public class OrderChangeListener {
    private final MongoTemplate mongoTemplate;

    @PostConstruct
    public void listen() {
        ChangeStreamRequest<Order> request = ChangeStreamRequest.builder(this::handleChange)
            .collection("orders")
            .build();
        messageListenerContainer.register(request, Order.class);
    }

    private void handleChange(ChangeStreamEvent<Order> event) {
        Order newOrder = event.getBody();
        notificationService.notifyRestaurant(newOrder.restaurantId(), newOrder.id());  // pushed to Spice Garden's screen instantly
    }
}
MongoTemplate

C) One combined report for ops → $lookup

🔴 The incident

Ops needs a weekly report of orders together with restaurant details (name, city) — which live in a different collection.

Why this happens: restaurants are edited independently (menus, addresses change), so they rightly live in their own collection — but reports sometimes need both sides at once.
💡 The fix

$lookup joins two collections inside an aggregation — used in the nightly report job, never on a page a customer is waiting for.

LookupOperation lookup = Aggregation.lookup("restaurants", "restaurantId", "_id", "restaurant");
Aggregation pipeline = Aggregation.newAggregation(lookup, Aggregation.limit(100));
List<Document> joined = mongoTemplate.aggregate(pipeline, "orders", Document.class).getMappedResults();
Rule QuickBite adopted: $lookup is allowed in batch jobs and admin reports; it is banned in customer-facing request paths, where the single-document design from 10.2 should already have the data together.

D) Menu photos disappearing → GridFS (and its honest limits)

🔴 The incident

Spice Garden uploads a new menu photo. It displays fine — until the next deployment, when the photo is simply gone.

Why this happens: the photo was saved to the app server's local disk. In modern deployments, servers are replaced on every deploy — local disk is temporary by design. Anything written there is guaranteed to vanish; it just isn't guaranteed WHEN.
💡 The fix

Store the file in a place that outlives app servers. GridFS keeps it inside MongoDB — shown here because it directly answers "files in Mongo." Honest note: for public images at scale, S3 + a CDN is usually the better production choice; GridFS fits best when files must live and die with specific documents.

@Autowired GridFsTemplate gridFsTemplate;

public String storeMenuImage(InputStream imageStream, String filename) {
    ObjectId id = gridFsTemplate.store(imageStream, filename, "image/jpeg");
    return id.toString();
}

10.9 · MongoRepository vs MongoTemplate — the playbook QuickBite settled on

By month 8, the team had made this call enough times to write it down as a rule everyone follows:

SituationUseWhy
Save, findById, delete, simple find-by-fieldMongoRepositoryOne method signature, Spring writes the query
Query name gets long/ugly (5+ conditions)MongoTemplateBuild the Query/Criteria in code instead of a giant method name
Aggregation pipeline (group, sum, join)MongoTemplateMongoRepository can't express pipelines
Dynamic query built from optional filters (search screen)MongoTemplateAdd Criteria conditionally, in a loop/if-chain
Bulk insert/update of many documentsMongoTemplateBulkOperations batches network calls
Need a specific read preference/read concern per callMongoTemplateRepository doesn't expose this per-query
Standard CRUD screen (90% of a typical app)MongoRepositoryLess code, easy to test, easy to read

The rule of thumb: start every new feature with MongoRepository. Drop down to MongoTemplate only when the query genuinely can't be expressed as a method name — don't reach for MongoTemplate by default just because it's more powerful.

10.10

War stories — mistakes QuickBite actually made

📖 Looking back

N+1 queries

The restaurant dashboard looped over orders and called restaurantRepository.findById() inside the loop — one query became hundreds. Fixed by embedding the fields actually needed, or batching with findAllById().

Missing index, silent slowdown

The "My Orders" bug from 10.6 worked perfectly in testing (a few hundred rows) and only broke in production at 50 million. Lesson: always run .explain() on a new query before shipping it.

An order that kept growing

A "combo mega-order" feature appended items to one order document indefinitely during a long catering event, creeping toward the 16 MB document limit. Fixed by capping embedded items and referencing overflow items in a separate collection.

@Transactional on a solo local MongoDB

A new engineer's local MongoDB was a single standalone node, not a replica set — @Transactional failed with a confusing runtime error, not a compile error, on their very first day.

10.11

Capstone — QuickBite's complete Order Service, end to end

📖 Month 9 · Putting everything together
🔴 The incident

A new engineer joins to build the single most important screen in the app: "Track My Order." It shows the customer's delivery name and phone, what was ordered, whether payment succeeded, and where the rider is right now — refreshing every few seconds, for every active order in the country at once. The new engineer's first draft uses four collections (users, orders, payments, deliveries) joined by IDs.

Why that draft would fail: it's the 10.2 slow-page problem multiplied — four round trips per refresh, per user, on the most-watched screen in the product. And with four separate reads, one can fail while the others succeed, showing users a half-loaded, inconsistent screen. The screen customers stare at the most would be the slowest and flakiest one.
💡 The decision: one order, one document, everything it needs
  1. Keep the full user profile in its own users collection — it's edited independently (login, saved addresses, preferences) and read at login.
  2. Embed a lightweight snapshot of the customer (name, phone) inside each order — it's only ever read as part of that order.
  3. Embed the payment record and the delivery record too — same reasoning: they belong to one specific order and are never read without it.
  4. Result: "Track My Order" becomes one findById. One round trip. Nothing to half-fail.
📄 One QuickBite order document — user, order, payment, and delivery, together
 quickbite.orders — one complete document
{
  "_id": ObjectId("665f1a2b8c9d4e001a3b5c7d"),

  // ---- ORDER ----
  "customerId": "cust#42",
  "restaurantId": "rest#77",
  "items": [
    { "name": "Biryani", "qty": 2, "price": 320 },
    { "name": "Raita",   "qty": 1, "price": 40  }
  ],
  "total": 680,
  "status": "OUT_FOR_DELIVERY",
  "placedAt": ISODate("2026-07-06T13:00:00Z"),

  // ---- USER (lightweight snapshot, not the full profile) ----
  "customer": { "name": "Aisha Khan", "phone": "+91-98xxxxxx10" },

  // ---- PAYMENT ----
  "payment": {
    "method": "UPI",
    "transactionId": "txn_9f21a",
    "status": "SUCCESS",
    "paidAt": ISODate("2026-07-06T13:00:02Z")
  },

  // ---- DELIVERY ----
  "delivery": {
    "riderId": "rider#12",
    "riderName": "Rahul",
    "address": { "line1": "Flat 12, MG Road", "city": "Pune", "pin": "411001" },
