A founder and a CTO · every decision, in the order it really happens

Building Amazon — from a rented store to 100 million users

Jay Bajaj is a businessman with a dream: he wants to build Amazon — an online store that sells phones, laptops, and accessories, with honest prices and fast delivery. Purusottam is the engineer he trusts, and the CTO of this journey. This document is the story of their conversations over five years: every problem the business runs into, how Purusottam thinks through it, which solution he picks, and — just as important — why he says "not yet" to the fancy solutions until the right moment arrives.

Chapter 0 · A coffee shop, day zero

The idea, and an answer Jay did not expect

Two people · savings in the bank · zero customers · zero code

It is a Saturday morning. Jay Bajaj arrives at the coffee shop carrying a notebook. Inside the notebook are drawings he made late at night: boxes labelled "order service," "payment service," "Kubernetes cluster." He has read blog posts about how big companies build their systems, and he wants to start the same way. Across the table sits Purusottam, sipping his coffee, listening quietly.

Jay
Purusottam, I want to build Amazon. Phones, laptops, accessories — good prices, same-day delivery. I have drawn the full architecture already. Microservices from day one, Kafka for events, everything on Kubernetes. If we build it properly from the start, we will never have to rebuild it. What do you think?
Purusottam
Jay, I love the dream. But let me ask you one honest question first: how many customers do we have today?
Jay
Well… zero. We haven't launched.
Purusottam
Exactly. Right now, our biggest risk is not "will the system scale?" Our biggest risk is "will anyone buy from us at all?" Kubernetes does not answer that question. A live store answers it. So here is my advice, and it may surprise you: we should build nothing this month.
Jay
Nothing? You are the CTO and you are telling me not to write code?
Purusottam
Yes — because writing code is not the goal. Selling phones is the goal. There are companies like Shopify whose whole business is giving people a ready-made online store: catalog, cart, checkout, payments, hosting — everything included, for a small monthly fee. We can be live by Monday. Every hour I spend building what Shopify already gives us for two thousand rupees a month is an hour stolen from finding suppliers and customers. We will write real code on the day Shopify starts saying "no" to something the business needs. And I promise you — I will tell you clearly when that day comes.
How Purusottam reached this decision

He asked himself one question: what is the cheapest way to learn whether this business works? Building a custom platform takes months and answers nothing about the business. Renting a store takes a weekend and answers everything — do customers come, do they buy, do they return? When you don't know if anyone wants your product yet, the smartest architecture is somebody else's architecture. This is not laziness; it is the discipline of solving the riskiest problem first.

The rule this chapter teaches: the first version of almost every store should be rented, not built. You are not building a technology platform yet — you are testing whether a business exists.
Chapter 1 · The first year

The Shopify year — and the day the platform starts saying "no"

0 → ~8,000 customers · ~40 orders every day · team: Jay, Purusottam, one operations person
What renting gave them

The store went live in a single weekend, exactly as promised. Shopify quietly handled everything technical: the product catalog, the shopping cart, checkout, the payment gateway, hosting, security certificates, even the automatic emails to customers who left items in their cart. For a full year, not one line of backend code was written.

And that was the point. Jay spent the year on the actual business: finding suppliers who gave good prices on phones, negotiating with two delivery partners, running Instagram ads, answering customer calls himself. By month ten, the store was doing ₹28 lakh in monthly sales. The rented store had done its job perfectly — it proved the business was real.

The "no" list — how a business slowly outgrows a rented platform

But around month eight, something began to change. Jay kept coming to Purusottam with ideas from the market — and Purusottam kept finding that the platform could not do them. Each "no" was small on its own. Together, they formed a pattern:

What Jay wantedWhat the platform said
"Exchange your old phone for a discount"No proper flow for valuing a used device and adjusting the price. Some third-party apps existed, but none fit how phone exchange actually works in India.
Track each phone by its serial number (IMEI) for warrantyThe platform counts stock as a number ("47 units"). It cannot attach a serial number to each individual unit and follow that unit through sale, return, and warranty claim.
"No-cost EMI, but only on certain bank cards"The checkout page is locked. Bank-specific EMI rules need checkout customisation that the plan does not allow.
Reduce payment feesAround 2% of every sale goes to platform and gateway fees. On ₹28 lakh a month, that is over ₹56,000 — every month, and growing with the business.
A flash sale for a new phone launchThe platform throttled the traffic during the sale. Customers saw errors before they even saw the product.
Jay
Purusottam, last night was the OnePlus launch. The brand gave us a special allocation, we promoted it for two weeks — and at the exact moment of the sale, the platform started throttling our own customers. We looked like amateurs. And I am still working around the exchange program with spreadsheets. Tell me honestly: is it time?
Purusottam
Yes, Jay. The day has come — and I want you to notice why it has come, because the reason matters. We are not leaving Shopify because Shopify is bad. We are leaving because our business now needs things that a general-purpose platform cannot give anyone: a custom exchange flow, per-unit serial tracking, our own checkout, and the ability to survive a launch-day crowd. Those needs are ours alone now. That is what "outgrowing a platform" actually means.
Jay
So now we finally build the big architecture from my notebook? Microservices, Kafka, all of it?
Purusottam
Not yet. We are three people, Jay. Microservices solve the problems of thirty-five engineers stepping on each other — we do not have that problem, so we should not pay its price. I will build one well-organised Spring Boot application and one MySQL database. But I will build it with clean internal boundaries, so that on the day we DO have thirty-five engineers, the split into services will be easy. Trust me on the order of things: monolith now, microservices when the team demands it.
How Purusottam decided it was time to leave

He used a simple test: does the platform's limit now cost more than an engineering team would? One "no" is an annoyance you work around. But by month ten, three "no"s were blocking revenue directly — the exchange program (a real competitive advantage), the launch-day sales (a relationship with brands), and the growing fee bill. When the cost of staying crossed the cost of building, the answer changed. Not fashion, not excitement — arithmetic.

⚖️ What leaving the platform costs
  • Everything Shopify did invisibly becomes Purusottam's job: uptime, security, payment compliance, backups, monitoring. The ₹2,000 per month was buying a great deal of quiet work.
  • A real migration project: exporting the catalog and customers, redirecting the old links so Google search rankings survive, and running both stores in parallel for a few weeks. Roughly two months of careful work.
  • The lesson to carry forward: the right time to leave a platform is when its limits cost you more than an engineering team does — and not one day earlier.
Chapter 2 · Year two

Building version one — one app, one database, and three data decisions that last for years

~10,000 customers · team grows to 4 engineers · Spring Boot 4 · Java 25 · MySQL on RDS · S3 + CloudFront

The migration is done. For the first time, when a customer taps "Buy" on the site, the request lands on code that Purusottam's team wrote. The architecture he builds is deliberately simple — one Spring Boot application, one MySQL database, product images in S3 served through CloudFront. But inside that simple shape, he makes three careful decisions about how the data is stored. These three decisions are the quiet heroes of this whole story: two of them will save the company in later chapters.

Decision one — how should we store PRODUCT data?
Jay
Here is something I don't understand. A phone has RAM, storage, camera details. A laptop has screen size, processor, graphics card. A charger just has wattage. Every product type is different. How can one "products" table hold all of them? Do we need one of those NoSQL databases I keep hearing about?
Purusottam
That is genuinely the right question, Jay — different products really do have different shapes. But before jumping to a new database, let me walk you through the three classic answers to this problem, because choosing between them is a famous design decision, and I want you to see why we will pick the middle one.

Purusottam explains the three options at the whiteboard:

OptionHow it worksWhy it fits or fails for us
1 · A column for every attributeAdd ram_gb, screen_inch, wattage… as real columns in the table✗ Within a year we would have 200+ columns, most of them empty for most products. And every new product category would need a schema change — a database surgery for every business idea.
2 · An "attributes" side-table (EAV)A table of (product_id, attribute_name, attribute_value) rows✗ Flexible, but every real question becomes a puzzle of joins. "Phones with 16GB RAM under ₹30,000" turns into slow, unreadable SQL. Teams that choose this usually regret it.
3 · Common columns + one JSON column ✓Fixed columns for what EVERY product has (name, brand, price, category), plus one specs JSON column holding whatever varies✓ Flexible like a document database, but the data stays in the SAME MySQL as orders and inventory — one transaction, one backup, one system for a team of four to operate.
4 · A separate document databasePut the catalog in MongoDB or DynamoDBA good answer LATER — in Chapter 5, when a dedicated catalog team can own it. Today it would mean two databases for four engineers. The right idea at the wrong time is still the wrong idea.
-- The chosen shape: fixed columns for what every product shares, JSON for what varies
CREATE TABLE products (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  brand VARCHAR(100), category VARCHAR(50),
  price_paise BIGINT NOT NULL,            -- money stored as whole paise. never as a decimal float.
  specs JSON,                              -- {"ram_gb":16,"storage_gb":256,"color":"black"}
  INDEX idx_cat_brand (category, brand)
);
-- and MySQL can still look INSIDE the JSON when a question needs it:
SELECT * FROM products WHERE category='phone' AND specs->>'$.ram_gb' >= 16;
How Purusottam reached this decision

He judged each option against the team they actually are — four engineers who must also sleep. Option 1 fails on flexibility, option 2 fails on query pain, option 4 fails on operational weight. Option 3 gives ninety percent of a document database's flexibility for zero new systems. His rule, which returns again in Chapter 6: the best new database is usually a feature of a database you already run.

Decision two — how should we store USER data?

Users, unlike products, all have the same shape — a name, an email, addresses, saved payment methods, order history. This is exactly what relational tables were born for, so the design is classic and calm: a users table, an addresses table, a payment_methods table joined by user id. The decisions that matter here are about safety, and they are made on day one, not after the first breach: passwords stored only as bcrypt hashes (never the password itself), card numbers never stored at all (only the token the payment gateway gives back), and personal columns encrypted at rest. Boring, correct, and compliant — exactly how user data should feel.

Decision three — the inventory table that will save Chapter 4

The third decision looks like a small detail today. The warranty and exchange programs need to track every phone individually — this specific box, with this specific serial number (IMEI), sold to this specific customer. A single number saying "47 units in stock" cannot answer a warranty claim. So alongside the usual stock count, Purusottam creates a table with one row per physical unit:

CREATE TABLE inventory_units (
  id BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  product_id BIGINT NOT NULL,
  serial_no VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE,            -- the IMEI — the reason this table exists today
  status ENUM('FREE','RESERVED','SOLD') DEFAULT 'FREE',
  order_id BIGINT NULL,
  INDEX idx_pick (product_id, status)
);

One hundred iPhones in the warehouse means one hundred rows, each marked FREE. Today, this table exists for warranty tracking and nothing more. Keep it in mind — in Chapter 4, on the most stressful day of the company's life, this exact table turns out to be a weapon nobody planned.

Chapter 3 · Year three

Growing pains — the database is doing jobs it was never meant to do

~100,000 customers · evening traffic hurts every day · team: 10 engineers

The business is genuinely working now. A hundred thousand customers, steady press coverage, and every evening between seven and ten, a wall of traffic. And every evening, the same two complaints arrive — one from customers, one from Jay himself.

Jay
Two things, Purusottam, and both embarrass me. First: in the evening, product pages take two full seconds to open — I timed it myself. Second: our search is honestly terrible. Yesterday I typed "ifone" with a spelling mistake, and it found nothing. Then I typed "iphone 15 pro" correctly, and the first result was a screen guard, not the phone. Customers are noticing.
Purusottam
Both complaints look different, Jay, but they are actually the same disease: we are asking MySQL to do jobs it is bad at. Think about the slow pages — the same bestseller product is being fetched from the database five thousand times an hour. Same question, same answer, and MySQL does the full work every single time, because a database has no memory of what it just answered. Remembering answers is a different job — that is what a cache does. And search — LIKE '%iphone%' is just text matching. It cannot forgive a spelling mistake, cannot rank a phone above a screen guard, and it reads the whole table to do even that badly. Searching is also a different job — that is what a search engine does. My plan is simple: hire one specialist for each job, and let MySQL go back to the one job it is great at — being the reliable source of truth.
💡 The changes — each one tied to a named pain
  1. Redis (ElastiCache), the rememberer: product pages and category lists are cached in memory with a ten-minute expiry. The first viewer pays the database price; the next five thousand get the answer in under a millisecond. Evening database CPU falls from 85% to 30%.
  2. OpenSearch, the finder: products are indexed in a real search engine. "ifone" now finds iPhones (typo tolerance), and the iPhone 15 Pro ranks above its screen guard (relevance plus sales ranking). The search box becomes a feature instead of an apology.
  3. A MySQL read replica: a live copy of the database that serves reports and order-history reads, so heavy reading never again competes with customers' orders on the primary.
  4. Docker, Prometheus and Grafana — the eyes: every service ships as the same container image everywhere, and one dashboard shows latency, errors, and cache hit rate. From this month on, the team learns about problems from alerts — not from Jay's phone calls.
🔴 Incident · the cache that kept selling at the old price

One Tuesday, a supplier corrects a pricing mistake: a phone listed at ₹4,999 should have been ₹6,999. The catalog team updates the price in MySQL immediately. And yet, for the next twenty-five minutes, customers keep seeing — and keep buying at — ₹4,999. Why? The cached copy of that product page was created before the correction, its expiry was set to thirty minutes, and nothing told the cache that the world had changed. The cache was not broken; it was doing exactly what it was told — remembering an answer that was no longer true.

The two rules that came out of that Tuesday: first, every piece of code that changes a product must also delete that product's cache entry in the same breath — delete rather than update, because a deletion can never write a wrong value, while an update can. The expiry time stays only as a safety net for mistakes. Second, the checkout re-checks the price against MySQL at the moment of payment — the cache is for displaying things quickly; decisions about money always go back to the source of truth.
Chapter 4 · Launch day ★

The flash sale — fifty thousand buyers, one hundred phones, and the hardest problem in this book

A new phone launches exclusively on the site · 100 units at ₹49,999 · 50,000 people waiting for 12:00 PM

This is the chapter everything has been building toward. A phone brand offers Jay an exclusive: one hundred units of their new flagship, sold only on his site, at a launch price. It is a huge vote of trust — and Jay knows this is exactly the kind of event that crushed them back in the Shopify days. He walks into Purusottam's room and closes the door.

Jay
The brand confirmed it. One hundred units, twelve o'clock, Friday. Our ads are already running — I expect fifty thousand people refreshing the page at noon. Purusottam, I need you to be brutally honest with me: if we sell a hundred and five phones when we only have a hundred, or if the site freezes at 12:01, we will never get another exclusive from any brand again. Can we handle it?
Purusottam
We can — but only if we respect how hard this problem really is, Jay. Let me show you something on the whiteboard. I am going to write the buying code three times. The first version looks correct and oversells badly. The second version is truly correct but chokes under the crowd. Only the third version is both correct AND fast — and it uses a table we built two years ago for a completely different reason. Walking through all three is the only way you will trust the final answer.
Version one — the code that oversells (and why it looks so innocent)

Here is the version almost everyone writes first. Read the stock, check it in Java, subtract one, write it back:

// Step 1: read. Step 2: check. Step 3: write. Looks harmless — but there is a GAP between the steps.
int qty = jdbc.queryForObject("SELECT quantity FROM inventory WHERE product_id=?", Integer.class, id);
if (qty > 0) {
    jdbc.update("UPDATE inventory SET quantity=? WHERE product_id=?", qty - 1, id);
    createOrder(...);
}

Why it fails: on a quiet Tuesday, this code works perfectly, which is exactly what makes it dangerous. At noon on launch day, hundreds of requests run this code at the same moment. They all perform step 1 together — and they all see the same number. Watch two of them race for the last phone:

TimeRequest ARequest Bquantity in the database
12:00:00.001reads → sees 1—1
12:00:00.002—reads → also sees 11
12:00:00.003check passes · writes 0 · order created ✓—0
12:00:00.004—check passed earlier · writes 0 · order created ✓0 — two phones sold, one existed

This is called a race condition — two requests racing through the same gap between reading and writing. With fifty thousand buyers, this code would not oversell by one phone. It would oversell by hundreds.

Version two — correct at last, but every buyer stands in one queue
Purusottam
The cure for a race condition is to close the gap — make the check and the subtraction happen as ONE step that nothing can interrupt. And MySQL can do exactly that, if we push the check inside the UPDATE statement itself.
// The check and the decrement fused into ONE atomic statement.
// MySQL locks the row while updating it, so requests execute on this row strictly one at a time.
int updated = jdbc.update(
    "UPDATE inventory SET quantity = quantity - 1 WHERE product_id = ? AND quantity >= 1", id);
if (updated == 0) throw new SoldOutException();   // zero rows changed = someone else took the last one

This version can never oversell. The WHERE quantity >= 1 is the check, the quantity - 1 is the write, and the row lock makes them one unbreakable action. If the stock is gone, the statement simply changes zero rows, and we tell the customer "sold out."

But now look at the new problem. One product means one row. One row means one lock. And one lock means fifty thousand requests forming a single-file queue, each waiting for the one before it to finish its whole transaction. The line moves — but it is a line. Lock-wait timeouts begin firing. The connection pool fills up with requests that are just standing in the queue, and now even customers buying other products are stuck, because all the connections are busy waiting. The site is correct and crawling at the same time.

Jay
So version one sells phones we don't have, and version two makes fifty thousand people stand in one line. Is there really a version where they don't queue at all?
Purusottam
There is — and here is the beautiful part, Jay. Remember the inventory_units table from two years ago? The one we built so every phone could carry its own IMEI for warranty claims? One hundred phones means one hundred separate ROWS in that table. And a lock in MySQL is per-row. So instead of everyone fighting over one row… what if every buyer locks a DIFFERENT row?
Version three — one row per unit, and the magic words SKIP LOCKED 
// Each purchase claims ONE free unit — and skips past rows that other buyers are holding right now
@Transactional
public Order buyFlashSale(String userId, long productId) {
    Long unitId = jdbc.query("""
        SELECT id FROM inventory_units
        WHERE product_id = ? AND status = 'FREE'
        LIMIT 1
        FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED""",                    -- the magic phrase
        rs -> rs.next() ? rs.getLong(1) : null, productId);

    if (unitId == null) throw new SoldOutException();   // no free, unlocked unit left = sold out

    jdbc.update("UPDATE inventory_units SET status='RESERVED', order_id=? WHERE id=?",
                orderId, unitId);
    return createOrder(userId, productId, unitId);       // this specific IMEI now belongs to this order
}

What SKIP LOCKED means, in plain words: "Find me a FREE row. If you reach a row that another transaction is holding at this moment — do not wait for it. Skip it, and take the next free one." So buyer one locks unit #1. Buyer two arrives a millisecond later, sees unit #1 is busy, and — instead of standing behind buyer one — instantly grabs unit #2. Buyer three grabs unit #3. One hundred buyers proceed at the same time, on one hundred different rows. The single-file queue becomes one hundred parallel checkout lanes. Buyer one hundred and one finds no free, unlocked row anywhere — and receives "sold out" immediately, without waiting behind anyone.

Here is what the table actually looks like three seconds into the sale — same product_id on every row, one row per physical phone, and a new buyer's query walking past the locked rows:

How Purusottam reached this solution

He followed the bottleneck, step by step. Version one's bottleneck was correctness — closed by making check-and-write atomic. Version two's bottleneck was contention — fifty thousand requests contending for one lock. The general cure for contention is always the same idea: spread the fighting across more things to fight over. One row cannot be shared, but a hundred rows can serve a hundred buyers at once. The inventory_units table — built two years earlier for warranty serial numbers — already held stock in exactly that shape. The lesson he repeats to the team afterwards: good data modelling is stored luck. Decisions made for one honest reason keep paying off for reasons nobody predicted.

The full launch-day defence — layers protecting layers
💡 What actually runs at 12:00 PM on Friday
  1. A rate limiter at the door (a Redis counter per user and per IP): bots and frantic refreshers receive HTTP 429 before touching anything expensive.
  2. A Redis gate in front of the database: DECR sale:stock — one atomic counter starting at 100. A negative answer means instant "sold out," served from memory in under a millisecond. Fifty thousand clicks become roughly one hundred database visitors; Redis absorbs the crowd so MySQL only ever meets the winners. (If a later step fails, the code gives the number back with INCR.)
  3. The SKIP LOCKED unit claim — the hundred winners each lock their own unit row in parallel, status moving to RESERVED with a five-minute expiry.
  4. Payment with an idempotency key — a unique key generated when the checkout screen opens, sent with every attempt, so a double-tap or a retry can never charge twice. On success the unit becomes SOLD. On failure or timeout, a small sweeper job flips the unit back to FREE and INCRs the Redis gate — the phone quietly returns to the shelf for the next buyer in line.
Jay
It's 12:04 PM. All hundred units sold. Not one oversold. The site never even blinked — and the brand manager just called me about the next launch. How are you feeling?
Purusottam
Relieved — and I want the team to remember WHY it worked. Not because of one clever trick, but because of layers: the rate limiter protected Redis, Redis protected MySQL, SKIP LOCKED removed the queue, the idempotency key protected the money, and the sweeper protected the stock. Every layer was built assuming the layer before it would leak a little. That assumption — that everything fails a little — is the real architecture.
Chapter 5 · Year four

Microservices and the event-driven order system — the split, done at the right time

~1 million customers · team: 35 engineers in 6 teams · EKS · Kafka (MSK)

The company is not small anymore. Thirty-five engineers work in six teams — catalog, orders, payments, search, delivery, and customer accounts. And a strange thing has happened: the codebase that once made four engineers fast is now making thirty-five engineers slow. Deploy day has become a three-hour ceremony where six teams ship together and pray together.

Jay
Purusottam, last Thursday the reviews team shipped a small bug — and it took down checkout for forty minutes. Reviews! Why should a bug in product reviews stop people from paying us? And my team leads tell me they wait days for a deploy slot. Four years ago you told me "microservices when the team demands it." Is the team demanding it now?
Purusottam
It is, Jay — loudly. And notice that the problem forcing us is exactly the one I predicted: not traffic, but people. One codebase means one deploy line, one failure zone, one scaling unit for six teams with completely different needs. The good news? Remember the clean packages I insisted on in Chapter 2 — catalog, cart, orders, payments, users kept strictly separate inside the monolith? Each of those packages now becomes its own service. We designed this split four years ago. We simply refused to pay for it before we had to.
💡 The split — and the rules that keep it sane
  1. Seven services, each owned by a team: User & Auth, Catalog, Cart, Order, Inventory, Payment, Notification — each running on Kubernetes (EKS), each deployed on its own schedule, each owning its OWN database. The golden rule, never broken: no service ever touches another service's tables. They talk through APIs and events only.
  2. The right database for each job, now that teams can own them: Catalog moves to a document store (the JSON pattern from Chapter 2 graduates into its own database). Cart lives in Redis — fast, expiring, and safe to lose. Order, Inventory, and Payment stay on MySQL, because money needs transactions. Search stays on OpenSearch.
  3. An API Gateway as the single front door: login checking, routing, and rate limiting live in ONE place, instead of being copied into seven services.
  4. Kafka (MSK) as the event backbone: when an order is placed, the Order service announces the fact — order-placed — and every interested service (inventory, notification, analytics) reacts on its own time, at its own speed, without the customer waiting for any of them.
The order flow — and the three traps hiding inside it

Purusottam explains to the team that an event-driven order system has three famous traps, and the design must answer all three before the first incident, not after:

Trap one — the lost event. The Order service writes the order to its database, and then publishes the event to Kafka. But what if the service crashes between those two steps? The order exists, yet no other service ever hears about it — no stock reserved, no email sent. The database and Kafka are two separate systems; there is no single transaction covering both. The answer is the Transactional Outbox: in the SAME database transaction that saves the order, also save the event into an outbox_events table. Either both are saved or neither is. A small relay process then reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka, retrying until it succeeds. The event can be late, but it can never be lost.

Trap two — the double order. A customer's "Pay" button times out on her screen, though the request actually succeeded on the server. She taps again — and gets charged twice. The answer is an idempotency key: the app generates a unique key when the checkout screen opens and sends it with every attempt. The Order service stores it with a unique constraint, so the second attempt collides with the first and simply returns the existing order. The same key travels to the payment gateway, so even the charge cannot be duplicated.

Trap three — the half-finished order. Stock is reserved, then the payment fails. Without care, that unit stays reserved forever. The answer is the saga pattern: every step in the flow has a compensating "undo" step. Payment failed → publish payment-failed → Inventory hears it and releases the unit → Order marks itself CANCELLED. The big transaction we cannot have across services is replaced by a chain of small local transactions, each with an undo.

🔴 Incident · the webhook that came twice — and sometimes never

The payment gateway confirms payments by calling back a URL — a "webhook." In the first month after the split, the team discovers the webhook's true personality: for some orders it arrives twice (the gateway retries generously), and for a few it never arrives at all (a network blip on the receiving side). Result: some customers charged once but shown two confirmations, and a few orders stuck forever at CREATED even though the money was taken.

The two habits that fixed it for good: first, webhooks are processed idempotently — the gateway's payment ID is the deduplication key, so a repeated webhook is a harmless no-op. Second, a reconciliation job runs every ten minutes: any order sitting in CREATED for more than fifteen minutes is checked directly against the gateway's API — paid means advance it, unpaid means cancel it and release the unit. The team's new motto: webhooks are an optimisation; reconciliation is the guarantee.
⚖️ What the split honestly costs
  • The monolith's problems are traded for distributed problems: events arriving twice, services seeing the world at slightly different moments, failures that are partial instead of clean. This trade is worth it ONLY at team scale — which is exactly why Purusottam refused it in Chapter 0 and Chapter 1.
  • A slow checkout is no longer one stack trace — it is a trail across four services. Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry) becomes day-one equipment, not a luxury.
  • The infrastructure bill takes a visible jump: EKS, Kafka, seven services with replicas. Cost dashboards per team start this quarter — so that Chapter 7's bill is never a mystery.
Chapter 6 · Year five

Recommendations — teaching the store to understand what things mean

~10 million customers · "customers also viewed" is now a serious revenue line
Jay
Purusottam, I was browsing our own site last night. I looked at three gaming laptops in a row — and the "you may also like" section offered me a phone case and a kitchen mixer. Meanwhile the big players seem to read my mind: gaming mouse, cooling pad, RAM upgrade. What machinery is behind that mind-reading, and can we afford it?
Purusottam
We can, and the machinery has a beautiful core idea: turn meaning into numbers. A model reads each product's title, description, and image, and produces a list of a few hundred numbers called an embedding — the product's "meaning coordinates." Products with similar meaning get similar numbers: gaming laptops land close to gaming mice and cooling pads, and far away from kitchen mixers. Your recent activity gets its own coordinates too. Then "what should we show Jay?" becomes a geometry question: which products sit nearest to Jay's current position in meaning-space? A vector database is simply a database built to answer that nearest-neighbour question very fast. The only real decision for us is which vector database — and I have a firm opinion shaped by everything we have built so far.
The decision — which vector database should we use?
OptionWhat it isBest whenPurusottam's verdict
pgvector (on Aurora/RDS)A vector column INSIDE PostgreSQLUp to a few million vectors, and you want vectors living beside your normal data✓ Start here. One system we already know how to run, plain SQL, joins with product data for free, zero new infrastructure.
OpenSearch k-NNA vector index inside the search cluster we ALREADY run (Chapter 3)Tens of millions of vectors, and you want text search and meaning search blended in one query✓ Graduate here. "iphone case" as words, blended with "similar in meaning" as vectors — one query, one cluster, and it is already ours.
Redis vector searchVectors inside ElastiCacheThe vector changes every few seconds and must be read with tiny latencyUsed for one thing only: the live session vector, which updates on every click.
A dedicated vector service (Pinecone and friends)A managed, vector-only databaseHundreds of millions of vectors and a dedicated ML platform teamNot yet. A new vendor, new bills, and data leaving our cloud — for a scale problem we do not have. We will know if that day comes.
How Purusottam reached this decision

The same rule that chose the JSON column in Chapter 2, applied five years later: the best new database is a feature of a database you already operate. pgvector lets the team learn embeddings with zero new systems. OpenSearch k-NN is the natural graduation because the cluster, the operations knowledge, and the on-call rotation already exist. A dedicated vector vendor is the answer to a scale the company has not reached — and adopting the answer before the question is how infrastructure bills become mystery novels.

Chapter 7 · The one-page memory

★ The playbook — five years of decisions on one page

ChapterThe pain that triggered itThe moveTechnology that arrived
0–1 · Idea → 8K customersThe riskiest question is "does the business exist?"Rent everything, build nothingShopify
1 · Month tenThe platform says "no": exchange flow, IMEI tracking, EMI checkout, launch sales, feesLeave — for arithmetic, not fashion—
2 · 10KCustom features need custom codeA boring monolith with careful data decisionsSpring Boot, MySQL (JSON specs, one row per unit), S3 + CloudFront
3 · 100KMySQL doing jobs it hates — remembering and findingOne specialist per jobRedis, read replica, OpenSearch, Docker, Prometheus + Grafana
4 · Launch day50,000 buyers, 100 phones, one hot rowLayers, plus 100 rows and SKIP LOCKEDRedis gate, FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, idempotency keys, the sweeper

6 · 10MGeneric recommendations leave money on the tableTurn meaning into numbersEmbeddings, pgvector → OpenSearch k-NN

The patterns that repeat forever

An atomic conditional UPDATE beats read-check-write. One row per unit plus SKIP LOCKED beats one hot row. Idempotency keys make retries safe. The outbox makes database-and-event atomic. Delete the cache, never update it. A reconciliation job stands behind every webhook. Same key, same partition, same order.

Purusottam's meta-rules

Rent until the platform says no. Adopt technology only when a named pain demands it. Draw clean boundaries years before you split along them. The best new database is one you already run. And design every layer assuming the layer before it leaks a little.

The one-line summary Jay gives investors: "We scaled by removing one bottleneck at a time, and only that one — first ownership, then the machine, then the database's extra jobs, then the hot row, then the monolith, then the generic experience. Every technology in our stack is simply the tool that removed one specific bottleneck, adopted on the day that bottleneck appeared."
Jay Bajaj and Purusottam's journey is a teaching story; the incidents are the industry's shared scars. Stack: Java 25 · Spring Boot 4 · AWS (EKS, RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch, MSK, S3, CloudFront, API Gateway) · Prometheus · Grafana.
Simple guide · With real systems

Kafka explained with real high-scale systems

0 Story1 What2 Architecture3 Producers/Consumers 4 Ordering5 Replication6 Guarantees 7 Rebalancing7.5 Who's in charge8 Serialization9 Storage 10 Streams11 Patterns12 Production12.5 Real problems13 Who uses it
Section 0 · Why Kafka exists

The story: too many pipes at LinkedIn

Around 2010, LinkedIn had a problem that every growing company hits sooner or later. Many systems created data: page views, clicks, profile edits, log files. Many other systems needed that data: search, recommendations, reports, monitoring. The teams connected them in the most natural way: they built one direct connection ("pipe") between each pair of systems.

Think about what happens as the company grows. With 10 systems creating data and 10 systems reading it, you can end up with close to 100 different pipes. Each pipe has its own format, its own bugs, and its own team fixing it in the middle of the night. Adding one new system means building ten new pipes for it.

Three engineers (Jay Kreps, Neha Narkhede, and Jun Rao) suggested a very different idea: build one central pipe for everything. Every system writes what happened to one shared place. Every system that wants data reads from that same place. The shared place itself is simple: it is just a log — a list of events, written one after another, saved on disk, never changed after writing.

That shared place became Kafka. It was made open source in 2011, and the founders later started a company around it called Confluent.

Real system · LinkedIn today

LinkedIn's Kafka now carries around 7 trillion messages every day. Every like, profile view, connection request, and log line flows through it. The "100 pipes" problem turned into "everyone talks to one log."

The one idea to hold onto for this whole guide: Kafka is like a shared diary. New entries are always written at the bottom. Nothing is ever erased or edited. Anyone can read the diary from any page, at their own speed, using their own bookmark. Almost everything else in Kafka is machinery to make this one simple idea fast, safe, and very, very big.
Section 1 · Basics

What exactly is Kafka?

What is it?

Kafka is a system for passing events between applications. An event is a small note that says something happened: "Aisha placed order #77213 for ₹680." One application writes the note. Other applications read the note and react to it. Kafka sits in the middle, holding the notes safely and handing them out.

People call Kafka a "distributed event streaming platform." Let's translate those words. Event: a note about something that happened. Streaming: the notes flow continuously, like water, not in big once-a-day batches. Distributed: Kafka runs on many computers working together, so it can handle huge amounts and survive a computer dying. Platform: it is a foundation other systems are built on.

Why is it needed?

Imagine our food delivery app, QuickBite, without Kafka. When Aisha places an order, the Order service must directly call the Notification service (tell the restaurant), the Inventory service (update stock), and the Analytics service (update reports). Three problems appear:

1) Everything must be awake. If the Analytics service is down, should Aisha's order fail? That makes no sense — analytics is not her problem. 2) The slowest one sets the speed. If Analytics is slow today, Aisha waits longer for her order confirmation. 3) Adding a listener means surgery. A new Fraud team wants order data? Someone must change the Order service's code.

With Kafka, the Order service writes ONE note — "order placed" — and moves on. It does not know or care who reads it. Every interested team reads the note on its own, at its own speed. If one reader is down for an hour, its notes wait for it. Adding a new reader changes nothing for anyone else.

How does it work?

Events are written to named lists called topics (think: one diary per subject — an "orders" diary, a "payments" diary). The diary lives on disk and is copied to several computers for safety. Every reader keeps a bookmark (called an offset) that remembers how far they have read. That is genuinely the whole model.

How do we use it?

The Order service sends an event to the topic orders-placed. The Notification, Inventory, Analytics, Fraud, and Loyalty services each subscribe to that topic and process every order their own way. None of them know the others exist.

Queue vs broadcast — Kafka is both

A queue gives each message to ONE worker (good for sharing work among copies of the same service). A broadcast gives each message to EVERY listener (good for many different teams). Kafka does both at once, using "consumer groups" — explained in Section 3.

Kafka is not a mailbox

In a normal mailbox, reading a letter removes it. Kafka does NOT delete a message when it is read. Messages stay for a set time (usually days) and can be read again and again, by anyone. It is a diary you can re-read, not a mailbox you empty.

Real system · QuickBite's order announcement

Aisha taps "Place Order." The Order service writes ONE event to the orders-placed topic. Five different teams' services read it: notifications (ping Spice Garden), inventory (reduce stock), analytics (update dashboards), fraud (check for risk), loyalty (add reward points). Next month a sixth team joins — and nobody has to change anything. They just start reading.

Section 2 · Architecture

Brokers, topics, partitions

What are they?

A broker is one Kafka server — one computer running the Kafka program. A cluster is a group of brokers working together as a team. A topic is one named stream of events, like orders-placed — think of it as one diary. A partition is one slice of that diary. A topic with 3 partitions is really 3 smaller diaries that together hold all the events of that topic.

Why are partitions needed?

Imagine one diary and one person allowed to write in it. No matter how fast they write, there is a limit — one hand, one pen, one book. Now imagine splitting the diary into 12 smaller diaries handled by 12 people. Twelve times the writing speed, twelve times the reading speed. That is exactly why Kafka splits topics into partitions and spreads them across brokers: so many computers can share the work in parallel.

If you have read the MongoDB or DynamoDB guides: partitions play the same role as shards in MongoDB and partitions in DynamoDB. Same idea, third system.

How does it work?

Every event lands in exactly one partition of its topic. Inside a partition, events keep their exact arrival order, and each gets a number: 0, 1, 2, 3... (this number is the offset). But there is a price for the parallel speed: order is only promised INSIDE one partition, not across partitions. Event #5 in partition 0 might have happened after event #2 in partition 1. Section 4 shows how to live with this happily.

How do we use it?

You choose the number of partitions when you create a topic. A simple rule: partitions should be at least the number of parallel workers you will ever want, because one partition can be read by at most one worker in a team (Section 3 explains this). QuickBite creates orders-placed with 12 partitions — room to grow to 12 parallel workers later.

Real system · Uber

Uber runs one of the world's largest Kafka setups — trillions of messages a day: trip events, driver GPS positions, price updates, payments. A busy topic like driver GPS is split across hundreds of partitions so hundreds of machines can share the load. It is QuickBite's 12 partitions, just at 100 times the scale.

Section 3 · Producers, consumers, groups, offsets

Who writes, who reads, and how reading scales

What are they?

A producer is any application that writes events into a topic. A consumer is any application that reads them. A consumer group is a team of identical consumers sharing one job — Kafka divides the topic's partitions among the team members. An offset is a bookmark: it remembers, for each partition, how far a group has read. "I have finished up to message number 4,502."

Why are consumer groups needed?

Here is the everyday problem. Your notification service reads order events. Traffic grows, one copy can't keep up, so you run 3 copies. But now there is a danger: will each order be processed 3 times? Will Spice Garden get 3 pings per order? The consumer group solves this. All 3 copies join the same group (named, say, notification-service). Kafka gives each copy its own share of the partitions. Every event is read by exactly ONE member of the group. The 3 copies now share the work instead of repeating it.

How does it work, step by step?
1Consumers start up and tell Kafka their group name
2Kafka gives each member some partitions — each partition goes to exactly one member
3Each member reads its partitions and regularly saves its bookmark ("commits its offset")
4Bookmarks are stored inside Kafka itself, in a hidden topic called __consumer_offsets
5If a member dies, its partitions are handed to the survivors (Section 7)

Different groups do not share bookmarks. The group notification-service and the group analytics-service BOTH read every event in orders-placed, each with their own bookmark, each at their own speed. This is how Kafka is a work-sharing queue (inside one group) and a broadcast (across groups) at the same time.

Offset management — the small detail with big consequences

WHEN you save your bookmark decides what happens after a crash. Read this table slowly — it is the seed of Section 6:

When you save the bookmarkIf you crash while processing a messageResult
BEFORE processingThe bookmark already moved past the message, so you never read it againThe message is lost. Called "at-most-once."
AFTER processingThe bookmark still points at the message, so you read it again after restartThe message may be processed twice. Called "at-least-once" — the sensible default.
Real system · QuickBite's three teams, one topic

The orders-placed topic (12 partitions) is read by: group notifications (3 copies — 4 partitions each), group analytics (1 copy — all 12 partitions), group fraud (6 copies — 2 partitions each). When analytics goes down for maintenance, its bookmark just waits. On restart, it catches up on everything it missed. No other team notices anything.

Section 4 · Ordering & partitioning

How events choose their partition — and stay in order

What decides which partition an event goes to?

The message key. When you send an event, you can attach a key — any string, like an order ID. Kafka turns the key into a number (this is called hashing — like a machine that turns any word into a number, the same number for the same word every time) and uses it to pick a partition. Same key → same partition, every single time. If you send no key, Kafka just spreads events around evenly, with no promise about order.

Why does this matter so much?

Remember Section 2's rule: order is only kept INSIDE one partition. Now imagine order #77213 goes through three steps: "placed", then "paid", then "shipped". If these three events land in three different partitions, three different workers read them in parallel — and one worker might apply "shipped" before another applies "paid". The order's status would jump around wrongly.

The fix is one simple rule: events that must stay in order must share the same key. Give every event of order #77213 the key "ord#77213", and they all land in one partition, one after another, read by one worker, in the right order. Always.

Try it yourself

Type a key below and press Enter to "send" a message. Watch which partition it lands in. Send the same key again — it always lands in the same place, stacking up in order:

Send the same key several times — it always stacks in the same partition, in order. Change one letter and it may jump to another partition. This little machine IS Kafka's whole ordering model.

The hot-key trap: keys spread evenly, but traffic may not. Imagine keying order events by restaurantId during a mega-restaurant's half-price promo: that one restaurant's partition gets flooded while the others sit idle. One overloaded partition while others rest is called a hot partition — the same trap as DynamoDB's hot partition in that guide. Choose keys that both give you the order you need AND have many different values.
Real system · Payments everywhere

Every payment system keys its events by account or order ID for exactly this reason: "money taken out, then money put in" must never be seen backwards. Photo-feed systems like Instagram do the opposite on purpose — likes from different users don't need any order between them, so they flow without keys for maximum speed.

Section 5 · Replication, ISR, ZooKeeper vs KRaft

How Kafka survives a dead computer

What is replication?

Replication means keeping copies. Every partition is copied onto several brokers — usually 3 copies. One copy is the leader: all writing and reading happens through it. The other copies are followers: their only job is to copy everything the leader writes, as fast as they can, so they are always ready to take over.

What is the ISR?

ISR stands for In-Sync Replicas — in plain words, "the list of copies that are fully caught up right now." Why keep such a list? Because when the leader's computer dies, Kafka must promote a follower to be the new leader — and it must pick one that has EVERYTHING, or acknowledged messages would be lost. The ISR is exactly that safe-to-promote list. A follower that falls behind (slow disk, network trouble) is temporarily dropped from the list until it catches up.

How does failover work, step by step?
1Broker 2, the leader of partition P1, crashes
2The cluster's coordinator notices its heartbeat stopped
3A fully-caught-up follower (from the ISR) is promoted to leader
4Producers and consumers automatically find the new leader and reconnect — it takes seconds, and no human is involved

ZooKeeper vs KRaft — who keeps track of the cluster

Someone has to keep the master list: which brokers are alive, and who is the leader of each partition. For many years, Kafka used a separate helper system called ZooKeeper for this. It worked, but it meant running and maintaining TWO systems instead of one — twice the setup, twice the patching, twice the 2 AM pages. It also became a bottleneck for very large clusters.

KRaft (short for "Kafka Raft") is the modern replacement, and the default today (ZooKeeper was fully removed in Kafka 4.0). The idea: let Kafka coordinate itself. A few brokers take the role of controllers, agree with each other using a well-known voting method called Raft, and store the cluster's master list as — fittingly — a Kafka log. One system instead of two, faster recovery, and support for far bigger clusters.

ZooKeeper eraKRaft era (today)
Systems to runKafka + ZooKeeperKafka only
Master list stored inZooKeeperAn internal Kafka log
Recovery after controller diesSlower — must reload stateNear-instant — standby controllers already have the log
Practical cluster size~200,000 partitionsMillions of partitions
Real system · Every 2 AM, everywhere

The value of all this shows up as a NON-event. A broker dies at 2 AM at QuickBite. Leaders fail over in seconds. Producers retry automatically. Consumers reconnect automatically. The on-call engineer sleeps through it and reads about it on the morning dashboard. That is the whole point of copies + a fast coordinator.

Section 6 · Delivery guarantees

At-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once

What question are we answering?

Computers crash, networks hiccup. The question is: if things break at the worst possible moment, does each event get processed zero times, one time, or two times? Kafka lets you choose the answer, and the choice is made by a few settings on the writing side and the reading side.

GuaranteeIn plain wordsWhen it is the right choice
At-most-onceNever doubled, but might be lostRider GPS pings — losing one is invisible, doubling one is pointless
At-least-onceNever lost, but might be doubledThe default for real work (orders, emails) — IF you handle doubles safely (see "idempotent" below)
Exactly-onceNever lost, never doubledMoney movements and counters — needs extra machinery
The writing side — three settings

acks ("acknowledgements") — how many copies must say "got it!" before the producer treats the message as saved. acks=0: don't wait at all (fire and forget). acks=1: wait for the leader only. acks=all: wait for all the caught-up copies (the ISR) — the safe choice. If you read the other guides: this is the same idea as MongoDB's w: majority and DynamoDB's "two of three copies" rule.

retries — if the network hiccups, the producer sends the message again. But here is a trap: what if the FIRST attempt actually arrived, and only the "got it!" reply was lost? The retry would create a duplicate.

enable.idempotence=true — the fix for that trap, called the idempotent producer. "Idempotent" is a fancy word for a simple idea: safe to do twice — doing it again changes nothing. The producer numbers each message; the broker remembers the numbers and quietly drops any repeat it has already stored. Retries stop creating duplicates. This is on by default in modern Kafka and costs almost nothing. Leave it on.

The reading side — when to save the bookmark

From Section 3: save the bookmark AFTER processing and you get at-least-once (nothing lost, maybe doubled). Since doubles are possible, your processing code must itself be idempotent — "handle order #77213" run twice must have the same effect as running once. A simple way: keep a small record of already-handled order IDs and skip repeats. This is the same discipline as the conditional writes in the MongoDB and DynamoDB guides.

Exactly-once — Kafka transactions

Some apps read from one topic, do some work, and write results to another topic (read → process → write). A crash in the middle can double the output. Kafka transactions fix this: the output messages AND the input bookmark are saved together, as one all-or-nothing package. Readers of the output set isolation.level=read_committed, which means: "only show me messages from packages that finished completely." Kafka Streams (Section 10) uses this machinery under the name exactly_once_v2.

An honest limit: exactly-once works within Kafka's world (topic to topic). The moment your code calls something outside — a bank's API, an email service — Kafka cannot help there. Kafka cannot un-send an email. Outside calls need their own "safe to do twice" protection.
Real system · QuickBite's wallet pipeline

Wallet events (money out, money in) run with transactions and read_committed readers — the Kafka twin of the ₹680 and ₹2,499 wallet fixes in the MongoDB and DynamoDB guides. Rider GPS pings run with acks=1 and no transactions — because nobody cares about one lost ping. Matching the guarantee to the data is the real skill here.

Section 7 · Rebalancing

What happens when readers come and go

What is it?

A rebalance is Kafka re-dealing the partitions among a group's members — like re-dealing cards when a player joins or leaves the table. It happens when a consumer starts, stops, crashes, or just LOOKS crashed (its heartbeat stopped, or it spent too long processing one batch).

Why can it hurt?

The old-style ("eager") rebalance is a full stop: EVERY member of the group stops reading, gives up ALL its partitions, and waits for the new deal — even members whose share doesn't change at all. Now picture deploying a new version of your service, restarting 3 copies one by one: that is multiple full stops in a row. A group that rebalances often spends its life reshuffling instead of working. The symptom on your dashboard: the reading backlog (lag) jumps on every deploy.

How is it fixed in modern Kafka?

Cooperative sticky rebalancing

Only the partitions that actually need to move, move. Everyone else keeps reading right through the reshuffle. This is the setting to choose today.

Static membership

Give each consumer a fixed name tag (group.instance.id). Now a quick restart — like a deploy — is not treated as "a member died." Kafka just waits for the member to come back. No rebalance at all.

Real system · The deploy that paused notifications

QuickBite deploys the notification service (3 copies, restarted one by one) right at dinner time. With old-style rebalancing: three full stops, notifications frozen each time, restaurants pinged late. With cooperative sticky + static membership: the deploy barely makes a ripple. This exact tuning is one of the most common real-world Kafka fixes.

Section 7.5 · Who is actually in charge

Two different managers: the Controller and the Group Coordinator

People mix these two up constantly, and it is a favourite interview trap. Kafka has two separate manager roles, and they look after completely different things. Knowing which is which — and what happens when each one dies — is what separates a confident answer from a shaky one.

What is the Controller?

The Controller is the manager of the whole cluster. There is exactly one active Controller at a time. Its job is cluster-wide bookkeeping: which brokers are alive right now, and who is the leader of every partition. When a broker dies, the Controller is the one that notices and picks a new leader from the ISR (Section 5). In modern KRaft mode, a small set of brokers act as controllers and agree using the Raft voting method; one of them is the active Controller and the others stand by, already holding the full state.

What is the Group Coordinator?

The Group Coordinator is the manager of one single consumer group. Its job is much narrower: run the rebalance for that group (who reads which partition), and keep that group's bookmarks (offsets). Each consumer group gets its coordinator by a simple rule — Kafka takes the group name, hashes it, and that points to one partition of the internal __consumer_offsets topic; whichever broker leads that partition is the coordinator for that group. So different groups can have different coordinators sitting on different brokers, spreading the load.

The one-line memory hook: the Controller looks after brokers and partition leaders (the whole cluster). The Group Coordinator looks after one consumer group's rebalancing and bookmarks. Different jobs, different scope.
What is __consumer_offsets?

It is a hidden, internal Kafka topic that acts as a ledger of bookmarks. Every time a group commits an offset ("order-consumer-group has finished up to message 4,502 on partition 3"), that fact is written here as an event. It is a normal, replicated Kafka topic — so it survives broker crashes like any other. Two things lean on it: consumers read it on restart to know where to resume (so they don't reprocess everything from zero), and it is the store a new coordinator reloads from after a failover.

How does each recover when it dies?
If this dies…What is affectedHow it recovers
The ControllerCluster-level decisions pause briefly (no new leader elections for a moment)A standby controller is promoted in seconds (KRaft standbys already hold the state). Producers and consumers keep working; leaders that were already assigned stay put.
A Group CoordinatorOnly THAT group — its in-flight rebalance and offset commits pause. Other groups are untouched.A new coordinator is elected from the brokers that hold replicas of that group's __consumer_offsets partition. It reloads the group's state from the ledger, the rebalance restarts, and the consumers reconnect on their next request. A short hiccup, then it resumes.
Key point: a Controller failure is a cluster event; a Coordinator failure is a single-group event. Neither one loses your data, because the state each relies on (the metadata log for the Controller, __consumer_offsets for the Coordinator) is itself replicated across brokers.
Real system · Purushottam's checkout cluster

Purushottam runs three consumer groups on one topic: order-processor, inventory-sync, and analytics. Their coordinators happen to land on three different brokers, so rebalancing work is spread out. One night the broker holding the analytics coordinator restarts. Only the analytics group briefly pauses and re-forms; order-processor and inventory-sync never notice, and no bookmark is lost — the new analytics coordinator simply reads the last committed offsets back out of __consumer_offsets.

Section 8 · Serialization & Schema Registry

What the bytes look like — and who guards the format

What is serialization?

Kafka moves and stores bytes — raw computer data. It does not know or care what is inside. So the writer must turn its Java object into bytes (like packing a box for shipping), and the reader must turn the bytes back into an object (unpacking the box). This packing and unpacking is called serialization and deserialization. Both sides must agree on the packing method, or the box comes out as nonsense.

FormatWhat it isThe trade
JSONPlain readable text: {"orderId": "77213"}Easy to start and debug by eye. But big, and there is no rulebook — if the writer renames a field, readers break silently.
AvroCompact binary (not human-readable) plus a written schema — a document describing exactly what fields existSmall and fast, with built-in rules for changing the format safely. The classic Kafka choice.
ProtobufGoogle's compact binary formatSame benefits as Avro; the natural pick if your company already uses Google's gRPC tools.
Why is a Schema Registry needed?

The real danger is not the format — it is change. One day a developer renames the field total to totalAmount in the writer. Every reader in the company breaks at the same time, at runtime, probably in the evening. The Schema Registry prevents this. It is a small service that stores the official schema (the format rulebook) for each topic, with version history — and, most importantly, it refuses to accept a new version that would break existing readers. The breaking change fails while the developer is still at their desk, not after it reaches production.

How does it work, step by step?

1) The writer registers its schema with the registry and gets back a small ID number. 2) Each message carries that tiny ID instead of the whole schema. 3) The reader sees the ID, asks the registry for the schema once, remembers it, and unpacks every message correctly. 4) A compatibility rule (most commonly BACKWARD) defines what changes are allowed. Adding a new optional field: allowed. Deleting or renaming a field readers depend on: refused.

Real system · The rename that never broke anything

A QuickBite intern renames a field in the order event. With plain JSON, that is a broken-evening incident for three consuming teams. With Avro + Schema Registry in BACKWARD mode, the registry refuses the new schema the moment the build tries to register it. The incident becomes a red X in the build and a one-line code review comment.

Section 9 · Storage internals

Segments, retention, compaction — and why Kafka is so fast

How is a partition stored on disk?

A partition is a folder of files called segments (each around 1 GB). Only the newest segment is being written; older segments are closed and never touched again. This makes deleting old data wonderfully cheap: Kafka just deletes whole old files, like throwing away full notebooks. Small companion index files let a reader jump straight to any message number without scanning.

Retention — how long events live

Kafka does not keep messages forever (unless you tell it to). The rules are per topic:

RuleIn plain wordsUsed for
delete + retention.msThrow away anything older than X (default 7 days)Normal event streams — orders, clicks
delete + retention.bytesNever let this partition use more than X disk spaceVery high-volume streams — GPS pings
compactFor each key, always keep at least the NEWEST message; older messages with the same key may be cleaned away"Current state" topics — latest status per order, latest price per product
Log compaction, in one picture

Imagine a compacted topic keyed by order ID. Order #77213 wrote three events over time: PLACED, then PAID, then SHIPPED. After compaction, only SHIPPED remains for that key. Why is this useful? A brand-new reader can read the topic from the start and get the current state of every order — without replaying weeks of history. This trick powers Kafka Streams' tables (Section 10), and Kafka's own bookmark storage (__consumer_offsets) is itself a compacted topic.

Why is Kafka so fast? Three honest tricks

1 · Writing only at the end

Disks are slow when you jump around, and surprisingly fast when you write in a straight line. Kafka ONLY appends to the end of files and reads forward — the one pattern disks love.

2 · Letting the OS cache files

Your operating system automatically keeps recently used file data in spare memory (the "page cache"). Kafka leans on that: recent messages are usually served straight from memory, without Kafka building any cache of its own.

3 · Zero-copy sending

Normally, sending file data over the network means copying it several times between memory areas. Kafka uses a shortcut where data goes almost directly from disk to network. Less copying, more speed.

+ Batching and compression

Producers group many small messages into one compressed package before sending. Fewer, fuller trips — the same "batch beats one-at-a-time" law from the MongoDB and DynamoDB guides.

Real system · Netflix

Netflix's event pipeline (called Keystone) pushes on the order of trillions of events per day through Kafka — playback signals, app events, service logs. Handling that volume affordably is only possible because of these exact tricks: straight-line writes, the OS cache, zero-copy sends, and compressed batches.

Section 10 · Kafka Streams

Doing math on the stream — inside your own app

What is it?

Kafka Streams is a Java library — not a separate server — for building apps that continuously read topics, transform or count what flows through, and write results to new topics. You add it to your Spring Boot app like any other library. Your app IS the stream processor.

Why is it needed?

A plain consumer is fine for "react to each event." It becomes painful for questions like "how many orders did each restaurant get in the last 5 minutes?" To answer that by hand you would need: counters kept somewhere safe, a clock for the 5-minute windows, a way to split the counting across app copies, and recovery when a copy crashes. That is months of tricky code. Kafka Streams gives you all of it as a library.

The two core ideas

KStream — the flow

Every event as it happens, one after another: "order placed", "order placed", "order placed"... Think of it as watching the river flow past.

KTable — the latest values

Only the newest value for each key: "order #77213 is currently SHIPPED." Think of it as a whiteboard where each order has one line that keeps being rewritten. Behind the scenes, it is backed by a compacted topic (Section 9).

How does it work?

You describe the pipeline in code: take the orders stream → group by restaurant → cut into 5-minute windows → count. The library then runs this across all copies of your app, splitting the work by partition. Each copy keeps its counters in a small local store (RocksDB — a fast on-disk key-value store), and every counter change is ALSO written to a backup topic in Kafka. If a copy crashes, another copy rebuilds its counters from the backup topic and carries on. Turn on exactly_once_v2 and the transactions from Section 6 make sure no count is ever doubled.

How do we use it?

QuickBite's live operations dashboard — "orders per restaurant, last 5 minutes, always current" — is about 10 lines of Kafka Streams code instead of a hand-built counting service. The Spring tab builds exactly this.

Real system · Fraud detection everywhere

Payment companies run fraud rules as stream processing: "more than 3 orders from the same card in different cities within 10 minutes" is a windowed count over a keyed stream. It fires in seconds, while the events are still flowing — not hours later in a nightly report.

Section 11 · Architecture patterns on Kafka

The six patterns interviews (and production) care about

1 · Pub/Sub — the foundation

Short for publish/subscribe: one event written once, read by many independent listeners. This is Section 1's whole point, and every pattern below is built on top of it.

2 · Event Sourcing

What it is: most systems store only the current state: "order #77213 = SHIPPED." Event sourcing stores the full story instead: PLACED, then PAID, then SHIPPED — the list of events IS the truth, and the current state is just what you get by reading the story from the start. Why: you get a perfect history (who did what, when), you can debug by replaying the past, and you can build brand-new views of the data later from the same story. Kafka's role: Kafka basically IS an event store — an ordered, replayable, safely-kept list of events. The honest cost: asking "what is the state right now?" needs extra work (pre-built views). Most teams event-source a few critical flows like payments and orders — not everything.

3 · CQRS — separate the writing from the reading

The initials stand for Command Query Responsibility Segregation, which is a heavy name for a simple idea: use one store for writing and different stores for reading. Writes go to one carefully-guarded place. Events then flow through Kafka to feed separate read-stores, each shaped for one screen. QuickBite example: orders are written to the main database; consumers copy them into a search engine (for the search screen), a fast cache (for "my active order"), and a data warehouse (for reports). A lovely bonus: any read-store can be thrown away and rebuilt by replaying the topic.

4 · Saga — a big action across many services, without one big transaction

The problem: "place an order" involves the Order service, Payment service, and Inventory service — each with its own database. There is no way to wrap all three in one database transaction. The pattern: break the big action into a chain of small local steps connected by events: OrderPlaced → Payment service takes the money → PaymentCompleted → Inventory service reserves the food → and so on. If a step fails, earlier steps are undone by compensating events — "undo notes": PaymentFailed → the Order service cancels the order and announces OrderCancelled. Kafka carries the chain; each service only ever has to keep its own house in order.

5 · Transactional Outbox

The problem (called the dual-write bug): a service needs to save an order to its database AND announce it on Kafka. Two different systems — no shared transaction covers both. If the app crashes between the two actions, the database has an order that Kafka never heard about. The pattern: in ONE database transaction, save the order AND insert the announcement into a table called outbox — same database, so both happen or neither does. A separate little publisher then reads the outbox table and sends the announcements to Kafka, marking each as sent. The database is the single source of truth, and the announcement can always be retried safely. (This is the same Transactional Outbox from the microservices notes — Kafka is the delivery half.)

6 · Dead Letter Topics and retry ladders

The problem: one broken message — bad data, a bug — fails every time you try to process it. And because a partition is a strict line, retrying it in place blocks everything behind it. One bad message can freeze thousands of good ones. The strategy is a ladder:

RungWhat happens
1 · Retry in placeTry a few times with short pauses — this heals temporary problems (a database hiccup)
2 · Retry topicsStill failing? Move the message to a side topic like orders-retry-1m, then orders-retry-10m — it gets retried later WITHOUT blocking the main line
3 · Dead Letter Topic (DLT)Given up? Park it in a special topic like orders.DLT — a parking lot for broken messages — with a note about the error. Alert a human. Replay after the bug is fixed.
Real system · The poison order

A malformed order event (a missing field from a buggy app release) hits QuickBite's notification reader and fails every attempt. Without the ladder: the partition is blocked, and ALL notifications behind it freeze — a full outage caused by one message. With the ladder: three quick retries, then the side topics, then the parking lot, one alert, and every other notification keeps flowing. The Spring tab builds this exact ladder.

Section 12 · Running Kafka for real

Tuning, monitoring, security, deployment

Performance tuning — the settings that matter

SettingSideWhat it does, in plain words
batch.size + linger.msProducer"Wait a few milliseconds to fill the box before shipping it." A tiny delay per message, a huge gain in total speed.
compression.typeProducerSqueeze the box before shipping (lz4 or zstd). Smaller boxes = less network and disk. Almost always worth it.
fetch.min.bytes / max.poll.recordsConsumerRead fuller boxes; and don't bite off more per mouthful than you can chew before Kafka thinks you died.
num.partitionsTopicYour maximum parallelism — hard to change later. Plan for growth, but don't create 1,000 "just in case" (they have real costs).
replication.factor=3, min.insync.replicas=2TopicKeep 3 copies; a safe write needs at least 2 of them. With acks=all, this survives one dead broker with zero loss. The standard safety pair.

Monitoring — the one number above all

Consumer lag = how far behind a reading group is: the newest message number minus the group's bookmark. If lag keeps growing, your readers can't keep up — or they are stuck. Lag is the earliest warning sign of almost every Kafka problem, which is why teams alert on it first. Track it per group and partition (common tools: Prometheus with a Kafka exporter, graphs in Grafana). Also worth watching: under-replicated partitions (a broker is in trouble), request latency, disk usage, and how often rebalances happen.

Security — three separate questions

LayerThe question it answersThe mechanism
Encryption (SSL/TLS)Can someone spying on the network read our messages?Encrypt the connection between apps and brokers — like sealing the envelope
Authentication (SASL)WHO is connecting?Every app proves its identity — username/password (SCRAM), tokens, or certificates — like showing ID at the door
Authorization (ACLs)What is this identity ALLOWED to do?Permission rules per topic: "order-service may WRITE to orders-*; analytics may only READ" — like a permissions list on the wall

Production rules: never allow unencrypted connections, give every service its own identity (never shared), and grant the minimum permissions each needs.

Deployment, scaling & golden rules

Deploy

At least 3 brokers, spread across different data-center zones; KRaft mode; own disks. Or skip running it yourself with a managed service (Confluent Cloud, AWS MSK) — the same buy-vs-run choice as MongoDB Atlas vs self-hosted.

Scale

Need more capacity? Add brokers and move some partitions onto them. Remember: reader parallelism is capped by partition count — more readers than partitions means some readers stand idle.

Golden rules

Key by the order you need. acks=all + idempotence for anything that matters. Readers safe-to-run-twice, always. A DLT on every consumer. Schema Registry from day one. Alert on lag.

Common mistakes

Using Kafka as a forever-database (endless retention "just in case"). One giant topic for everything. Ignoring rebalance storms. One shared password for every service.

Section 12.5 · Concept ↔ real problem

Why each concept exists — a real production problem for every one

Every Kafka idea was born from a real pain in a real system at scale. This is the fastest way to remember them: don't memorise the concept — remember the problem it was invented to solve. Tap any system below to see the exact production problem, why it hurts, and the Kafka concept that fixes it. Each one links to the full section.

How to read these: the scenarios are framed as "a system like Instagram / Amazon / YouTube." The shape of each problem is exactly what these products face at scale; the point is the problem→concept mapping, not any one company's internal tech choices.
Section 13 · Quick recall

Who runs what on Kafka — memory hooks

CompanyWhat flows through KafkaThe concept it proves
LinkedIn~7 trillion messages/day — Kafka's birthplaceOne shared log replaces a hundred custom pipes
UberTrip events, driver GPS, pricing — trillions/dayPartitions = parallel speed; keys keep each trip's story in order
NetflixPlayback signals and logs (the Keystone pipeline)Why the storage tricks (Section 9) matter at scale
Banks / payment firmsPayment event chainsKeys for order; transactions; exactly-once; sagas
QuickBite (our example)orders-placed, read by 5+ teamsPub/sub, groups, the DLT ladder, outbox, a Streams dashboard

One-line answers to say in an interview

What is Kafka?

"A shared, copied, append-only log. Writers add to the end; groups of readers share the work with their own bookmarks; order holds inside a partition, chosen by the message key."

Why is it fast?

"It writes in a straight line, leans on the OS's file cache, sends data disk-to-network with almost no copying, and ships compressed batches."

Why is it safe?

"Three copies per partition, new leaders picked only from fully caught-up copies, acks=all with min 2 in-sync copies, duplicate-proof producers, and transactions when exactly-once matters."

Where are its sharp edges?

"No order across partitions, hot keys overload one partition, careless setups rebalance constantly, and exactly-once stops at Kafka's border — outside calls still need their own protection."

Section 14 · Hands-on · Spring Boot 4 · Java 25 · Two stories · Sixteen chapters

Spring Boot 4 + Java 25 Implementation

We're the backend team of Tinder — the dating app. Users swipe left or right on profiles; when two people swipe right on each other, they match and can start chatting. Millions of swipes an hour, matches must never be lost, chats must stay in order. Chapters 14.1–14.10 are real production incidents from Tinder's Kafka platform — the story, why it happened, the fix, the code, and a diagram to lock the mental model.

Then, from 14.11, a second running example — Purushottam's e-commerce checkout (place order → pay → reserve stock → notify).
