These chapters cover the production-grade consumer patterns that decide whether a checkout is correct under crashes and retries: idempotent consumers, non-blocking processing, safe calls to a payment gateway, and the whole flow end to end.

How to read each chapter: the incident (what went wrong on a real day), why it happened (in plain words), the fix, step by step, a diagram to see the shape, then the code and a walkthrough. Where settings matter, a table shows what each one really controls.

14.1 Setup 14.2 First Producer & Consumer 14.3 Consumer Groups 14.4 Ordering & Keys 14.5 Delivery Guarantees 14.6 Retries & DLT 14.7 Transactions & Outbox 14.8 Avro & Schema Registry 14.9 Kafka Streams 14.10 Spring Cloud Stream 14.11 Idempotent Consumer 14.12 Non-blocking Processing 14.13 Idempotent Payments 14.14 Checkout End-to-End ★ 14.15 Decision Guide 14.16 Capstone
14.1

Project setup & connection

Getting Kafka running in Spring Boot is mostly configuration, not code. You add one dependency, put the connection and a few settings in application.yml, and Spring auto-builds the producer and consumer for you — no factory code in Java. The one golden rule: keep configuration outside code, so the broker address comes from the environment and the same build runs on a laptop and in production.

💡 The fix
  1. Add two dependencies — spring-kafka gives us producers, consumers, listener containers, and admin. spring-boot-starter gives us configuration binding from YAML.
  2. Put every setting in application.yml, with the broker address coming from an environment variable — never hardcoded.
  3. Let Spring auto-configure the producer and consumer factories from that YAML. Zero factory code in Java.
// pom.xml — Spring Boot 4 on Java 25
<properties>
    <java.version>25</java.version>
    <spring-boot.version>4.0.0</spring-boot.version>
</properties>

<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.kafka</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-kafka</artifactId>
</dependency>
# application.yml — one truth for Tinder's Kafka config
spring:
  application:
    name: tinder-swipes-service
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: ${KAFKA_BROKERS:localhost:9092}   # env-var wins; laptop default
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      acks: all                                           # see chapter 14.5
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true                          # retries won't create duplicates
    consumer:
      group-id: swipes-processor
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      enable-auto-commit: false                           # we commit manually — chapter 14.5
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.json.trusted.packages: "com.tinder.events"
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. ${KAFKA_BROKERS:localhost:9092} — Spring reads the env var if set, else falls back to laptop. Same YAML file works everywhere; only the environment differs.
  2. Zero factory code in Java — auto-configuration reads the YAML and builds ProducerFactory, ConsumerFactory, KafkaTemplate beans automatically. Your service just @Autowireds them.
  3. One central source of truth — if we ever need to change acks or bootstrap servers across all four services, we change the shared config, not four Java files.
14.2

First producer & consumer — the swipe event

📖 Week 1 · Aisha's first right-swipe
🔴 The incident

Aisha opens Tinder at 8:47 PM and swipes right on Rahul's profile. The first version of our backend does everything in one HTTP request: save swipe to database, check if Rahul also swiped right on Aisha, if yes create a match, then send a push notification, then update the analytics counter. Total time: 9 seconds. Aisha's screen is frozen. She closes the app. We lose a customer because we tried to do everything at once.

Why this happens: the HTTP request is doing five services' worth of work in a straight line. The notification service, the match service, the analytics service — none of them need to happen while Aisha's phone is waiting for a response. They just need to happen eventually. This is exactly what Kafka is for: publish one small event, return to Aisha in 40 milliseconds, let downstream services react on their own time.
💡 The fix
  1. The API only writes the swipe to the DB and publishes ONE event to swipes-registered. It returns to Aisha in ~40ms.
  2. Downstream services subscribe to that topic and each do their own job — match check, notifications, analytics — in parallel, none blocking Aisha's phone.
  3. KafkaTemplate is the producer helper. @KafkaListener is the consumer helper. Almost no boilerplate.
// Java 25 record — the event we publish
package com.tinder.events;
public record SwipeEvent(String swiperId, String swipedOnId, String direction,   // "RIGHT" or "LEFT"
                          Instant swipedAt) {}
// SwipeService.java — save + publish, then return to Aisha
@Service
public class SwipeService {

    private final SwipeRepository repo;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, SwipeEvent> kafka;

    public SwipeService(SwipeRepository repo, KafkaTemplate<String, SwipeEvent> kafka) {
        this.repo = repo;
        this.kafka = kafka;
    }

    public void recordSwipe(String swiperId, String swipedOnId, String direction) {
        repo.save(new Swipe(swiperId, swipedOnId, direction, Instant.now()));           // DB write
        var event = new SwipeEvent(swiperId, swipedOnId, direction, Instant.now());
        kafka.send("swipes-registered", swiperId, event);                          // key = swiperId (chapter 14.4)
    }
}
// MatchDetector.java — one of many downstream consumers
@Component
public class MatchDetector {

    private final SwipeRepository swipeRepo;
    private final MatchService matchService;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "swipes-registered", groupId = "match-detector")
    public void onSwipe(SwipeEvent event) {
        if (!"RIGHT".equals(event.direction())) return;                            // only right-swipes can match

        // Did the OTHER person already right-swipe on us?
        boolean reciprocated = swipeRepo.existsRightSwipe(event.swipedOnId(), event.swiperId());
        if (reciprocated) matchService.createMatch(event.swiperId(), event.swipedOnId());
    }
}
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. The API returns to Aisha in 40ms — she sees "you swiped right" instantly. The 9-second wait is gone.
  2. @KafkaListener is the whole consumer — one annotation, one method, Spring runs a pool of threads that read partitions and hand each event to your method.
  3. The event was keyed by swiperId — all of Aisha's swipes go to the same partition, in order. We'll need this in chapter 14.4.
  4. Three separate consumer groups (match-detector, notifications, analytics) each read every event independently — the broadcast pattern from Diagram 3.
14.3

Consumer groups — scaling the readers

📖 Month 2 · The Friday-night lag spike
🔴 The incident

Tinder's traffic follows a beautiful curve: quiet on Monday mornings, insane on Friday nights. Last Friday at 9 PM the notification consumer's lag hit 42,000 messages. Aisha matched with Rahul at 9:03 PM — she got the "It's a match!" push at 9:14 PM. Eleven minutes late. Rahul had already gone to bed. The dashboard showed one lone consumer trying to process a partition-8 firehose alone.

Why this happens: our topic has 8 partitions but we deployed only ONE notification consumer. So one worker was reading all 8 partitions serially — no parallelism, no scaling. Kafka's whole promise is "add more workers to the same consumer group, they share the partitions." We just had to actually do it.
💡 The fix
  1. Deploy 4 copies of the notification service, all with the same groupId. Kafka gives each copy 2 of the 8 partitions.
  2. Inside each copy, set concurrency=2 — one JVM handles both its partitions in parallel.
  3. Add CooperativeStickyAssignor — during deploys, only partitions that must move actually move (Section 7).
// application.yml — notification service
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      group-id: notifications                       # all 4 copies share this — Kafka splits partitions among them
      properties:
        partition.assignment.strategy: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
        group.instance.id: ${HOSTNAME}              # static membership — deploys don't trigger rebalance (Section 7)
    listener:
      concurrency: 2                                # each JVM handles its 2 partitions in parallel
// NotificationConsumer.java — the code is unchanged; scaling is a CONFIG win
@Component
public class NotificationConsumer {

    private final PushGateway push;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "swipes-registered", groupId = "notifications")
    public void handle(SwipeEvent event) {
        if ("RIGHT".equals(event.direction())) {
            push.sendYouWereLiked(event.swipedOnId());   // "Someone liked you!"
        }
    }
}
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. 4 copies × concurrency 2 = 8 parallel readers, matching our 8 partitions. Each reader owns exactly one partition — the maximum parallelism for this topic.
  2. Same groupId across all copies is what makes them share the work. Change groupId, and each copy would read EVERY event — not what you want here.
  3. Static membership + cooperative sticky means a Friday-evening deploy doesn't cause a lag spike from constant reshuffling.
  4. Measured result: Friday lag dropped from 42,000 to ~120. Rahul now gets the match ping in ~500ms.
14.4

Ordering & keys — the ghost-match bug

📖 Month 3 · The match that should not have existed
🔴 The incident

Aisha swiped right on Rahul, then a second later she second-guessed herself and swiped LEFT on him (Tinder has an "undo" feature that publishes a fresh LEFT swipe). Both events were published: right first, then left. But the events landed in different partitions, read by different workers. The LEFT was processed BEFORE the RIGHT. When RIGHT arrived later, the match detector saw "she just liked him — and he already liked her — MATCH!" A push went out. Rahul got excited. Aisha was confused because she had explicitly un-liked him. Support ticket: "your app matched me with someone I rejected."

Why this happens: Kafka only promises order INSIDE a single partition (Section 4). Without a key, events are spread randomly across partitions. Aisha's two swipes ended up on partitions 3 and 6, being read by two different workers running side by side. The one on partition 3 finished first — even though it happened SECOND — and produced a wrong result. The fix is Section 4's one rule: give related events a shared key.
💡 The fix
  1. Key every swipe by swiperId — all of Aisha's swipes now land on the same partition, one after another, in the exact order she performed them.
  2. One worker reads that partition — sees RIGHT, then LEFT, in order. No ghost matches possible.
  3. Set max.in.flight.requests.per.connection=5 combined with idempotence — the producer guarantees no in-partition reordering even under retries.
// SwipeService.java — one line change fixes the ghost-match bug
public void recordSwipe(String swiperId, String swipedOnId, String direction) {
    repo.save(new Swipe(swiperId, swipedOnId, direction, Instant.now()));
    var event = new SwipeEvent(swiperId, swipedOnId, direction, Instant.now());

    // KEY = swiperId. All of Aisha's actions now land on the same partition, in order.
    kafka.send("swipes-registered", swiperId, event);
}
# application.yml — belt-and-braces settings for perfect ordering
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true                        # retries won't reorder
        max.in.flight.requests.per.connection: 5        # safe together with idempotence
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. swiperId as the key is the whole fix. Kafka hashes "aisha" to a partition number, and every one of her events goes there. Rahul's events go to whatever partition hash("rahul") points at — a different one, so his flow doesn't slow hers down.
  2. Traffic still spreads well because there are millions of user IDs. No single user creates enough traffic to make one partition hot.
  3. Ordering is now user-level, not global — that's exactly what we needed. Aisha's actions in order; Rahul's actions in order; but Aisha's and Rahul's may interleave (which is fine).
14.5

Delivery guarantees — 31 matches disappeared

📖 Month 4 · Sunday morning post-mortem
🔴 The incident

Saturday evening a broker restarted for a routine patch. Sunday's report showed 31 matches missing — 31 pairs of users had matched on Saturday evening, but the notification never fired and the match never appeared in either user's inbox. Support flooded with "did I actually match with someone?" tickets. Our producer had acks=1, so the producer treated a message as saved the moment the leader confirmed — even if no follower had copied it yet. When the leader restarted, those in-flight matches were gone forever.

Why this happens: acks=1 only waits for the leader broker to write the message. If the leader dies before followers copy it, the message vanishes. For a swipe-ping this is fine (Rahul won't miss one ping). For a MATCH — a mutual right-swipe, the app's core promise — it is catastrophic. And on the consumer side, we were auto-committing offsets before actually processing, so a crash mid-processing meant "the bookmark moved past a match we hadn't handled yet."
💡 The fix
  1. Producer: acks=all + enable.idempotence=true — no match is confirmed until the whole ISR has a copy, and retries can't create duplicates.
  2. Consumer: enable-auto-commit=false + MANUAL_IMMEDIATE — we only commit the offset AFTER our processing succeeded. If we crash mid-processing, we re-read the message.
  3. Idempotent processing on our side too — record processed match IDs in the DB with a unique constraint, so re-reads don't create duplicates.
# application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        max.in.flight.requests.per.connection: 5
    consumer:
      enable-auto-commit: false                       # we control WHEN the bookmark moves
    listener:
      ack-mode: MANUAL_IMMEDIATE                       # give us an Acknowledgment we call ourselves
// MatchConsumer.java — manual ack + dedupe
@Component
public class MatchConsumer {

    private final MatchService matchService;
    private final ProcessedMatchStore processed;   // backed by a unique-key DB table

    @KafkaListener(topics = "matches-created", groupId = "match-inbox")
    public void handle(ConsumerRecord<String, MatchCreated> record, Acknowledgment ack) {
        var event = record.value();
        String matchId = event.matchId();

        if (processed.wasProcessed(matchId)) {         // re-read after crash? just skip.
            ack.acknowledge();
            return;
        }

        matchService.deliverToInboxes(event);          // business work
        processed.markProcessed(matchId);              // records the ID in DB with UNIQUE constraint

        ack.acknowledge();                              // only NOW move the bookmark forward
    }
}
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. acks=all is the difference between "the leader has it" (fragile) and "the whole ISR has it" (durable). One extra millisecond per publish; zero matches ever lost.
  2. MANUAL_IMMEDIATE + ack.acknowledge() at the end means a crash mid-processing simply causes a re-read after restart — matching Section 6's "at-least-once with idempotent processing."
  3. The dedupe table is what turns at-least-once into effectively exactly-once — a repeated event is silently ignored because its match ID is already recorded.
14.6

Retries & Dead Letter Topic — the poison message

📖 Month 5 · One bad event stopped everything
🔴 The incident

3:14 AM alarm: swipe processing lag climbing at 500/sec. Investigation shows a single malformed swipe event — a corrupt JSON blob from a beta client — is throwing an exception in the consumer. The consumer catches the exception, retries the same message, fails again, retries... in a tight loop. Meanwhile, ALL messages behind it in the partition are waiting. One bad message froze the whole line. This is called a poison message.

Why this happens: the default behavior of a Kafka consumer is to stop and retry a failed message forever, because moving on would look like data loss. But some messages will never succeed (bad format, referenced user was deleted, business rule violated). Endless retries pile up behind them and paralyze the partition. The clean fix is a "retry ladder" — try a few times with delays, then give up and route the message to a Dead Letter Topic where humans can look at it, while the main flow moves on.
💡 The fix
  1. @RetryableTopic — Spring for Kafka creates helper topics automatically: swipes-registered-retry-0, -retry-1, -retry-2, and finally -dlt.
  2. Attempts + backoff: try 4 times total, waiting 1s, 3s, 9s (exponential).
  3. Skip retries for "business" errors (validation failures) — those should go straight to DLT, no wait.
  4. A @DltHandler receives poisoned messages so we can log them, alert, or move them to a debug tool.
// SwipeConsumer.java — with retry topics + DLT handler
@Component
public class SwipeConsumer {

    @RetryableTopic(
        attempts = "4",                                    // original + 3 retries
        backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 3),      // 1s, 3s, 9s
        exclude = { ValidationException.class }                // business errors go straight to DLT
    )
    @KafkaListener(topics = "swipes-registered", groupId = "swipes-processor")
    public void handle(SwipeEvent event) {
        swipeProcessor.process(event);                         // throws on failure — retry ladder kicks in
    }

    @DltHandler
    public void onDeadLetter(SwipeEvent event,
                              @Header(KafkaHeaders.EXCEPTION_MESSAGE) String reason) {
        log.error("Dropped swipe: {} reason: {}", event, reason);
        alerts.notifyOncall(event, reason);
        deadLetterStore.save(event, reason);                   // for later inspection / replay
    }
}
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. @RetryableTopic auto-creates three retry topics + one DLT — you don't manage them. A failure moves the message to retry-0, waits 1s, retries. Fails again → retry-1, waits 3s. And so on.
  2. Exponential backoff (× 3) gives transient issues (network hiccup, brief DB slowdown) time to heal without hammering the system.
  3. The main partition is never blocked — a poison message steps out of the main line into retry topics; the next messages behind it flow freely.
  4. @DltHandler is the safety net — messages that fail 4 times aren't silently dropped. They land here, get logged, alert on-call, and are stored for investigation.
14.7

Transactions & Outbox — “I paid but never got the notification”

📖 Month 6 · The Tinder Gold upgrade
🔴 The incident

Aisha buys Tinder Gold (₹499/month) to see who liked her. The code does two things: write "isGold=true" to the users table, then publish a subscription-activated event to Kafka so the notification service can send her a welcome message. Yesterday, seven users complained: money was charged, database showed Gold, but no welcome and no Gold features unlocked. The reason: the DB write succeeded, and BETWEEN the DB commit and the Kafka publish, the pod restarted. The event was never sent. DB and Kafka are two different systems; there's no single transaction across them.

Why this happens: a normal database transaction cannot include "publish to Kafka" as one of its steps — they are separate systems with separate commit protocols. Two options exist: (1) Kafka transactions covering read+process+write across topics (useful within Kafka), or (2) the Transactional Outbox pattern — save the event to an OUTBOX table in the SAME database transaction as the business write. A separate small process reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka. Now either both save, or neither.
💡 The fix — Transactional Outbox
  1. Add an outbox_events table to the same DB as the users table.
  2. In one JPA transaction: update the user AND insert a row into outbox_events. Either both commit or both roll back.
  3. A tiny relay component, on a schedule (or listening to DB change events), reads unpublished outbox rows, sends them to Kafka, marks them published.
  4. Result: the event either goes out (eventually) or the DB write never happened. Never one without the other.
// SubscriptionService.java — the write side, one transaction
@Service
public class SubscriptionService {

    private final UserRepository userRepo;
    private final OutboxRepository outboxRepo;

    @Transactional        // user update + outbox insert = one atomic step
    public void activateGold(String userId) {
        userRepo.markGold(userId);

        var event = new OutboxEvent(
            UUID.randomUUID(),
            "subscription-activated",                    // topic name
            userId,                                            // key
            new SubscriptionActivated(userId, Instant.now())   // payload
        );
        outboxRepo.save(event);
    }
}
// OutboxRelay.java — reads unpublished rows and sends to Kafka
@Component
public class OutboxRelay {

    private final OutboxRepository outboxRepo;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, Object> kafka;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)      // every half-second
    public void publishPending() {
        List<OutboxEvent> batch = outboxRepo.findUnpublished(100);
        for (var event : batch) {
            kafka.send(event.topic(), event.key(), event.payload())
                 .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
                     if (ex == null) outboxRepo.markPublished(event.id());
                     // on failure: leave it — the next tick will retry
                 });
        }
    }
}
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. @Transactional wraps BOTH writes. If saving the outbox row fails, the user update rolls back. If the whole method throws, nothing was committed. This is the atomic promise we needed.
  2. The relay's job is boring on purpose — read, send, mark done. It survives its own crashes because unpublished rows just wait for the next tick.
  3. Duplicates are possible if Kafka accepted the message but the relay crashed before marking it published. Downstream idempotent processing (14.5) handles that.
  4. The seven complaints stopped that same week. Zero missed Gold activations since.
14.8

Avro & Schema Registry — the field rename that took down everything

📖 Month 8 · The 6 PM outage
🔴 The incident

A well-meaning developer renamed a field in the SwipeEvent record: swipedOnId → targetUserId. The change went out at 6 PM (obviously). Every downstream consumer immediately started throwing UnrecognizedPropertyException and dying. Notifications stopped. Match detection stopped. Analytics stopped. All 6 PM Friday-evening peak swipes were piling up unprocessed. The rollback took 20 minutes. In hindsight the bug was obvious: the producer changed but the consumers still expected the old field.

Why this happens: when events are just JSON, nothing checks that a producer's shape matches what consumers expect. Renaming a field, removing a required field, or changing a type is a breaking change — and there is no automatic guard. The industry-standard fix is a Schema Registry: producers must register the schema of every event; consumers fetch schemas by ID. Before accepting a new schema version, the registry checks it is COMPATIBLE with the previous one. Backward-incompatible changes are refused at deploy time — not at 6 PM in production.
💡 The fix
  1. Move from JSON to Avro — a compact binary format that requires a schema.
  2. Publish schemas to a Schema Registry (Confluent Schema Registry or Redpanda's version).
  3. Set compatibility to BACKWARD — new schemas may add optional fields with defaults, but never break existing consumers.
  4. Result: attempting to rename a field at build time fails the build, not at 6 PM in prod.
// user-registered.avsc — the schema, checked into git next to the code
{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "SwipeEvent",
  "namespace": "com.tinder.events",
  "fields": [
    { "name": "swiperId",    "type": "string" },
    { "name": "swipedOnId",  "type": "string" },
    { "name": "direction",   "type": "string" },
    { "name": "swipedAt",    "type": "long", "logicalType": "timestamp-millis" }
  ]
}
# application.yml — point producers & consumers at the registry
spring:
  kafka:
    producer:
      value-serializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroSerializer
      properties:
        schema.registry.url: ${SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL}
        auto.register.schemas: false                     # CI registers; runtime just reads
    consumer:
      value-deserializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroDeserializer
      properties:
        schema.registry.url: ${SCHEMA_REGISTRY_URL}
        specific.avro.reader: true
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. The registry is a small HTTP service keeping a versioned list of schemas per topic. Producers write the schema's numeric ID at the start of each message; consumers fetch the schema for that ID and decode.
  2. Compatibility check is the whole trick — BACKWARD means "the new schema can be read by consumers using the old schema." Adding an optional field with a default is fine. Renaming a field is not — the check fails at build time.
  3. Avro is also ~5× smaller than equivalent JSON — network and storage bonus on top of the safety.
  4. Since we adopted this, we've had zero schema-related production incidents. Bad changes are caught in CI, not at 6 PM.
14.9

Kafka Streams — real-time match detection

📖 Month 10 · From "matches every hour" to "matches now"
🔴 The incident

Tinder's original match detector ran as a batch job every hour: read all new swipes, find mutual right-swipes, create matches, send notifications. Users complained: "I swiped right on someone at 8 PM — got the match ping at 9 PM." The magic of a dating app is the instant "It's a match!" moment. A one-hour delay kills that magic. We needed something that reacts as each swipe arrives, and can efficiently ask "did the OTHER person swipe right on me recently?" — without a batch job and without hitting the DB for every event.

Why this happens: a batch job trades freshness for simplicity — and for a live feature, the trade is wrong. What we need is a stream processor: something that reads swipes continuously, keeps a small in-memory state ("recent right-swipes per user"), and, for every incoming right-swipe, checks if the target already right-swiped the source. Kafka Streams is exactly this: a Java library (not a separate server) that runs inside your Spring Boot app, does the stateful work, and stores its state locally with automatic Kafka-backed recovery.
💡 The fix
  1. Add spring-kafka-streams and enable it with @EnableKafkaStreams.
  2. Build a topology that reads swipes-registered, keeps a KTable of "right-swiped whom" per user, and, for each new right-swipe, checks that KTable for reciprocity.
  3. Publish matches to matches-created the instant reciprocity is detected.
  4. Set processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 — Kafka Streams' transaction wrapper prevents duplicate matches even on retries.
// StreamsConfig.java
@Configuration
@EnableKafkaStreams
public class StreamsConfig {

    @Bean
    public KafkaStreamsConfiguration streamsConfig() {
        Map<String, Object> props = new HashMap<>();
        props.put(APPLICATION_ID_CONFIG, "tinder-match-detector");
        props.put(BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS_CONFIG, "${KAFKA_BROKERS}");
        props.put(PROCESSING_GUARANTEE_CONFIG, "exactly_once_v2");   // no duplicate matches
        return new KafkaStreamsConfiguration(props);
    }
}
// MatchDetectorTopology.java — the streaming pipeline itself
@Component
public class MatchDetectorTopology {

    @Autowired
    public void buildTopology(StreamsBuilder builder) {

        // Only right-swipes matter
        KStream<String, SwipeEvent> rightSwipes = builder
            .stream("swipes-registered", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), swipeSerde))
            .filter((key, swipe) -> "RIGHT".equals(swipe.direction()));

        // Re-key by swipedOnId so all "who did rahul right-swipe" land together
        KTable<String, Set<String>> rightSwipedByUser = rightSwipes
            .groupBy((k, swipe) -> swipe.swiperId(), Grouped.with(Serdes.String(), swipeSerde))
            .aggregate(HashSet::new,
                       (userId, swipe, set) -> { set.add(swipe.swipedOnId()); return set; },
                       Materialized.as("right-swipes-per-user"));

        // For each right-swipe: check if the target already right-swiped ME
        rightSwipes
            .selectKey((k, swipe) -> swipe.swipedOnId())   // look up by the OTHER person
            .join(rightSwipedByUser,
                  (swipe, othersRightSwipes) ->
                      othersRightSwipes.contains(swipe.swiperId())
                          ? new MatchCreated(swipe.swiperId(), swipe.swipedOnId(), Instant.now())
                          : null)
            .filter((k, match) -> match != null)
            .to("matches-created", Produced.with(Serdes.String(), matchSerde));
    }
}
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. The KTable is our "who has right-swiped whom" state, kept locally by Streams and backed up to Kafka automatically for recovery.
  2. Every new right-swipe from Aisha triggers: re-key to Rahul's ID, look up Rahul's right-swipes, does it contain Aisha? Emit a match. All within milliseconds.
  3. exactly_once_v2 uses Kafka transactions under the hood — the input offset, the KTable update, and the output message all commit together, or none do.
  4. Match delay dropped from "up to 1 hour" to ~200ms end-to-end. Aisha now sees "It's a match!" while Rahul is still on her profile.
14.10

Spring Cloud Stream — the functional style

📖 Month 11 · A cleaner API for the analytics team
🔴 The incident

The analytics team needs to build 12 small consumers — "count active users per city," "swipes per hour," "median match age," and so on. Each is basically the same shape: read topic X, transform, publish topic Y. Writing them with @KafkaListener plus KafkaTemplate works fine, but the analytics team keeps duplicating boilerplate: consumer config, producer config, error handling. They ask: is there a lighter API where a consumer is just a Function<A, B>?

Why this happens: when you have MANY small stateless read → transform → write pipelines, the imperative @KafkaListener + template.send pattern is repetitive. Spring Cloud Stream is a higher-level layer: you write a Function<In, Out>, and Spring binds it to Kafka topics via configuration alone. Same runtime (Spring for Kafka underneath), less code, cleaner APIs — perfect for a portfolio of small pipelines.
💡 The fix
  1. Add spring-cloud-stream-binder-kafka.
  2. Write a Function<A, B> bean — that IS the consumer + producer.
  3. Bind it to topics in YAML — input from matches-created, output to loyalty-points-earned. Zero glue code.
// LoyaltyPointsFunction.java — the ENTIRE pipeline
@Configuration
public class LoyaltyPointsFunction {

    @Bean
    public Function<MatchCreated, LoyaltyPoints> loyaltyPoints() {
        return match -> new LoyaltyPoints(
            match.userA(),
            10,                              // 10 points per match
            "match-created",
            Instant.now()
        );
    }
}
# application.yml — bindings connect the bean to real topics
spring:
  cloud:
    stream:
      bindings:
        loyaltyPoints-in-0:
          destination: matches-created           # reads from here
          group: loyalty-points-consumer
        loyaltyPoints-out-0:
          destination: loyalty-points-earned     # writes to here
@KafkaListener + KafkaTemplateSpring Cloud Stream (Function)
BoilerplateConsumer, template, error handlerJust a Function bean
Best forComplex flows, custom acks, transactionsMany small stateless read → transform → write
RuntimeSpring for KafkaSpring for Kafka (same underneath!)
Chapters 14.11–14.14 · A second running example

Purushottam's e-commerce checkout

The Tinder chapters showed the moving parts. These four show the patterns that decide whether a checkout stays correct when things crash and retry. Meet Purushottam, placing a ₹2,499 order. Behind that one tap: place the order, take the payment, reserve the stock, send the confirmation — four services, four topics, and every "safe to run twice" trick in the book. Same house style: the incident, why it happened, the fix, the code, a diagram.

14.11

Idempotent consumer — the stock that dropped twice

📖 Purushottam's shop · The phantom decrement
🔴 The incident

The inventory service read order #A-3391 from orders-placed, ran UPDATE product SET stock = stock - 1, and the database committed. Then — a routine deploy — the pod was killed before it could commit its Kafka offset. On restart, Kafka redelivered the exact same order event. Stock dropped a second time. A product that really had 3 units now showed 1. One order, two decrements, one very confused warehouse.

Why this happens: we commit the offset after processing — that is at-least-once (Section 6), the sensible default that never loses a message. The price is that a crash between "work done" and "offset committed" causes a redelivery. Kafka cannot fix this for you: it does not know that your UPDATE already ran. The consumer's own code must be idempotent — handling the same event twice must have the same effect as handling it once.
💡 The fix — a dedup ledger + one transaction
  1. Add a processed_events table with a UNIQUE key on the event's id. This is the "have I seen this before?" ledger.
  2. In ONE @Transactional method: record the event id AND do the business write (decrement stock) together. Either both commit or neither does.
  3. If the event id is already there → skip. The first run already did the work; the second run does nothing.
  4. Commit the offset only after the method returns cleanly.
// ProcessedEvent.java — one row per handled event (the dedup ledger)
@Entity @Table(name = "processed_events")
public class ProcessedEvent {
    @Id private String eventId;      // the order event's unique id = the dedup key
    private Instant processedAt;
    // constructors / getters …
}
// InventoryService.java — dedup check + business write in ONE transaction
@Service
public class InventoryService {

    private final ProcessedEventRepository seen;
    private final ProductRepository products;

    @Transactional        // ledger insert + stock decrement = all-or-nothing
    public void reserveOnce(OrderPlaced event) {

        // 1) have we already handled this exact event?
        if (seen.existsById(event.eventId())) {
            log.info("Duplicate order event {}, skipping", event.eventId());
            return;                              // first run already did the work
        }
        seen.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId(), Instant.now()));

        // 2) the real work — same transaction, so it can't half-happen
        products.decrementStock(event.productId(), event.quantity());
    }
}
// InventoryConsumer.java — the listener just delegates
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders-placed", groupId = "inventory-sync")
public void handle(OrderPlaced event) {
    inventoryService.reserveOnce(event);   // safe to call twice
}
The UNIQUE index does the real work. The existsById check is a fast path, but under a true race — two pods handling the same event at the same instant — both might pass the check. The database's UNIQUE constraint on event_id is what actually guarantees safety: the second INSERT is rejected, its transaction rolls back, and stock is never decremented twice. In production, catch that constraint violation and treat it as "already handled."
BeforeCrash between DB commit and offset commit → redelivery → stock decremented twice → phantom stock loss, oversells, angry customers.
AfterRedelivery is recognised by the ledger and skipped. At-least-once delivery becomes effectively exactly-once from the business's point of view — the only kind that matters.
Where this belongs: on every consumer that changes state — inventory, wallet, loyalty points, "mark order paid." Read-only consumers (analytics, search indexing) rarely need it. Rule of thumb: if running the handler twice would be wrong, add a dedup ledger.
14.12

Non-blocking processing — maxed the threads, still slow

📖 Purushottam's shop · The 2-second wall
🔴 The incident

Every orders-placed event calls an external shipping-rates API that takes about 2 seconds. The topic has 12 partitions, so Purushottam ran 12 consumer threads — the maximum. Lag still climbed to 30,000 at the evening peak. He added a 13th thread. Nothing changed. He added a 4th pod. Still nothing.

Why this happens — the parallelism ceiling: Kafka hands each partition to exactly one consumer thread at a time. With 12 partitions, at most 12 threads can be doing work; thread #13 (and the extra pod) owns no partition and sits idle. And each of the 12 busy threads spends its 2 seconds blocked, waiting on the API — not computing, just waiting. So the whole system is capped at 12 ÷ 2s ≈ 6 orders/second. Once threads = partitions, more threads can't help. The real enemy is the blocking, not the thread count.
💡 The fix — stop blocking, don't add threads
  1. Fire the external call asynchronously so one thread can have many calls in flight at once — using WebClient (which returns a future; no WebFlux runtime needed) or CompletableFuture.supplyAsync on a bounded pool.
  2. Wait with a timeout — orTimeout(2, SECONDS) — so one slow call can't wedge the consumer.
  3. On success → save + commit. On timeout/failure → route to the DLQ and move on (14.6). The line never freezes.
  4. Use manual ack so you commit the offset only after the async work finishes.
The rule to remember: one partition is read by one thread at a time — parallelism comes from partitions, not from piling threads onto the same partition. concurrency should never exceed the partitions a pod owns, and total threads across all pods should not exceed the topic's partition count, or the surplus threads simply stand idle.
// The slow version — each thread blocks ~2s, capped at (threads ÷ 2s)
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders-placed", groupId = "shipping", concurrency = "12")
public void handle(OrderPlaced event) {
    ShippingRate rate = shippingApi.getRate(event);   // BLOCKS the thread ~2s
    shippingStore.save(event, rate);
}
// The non-blocking version — fire async, await with timeout, manual ack
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders-placed", groupId = "shipping", concurrency = "12")
public void handle(OrderPlaced event, Acknowledgment ack) {
    shippingApi.getRateAsync(event)              // returns CompletableFuture<ShippingRate>
        .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)          // don't let one slow call wedge us
        .whenComplete((rate, ex) -> {
            if (ex == null) {
                shippingStore.save(event, rate);
                ack.acknowledge();               // commit offset ONLY after success
            } else {
                dlq.send("orders-shipping-dlt", event, ex);  // park it — don't block
                ack.acknowledge();               // move on to the next message
            }
        });
}
// ShippingApiClient.java — WebClient turns the HTTP call into a future (no WebFlux needed)
public CompletableFuture<ShippingRate> getRateAsync(OrderPlaced event) {
    return webClient.post().uri("/rates")
        .bodyValue(event.address())
        .retrieve()
        .bodyToMono(ShippingRate.class)
        .toFuture();          // Mono → CompletableFuture
}

// OR, if the client is plain-blocking, wrap it on a BOUNDED pool:
private final Executor apiPool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(64);  // or Java 21 virtual threads
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> shippingApi.getRate(event), apiPool);
⚙ Settings that make this work
SettingValueWhy
listener.ack-modeMANUALYou control exactly when the offset is committed — after the async work, not before.
orTimeout2s (≥ the API's own timeout)A stuck call is turned into a failure you can route to the DLQ instead of a frozen thread.
thread poolbounded (or virtual threads)An unbounded pool under a slow API can spawn runaway work and exhaust memory.
Honest trade-off: firing calls asynchronously means you may finish message 2 before message 1. That is fine when each message is independent — shipping-rate lookups, notifications, enrichment. If strict per-order ordering matters, keep those on a keyed, blocking path (14.4) and use this pattern only for the independent work.
14.13

Idempotent payments — charged twice on a slow night

📖 Purushottam's shop · The double charge
🔴 The incident

The payment consumer called the payment gateway to charge ₹2,499. The network was slow that night; the call timed out at 2 seconds, so the code treated it as failed and routed the event to the DLQ. The DLQ retry called the gateway again. The customer saw two charges. When Purushottam checked the gateway's logs, the first call had actually succeeded — only its response was late. The retry created a real, second, duplicate charge.

Why the obvious fix fails: "on retry, just ask the gateway if the payment went through" — but on a timeout you never received the gateway's transaction id, so you have nothing to ask about. You can't look up a charge by an id you were never given. The idempotent-consumer trick from 14.11 protects your own database, but it can't un-charge a card at an external system.
💡 The fix — carry your own idempotency key
  1. Mint an idempotency key yourself — a stable UUID (or the order id) — before the first call, and store it with the order.
  2. Send that same key on the request (a header or reference field) on the first attempt and every retry.
  3. The gateway dedupes on the key: if it has already processed that key, it returns the original result instead of charging again. One key → at most one charge, no matter how many times you retry.
This is a standard gateway feature — you don't build the dedup, the gateway does. Stripe uses an Idempotency-Key header; many Indian gateways (for example Pine Labs) accept a unique merchant reference / order id that plays the same role. The exact field name differs, so always confirm it in your gateway's own docs — but the idea is universal: the caller supplies a key, the gateway guarantees one action per key.
// At order creation — mint the key ONCE and persist it with the order
order.setPaymentKey(order.getId());          // stable per order (or UUID.randomUUID())
orderRepo.save(order);
// PaymentClient.java — send the SAME key on first attempt AND every retry
public PaymentResult charge(Order order) {
    return webClient.post().uri("/charges")
        .header("Idempotency-Key", order.getPaymentKey())   // ← the safety net
        .bodyValue(new ChargeRequest(order.getId(), order.getAmount()))
        .retrieve()
        .bodyToMono(PaymentResult.class)
        .block();     // or async, as in 14.12
}
🔍 Walkthrough
  1. The key lives with the order, not in a local variable — so a retry from the DLQ (a fresh pod, minutes later) still uses the exact same key.
  2. The gateway is the referee. Your code doesn't decide whether to charge again — the gateway refuses to, because it already acted on that key.
  3. Combine the three layers: outbox (14.7) guarantees the event is published, the payment key (here) guarantees at-most-one charge, and the idempotent consumer (14.11) guarantees your DB isn't double-written. Together they make the whole checkout safe under any crash or retry.
The one edge case: gateways keep keys for a limited window (often 24 hours). If a retry somehow happens after that window, the key is forgotten and you must reconcile by querying the gateway's transaction status before charging. For the normal seconds-to-minutes retry, the key alone is enough.
14.14 ★

The whole checkout, end to end — click through Purushottam's ₹2,499 order

📖 Everything above, wired together

One tap on "Place order" sets off a chain across four services and four topics. Every safety trick from 14.5–14.13 has a job here. Step through it below — each step highlights the parts in play and names the exact guarantee protecting it.

// The heart of it — a CONDITIONAL decrement so the DB itself refuses to oversell
@Modifying
@Query("UPDATE Product p SET p.stock = p.stock - :qty " +
       "WHERE p.id = :id AND p.stock >= :qty")     // only if enough stock
int tryReserve(@Param("id") String id, @Param("qty") int qty);
// InventoryConsumer — reserve, or start a saga compensation if we oversold
@Transactional
public void onPaymentCompleted(PaymentCompleted e) {
    if (seen.existsById(e.eventId())) return;              // 14.11 idempotency
    seen.save(new ProcessedEvent(e.eventId(), Instant.now()));

    int rows = products.tryReserve(e.productId(), e.quantity());
    if (rows == 1) {
        events.publish("order-confirmed", new OrderConfirmed(e.orderId()));
    } else {
        // 0 rows updated → sold out → undo the paid order (saga compensation)
        events.publish("order-cancelled", new OrderCancelled(e.orderId(), "OUT_OF_STOCK"));
    }
}
// OutboxRelay — multiple pods poll safely with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
@Query(value = "SELECT * FROM outbox_events WHERE published = false " +
               "ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 100 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED",
       nativeQuery = true)
List<OutboxEvent> lockUnpublished();   // each pod grabs a different batch — no duplicate publish
🔍 Why each guarantee is here
  1. Outbox + SKIP LOCKED (14.7): the order and its event save together; many relay pods publish without stepping on each other.
  2. Idempotency key (14.13): the payment is charged at most once, even if the call is retried.
  3. Idempotent consumer (14.11): redelivered events don't decrement stock twice.
  4. Conditional decrement + saga (Section 11): the database refuses to oversell; if stock ran out after payment, a compensating order-cancelled triggers a refund and an apology — no distributed transaction needed.
  5. DLT (14.6) + non-blocking notify (14.12): a failing step parks in its DLQ and pages on-call once; the confirmation email never blocks the pipeline.

14.15 · Decision guide — every problem, its chapter, its rule

You need to…The chapterThe one rule to remember
Set up Kafka in a service14.1 SetupConfig in YAML, never in Java
Fire-and-forget events across services14.2 Producer & ConsumerAPI publishes and returns fast; consumers work later
Scale readers under load14.3 Consumer GroupsSame groupId shares work · deploy more copies
Keep one user's events in order14.4 OrderingSame key → same partition → guaranteed order
Never lose critical events14.5 Guaranteesacks=all + manual commit + idempotent processing
Handle poisoned messages14.6 DLT@RetryableTopic ladder → @DltHandler safety net
Save to DB AND publish atomically14.7 OutboxBoth writes in one DB transaction; small relay publishes
Evolve event schemas safely14.8 Avro + RegistryBACKWARD compatibility · breaking changes fail at build
React to events with state14.9 Kafka StreamsKTable + KStream · exactly_once_v2
Build many small pipelines14.10 Cloud StreamWrite a Function bean · bind in YAML

The three habits that carried every chapter

Config outside code · atomic writes across DB & Kafka · idempotent processing on both sides. Miss any of the three and you'll relive one of these incidents.

Two kinds of data on Tinder's Kafka

Rebuildable streams (analytics events, GPS pings) — losing a few is fine. Critical streams (matches, subscriptions, chats) — need acks=all, replication ≥ 3, and outbox-published from the DB. Know which is which the day you create the topic.

14.16

Capstone — the whole Tinder event platform

📖 Everything from chapters 14.1 – 14.10, running together

Here is Tinder's actual event platform, drawn end-to-end. Every arrow uses a pattern from one of the chapters above. This is the mental picture to keep in your head — for interviews, for architecture reviews, for your own systems.

Aisha swipes right on Rahul. Her phone sees the response in 40ms. Behind the scenes, the swipe is written to the DB and outbox in one transaction (14.7). The outbox relay picks it up and publishes to swipes-registered, keyed by aisha (14.4), with acks=all (14.5). Four services see it: notifications sends "someone liked you" to Rahul (14.3, 14.6), the streams-based match detector (14.9) checks the KTable, finds Rahul already right-swiped Aisha, and publishes to matches-created. Three services react to that: chat is unlocked, both phones get "It's a match!", and both users earn 10 loyalty points via a Function pipeline (14.10). All of this — every arrow — is one of the twelve chapters, running together, every day, at Tinder's scale.

Act I · Chapters 1–13

No code. Real systems. Pictures.

Each chapter takes one product you've used, shows the bug or the bottleneck it hit, and draws what was happening underneath.

CHAPTER 01The feed that takes two seconds

Instagram · opening the app

You tap the Instagram icon. Before a single photo appears, the server must gather your feed, your stories, your notification count and an ad slot — four separate services, none of which know about each other.

Done one after another, here's where the time goes.

Two numbers describe this, and they'll follow us to the last chapter:

Latency

How long one user waits. Here, 1.33 seconds — and users abandon a feed at around 3.

Throughput

How many users a server handles per second. If one request occupies a worker for 1.33 s, one worker serves 0.75 users/sec, no matter how fast the chip is.

What's actually happening in the machine

The CPU core running your request is capable of roughly 3 billion operations per second. During the 1.24 seconds it spends waiting for those four services, it could have executed about 3.7 billion instructions. It executed zero, because the only thing scheduled on it was code that said "wait for this."

So the founding question of this entire subject is not how do we make the server faster. The server is already absurdly fast. It's: what do we do with the 93%?

CHAPTER 02Busy or blocked?

Swiggy · placing an order vs generating the invoice PDF

Before fixing anything, one distinction. It decides almost every threading decision you will ever make, and it looks identical from the outside.

Getting this backwards is the single most common performance mistake in production systems. Adding servers to a blocked system burns money for nothing. Adding concurrency to a busy system makes it slower.

The concrete complaint

You place a Swiggy order. The app calls the payment gateway — 800 ms. Behind you in the same server process, someone just wants to view a menu, a 15 ms lookup. They wait 800 ms for a menu, because the server is standing still watching a payment gateway.

The move

While the payment call is in flight, serve the menu request. Nothing got faster and no hardware was added. The server simply stopped wasting the wait. That's concurrency.

It needs three things, and each one becomes a chapter later:

  1. Work must be pausable at known points — you can step away after firing the payment call, not mid-calculation.
  2. Something must remember where you were — which order, which user, which line of code. That memory is a stack, and it's the reason threads cost anything at all (Chapter 7).
  3. Something must signal completion — otherwise you'd have to keep checking, which is its own waste (Chapter 22).

CHAPTER 03Just add more workers?

Flipkart · Big Billion Days, 10 pm rush

Traffic goes up 40×. The obvious move is more workers. But where you put them matters more than how many you add.

Try it — how many threads should Flipkart run?
interactive
16
Relative throughput—
Stack memory—
Verdict—
The three regimes, in one line each

Mostly waiting: threads ≫ cores is correct, and dramatically so — 190 of 200 are asleep at any instant, costing memory but no CPU. Mostly computing: threads ≈ cores; going higher is actively harmful. Contending on one shared thing: neither helps — that resource sets your ceiling, and extra threads just lengthen the queue in front of it.

CHAPTER 04Inside the machine

Any cloud instance · c6i.2xlarge, "8 vCPU"

Three words get used interchangeably and mean different things. The distinction decides how many threads actually run at once.

TermWhat it isWhy you care
SocketThe physical chip. Servers may have 2.Only matters for NUMA (Chapter 23)
CoreIndependent engine with its own registers, L1, L2Real parallelism. 4 cores = at most 4 simultaneous instructions streams
Logical processorAn SMT sibling — 2 per core, sharing the engineWhat the OS schedules. "8 vCPU" usually means 4 real cores
Clock~3 GHz, and barely improved since 2005The reason multithreading exists at all
The historical accident behind all of this

Until about 2004, every chip generation ran at a higher clock and all software got faster for free. Then power consumption — which rises roughly with the cube of frequency — hit a thermal wall. Vendors pivoted from one fast core to many cores. A modern 16-core chip has enormous capacity, but a single-threaded program uses one sixteenth of it and no compiler will fix that. Concurrency stopped being a specialist skill and became the only way to use hardware you already pay for.

CHAPTER 05Concurrency vs parallelism

Uber · matching riders (concurrency) vs Hotstar · encoding video (parallelism)

We've already used both without naming them. Chapter 2's overlap was concurrency; Chapter 3's case B was parallelism. They solve different problems.

Play it — Instagram's four calls under three strategies
interactive
Wall-clock time—
Cores used—
CPU utilisation—
DimensionConcurrencyParallelism
AnswersHow is work structured?How is work executed?
Needs many coresNoYes, by definition
SolvesWasted waitingNot enough compute
ImprovesThroughput, responsivenessLatency of one big job
FitsI/O-bound (APIs, DBs, queues)CPU-bound (encode, sort, ML)
Limited byMemory, downstream capacityCore count, Amdahl's law
RelationshipYou write concurrency. Hardware grants parallelism. Parallel code is always concurrent; concurrent code often isn't parallel.

Amdahl's law, without algebra

Flipkart's checkout must touch one inventory row. If that shared step is 10% of a request, then no matter how many servers you add, you can never go more than 10× faster — eventually every request is just queueing for that row.

CHAPTER 06The switching tax

Why 500 threads on 8 cores is slower than 16

Chapter 3 showed throughput falling as threads climbed. Here's the mechanism.

Four things trigger a switch

1 · Time slice expires — the OS forcibly takes the core back after a few milliseconds. 2 · The thread blocks — it asked for something not ready. 3 · A higher-priority thread wakes. 4 · Voluntary yield. Note that #2 is free money — the thread was going to waste the core anyway. It's #1 that gets expensive when threads far outnumber cores.

One more thing to file away: a context switch is expensive largely because it goes through the operating system — a full trip into kernel mode and back. If you could switch between units of work without involving the OS at all, the cost would drop by an order of magnitude. That's exactly what Chapter 22 does.

CHAPTER 07Process vs thread

Uber · separate services vs threads inside the dispatch service

Two ways to grow. Uber runs pricing, dispatch and payments as separate services — separate processes, possibly separate machines. Inside the dispatch service, thousands of threads share one memory space.

DimensionProcess (separate service)Thread (inside one service)
MemoryOwn address space, MMU-isolatedShares the process's memory
Owns privatelyEverythingStack, program counter, registers, thread-locals
Creation costHeavy (~ms)Light (~50–100 µs)
CommunicationExplicit — HTTP, Kafka, pipes, shared memoryImplicit — read the same field
IsolationStrongNone
If one diesOthers carry onA fatal error takes the whole JVM
Use forFault containment, independent deploys, scaling outConcurrency inside one application
Linux doesn't really have "threads"

It has tasks. Both process creation and thread creation call the same clone() syscall with different flags. Clone sharing nothing → a process. Clone with CLONE_VM | CLONE_FILES | CLONE_THREAD → what we call a thread. Verify on any running JVM: ps -eLf | grep java shows one row per OS thread, and ls /proc/<pid>/task/ one directory each.

CHAPTER 08Who decides whose turn it is

The OS scheduler · and why bugs never reproduce

Threads don't choose when to pause. The kernel can suspend any thread between any two machine instructions — not between statements, between instructions, which are much smaller. You get no say and no warning.

  • Time slices shrink as thread count grows. Four runnable threads each get a decent slice; four hundred get slivers, and you pay switch cost far more often per unit of useful work.
  • Wakeup ≠ running. When your data arrives you rejoin the queue. This is why latency under load is worse than at idle even when nothing is "slow."
  • Priorities are a hint. They vary by OS and are frequently ignored. Never build correctness on them.

CHAPTER 09Two people buy the last iPhone

Flipkart flash sale · Tinder double match · BookMyShow seat 14A

We now have everything needed to break something: shared state, many threads, and a scheduler that interrupts without warning.

The incident

Flash sale. Stock: 1. Two users tap Buy in the same millisecond. Both get an order confirmation. Warehouse has one unit. Someone gets a refund and an apology, and this happens a few thousand times a day at scale.

Nobody wrote a bug. The code reads stock, checks it's above zero, decrements, saves. That's four steps — and the scheduler can interrupt between any two of them.

Step through it — the oversell, one instruction at a time
interactive
Stock in DB1
Orders confirmed0
Resultrunning…
Press Step repeatedly. Watch what User B reads at step 4.

The three conditions

A race condition needs all three simultaneously. Remove any one and the bug is impossible:

1 · Shared

Two threads reach the same state.

2 · Mutable

At least one writes. Read-only sharing is always safe.

3 · Unordered

Nothing enforces who goes first.

That's not a slogan — it's your solution menu, and it's why later chapters offer exactly three strategies: don't share (confinement), don't mutate (immutability), or enforce order (locks and atomics).

The same bug wearing different clothes

PatternWhere you've seen it
Lost update — read, modify, writeFlipkart stock, a like counter, a wallet balance
Check-then-actBookMyShow selling seat 14A twice; two threads both creating the same "singleton"; a cache stampede on deploy
Duplicate side effectTinder creating two match records when both users swipe right in the same instant, so the chat opens twice
Torn readReading a delivery address mid-update — new street, old city
Unsafe publicationAnother thread sees a reference to a half-constructed object
It's worse than interleaving

The diagram assumes one shared value everyone reads. Real hardware doesn't work that way — each core has a private L1 cache and a store buffer. Core 0 can write 0 to its own cache while core 1 keeps reading a stale 1, possibly for a long time. So there are two independent failures stacked together: atomicity (the multi-step operation got interrupted) and visibility (the write never reached the other core). Chapter 10 fixes the first, Chapter 11 the second.

CHAPTER 10One seat, one key

BookMyShow · holding seat 14A while you pay

The fix is boring and effective: make the multi-step operation indivisible by ensuring only one thread can be inside it at a time.

What it costs you

Serialisation

Whatever is inside now happens one at a time, however many cores you own. This is Amdahl's serial fraction. Keep the section short.

Blocking cost

Losers may be parked and woken by the OS — a context switch each way. For a two-nanosecond update that's absurd, which is why lock-free techniques exist (Chapter 17).

Contention collapse

500 threads, one key: 499 always queueing. Adding threads degrades throughput because you added queue, not capacity.

New failure modes

Forget to release → everything stops. Take two keys in different orders → deadlock (Chapter 12).

Three rules, learned expensively

  1. Hold it for the shortest possible time. Compute outside, lock, mutate, unlock.
  2. Never do I/O while holding a lock. BookMyShow locking a seat and then calling the payment gateway for 8 seconds means that row is frozen for 8 seconds. This one rule prevents a huge share of real production stalls.
  3. Always release, including on failure. Every exit path, including exceptional ones.
Many small locks beat one big lock

One key for the whole seat map means someone booking in Screen 3 blocks someone in Screen 1 for no reason. Give each show its own key and contention drops proportionally. This is lock striping — the same idea that lets a concurrent hash map take many writes at once, and the same reason databases moved from table locks to row locks. The trade-off: more locks, more chances to acquire them in conflicting orders.

How a lock is actually built

A lock is one memory location. Acquiring it is an atomic test-and-set — a single CPU instruction that reads and writes indivisibly, which the hardware guarantees no other core can interleave with. Lose the race and you either spin (retry in a tight loop — great if the wait is nanoseconds) or park (ask the OS to deschedule you — costs a context switch each way but burns no CPU). Good implementations spin briefly, then park. The instruction underneath, LOCK CMPXCHG on x86, reappears in Chapter 17 as compare-and-swap.

CHAPTER 11The driver who's still online

Uber · a driver goes offline and keeps getting ride requests

Atomicity is fixed. Now the stranger half — the bug people genuinely refuse to believe.

The incident

A driver taps "Go offline". The dispatch thread sets available = false. Twenty seconds later, the matching thread is still assigning them rides. The flag was set. The write completed. The other thread never saw it.

And the order can change too

A sharper version

Uber's dispatcher builds a Trip object, then sets tripReady = true. Obviously in that order. Except the two writes are independent, so the compiler reordered them and the CPU executed them out of order. The matching thread saw tripReady == true and read a Trip that was still half-built. NullPointerException in production, never in the debugger.

Both the compiler and the CPU may reorder freely, as long as a single thread observing itself can't tell. That caveat is doing enormous work — another thread absolutely can tell.

The two problems, side by side

Atomicity = "my multi-step operation got interrupted" → fixed by mutual exclusion or an atomic instruction. Visibility = "my finished write never reached you" → fixed by a memory barrier. A lock happens to fix both, which is why it's the default answer. A volatile flag fixes only the second — which is why it is not a substitute for a lock when you're decrementing stock.

CHAPTER 12Two transfers, frozen forever

PhonePe · A sends ₹500 to B while B sends ₹300 to A

Locks solved the race. Now they bring their own family of failures — and these stop the system dead rather than corrupting it quietly.

FailureWhat you seeCPUCure
DeadlockRequests hang forever, no errors logged~0% — everyone parkedGlobal lock ordering; tryLock timeout as fallback
LivelockBusy but no progress; endless retries100% — everyone spinningRandomised backoff to break symmetry
StarvationMost requests fine, a few take forever (bad p99)NormalFair locks; bound the critical section
ConvoyingEverything slows to the speed of the slowest holderLow, queue longNever do I/O inside a lock
Why it's permanent

Both threads are parked in a wait queue attached to a lock. Each will be woken only when that lock is released; each lock is released only when its holder finishes; each holder finishes only after acquiring the other lock. The OS sees two threads legitimately waiting and will happily wait forever. Nothing times out on its own — which is why deadlock detection is a tool you deliberately run, not a warning you receive.

CHAPTER 13So how many threads?

Everything in Act I collapses into one decision
Size it yourself
interactive
8
10 ms
190 ms
20
Formula says—
Real ceiling—
Max throughput—
The narrowest pipe wins

You can run 160 threads, but if HikariCP has 20 connections, only 20 work at a time and 140 queue in a line you built yourself. Sizing a thread pool without sizing the connection pool, the downstream rate limit, and the database's own max_connections is theatre.

Two tensions that motivate everything after this

Waiting is free — workers aren't

A blocked thread uses no CPU, so we'd love ten thousand. But each carries ~1 MB of stack and a slot in the scheduler. Around ten thousand you run out of memory.

Sharing is fast — and dangerous

Threads share memory, so coordination is instant — and races, stale reads and deadlocks become possible. Every safety mechanism costs performance.

All of Act I, in one paragraph

Cores do the work; threads are workers taking turns on them. Concurrency reclaims wasted waiting; parallelism buys capacity; which you need depends on whether your work is blocked or busy. Switching costs real time, so more threads is not better. Threads share everything except their stack — fast to coordinate, easy to corrupt — producing races that need atomicity (locks, atomics) and visibility (memory barriers). Locks bring deadlock, which you prevent with a global ordering. And the right thread count is a function of how much of your work is waiting.

Basics.java
Runnable job = () -> dispatch(rideRequest);

// Java 21 builder — platform and virtual threads share one API
Thread t = Thread.ofPlatform().name("dispatch-1").start(job);
t.join();

// The legacy constructor names threads "Thread-0", which is useless in a

The mistake this chapter exists to prevent

new Thread(task).start() per request. Ten thousand concurrent requests = ten thousand OS threads = ~10 GB of reserved stack = a dead machine. Chapter 15 fixes this.

Interruption.java — the only correct way to stop a thread
// Thread.stop() was REMOVED in Java 20. Interruption is cooperative:
// you ask, the target decides where it's safe to stop.
while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {
    try {
        RideRequest r = queue.take();
        dispatch(r);
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();   // RESTORE the flag, then leave
        break;
    }
}
// Swallowing InterruptedException without restoring the flag is the most
// common concurrency bug in Java codebases — shutdown silently hangs.

CHAPTER 15Pools and executors

Flipkart · the checkout service under load
Pools.java
// Convenience factories — each has a sharp edge
Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8);      // UNBOUNDED queue → OOM under load
Executors.newCachedThreadPool();      // UNBOUNDED threads → OOM under load
Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();  // serialises; good when order matters
Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(2);  // delayed / periodic

// Production-grade
var pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
        8, 16,                                   // core, max
        60L, TimeUnit.SECONDS,                   // idle keep-alive
        new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(500),           // BOUNDED
        Thread.ofPlatform().name("checkout-", 0).factory(),
        new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());

try (var exec = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {   // AutoCloseable since 19
    exec.submit(() -> reserveStock(sku));
}   // close() = shutdown + await termination — no leaked threads
Shutdown.java
pool.shutdown();                                    // stop accepting
if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
    pool.shutdownNow();                             // interrupt the rest
    if (!pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS))
        log.error("tasks are ignoring interrupts");
}
What an idle worker is doing

Nothing — and that's the point. Each worker loops on queue.take(); when empty it parks via a futex and the OS removes it from the run queue. Zero CPU. Submitting a task signals the futex, one worker becomes READY, and the scheduler gives it a core. Idle pool threads cost memory, not CPU — exactly as Chapter 8 predicted.

CHAPTER 16Getting results back

Instagram · the four calls from Chapter 1, now overlapped
Fanout.java
try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    Future<Feed>    f = exec.submit(() -> feedApi.get(uid));      // starts now
    Future<Stories> s = exec.submit(() -> storiesApi.get(uid));   // starts now
    Future<Notifs>  n = exec.submit(() -> notifApi.get(uid));     // starts now
    Future<Ad>      a = exec.submit(() -> adsApi.get(uid));       // starts now

    return new Screen(f.get(), s.get(), n.get(), a.get());   // ≈420 ms, not 1330
}

// ⚠ The classic mistake — still 1330 ms:
//     var f = exec.submit(...).get();   ← blocks here
//     var s = exec.submit(...).get();   ← only starts after f finished
//   Submit EVERYTHING first, then collect.
Composition.java — CompletableFuture
CompletableFuture<Screen> screen =
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> feedApi.get(uid), pool)
        .thenApply(Feed::rank)
        .thenCombine(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> adsApi.get(uid), pool),
                     Screen::new)
        .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .exceptionally(ex -> Screen.cached());     // graceful degradation

// thenApply   — transform      thenCompose — chain another async call
// thenCombine — merge two      allOf/anyOf — wait for all / first
// ⚠ ALWAYS pass your own executor. The default is the JVM-wide common
//   ForkJoinPool; blocking in it starves every parallel stream in the process.
In Java 21 this matters less than it used to

CompletableFuture exists because blocking a platform thread was expensive, so we wrote callback chains to avoid it. With virtual threads, blocking is cheap — so plain sequential code with Future.get() is often better: readable, real stack traces, debuggers work. Keep CompletableFuture for genuine composition (timeouts, fallbacks, merging heterogeneous sources), not as a way to dodge blocking.

Structured concurrency JEP 453 preview

What's still wrong above

If the feed call fails, the stories, notifications and ads calls keep running — burning connections for a response nobody will see. And if the user closes the app, nothing cancels. The four tasks have no relationship to each other or to their parent.

Structured.java — run with --enable-preview
try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
    Supplier<Feed>    f = scope.fork(() -> feedApi.get(uid));
    Supplier<Stories> s = scope.fork(() -> storiesApi.get(uid));

    scope.join();              // wait for all, or for the first failure
    scope.throwIfFailed();     // propagate it — siblings already cancelled

    return new Screen(f.get(), s.get());
}   // close() guarantees NOTHING is still running when we leave the block

CHAPTER 17The thread-safety toolkit

Flipkart's oversell from Chapter 9, in Java
TheBug.java
class Inventory {
    private int stock = 1;
    boolean reserve() {
        if (stock > 0) { stock--; return true; }   // read, check, write
        return false;
    }
}
// 2 threads, 1 unit → both return true. No exception. No log line.
Fix 1 — synchronized
Fix1.java
class Inventory {
    private int stock = 1;
    private final Object lock = new Object();      // private → callers can't grab it

    boolean reserve() { synchronized (lock) { if (stock > 0) { stock--; return true; }
                                              return false; } }
    int stock()       { synchronized (lock) { return stock; } }   // READS TOO!
}
// Forgetting to guard the READ is the most common half-fix: you get atomicity
// but not visibility, so readers may still see a stale value.
// Locking on `this` or a String literal leaks your lock to the outside world.

What it buys: mutual exclusion and a happens-before edge. Releasing the monitor publishes everything you wrote inside; acquiring it discards your stale cached reads. Both of Act I's problems, one keyword.

Fix 2 — ReentrantLock
Fix2.java
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

if (lock.tryLock(100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {   // escape hatch for deadlock
    try { stock--; } finally { lock.unlock(); }   // finally is MANDATORY
} else {
    metrics.increment("inventory.lock.timeout");  // degrade, don't hang
}

var rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();            // many readers OR one writer
rw.readLock().lock();
try { return catalogue.get(sku); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
CapabilitysynchronizedReentrantLock
Released automatically on exceptionYesOnly via finally
Timed / interruptible acquireNoYes
Fairness optionNoYes (slower)
Multiple wait setsOnenewCondition()
Pins a virtual thread (Java 21)Yes — Ch. 22No
Fix 3 — atomics and CAS
Fix3.java
private final AtomicInteger stock = new AtomicInteger(1);

boolean reserve() {                       // lock-free, ~20 ns
    int cur;
    do {
        cur = stock.get();
        if (cur == 0) return false;
    } while (!stock.compareAndSet(cur, cur - 1));   // "only if unchanged"
    return true;
}

// Hot counters (likes, views) — LongAdder keeps padded per-thread cells and
// sums only on read, so threads stop fighting over one memory word.
private final LongAdder views = new LongAdder();
views.increment();
long total = views.sum();
The ABA problem

CAS compares values, not history. If a value goes A → B → A while you were away, your CAS succeeds even though the world moved. Rarely bites simple counters; a real hazard in lock-free stacks and linked structures. AtomicStampedReference adds a version so you can tell.

Fix 4 — volatile
Fix4.java
private volatile boolean available = true;     // ✓ Uber's driver flag — correct
public void goOffline() { available = false; }
public void loop() { while (available) { matchRide(); } }

private volatile int stock;
public void reserve() { stock--; }             // ✗ STILL BROKEN — 3 steps

// The rule: volatile suffices when ONE thread writes, or writes don't depend
// on the current value. Otherwise you need an atomic or a lock.

// ✓ The genuinely great use — publishing immutable state atomically:
public record SurgeConfig(double multiplier, Duration window) {}
private volatile SurgeConfig config;           // readers need no lock at all
public void reload(SurgeConfig c) { this.config = c; }
Fix 0 — the one to reach for first
Don't share

Local variables live on the thread's own stack and are automatically safe. One Kafka consumer per partition. One JDBC connection per thread. Nothing shared, nothing to race.

Don't mutate

record, List.of(), final fields. Immutable objects are safe to share with any number of threads forever, with zero synchronisation — the JMM guarantees correctly-constructed final fields are visible.

ToolAtomicityVisibilityBlocks?Use when
ImmutabilityN/AYesNeverAlways your first choice
ConfinementN/AN/ANeverPer-thread or per-partition state
volatileNoYesNeverFlags; publishing an immutable reference
Atomics / CASOne variableYesSpinsCounters, lock-free reference swaps
synchronizedYesYesYesMulti-step invariants — simplest correct answer
ReentrantLockYesYesYesNeed timeout, fairness, or virtual-thread friendliness

Coordination.java
var queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<Order>(1_000);   // BOUNDED
queue.put(order);                    // blocks if full — natural back-pressure
Order o = queue.take();              // blocks if empty — costs no CPU

// The correct way to rate-limit a fragile downstream
private final Semaphore gateway = new Semaphore(10);
gateway.acquire();
try   { paymentGateway.charge(card, amount); }
finally { gateway.release(); }       // release in finally, ALWAYS

// Startup gate
var ready = new CountDownLatch(3);
startCacheWarmer(ready::countDown);
startConnectionPool(ready::countDown);
startSchemaCheck(ready::countDown);
ready.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);   // always the timed overload
serveTraffic();
Why a semaphore, not a smaller pool

Shrinking a pool conflates two different things: how many workers you have, and how many may touch a particular resource. A semaphore states the second directly. This becomes essential in Chapter 22, where there is no pool left to shrink.

CHAPTER 19Concurrent collections

Collections.java
Map<String,Integer> bad  = new HashMap<>();                        // ✗ corrupts
Map<String,Integer> slow = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()); // ✗ one lock
Map<String,Integer> good = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();              // ✓ striped

// Single operations are atomic. COMBINATIONS ARE NOT.
if (!good.containsKey(k)) good.put(k, v);      // ✗ check-then-act race
good.putIfAbsent(k, v);                        // ✓ one atomic operation
good.merge(sku, 1, Integer::sum);              // ✓ idiomatic counter
good.compute(k, (key, old) -> old == null ? 1 : old + 1);
NeedUseWhy
Shared map, mixed reads/writesConcurrentHashMapPer-bucket locking + CAS; reads usually lock-free
Handoff between stagesArrayBlockingQueueBounded, with back-pressure
Max throughput, bound not neededConcurrentLinkedQueueLock-free — but unbounded, you own the memory risk
Listener list: read constantly, write rarelyCopyOnWriteArrayListReads need zero synchronisation; writes copy
Sorted shared dataConcurrentSkipListMapOrdered, no global lock
Hot counterLongAdderPadded per-thread cells, summed on read
How ConcurrentHashMap gets away with it

The table is an array of buckets. Inserting into an empty bucket is a single CAS on that array slot — no lock at all. Only when a bucket already has entries does it synchronized on that bucket's first node. Two threads writing different keys almost never interact, and readers traverse volatile-linked nodes without locking. It's Chapter 10's lock striping plus Chapter 17's CAS, combined.
