DeadlockFix.java
// ✓ Global ordering — rank by something stable and total
void transfer(Account from, Account to, BigDecimal amt) {
    Account first  = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;
    Account second = from.id() < to.id() ? to   : from;
    synchronized (first) { synchronized (second) { from.debit(amt); to.credit(amt); } }
}

// ✓ Health check — returns null when healthy, cheap enough to run every 30 s
var mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long[] stuck = mx.findDeadlockedThreads();
if (stuck != null)
    for (ThreadInfo i : mx.getThreadInfo(stuck, true, true))
        log.error("DEADLOCK: {} blocked on {} held by {}",
                  i.getThreadName(), i.getLockName(), i.getLockOwnerName());

CHAPTER 21Divide and conquer

Flipkart · re-scoring 10 million products for the sale ranking
Parallel.java
long flagged = products.parallelStream().filter(Product::needsReview).count();

// ⚠ Uses the JVM-wide COMMON ForkJoinPool. Blocking I/O in here starves every
//   other parallel stream in the process. Pure CPU work, large datasets only.

var pool = new ForkJoinPool(Runtime.getRuntime().availableProcessors());
long n = pool.submit(() -> products.parallelStream().filter(...).count()).get();

class ScoreTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 10_000;    // too small → splitting
    protected Long compute() {                      // costs more than the work
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) return scoreSequentially(lo, hi);
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        var left = new ScoreTask(lo, mid);
        left.fork();                                // queue for stealing
        long right = new ScoreTask(mid, hi).compute();
        return right + left.join();
    }
}
When parallel streams lose

Small collections (split and merge cost more than the work). LinkedList and other sources that can't split evenly. Shared mutable state or ordering requirements. And anything doing I/O. parallel() is a one-word change that can easily make code three times slower — benchmark it.

CHAPTER 22The wall — and virtual threads JEP 444

Hotstar · 5 crore concurrent viewers during an India–Pakistan match

This is the chapter Act I was built for. Chapter 13 left a tension: waiting is free in CPU terms, but each waiting thread costs ~1 MB of stack and a slot in the scheduler. Watch it become a hard wall.

The incident

An API gateway. Every request calls three services, ~100 ms each. Actual computation: under 2 ms. Tomcat runs the default 200 threads on 8 cores.

Concurrency reaches 5,000. CPU sits at 6%. Latency is eleven seconds. The machine is almost entirely idle and the service is effectively down.

Drag it — what 1 million concurrent users costs
interactive
10 000
platform
virtual
Platform threads—
Virtual threads—
OS threads needed—

The idea

The move

Chapter 6: switching is expensive mainly because it goes through the kernel. Chapter 7: the only truly private thing a thread owns is its stack. Put them together — keep the stack on the Java heap and let the JVM decide which work runs on a real OS thread. Now a "thread" is just an object. Creating one is an allocation. Switching never enters the kernel. And a blocked one occupies no OS thread at all.

One request, step by step
  1. You submit a task. The JVM allocates a VirtualThread object on the heap. No syscall.
  2. The scheduler mounts it on a carrier — its frames are copied onto that carrier's real OS stack.
  3. Your code runs as ordinary JIT-compiled Java on a real core. Full speed; no emulation.
  4. You hit a blocking call. The JDK's I/O layer intercepts it instead of letting the thread wait.
  5. The runtime unmounts — frames copied back to the heap, carrier released immediately to run something else.
  6. epoll reports readiness. The continuation is resubmitted and resumes on the next line, often on a different OS thread.
~1 KB
Footprint

vs ~1 MB reserved for a platform thread.

~1 µs
Creation

An allocation, vs ~50–100 µs for a syscall.

~200 ns
Switch

User-space continuation swap, vs 1–5 µs plus cache damage.

VirtualThreads.java
Thread vt = Thread.ofVirtual().name("stream-1").start(() -> serve(viewer));
// VirtualThread[#31,stream-1]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-3

try (var exec = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    IntStream.range(0, 1_000_000).forEach(i ->
        exec.submit(() -> { Thread.sleep(Duration.ofSeconds(1)); return i; }));
}
// A million, on a laptop, in seconds. Platform threads die around 10 000 with
// OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread

Shrink the pool to rate-limitSemaphoreNo pool to shrink — express the real constraint
Avoid blocking callsBlocking is fine againBlocking unmounts instead of parking an OS thread

Pinning — the one real gotcha on Java 21

Pinning.java
// ✗ PINNED
synchronized (lock) { jdbcTemplate.query(...); }

// ✓ NOT PINNED
lock.lock();
try   { jdbcTemplate.query(...); }
finally { lock.unlock(); }

Version note worth knowing for interviews

On Java 21, synchronized pins. From Java 24 (JEP 491) the runtime can unmount inside monitors and the problem largely disappears. On 21 — audit your libraries, especially older JDBC drivers and connection pools.

✗ Don't use for CPU-bound work

No waiting to overlap; a fixed pool sized to cores is correct.

✗ Don't use with heavy ThreadLocal

Per-thread state multiplies by task count, not pool size.

✗ Not where a small pool was the rate limit

Replace with a semaphore first, or you'll fire 50,000 concurrent calls at a fragile downstream.

✓ Enable in Spring Boot 3.2+

spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true — Tomcat, @Async and @Scheduled all switch over.

If L1 were 1 second—
Wasted instructions—

Because a cache miss fetches a whole 64-byte line, sequential access is nearly free after the first read. That's why an int[] scan beats a LinkedList<Integer> scan tenfold — identical Big-O, but pointer chasing misses on every hop while the array streams.

Locality.java
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)                 // ✓ row-major — sequential
    for (int j = 0; j < N; j++) sum += m[i][j];

for (int j = 0; j < N; j++)                 // ✗ column-major — miss every read
    for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) sum += m[i][j];   // often 5–10× slower

False sharing

FalseSharing.java
class Counters { volatile long a; volatile long b; }              // ✗ one line
class Padded { volatile long a; long p1,p2,p3,p4,p5,p6,p7;
               volatile long b; }                                 // ✓ padded
var hits = new LongAdder();   // ✓ best — its internal Cell is already @Contended
  • SMT: mixed workloads gain 15–30%; tight CPU loops gain nearly nothing. availableProcessors() returns the logical count — benchmark CPU pools against physical too.
  • Affinity: taskset -c 2,3 java -jar app.jar pins the JVM so threads keep warm caches. Latency-critical paths only.
  • NUMA: multi-socket machines pay 1.5–2× to reach the other socket's memory. Check numactl --hardware; mitigate with -XX:+UseNUMA.
Keep this in proportion

For the vast majority of Java services this chapter is not your bottleneck — a missing index, an N+1 query, or a connection pool of 10 is. Reach for cache-line reasoning only after a profiler points here.

CHAPTER 24Multiprocessing and scaling out

Java has no global interpreter lock, so unlike Python you don't need multiple processes to use multiple cores. You need them for different reasons entirely.

Fault isolation

An OOM, a JNI segfault or a pathological GC kills one pod, not all traffic.

Heap ceilings

Four 8 GB JVMs often beat one 32 GB JVM — shorter GC pauses, better locality, each may fit one NUMA node.

Untrusted / native code

Run video transcoding or a fragile C library in a child so a crash can't take the service down.

Independent lifecycle

Deploy, scale and roll back on separate schedules.

Processes.java
Process p = new ProcessBuilder("ffmpeg", "-i", in, out)
        .redirectErrorStream(true).start();
try (var r = p.inputReader()) { r.lines().forEach(log::info); }   // MUST drain
if (!p.waitFor(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) p.destroyForcibly();        // bound it
The hang that catches everyone once

Don't consume the child's stdout and its 64 KB pipe buffer fills, the child blocks writing, and waitFor() never returns.

IPCJava APISpeedUse when
Pipes / stdioProcessBuilder streamsMediumWrapping a CLI tool
TCP / HTTP / gRPCSocket, HTTP clientSlowerCross-machine — the microservices default
Unix domain socketsUnixDomainSocketAddress 16+FastSame host, skips the TCP stack
Shared memoryFileChannel.map()FastestBulk or low-latency; you own framing and ordering
Message brokerKafka, RabbitMQSlowerDurability, decoupling, replay
The honest answer for most Java systems

"Multiprocessing" in practice means horizontal scaling: N identical JVMs behind a load balancer, or N members of a Kafka consumer group. Your IPC is the network protocol you already have.

Act III · Chapter 25

Six real outages

Symptom → diagnosis → code → what changed at the OS and CPU level. These are the scenarios interviews are drawn from.

CHAPTER 25Six real failures

1 · The gateway that idles at 6% CPU Hotstar-style

Symptom

p99 latency 11 s. CPU 6%. Memory fine. No errors. Downstream services report normal latency. More pods barely help.

Diagnosis

Thread dump: 200 Tomcat threads, nearly all RUNNABLE in socketRead0 — which means blocked on I/O, not computing. 200 × 300 ms = ~660 req/s ceiling; the rest queues at the accept socket.

Fix
// application.properties → spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true
@GetMapping("/watch/{id}")
public Stream watch(@PathVariable String id) {
    var meta  = catalogClient.fetch(id);      // unmounts while waiting
    var drm   = drmClient.token(id);
    var edge  = cdnClient.pick(id);
    return Stream.of(meta, drm, edge);
}
// 2 000 platform threads would need ~2 GB of stack. 20 000 virtual threads
// cost ~20 MB of heap.
At the OS/CPU level

Before: 200 kernel tasks parked in socket reads, each holding ~1 MB, caches evicted on every switch. After: 8 carriers stay resident on 8 cores with warm caches; waiting requests are heap objects in one epoll set. Kernel thread count stops growing with traffic, and throughput becomes bounded by the downstream — the correct bottleneck.

2 · Kafka lag that won't come down Swiggy order events

Symptom

Consumer lag climbing. You scale from 6 pods to 20. Lag doesn't move. The 14 new pods log nothing.

Diagnosis

The topic has 6 partitions. Within a consumer group each partition goes to exactly one consumer, so consumers 7–20 are assigned nothing. Partitions, not pods, are the unit of parallelism.

KafkaScaling.java
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", concurrency = "24")   // after raising to 24 partitions
public void consume(OrderEvent e) { process(e); }

// NEVER poll() from two threads — KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe.
// ⚠ If a batch exceeds max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 min) the broker
//   rebalances and you reprocess. Make handlers idempotent.

3 · Connection pool starvation Flipkart checkout

Symptom

SQLTransientConnectionException: request timed out after 30000ms, intermittently. The database shows low load and fast queries.

Diagnosis

200 app threads, HikariCP max 10. 190 queue in getConnection(). The thread pool was never the bottleneck — Chapter 13's narrowest pipe was.

PoolSizing.java
// More connections is NOT better — each is a backend process with its own locks.
// Postgres guidance ≈ (cores × 2) + spindles → usually 10–30.
private final Semaphore dbGate = new Semaphore(20);   // == Hikari max

<T> T withDb(Callable<T> c) throws Exception {
    if (!dbGate.tryAcquire(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) throw new TooBusyException();
    try { return c.call(); } finally { dbGate.release(); }
}
// ⚠ A JDBC Connection is NOT thread-safe. And Spring binds the transaction to
//   the CURRENT thread, so @Transactional does NOT propagate into
//   executor.submit(...) — each task needs its own transaction.

4 · The batch that got slower when parallelised

Symptom

A nightly job took 40 min. Someone added .parallel(). Now 55 min — and unrelated HTTP endpoints in the same JVM slowed down too.

Diagnosis

The pipeline does a DB lookup per row. parallelStream() uses the JVM-wide common ForkJoinPool, so blocking I/O starved every other parallel stream — including on the request path. And the round-trips, not the CPU, were always the cost.

BatchFix.java
// ✓ Separate the two kinds of work
try (var io = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    var enriched = rows.stream()
        .map(r -> io.submit(() -> withDb(() -> enrich(r))))
        .toList().stream().map(Future::resultNow).toList();

    enriched.parallelStream().map(Scorer::score).forEach(sink::write);  // pure CPU
}
// ✓ Better still: batch the lookups. 10 000 single-row queries → 10 queries of
//   1 000 rows. Removing round-trips beats parallelising them, every time.

5 · The payment gateway that started 429-ing PhonePe integration

Symptom

After migrating to virtual threads, the provider returns 429 Too Many Requests and eventually blocks the account. Nothing changed but the executor.

Diagnosis

The old newFixedThreadPool(10) was doing double duty — managing threads and silently capping outbound concurrency at 10. Removing the pool removed a rate limit nobody had written down. Now 8,000 virtual threads call at once.

RateLimit.java
private final Semaphore gateway = new Semaphore(10);   // the REAL constraint

PaymentResult charge(Card c, Money m) throws Exception {
    gateway.acquire();
    try { return providerClient.charge(c, m); } finally { gateway.release(); }
}
// Add a circuit breaker too: when the provider IS down you want to stop calling,
// not hold 8 000 threads open waiting for timeouts.
The general rule

Every implicit limit becomes explicit when you adopt virtual threads. Before migrating, list every place a small pool was quietly protecting something and replace each with a semaphore that says so.

6 · Cache stampede on deploy

Symptom

Every deploy, database CPU spikes to 100% for 90 seconds and requests time out. Steady state afterwards is fine.

Diagnosis

Chapter 9's check-then-act race at scale. On a cold cache, 2,000 concurrent requests all miss and all issue the same expensive query. One value computed 2,000 times.

Stampede.java
// ✗ 2 000 threads pass the null check simultaneously
Report r = cache.get(key);
if (r == null) { r = expensiveQuery(key); cache.put(key, r); }

// ✓ atomic PER KEY — exactly one thread computes, the rest wait for that result
Report r = cache.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> expensiveQuery(k));

// ⚠ CHM holds the bucket lock during the mapping function — and on Java 21
//   that PINS a virtual thread. For slow loads, block on a future instead:
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<Report>> inFlight
        = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
CompletableFuture<Report> load(String key) {
    return inFlight.computeIfAbsent(key, k ->
        CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> expensiveQuery(k), ioPool)
                         .whenComplete((v, e) -> inFlight.remove(k)));
}
GracefulShutdown.java — half of "deploy caused an incident"
Runtime.getRuntime().addShutdownHook(Thread.ofPlatform().unstarted(() -> {
    server.stopAcceptingNewRequests();
    pool.shutdown();
    try { if (!pool.awaitTermination(25, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) pool.shutdownNow(); }
    catch (InterruptedException e) { pool.shutdownNow(); Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
}));
// Spring Boot: server.shutdown=graceful
// Kubernetes: add a preStop sleep so the LB removes the pod BEFORE the JVM
//             starts refusing connections.

CHAPTER 28Cheat sheet

Concurrency vs parallelism?

Concurrency is a structuring property — several tasks in progress, achievable on one core by interleaving; it solves wasted waiting and fits I/O-bound work. Parallelism is an execution property — several tasks at the same instant, requiring multiple cores; it solves insufficient compute and fits CPU-bound work. Parallelism is one possible outcome of a concurrent design.

Process vs thread, and which does Java use?

A process owns an isolated address space enforced by the MMU. Threads share heap, statics and file descriptors, keeping private only a stack, program counter, registers and thread-locals. Java's concurrency is thread-based — one JVM is one process. On Linux both come from the same clone() syscall with different flags. "Multiprocessing" in Java usually means scaling identical JVMs horizontally.

Why is a context switch expensive?

The direct cost — saving and restoring registers plus scheduler bookkeeping — is only 1–5 µs. The bigger cost is indirect: the incoming thread evicts the outgoing thread's data from L1 and L2, so on resume hundreds of reads miss cache at ~250 cycles each. That's why a pool far larger than the core count reduces throughput on CPU-bound work.

What exactly is a race condition?

Correctness depending on the relative timing of threads. It needs three things at once: shared state, at least one writer, and no enforced ordering. Remove any one and it's impossible — hence the three strategies: don't share, don't mutate, or enforce order. Remember that decrementing stock is read-check-write, and preemption can land between any two steps.

volatile vs synchronized vs AtomicInteger?

volatile gives visibility and ordering but not atomicity — correct for a flag, wrong for a counter. synchronized gives mutual exclusion and visibility but may park threads in the kernel. Atomics give lock-free single-variable updates via CAS with no blocking, but the retry loop burns CPU under heavy contention, where LongAdder wins because it keeps padded per-thread cells.

Explain CAS and its downsides.

Compare-and-swap atomically sets a value to Y only if it currently equals X, else reports failure so you retry. It compiles to a single LOCK CMPXCHG — no syscall, no context switch. Downsides: retries waste CPU under contention, the cache line ping-pongs between cores, and it's vulnerable to ABA, where a value changes away and back so the CAS succeeds despite the world having moved. AtomicStampedReference adds a version to fix that.

What is happens-before?

The Java Memory Model's ordering guarantee: if A happens-before B, A's effects are visible to B and appear to have occurred first. Without such an edge, compiler, JIT and CPU may reorder legally. The edges: program order within a thread; monitor unlock before any later lock of the same monitor; volatile write before any later read; start() before the thread body; the body before join() returns; correctly-constructed final fields; and transitivity, which lets one volatile write publish everything written before it.

How do virtual threads work internally?

The stack is a continuation object on the Java heap, scheduled by a JVM-managed ForkJoinPool of carrier threads — one per core by default. To run, it's mounted: frames are copied onto a carrier's real OS stack and execute as ordinary JIT-compiled code at full speed. On a blocking call the JDK intercepts, copies frames back to the heap and unmounts, freeing the carrier instantly. The fd is registered with epoll; on readiness the continuation is resubmitted and resumes on any free carrier — often a different OS thread.

Should you pool virtual threads?

No. Pooling amortises expensive creation, and a virtual thread costs about a microsecond — pooling reintroduces the ceiling you removed. Use Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(). To limit concurrency against a downstream, use a Semaphore, which expresses the actual constraint rather than encoding it in a thread count.

What is pinning?

A virtual thread that cannot unmount from its carrier. On Java 21 this happens inside a synchronized block or a native frame. If it then blocks on I/O, the carrier blocks too — and there are only as many carriers as cores, so enough pinning stalls the application while CPU sits idle. Detect with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full or the jdk.VirtualThreadPinned JFR event; fix by converting hot synchronized blocks to ReentrantLock. JEP 491 in Java 24 largely removes it.

When would you NOT use virtual threads?

CPU-bound work — no waiting to overlap, so a fixed pool sized to cores is right. Code holding large per-thread state in ThreadLocal, since it multiplies by task count. Anywhere a small pool was deliberately rate-limiting, until you replace it with a semaphore. And hot paths still holding a monitor across blocking I/O on Java 21.

How do you size a thread pool?

Threads = cores × utilisation × (1 + wait/service). CPU-bound means threads ≈ cores; I/O-bound with 190 ms waiting and 10 ms computing on 8 cores gives about 160. But the honest answer is the pool is rarely the binding constraint — the connection pool, downstream rate limit, or database max_connections usually is. Size to the narrowest pipe and validate under load.

What's wrong with newFixedThreadPool?

It uses an unbounded queue, so tasks accumulate in memory under overload until OOM with no back-pressure. Worse, because ThreadPoolExecutor only grows past core size when the queue is full, an unbounded queue makes maximumPoolSize dead configuration. Construct ThreadPoolExecutor directly with a bounded queue, a named thread factory and an explicit rejection policy.

How do you prevent and detect deadlock?

Give every lockable resource a total order and always acquire ascending — that breaks circular wait and is checkable locally in each function. Also hold as few locks as possible, never do I/O inside one, and use tryLock with timeout and randomised backoff as a fallback. Detect with jcmd <pid> Thread.print, which explicitly reports Java-level deadlock cycles, or ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads() in a health check.

Deadlock vs livelock vs starvation?

Deadlock is a cycle of threads each waiting on a lock another holds — permanent, CPU at zero. Livelock is threads repeatedly reacting to each other without progressing — CPU at 100%, cured by randomised backoff. Starvation is one thread never getting its turn — it shows as a bad p99 rather than a hang, cured by fair locks and short critical sections.

What is false sharing?

Two threads writing different variables that share a 64-byte cache line. Coherence works at line granularity, so each write invalidates the line in the other core's cache and it ping-pongs between them despite no logical sharing. Typical in per-thread counter arrays and ring-buffer cursors. Fix with padding, @Contended, or LongAdder, whose cells are already padded.

Why can't you just add more Kafka consumers?

Within a consumer group each partition goes to exactly one consumer, so consumers beyond the partition count idle. Partitions are the unit of parallelism, and KafkaConsumer isn't thread-safe so you can't poll from several threads either. To go faster you add partitions, or poll on one thread and dispatch to workers — sacrificing per-partition ordering and forcing careful offset management.

What happens at the OS level when a Java thread blocks on I/O?

Platform thread: the read syscall traps into the kernel, the task is marked non-runnable and removed from the run queue, and the scheduler switches away. The OS thread and its ~1 MB stack sit idle until data arrives. Virtual thread: the JDK registers the fd with epoll, copies frames to the heap and unmounts, so the carrier immediately runs another virtual thread. No OS thread is parked at all — that's the whole point.

200 threads, 15% CPU, terrible latency. Diagnose it.

Low CPU with high latency means threads are blocked, not computing. Take a thread dump and read the distribution: mostly RUNNABLE in socket reads means a slow downstream; WAITING in getConnection means the JDBC pool is too small; many BLOCKED on one monitor means lock contention. The fix follows the finding — right-size the connection pool, add timeouts and a circuit breaker, shrink the critical section, or move to virtual threads. Raising the thread count before diagnosing usually makes it worse.

Mistakes that cause most real incidents

MistakeCausesInstead
Unbounded queue in a poolMemory growth then OOM, no back-pressureBounded queue + rejection policy
Guarding the write but not the readStale reads under load onlyGuard both, or make it volatile
Swallowing InterruptedExceptionShutdown hangs, JVM won't exitRestore the flag
Blocking I/O inside a lockConvoying — everything queues behind one callCompute outside, lock only to mutate
Blocking I/O in a parallel streamStarves the JVM-wide common poolOwn executor, or virtual threads for the I/O half
containsKey then putCheck-then-act race, cache stampedecomputeIfAbsent, merge
Sizing threads but not connectionsTimeouts, pool exhaustionFind the narrowest pipe first
Locking on this or a String literalOutsiders can lock you; interned strings are globalA private final Object lock
Pooling virtual threadsReinstates the ceiling you removedOne per task + Semaphore
Unnamed threadsDumps full of "Thread-42" — undiagnosableThread.ofPlatform().name("api-", 0).factory()
Testing for thread safetyFalse confidence — races hide for millions of runsReason about the three conditions
The mental model

Cores do the work; threads take turns on them. Concurrency reclaims waiting; parallelism buys capacity. Switching costs real time. Threads share everything but their stack.

The two problems

Atomicity — my multi-step operation got interrupted (lock or atomic). Visibility — my write never reached you (memory barrier). A lock fixes both; volatile only the second.

Default choices

I/O-bound → virtual threads + semaphore. CPU-bound → fixed pool = cores. Counter → LongAdder. Map → ConcurrentHashMap. Config → immutable record behind volatile.

Diagnosis kit

jcmd <pid> Thread.print · top -H -p · vmstat 1 · -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full · JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned

Where the story ends

We started with Instagram's feed wasting 93% of a request on waiting. Everything since has answered that: overlap the waits, add cores where work is real, don't over-hire, protect shared state, make sure writes are seen, agree on lock order — and finally, make the worker so cheap that a million of them waiting costs almost nothing. That last step is Java 21, and it's why the simple blocking code you'd write on day one is, once again, the right answer.

Tab 01 · Fast overview

Eleven protocols that actually matter

Every protocol here answers one of three questions: how do bytes reach the other machine, who guarantees they arrive, and what do the bytes mean. Each section is traced through a system you already use — Instagram's feed, WhatsApp's chat, PayPal's authorization, Amazon's checkout.

L3Addressing & routing — IP
L4Delivery contract — TCP, UDP, QUIC
L5/6Identity & secrecy — TLS 1.3
L7Meaning — HTTP/2, HTTP/3, WS, gRPC, Kafka, AMQP
Why HTTP/1.1 isn't a section hereIt's still on the wire (roughly a quarter of requests, mostly bots, proxies and legacy middleboxes), but nothing about it is a design decision you'd make today. It appears only where it explains HTTP/2 — as the problem HTTP/2 was built to delete.

One request, every layer

Opening Instagram traced from the tap to the pixel — with the real bytes each layer adds and who reads them.

Encapsulation · Instagram feed request, layer by layer
L3 network L4 transport L5/6 security L7 application

IP Layer 3 · Network

The postal system of the internet — addresses and routes, no promises.

What & why

IP gives every interface a globally routable address and a packet format any router can forward. Without it there is no "somewhere else" to send bytes to.

It is deliberately dumb and best-effort: packets may be dropped, duplicated, delayed or reordered. All intelligence is pushed to the endpoints — which is exactly why the internet scaled to billions of devices.

How it works

  • Sender builds a packet: src IP, dst IP, TTL, protocol number (6=TCP, 17=UDP) + payload.
  • Each router does a longest-prefix match against its routing table, decrements TTL, forwards to the next hop. It keeps no per-flow state.
  • Too big for a link's MTU → fragment, or drop with an ICMP "fragmentation needed".
  • TTL reaches 0 → packet dies and ICMP comes back. That's how traceroute draws its map.

Key characteristics

Model
Connectionless, per-packet, best effort
IPv4
32-bit, exhausted → NAT everywhere
IPv6
128-bit, no NAT, simpler header
Private
10/8, 172.16/12, 192.168/16 — your VPC
MTU
1500 B typical; ~1460 B usable by TCP payload

Real-world use case

PayPal's VPC. Payment pods live in 10.0.1.0/24, the ledger database in 10.0.9.0/24. Security groups and route tables are pure L3 rules — they match IP and port and never look at your JSON.

Amazon's edge. A shopper in Pune reaches amazon.in via anycast: the same IP is announced from dozens of locations, and BGP steers each user to the nearest one. Pure L3 load balancing, before a single TCP packet is sent.

Pune → Singapore · what each hop does, and what nobody does
Interview line"IP is a stateless, best-effort datagram service. Routers hold no per-flow state, which is why the internet scales — but it means loss, duplication and reordering are normal, not exceptional. Everything above L3 exists to compensate."

TCP Layer 4 · Transport

Turns an unreliable packet stream into a reliable, ordered byte stream — and paces itself so the network survives.

What & why

TCP sells the application one illusion: a bidirectional pipe of bytes that arrive exactly once, in order. HTTP/2, TLS, WebSocket, gRPC, Kafka, AMQP and JDBC are all built on that illusion.

It also protects the network from you. Congestion control means a million clients sharing a link converge on a fair rate instead of collapsing it.

How it works

  • Connect: SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. One full RTT before any data moves.
  • Reliability: every byte numbered; receiver ACKs; unacked data retransmitted after an RTO or 3 duplicate ACKs.
  • Ordering: out-of-order segments are buffered and released to the app only in sequence → head-of-line blocking.
  • Flow control (rwnd): "don't exceed my buffer." Congestion control (cwnd): "don't exceed the network."
  • Slow start doubles cwnd per RTT, then CUBIC/BBR takes over. A brand-new connection is slow on purpose.
  • Close: FIN/ACK each way; the closer waits ~60 s in TIME_WAIT.

Key characteristics

Guarantees
Ordered, reliable, deduplicated byte stream — no message boundaries
Setup cost
1 RTT, plus 1 more for TLS 1.3
Header
20–60 B: ports, seq, ack, flags, window
Weakness
HOL blocking; slow recovery on lossy mobile links
Limit
~28k ephemeral ports per client IP → pool your connections

Real-world use case

Amazon checkout. order-service calls payment-service 8,000 times a second. Without pooling, each call pays a handshake plus TLS — roughly 12 ms of pure setup — and leaves thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT. With a warm pool, setup cost is zero and cwnd is already large.

This is the entire reason HikariCP, connection pools and keep-alive exist: a handshake is a round trip you can only avoid by not doing it again.

Full lifecycle · handshake, slow start, loss recovery, teardown
control data / window growth acknowledgement loss & recovery
The trap they will setTCP is a byte stream, not a message stream. Two write() calls can arrive as one read; one write can arrive split in three. Every protocol above TCP invents its own framing — Content-Length, chunked encoding, HTTP/2 frame headers, Kafka's length prefix. If you build a raw TCP protocol and forget framing, it works in testing and corrupts in production.

UDP Layer 4 · Transport

A thin envelope over IP: ports and a checksum. Its value is everything it refuses to do.

What & why

UDP adds only ports (so the kernel knows which process gets the packet) and an optional checksum. No handshake, no ACKs, no ordering, no congestion control.

When late data is worthless — a voice packet, a GPS ping, a metric — retransmitting it is worse than dropping it. UDP is also the only way to build a custom transport in userspace, which is precisely what QUIC does.

How it works

  • App hands a datagram to the socket; kernel adds an 8-byte header and sends it. No state is kept.
  • Message boundaries are preserved — one send equals one receive, or nothing at all.
  • Lost, duplicated, reordered? The application decides whether it cares.
  • Supports broadcast and multicast; TCP cannot.
  • Keep datagrams under ~1200 B so they never fragment.

Key characteristics

Header
8 bytes vs TCP's 20–60
Setup
0 RTT — the first packet carries payload
Delivery
Unreliable, unordered, datagram-oriented
State
None on either side — millions of senders cost nothing
Users
QUIC/HTTP3, DNS, RTP/voice, DTLS, StatsD, syslog

Real-world use case

WhatsApp voice and video calls. Audio travels as RTP over UDP. If one 20 ms packet vanishes, the codec conceals it and you hear a tiny artefact. If TCP retransmitted it, the entire call would stall for a round trip to deliver audio that is already in the past.

Uber driver telemetry. Two million drivers pinging GPS every four seconds: over TCP that's two million live sockets and keep-alives; over UDP it's stateless datagrams, and a lost ping is superseded four seconds later by a more accurate one.

Same 2% packet loss on a WhatsApp call · TCP recovers, UDP conceals

HTTPS / TLS 1.3 Session & security

HTTPS isn't a protocol — it's HTTP inside a TLS tunnel. TLS gives you three things, and you should name all three.

What & why

Confidentiality — nobody reads it. Integrity — nobody edits it. Authentication — you're talking to the real server, proven by a CA-signed certificate.

Without the third, the first two are worthless: you'd have a perfectly private conversation with an attacker.

How it works

  • ClientHello: versions, cipher suites, SNI (which hostname), ALPN (h2/h3) and an ECDHE key share guessed upfront — this guess is what saves a round trip versus TLS 1.2.
  • ServerHello: chosen cipher + its key share. Both sides independently derive the same secret; it never crosses the wire.
  • Server sends its certificate chain and signs the transcript, proving it holds the private key. Client validates chain, hostname, expiry, revocation.
  • All application data is AEAD-encrypted (AES-GCM / ChaCha20-Poly1305) — encryption and integrity in one operation.
  • mTLS: the server demands a client certificate too — standard for bank and payments service-to-service.

Key characteristics

Cost
TLS 1.3 = 1 RTT (1.2 needed 2); 0-RTT on resume
PFS
Ephemeral keys — stealing the server key later can't decrypt yesterday
SNI
Hostname in ClientHello lets one IP serve many certs
ALPN
Negotiates h2 vs h3 vs http/1.1, free, in the handshake
Where
Terminated at ALB/CDN; mTLS re-established inside the mesh

Real-world use case

PayPal. The browser's padlock is the client verifying that the certificate for paypal.com chains to a trusted root and matches the hostname. That check — not the encryption — is what stops a lookalike domain from silently proxying your login.

Inside PayPal's cluster, payment-svc presents its own certificate to ledger-svc, which authorizes on the certificate's identity rather than the source IP. A compromised pod elsewhere still can't post a journal entry.

TLS 1.3 handshake · what is sent, what is encrypted, what is verified
Common misconceptionTLS does not hide who you talk to. The destination IP, and classically the SNI hostname, are visible on the wire. It hides what you say, not whom you say it to.

HTTP/2 Layer 7 · Application

Same semantics as HTTP/1.1, new wire format: binary frames multiplexed over one TCP connection. Still the majority of real web traffic.

What & why

HTTP/1.1 could carry one request at a time per connection, so browsers opened six sockets per origin and still queued. HTTP/2 keeps methods, status codes and headers identical and replaces only the encoding.

Result: one connection per origin, hundreds of concurrent requests, one TLS handshake, one warm congestion window — and no application code changes.

How it works

  • Binary framing: everything is a typed frame (HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM, PING) tagged with a stream ID.
  • Streams: each request/response is an independent stream; frames from different streams interleave freely on one socket.
  • HPACK: a shared dynamic table means a repeated header costs an index byte instead of the full string.
  • Flow control per stream and per connection; RST_STREAM cancels one request without killing the connection.
  • Negotiated during TLS via ALPN (h2). Server push existed and is now dead — mention it, don't recommend it.

Key characteristics

Concurrency
~100 streams on one socket by default
Headers
HPACK cuts repeated header bytes ~85–90%
Still TCP
Transport HOL remains — one lost segment stalls every stream
Reality
Browsers require TLS; ~52% of all requests today
Bonus
Long-lived bidirectional streams — the foundation gRPC is built on

Real-world use case

Instagram feed load. One screen pulls 60+ resources: feed JSON, stories ring, avatars, thumbnails, like counts. Over HTTP/1.1 that's six connections, six handshakes and a queue; over h2 it's one connection with 60 interleaved streams and one handshake.

Amazon's internal mesh. Service-to-service gRPC rides h2, so thousands of concurrent RPCs share a single warm connection between two pods instead of thrashing a socket pool.

Instagram feed · HTTP/1.1 six connections vs HTTP/2 one connection
handshake / blocked API + avatars stories + thumbs large media completed faster
The one thing HTTP/2 could not fix · TCP still delivers strictly in order
Interview line"HTTP/2 eliminated head-of-line blocking at the HTTP layer but inherited it from TCP. On a clean datacentre link that's irrelevant; on a lossy 4G link it's the dominant cost — which is exactly the gap HTTP/3 was designed to close."

HTTP/3 + QUIC L4 in userspace L7

The newest version. Rebuilds transport on UDP so streams are genuinely independent — and connections survive changing networks.

What & why

HTTP/2's remaining flaw is TCP, and TCP lives in the kernel where nobody can iterate on it. QUIC re-implements transport in userspace over UDP: reliability, ordering, congestion control and TLS 1.3, fused into one protocol.

HTTP/3 is HTTP semantics mapped onto QUIC streams. Two headline wins: no transport head-of-line blocking and connection migration.

How it works

  • Every QUIC stream has its own sequence space — loss on stream 3 never blocks stream 5.
  • TLS 1.3 is built in, not layered on: handshake and crypto complete in 1 RTT, or 0-RTT on resumption.
  • Connections are keyed by a Connection ID, not the IP/port 4-tuple — so changing network keeps the session alive.
  • QPACK replaces HPACK, designed to tolerate out-of-order delivery.
  • Discovered via Alt-Svc: h3=":443" or a DNS HTTPS record; silently falls back to h2 where UDP is blocked.

Key characteristics

Transport
UDP + QUIC in userspace — upgradeable without kernel changes
Handshake
1 RTT, or 0-RTT on resume (replay-unsafe for writes)
HOL
Eliminated at the transport level
Mobility
Connection migration across IP changes
Cost
More CPU (userspace crypto); ~20% of requests, and some networks throttle UDP

Real-world use case

WhatsApp on a moving train. The phone hands over between towers, so its IP changes repeatedly. Over TCP each change kills the connection and forces a fresh handshake mid-chat; over QUIC the Connection ID keeps the session and its crypto state alive.

Instagram on 4G. Loss is high, so under h2 a single dropped segment stalls every image at once. Under h3 only the affected image pauses, and the rest of the feed keeps painting.

QUIC · the stack it replaces, the round trips it saves, the stalls it removes
Connection migration · WhatsApp keeps the session when the network changes
Interview line"HTTP/2 solved head-of-line blocking at the application layer; HTTP/3 solves it at the transport layer by giving each stream its own sequence space inside QUIC. The price is userspace CPU and UDP-hostile middleboxes — which is why HTTP/3 is newest but HTTP/2 still carries more traffic."

WebSockets Layer 7 · Application

Upgrade one HTTP request, then keep a full-duplex message pipe open for hours.

What & why

HTTP is client-initiated: the server can't speak first. Polling wastes requests, long-polling wastes connections. WebSocket upgrades a single HTTP request into a persistent, bidirectional, message-oriented channel on the same TCP socket.

It starts as HTTP on port 443 so it survives proxies and firewalls — then stops being HTTP entirely.

How it works

  • Client sends GET /ws with Upgrade: websocket and a Sec-WebSocket-Key.
  • Server replies 101 Switching Protocols with the hashed accept value. The socket is now a WebSocket.
  • Data travels as frames with an opcode (text/binary/ping/pong/close). Message boundaries are preserved, unlike raw TCP.
  • Either side may send at any time. Ping/pong stops NAT and proxies reaping an idle socket.
  • Scaling out needs a broker: a connection is pinned to one pod, so a message for a user on another pod must be relayed.

Key characteristics

Duplex
Full — server push without a request
Overhead
2–14 B frame header vs ~700 B of HTTP headers
State
Stateful — sticky routing, reconnects, backpressure
Scheme
wss:// in production, always
Alternative
SSE if you only need server→client; simpler, auto-reconnects

Real-world use case

WhatsApp Web. Messages, typing indicators, read receipts and presence all arrive unprompted. A 2-second poll from 10M clients would be 5M req/s of mostly-empty responses; a WebSocket sends bytes only when something actually happened.

Amazon live order tracking and Instagram live-stream comments use the same shape: one long-lived socket, server pushes, client reconnects with a cursor.

Polling vs WebSocket · and the frame that replaces 700 bytes of headers
WhatsApp at scale · the six steps a message takes between two pods

DNS Layer 7 · Application

A globally distributed, cache-heavy key-value store — and the first hop of literally every request.

What & why

Humans and configs use names; IP needs addresses. DNS is the indirection that lets you move, scale and fail over infrastructure without changing a single client.

It's also a traffic-steering tool: weighted, latency-based, geo and failover routing all happen here, long before your service sees a packet.

How it works

  • Stub resolver → recursive resolver (ISP, 8.8.8.8, or your VPC's .2 address) which does the walking.
  • Root → TLD (.com) → authoritative nameserver, each returning a referral until an answer appears.
  • Every answer carries a TTL. TTL is simultaneously your failover speed and your stale-record risk.
  • Runs over UDP:53, falling back to TCP for large answers. DoT/DoH encrypt it.
  • Records: A/AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT, SRV (host+port), NS, SOA.

Key characteristics

Model
Hierarchical, delegated, eventually consistent
Caching
Four layers deep: browser, OS, JVM, resolver
TTL
60 s is the common compromise between agility and load
JVM trap
Old defaults cache a successful lookup forever
K8s
CoreDNS: svc.ns.svc.cluster.local; headless returns pod IPs

Real-world use case

Amazon multi-region failover. Route 53 health-checks both regions and stops returning the unhealthy one. With a 60-second TTL, a regional outage drains in about a minute — no deploy, no client change.

Inside any Kubernetes cluster, calling http://ledger-svc:8080 works because CoreDNS resolves it to the current ClusterIP, letting pods be rescheduled freely underneath.

Cold resolution vs cached · and the four caches that can lie to you
Production trapOlder JVMs cache successful lookups permanently (networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1). After a Route 53 failover your pods keep hammering the dead IP until someone restarts them. Set -Dnetworkaddress.cache.ttl=30 and negative.ttl=0.

gRPC RPC over HTTP/2

Contract-first, binary, streaming RPC — the default for internal service-to-service calls.

What & why

REST+JSON is right at the edge and wasteful in the middle: text parsing, no enforced schema, no streaming, hand-written clients. gRPC declares the API in a .proto file, generates typed stubs in every language, and serializes with Protocol Buffers.

Riding HTTP/2 gives it multiplexing and long-lived bidirectional streams for free.

How it works

  • .proto → protoc → stubs. A remote call looks like a local method call.
  • Each RPC is one HTTP/2 stream: path /pkg.Service/Method, metadata in headers, length-prefixed protobuf in DATA, status in trailers.
  • Four modes: unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, bidirectional.
  • Built-in deadlines that propagate across hops, cancellation, retries, interceptors for auth and tracing.
  • Schema evolution: add fields with new tag numbers; never reuse or renumber a tag.

Key characteristics

Payload
Binary protobuf — typically 3–10× smaller than JSON
Transport
HTTP/2, one warm connection per peer
Contract
Compile-time enforced across languages
Weakness
Not browser-native, not curl-friendly, opaque on the wire
Balancing
L4 LBs pin long-lived h2 conns → use client-side LB or a mesh

Real-world use case

Amazon checkout fan-out. One POST /checkout triggers pricing, tax, fraud and inventory calls inside a 300 ms budget. Protobuf over one multiplexed connection removes both serialization cost and pool churn.

Uber driver channel. Bidirectional streaming: drivers push GPS continuously while the server pushes ride offers down the same stream — one connection instead of a poll loop plus a push channel.

gRPC · wire size, call types, and the deadline that saves the request budget

Kafka Binary protocol over TCP

A distributed, replicated, append-only log. Not a queue — a re-readable event stream.

What & why

Kafka's core idea is that consuming doesn't delete. Messages append to a partitioned log and are retained by time or size; each consumer group tracks its own offset. Ten teams read the same event independently, and a new team can replay from the beginning.

That makes it the backbone for event-driven cores, CDC, stream processing and audit trails — not just background jobs.

How it works

  • Topic → N partitions, each an ordered immutable log on disk. Ordering is guaranteed per partition only.
  • Producer picks the partition by hash(key) — same key means same partition means ordered per entity.
  • Each partition has a leader plus followers; acks=all waits for the in-sync replica set.
  • Consumer group: each partition goes to exactly one consumer in the group, so parallelism is capped by partition count.
  • Speed comes from sequential disk writes, zero-copy sendfile, batching and compression.

Key characteristics

Model
Pull-based durable log, replayable
Ordering
Per partition (per key), never global
Delivery
At-least-once by default; exactly-once inside Kafka via transactions
Throughput
Millions of msg/s; scale by adding partitions
Weak at
Per-message routing, priorities, per-message TTL

Real-world use case

Amazon order pipeline. One order.placed event feeds payments, inventory, warehouse, notifications, fraud scoring and the analytics lake — each as its own consumer group. Adding loyalty points next quarter means adding a consumer, not touching the producer.

Instagram engagement. Every like and comment is an event; the feed ranker, notification service and analytics all replay the same stream at their own pace.

The log, the key, the groups · and why replay is the feature queues can't copy

RabbitMQ / AMQP Binary protocol over TCP

A smart broker with real routing: exchanges, bindings, queues, acks, delays and dead letters.

What & why

Kafka is a dumb log with smart consumers; RabbitMQ is a smart broker with dumb consumers. It excels at task distribution: give work to whoever is free, retry on failure, park it in a dead-letter queue if it keeps failing, delete it once acked.

Its routing model is genuinely expressive — per-message routing keys, priorities, TTLs, delayed delivery. Kafka does none of these natively.

How it works

  • Publish to an exchange with a routing key. Exchanges store nothing.
  • Bindings connect exchange to queue: direct (exact), topic (payment.*), fanout (broadcast), headers.
  • Messages are pushed to consumers up to a prefetch limit; consumers ack on success, nack on failure.
  • Nack/reject/expire routes the message to a dead-letter exchange. Pair that with a TTL queue and you get backoff retries with zero application state.
  • Publisher confirms + durable queues + persistent messages = no silent loss. Quorum queues replicate via Raft.

Key characteristics

Model
Push-based queue, deleted after ack
Routing
Rich, per-message, decided by the broker
Ordering
Only with one consumer per queue
Throughput
Tens of thousands msg/s — an order below Kafka
Superpower
Retry, DLQ, priority and TTL semantics for free

Real-world use case

PayPal capture retries. A capture call to an acquiring bank times out on ~2% of attempts. The message is nacked into a 30-second delay queue, dead-letters back to the work queue and retries. After five attempts it parks in a DLQ for ops. No cron, no retry_count column.

Amazon invoice and email generation is the same shape: one worker should do this once, not everyone should read it.

Routing, then the retry ladder · PayPal capture
DimensionKafkaRabbitMQ / AMQP
Mental modelDurable, replayable logTransient work queue
After consumptionStays until retention expiresDeleted on ack
DeliveryConsumer pulls at its own paceBroker pushes up to prefetch
RoutingTopic + partition key onlyDirect / topic / fanout / headers, per message
Retry & DLQYou build it (retry topics)Built in (nack, TTL, DLX)
OrderingGuaranteed per partitionOnly with one consumer per queue
ScaleMillions/s via partitionsTens of thousands/s per queue
Choose whenEvent streaming, many independent consumers, replay, CDC, analyticsTask queues, per-message routing, priority, complex retry

Synchronous vs asynchronous Architecture

The most reused question in system design. Answer it with coupling, not with speed.

Synchronous

HTTP · gRPC unary · JDBC. Caller blocks until the callee answers. Simple, immediately consistent, easy to debug.

Availability = A₁ × A₂ × A₃

Three 99.9% dependencies in a chain give 99.7%. Every hop adds latency and failure probability.

Asynchronous

Kafka · RabbitMQ. Caller hands the message to a broker and returns. The consumer works later, possibly much later.

Producer up + broker up = accepted

Consumer downtime becomes lag, not an outage. Cost: eventual consistency and no natural response.

The real rule

Sync when the user's next screen depends on the answer — payment authorization, seat availability, login.

Async when it merely must happen — invoice email, warehouse pick, loyalty points, search reindex.

Most real flows are both: sync for the decision, async for the consequences.

Amazon checkout, both ways · same business logic, very different failure behaviour
PatternProtocolDirectionCouplingUse when
Request/responseHTTP/2, gRPC unaryClient → ServerTemporal + availabilityYou need the answer to continue
Long-lived duplexWebSocket, gRPC bidiBoth ways, anytimeSession-bound (sticky)Chat, live tracking, tickers, collab
Server push onlySSEServer → ClientLoose, HTTP-nativeNotifications, progress, feeds
Pub/sub logKafkaProducer → many groupsVery loose, replayableEvent-driven core, fan-out, CDC
Work queueRabbitMQ/AMQPProducer → one workerLoose, transientRetryable jobs, routing, priority
Say this in the interview"I make a call synchronous only when the caller cannot proceed without the result. Everything else becomes an event, because synchronous coupling multiplies failure probability and latency, while asynchronous coupling converts a downstream outage into consumer lag."

One-screen decision table

NeedReach forBecause

Broadcast an event to many teams, replayableKafkaRetained log, independent consumer offsets
