Find a service without hardcoding IPsDNSIndirection + TTL-based failover
Prove who is calling, not just encryptmTLSIdentity from the certificate, not the source IP
Tab 02 · Implementation

The mechanisms that actually decide behaviour

Not every protocol needs code. IP, TCP and UDP show up as configuration and failure modes, never as classes you write. What genuinely deserves implementation depth is what happens between the socket and your controller: connection handling, segment and frame processing, multiplexing, and the messaging patterns built on top.

Boot 3.xJava 21 · Spring Framework 6
TomcatNIO connector, blocking servlets
NettyWebFlux · gRPC · QUIC paths

IP, TCP and UDP: no implementation, only consequences L3 / L4

You never write these protocols. You configure them — and you get paged when the configuration is wrong.

LayerWhere it surfaces in a Spring Boot appThe failure it causes when ignored
IP Bind address, VPC/security-group reachability, and the real client IP behind proxies (server.forward-headers-strategy: native + trusted proxy ranges) Rate limiter sees the load balancer's IP, so it throttles every user on the planet as one client
TCP Connection pools (maxConnPerRoute, HikariCP), connect and read timeouts, keep-alive, Tomcat threads.max and accept-count No read timeout → every worker thread parks in read() → a slow downstream becomes your outage
UDP Metrics export (StatsD:8125), DNS lookups, QUIC at the edge, occasionally a telemetry listener Datagrams over ~1200 B fragment; a single lost fragment silently discards the whole message

The only TCP config that matters

application.yml
server:
  tomcat:
    threads: { max: 200, min-spare: 20 }
    accept-count: 100          # OS backlog once all threads are busy
    max-connections: 8192      # sockets held open
    keep-alive-timeout: 60s    # reuse beats re-handshaking
  forward-headers-strategy: native
spring:
  datasource:
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20    # connections = throughput × latency
      connection-timeout: 3000
      max-lifetime: 1800000    # recycle before the LB reaps them

Sizing, not guessing

Little's Law: connections = throughput × latency.

500 rps at 40 ms → 20 concurrent calls → pool of ~25. An oversized pool doesn't speed anything up; it just hides a slow downstream until the database runs out of connections.

connectTimeout 2s socketTimeout 3s evict idle 30s circuit breaker around it
The classic outage, in one sentenceA downstream stops responding but never closes the socket; with no socketTimeout, all 200 Tomcat threads block inside read(), the accept queue fills, health checks fail, and Kubernetes restarts a pod that was never broken.

Connection handling Tomcat NIO internals

What happens between the TCP handshake and your @GetMapping — and why threads.max is your real concurrency limit.

Real-world use case

Amazon product API during a sale. 20,000 sockets are open but only a few hundred requests are active at any instant. Tomcat can hold all 20,000 because idle keep-alive connections cost a selector registration, not a thread — but the moment each one sends a request, only threads.max of them can be processed concurrently.

Tomcat NIO · acceptor, poller and worker — three different bottlenecks
selector — scales with memory worker threads — the real ceiling reuse teardown cost
application.ymlJava 21 — remove the thread ceiling entirely
spring:
  threads:
    virtual:
      enabled: true      # each request gets a virtual thread, not a pooled platform one
server:
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 200           # now largely irrelevant for I/O-bound work
  shutdown: graceful
ConnectionInsight.javaobserve the pool before you tune it
@Component
public class ConnectionInsight {

    /**
     * The three numbers that tell you whether you have a connection problem
     * or a downstream problem. Scrape them before changing any config.
     */
    ConnectionInsight(MeterRegistry registry, TomcatWebServer server) {

        Gauge.builder("tomcat.threads.busy", server,
                s -> ((AbstractProtocol<?>) s.getTomcat().getConnector()
                        .getProtocolHandler()).getExecutor() instanceof ThreadPoolExecutor tpe
                        ? tpe.getActiveCount() : 0)
             .description("Workers blocked right now — approaching threads.max means queuing")
             .register(registry);
    }
}

// What each metric actually tells you:
//   tomcat.threads.busy   → near max?  requests are queuing, not failing (yet)
//   hikaricp.connections.pending → > 0? the DB pool, not Tomcat, is the bottleneck
//   http.server.requests p99 vs p50 gap → a queue exists somewhere upstream of the CPU
Why virtual threads change the shapeWith platform threads, 200 concurrent slow requests exhaust the pool. With virtual threads, a blocked call parks the virtual thread and frees the carrier — so concurrency is bounded by memory and downstream capacity instead of an arbitrary pool size. Caveat: unbounded concurrency downstream is its own outage, so keep a semaphore or circuit breaker around the slow dependency.

Segment & frame processing Socket → request object

The single most useful mental model to own: TCP hands you an arbitrary pile of bytes, and every layer above re-cuts it into its own units.

Real-world use case

Instagram feed request over HTTP/2. One read() from the socket returns 2,914 bytes. That is not "a request". It's the tail of a previous TLS record, one complete record containing two HTTP/2 frames, and 40 bytes of a third frame that hasn't finished arriving. Every layer must handle "partial" as a normal case.

One read() from the socket · four re-framings on the way to your controller
FramingDemo.javathe lesson, in code you could actually write
/**
 * Why every protocol above TCP invents framing.
 * This is the bug people ship when they build a raw TCP protocol.
 */
class NaiveHandler {
    void wrong(SocketChannel ch) throws IOException {
        var buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(4096);
        ch.read(buf);
        // ✕ ASSUMES one read() == one message.
        // In production this splits a JSON object in half, or glues two together.
        handle(new String(buf.array(), 0, buf.position()));
    }
}

class LengthPrefixedHandler {
    private final ByteBuffer acc = ByteBuffer.allocate(64 * 1024);

    void right(SocketChannel ch) throws IOException {
        ch.read(acc);                       // may be partial, may be several messages
        acc.flip();
        while (acc.remaining() >= 4) {      // ✓ length prefix = self-delimiting
            acc.mark();
            int len = acc.getInt();
            if (acc.remaining() < len) { acc.reset(); break; }  // wait for the rest
            byte[] msg = new byte[len];
            acc.get(msg);
            handle(new String(msg, StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
        }
        acc.compact();                      // keep the partial tail for the next read
    }
}

// HTTP/1.1 solves this with Content-Length / chunked encoding.
// HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 solve it with a fixed-size frame header.
// Kafka and gRPC solve it with an explicit length prefix — exactly the code above.
Interview line"TCP delivers an ordered byte stream with no message boundaries, so every protocol above it defines framing — Content-Length in HTTP/1.1, a 9-byte frame header in HTTP/2, a length prefix in gRPC and Kafka. A parser that assumes one read equals one message passes every test and corrupts data under load."

HTTP/2 in Spring Boot Multiplexing

Two lines to enable on the server. The part people miss is the client, which silently stays on HTTP/1.1.

Real-world use case

Instagram-style feed BFF. One screen fires 30–60 backend calls. Over h2 they share one connection with interleaved streams, ~85% fewer header bytes and one TLS handshake — and with virtual threads you can issue them all concurrently without a thread pool.

Server — enable and verify

application.yml
server:
  http2:
    enabled: true       # ALPN negotiates h2 during the TLS handshake
  ssl:
    enabled: true       # browsers require TLS for h2
    bundle: server
spring:
  ssl:
    bundle:
      pem:
        server:
          keystore:
            certificate: classpath:certs/tls.crt
            private-key: classpath:certs/tls.key
verify.sh
curl -I --http2 https://localhost:8443/api/feed -v 2>&1 \
  | grep -iE "ALPN|HTTP/2"
# ALPN: server accepted h2
# HTTP/2 200          ← if this says HTTP/1.1, ALPN failed

Client — the half everyone forgets

Http2ClientConfig.java
@Bean
RestClient feedClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {
    // Apache HttpClient 4/5 defaults to HTTP/1.1.
    // The JDK client negotiates h2 via ALPN out of the box.
    var jdk = java.net.http.HttpClient.newBuilder()
        .version(java.net.http.HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
        .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
        .build();

    return builder
        .baseUrl("https://feed.internal")
        .requestFactory(new JdkClientHttpRequestFactory(jdk))
        .build();
}

Enabling h2 only on the server buys you nothing for service-to-service traffic — both ends must speak it.

FeedController.javamultiplexing is free — actually use it
@RestController
public class FeedController {

    private final RestClient client;
    FeedController(RestClient feedClient) { this.client = feedClient; }

    @GetMapping("/api/feed/{userId}")
    public FeedResponse feed(@PathVariable String userId) {

        // 4 real HTTP calls · 4 HTTP/2 streams · ONE socket · 4 virtual threads.
        // Total latency ≈ the slowest call, not the sum.
        try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
            var posts   = scope.fork(() -> get("/posts?u=" + userId, PostList.class));
            var stories = scope.fork(() -> get("/stories?u=" + userId, StoryList.class));
            var profile = scope.fork(() -> get("/profile/" + userId, Profile.class));
            var suggest = scope.fork(() -> get("/suggest?u=" + userId, Suggestions.class));

            scope.join().throwIfFailed();
            return new FeedResponse(posts.get(), stories.get(), profile.get(), suggest.get());
        } catch (Exception e) {
            throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.BAD_GATEWAY, "feed unavailable", e);
        }
    }

    private <T> T get(String uri, Class<T> type) {
        return client.get().uri(uri).retrieve().body(type);
    }
}
Inside the app · four calls, one connection, and where the LB can ruin it

HTTP/3 in Spring Boot Edge termination

The honest production answer: you terminate QUIC at the edge and change nothing in Tomcat. Saying that is the strong answer.

Real-world use case

Amazon order tracking on Indian mobile networks. Enabling h3 at CloudFront cut tail latency on lossy links and stopped connections dying at every tower handover — with zero application changes, because the CDN speaks h3 to phones and h2 to the origin.

Where h3 is actually turned on

edge — nginx / CloudFront / Envoy
listen 443 quic reuseport;        # UDP/443 — HTTP/3
listen 443 ssl;                   # TCP/443 — HTTP/2 fallback
http3 on;
add_header Alt-Svc 'h3=":443"; ma=86400';
proxy_pass https://order-svc.internal:8443;   # origin stays h2

Why not in Tomcat

Tomcat has no HTTP/3 support. Only the reactive Netty stack can terminate QUIC, via incubating codecs plus a native binary — fine for a demo, not something to volunteer as a production design.

tomcat — h1, h2 only netty — h3 incubating edge — the real answer
Http3Support.javawhat your Boot app genuinely contributes
/** 1. Advertise h3 so clients upgrade on their next request. */
@Component
class Http3Advertiser extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        res.setHeader("Alt-Svc", "h3=\":443\"; ma=86400");
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }
}

/** 2. Refuse 0-RTT early data for anything that mutates state. */
@Component
class ZeroRttGuard extends OncePerRequestFilter {

    private static final Set<String> SAFE = Set.of("GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS");

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        // QUIC 0-RTT payloads are replayable by an attacker. A replayed GET is
        // harmless; a replayed POST /payments charges the customer twice.
        if ("1".equals(req.getHeader("Early-Data")) && !SAFE.contains(req.getMethod())) {
            res.setStatus(425);            // 425 Too Early → client retries post-handshake
            return;
        }
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }
}
Where the protocol actually changes · and where the benefit actually lands

HTTPS / mTLS in Spring Boot Identity

Server TLS is config. mTLS is the part worth knowing — it turns "which IP called me" into "which service called me".

Real-world use case

PayPal ledger writes. Public traffic terminates TLS at the ALB. Inside the cluster, payment-svc presents a client certificate to ledger-svc, which authorizes on the certificate identity rather than the source IP. A compromised pod in another namespace still cannot post a journal entry.

Server — require a client certificate

application.yml — ledger-svc
server:
  port: 8443
  ssl:
    enabled: true
    key-store: classpath:ledger-keystore.p12
    key-store-password: ${KEYSTORE_PASSWORD}
    key-store-type: PKCS12
    client-auth: need              # need | want | none  ← this is mTLS
    trust-store: classpath:internal-ca-truststore.p12
    trust-store-password: ${TRUSTSTORE_PASSWORD}
    enabled-protocols: TLSv1.3,TLSv1.2

Client — present one

application.yml — payment-svc
spring:
  ssl:
    bundle:
      jks:
        ledger:
          key: { alias: payment-svc }
          keystore:
            location: classpath:payment-keystore.p12
            password: ${KEYSTORE_PASSWORD}
          truststore:
            location: classpath:internal-ca-truststore.p12
            password: ${TRUSTSTORE_PASSWORD}
          reload-on-update: true      # short-lived certs rotate without a restart
LedgerSecurity.javaauthorize on certificate identity, not on network position
@Configuration
public class LedgerClientConfig {
    @Bean
    RestClient ledgerClient(RestClient.Builder builder, SslBundles bundles) {
        var settings = ClientHttpRequestFactorySettings.defaults()
                .withSslBundle(bundles.getBundle("ledger"));   // sends our client cert
        return builder.baseUrl("https://ledger-svc:8443")
                .requestFactory(ClientHttpRequestFactoryBuilder.detect().build(settings))
                .build();
    }
}

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
class LedgerSecurity {
    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .x509(x -> x.subjectPrincipalRegex("CN=(.*?)(?:,|$)")    // CN becomes the username
                        .userDetailsService(cn -> new User(cn, "",
                                List.of(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_SERVICE")))))
            .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health").permitAll()
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/ledger/entries").access(
                    (auth, ctx) -> new AuthorizationDecision(
                            "payment-svc".equals(auth.get().getName())))
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .build();
    }
}
Operational realitymTLS is easy to enable and hard to run — certificate rotation is the failure mode. Either issue short-lived certs from cert-manager/Vault and reload the SSL bundle, or let a service-mesh sidecar do mTLS transparently and keep it out of your application entirely.

WebSockets in Spring Boot STOMP

STOMP over WebSocket gives you routing, subscriptions and a broker abstraction so you're not hand-rolling a message protocol.

Real-world use case

WhatsApp-style 1:1 chat. Amit's socket lives on pod-1, Raj's on pod-2. Pod-1 must deliver to a socket it does not own. The answer is always the same shape: authenticate once at CONNECT, route by user, relay across pods through a broker.

Dependencies

pom.xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-websocket</artifactId>
</dependency>

The ingress must allow the upgrade

ingress
proxy_http_version 1.1;
proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
proxy_read_timeout 3600s;        # or the LB reaps idle sockets
nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/affinity: "cookie"   # stickiness
WebSocketConfig.javaendpoint · broker · authenticate at CONNECT
@Configuration
@EnableWebSocketMessageBroker
public class WebSocketConfig implements WebSocketMessageBrokerConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void registerStompEndpoints(StompEndpointRegistry registry) {
        registry.addEndpoint("/ws")                       // the HTTP → 101 upgrade URL
                .setAllowedOriginPatterns("https://*.chat.com");
    }

    @Override
    public void configureMessageBroker(MessageBrokerRegistry registry) {
        registry.setApplicationDestinationPrefixes("/app");   // client → server
        registry.setUserDestinationPrefix("/user");           // per-user routing
        // Single pod only:
        // registry.enableSimpleBroker("/topic", "/queue");
        // Multi-pod — the message crosses pods through the broker:
        registry.enableStompBrokerRelay("/topic", "/queue")
                .setRelayHost("rabbitmq").setRelayPort(61613);
    }

    @Override
    public void configureClientInboundChannel(ChannelRegistration reg) {
        reg.interceptors(new ChannelInterceptor() {
            @Override public Message<?> preSend(Message<?> msg, MessageChannel ch) {
                var acc = MessageHeaderAccessor.getAccessor(msg, StompHeaderAccessor.class);
                // There are no per-message HTTP headers — authenticate ONCE, at upgrade.
                if (StompCommand.CONNECT.equals(acc.getCommand())) {
                    acc.setUser(JwtUtils.toPrincipal(acc.getFirstNativeHeader("Authorization")));
                }
                return msg;
            }
        });
    }
}
ChatController.javapersist first, deliver second
@Controller
public class ChatController {

    private final SimpMessagingTemplate messaging;
    private final ChatService chat;

    ChatController(SimpMessagingTemplate messaging, ChatService chat) {
        this.messaging = messaging; this.chat = chat;
    }

    @MessageMapping("/chat.send")                       // client sends to /app/chat.send
    public void send(@Payload ChatMessage msg, Principal sender) {
        var saved = chat.persist(msg.withFrom(sender.getName()));   // durable BEFORE delivery

        // Routed to /user/{recipient}/queue/messages on whichever pod owns that session
        messaging.convertAndSendToUser(msg.to(), "/queue/messages", saved);
        messaging.convertAndSendToUser(sender.getName(), "/queue/ack",
                new Ack(saved.id(), "DELIVERED"));
    }

    @MessageMapping("/chat.typing")
    public void typing(@Payload TypingEvent e, Principal sender) {
        messaging.convertAndSendToUser(e.to(), "/queue/typing",
                new TypingEvent(sender.getName(), true));   // ephemeral, never persisted
    }

    @EventListener
    public void onDisconnect(SessionDisconnectEvent event) {
        chat.markOffline(event.getUser().getName());
    }
}
Pre-empt the follow-up"What if the socket drops mid-send?" — persist before delivering, give every message a client-generated id, and have the client re-sync from lastMessageId on reconnect. The socket is a transport, never the source of truth.

gRPC in Spring Boot RPC

Contract in .proto, stubs generated at build time, server on its own port.

Real-world use case

Amazon checkout under a 300 ms budget. checkout-svc calls pricing on every request. Protobuf plus one warm HTTP/2 connection removes both serialization cost and pool churn, and the propagated deadline means a slow dependency is cancelled instead of blowing the whole budget.

Dependencies

pom.xml
<dependency>
  <groupId>net.devh</groupId>
  <artifactId>grpc-server-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>net.devh</groupId>
  <artifactId>grpc-client-spring-boot-starter</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- protobuf-maven-plugin compiles src/main/proto into stubs -->

Configuration

application.yml
grpc:
  server:
    port: 9090                  # separate from server.port (HTTP 8080)
  client:
    pricing-svc:
      address: 'dns:///pricing-svc:9090'   # DNS-based client-side LB
      negotiation-type: plaintext          # tls inside a mesh
      enable-keep-alive: true
      deadline: 200ms
pricing.protoboth services compile against this
syntax = "proto3";
package pricing;
option java_multiple_files = true;
option java_package = "com.shop.pricing.grpc";

service PricingService {
  rpc Quote (QuoteRequest) returns (QuoteResponse);              // unary
  rpc StreamSurge (SurgeRequest) returns (stream SurgeUpdate);   // server streaming
}

message QuoteRequest {
  string cart_id = 1;
  string customer_id = 2;
  string postcode = 3;      // add field 4 later — never renumber 1-3
}

message QuoteResponse {
  int64 total_paise = 1;
  int64 tax_paise = 2;
  string quote_id = 3;
}
PricingGrpcService.java + CheckoutService.java
@GrpcService
public class PricingGrpcService extends PricingServiceGrpc.PricingServiceImplBase {

    private final FareCalculator calculator;
    PricingGrpcService(FareCalculator calculator) { this.calculator = calculator; }

    @Override
    public void quote(QuoteRequest req, StreamObserver<QuoteResponse> obs) {
        // Caller already gave up? Don't burn CPU on an answer nobody will read.
        if (Context.current().isCancelled()) {
            obs.onError(Status.CANCELLED.asRuntimeException());
            return;
        }
        var q = calculator.quote(req.getCartId(), req.getPostcode());
        obs.onNext(QuoteResponse.newBuilder()
                .setTotalPaise(q.total()).setTaxPaise(q.tax()).setQuoteId(q.id()).build());
        obs.onCompleted();
    }
}

@Service
class CheckoutService {

    @GrpcClient("pricing-svc")
    private PricingServiceGrpc.PricingServiceBlockingStub pricing;

    public Quote price(Cart cart) {
        return pricing
            .withDeadlineAfter(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)   // propagates to every deeper hop
            .quote(QuoteRequest.newBuilder()
                    .setCartId(cart.id())
                    .setCustomerId(cart.customerId())
                    .setPostcode(cart.postcode())
                    .build())
            .pipe(Quote::from);
    }
}
Expose bothA common production shape: gRPC on 9090 for internal callers, REST on 8080 for the mobile BFF and for humans with curl. Same service beans behind both — only the transport adapter differs.

Kafka in Spring Boot Events

KafkaTemplate to publish, @KafkaListener to consume. The hard parts are ordering, idempotency and retries.

Real-world use case

Amazon order placement. order-svc publishes one order.placed event; payments, inventory, notifications, warehouse and analytics each consume it as an independent group. Adding a loyalty-points consumer requires no change to the producer at all.

Producer

application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: kafka-1:9092,kafka-2:9092,kafka-3:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.JsonSerializer
      acks: all                          # all in-sync replicas
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true         # no duplicates on internal retry
        linger.ms: 10                    # batch for throughput
        compression.type: lz4

Consumer

application.yml
spring:
  kafka:
    consumer:
      group-id: payment-service
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      enable-auto-commit: false          # commit AFTER the work succeeds
      max-poll-records: 100
    listener:
      ack-mode: manual_immediate
      concurrency: 3                     # ≤ partition count
OrderEventProducer.java + PaymentListener.javakey = ordering · dedupe = correctness
@Service
public class OrderEventProducer {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafka;
    OrderEventProducer(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafka) { this.kafka = kafka; }

    public void publish(Order order) {
        // The key decides the partition. Same orderId → same partition → strict order,
        // so order.cancelled can never be processed before order.placed.
        kafka.send("order.placed", order.id(), OrderPlaced.from(order))
             .whenComplete((res, ex) -> {
                 if (ex != null) outbox.markPending(order.id());
                 else log.info("published {} → p{} offset {}", order.id(),
                         res.getRecordMetadata().partition(), res.getRecordMetadata().offset());
             });
    }
}

@Component
class PaymentListener {

    private final PaymentService payments;
    private final ProcessedEventRepo processed;

    @KafkaListener(topics = "order.placed", groupId = "payment-service")
    public void onOrderPlaced(@Payload OrderPlaced event, Acknowledgment ack) {

        // Kafka is at-least-once. Redelivery WILL happen — the handler must be idempotent.
        if (processed.existsById(event.eventId())) { ack.acknowledge(); return; }

        payments.charge(event.orderId(), event.amount());
        processed.save(new ProcessedEvent(event.eventId(), Instant.now()));

        ack.acknowledge();   // commit only once the work is durable
    }
}

@Configuration
class KafkaErrorConfig {
    /** 3 retries with exponential backoff, then park in order.placed.DLT */
    @Bean
    DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<String, Object> template) {
        var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
                (rec, ex) -> new TopicPartition(rec.topic() + ".DLT", rec.partition()));
        var backoff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(3);
        backoff.setInitialInterval(1000); backoff.setMultiplier(2.0);

        var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backoff);
        handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(IllegalArgumentException.class);  // bad payload
        return handler;
    }
}
Publish path, failure path, and the dual-write problem you must name

RabbitMQ in Spring Boot Work queues

Declare the topology as beans and let the broker own retries, delays and dead letters.

Real-world use case

PayPal capture retries. The acquiring bank times out on ~2% of captures. Each failure nacks into a 30-second delay queue, dead-letters back to the work queue, and retries up to five times before parking for ops. No cron, no retry_count column, no scheduler.

RabbitTopologyConfig.javaexchange · queue · DLX · delay queue
@Configuration
public class RabbitTopologyConfig {

    @Bean TopicExchange payments() { return new TopicExchange("payments.topic", true, false); }
    @Bean TopicExchange retryEx()  { return new TopicExchange("payments.retry", true, false); }

    /** Work queue. Failures dead-letter into the retry exchange. */
    @Bean Queue capture() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable("q.payment.capture")
                .deadLetterExchange("payments.retry")
                .deadLetterRoutingKey("payment.capture")
                .build();
    }

    /** No consumer. Messages expire after 30s and dead-letter BACK to the work queue. */
    @Bean Queue captureRetry() {
        return QueueBuilder.durable("q.payment.capture.retry")
                .ttl(30_000)
                .deadLetterExchange("payments.topic")
                .deadLetterRoutingKey("payment.capture")
                .build();
    }

    @Bean Queue captureDlq() { return QueueBuilder.durable("q.payment.capture.dlq").build(); }

    @Bean Binding b1() { return BindingBuilder.bind(capture()).to(payments()).with("payment.capture"); }
    @Bean Binding b2() { return BindingBuilder.bind(captureRetry()).to(retryEx()).with("payment.capture"); }

    @Bean
    RabbitTemplate template(ConnectionFactory cf) {
        var t = new RabbitTemplate(cf);
        t.setMessageConverter(new Jackson2JsonMessageConverter());
        t.setConfirmCallback((corr, acked, cause) -> {
            if (!acked) log.error("broker rejected {}: {}", corr, cause);   // republish
        });
        return t;
    }
}
CaptureListener.javaack · nack · park — the only three outcomes
@Component
public class CaptureListener {

    private static final int MAX_ATTEMPTS = 5;
    private final AcquirerClient acquirer;
    private final RabbitTemplate rabbit;

    @RabbitListener(queues = "q.payment.capture")
    public void onCapture(CaptureCommand cmd, Message raw, Channel channel) throws IOException {
        long tag = raw.getMessageProperties().getDeliveryTag();
        int attempts = deathCount(raw);              // x-death header, maintained by the broker

        try {
            acquirer.capture(cmd);                   // idempotent at the acquirer too
            channel.basicAck(tag, false);            // ⇒ deleted from the queue

        } catch (TransientAcquirerException e) {     // might work later
            if (attempts >= MAX_ATTEMPTS) {
                rabbit.convertAndSend("q.payment.capture.dlq", cmd);
                channel.basicAck(tag, false);
            } else {
                channel.basicNack(tag, false, false);  // → DLX → 30s delay → back here
            }

        } catch (PermanentAcquirerException e) {     // card blocked: retrying is pointless
            rabbit.convertAndSend("q.payment.capture.dlq", cmd);
            channel.basicAck(tag, false);
        }
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    private int deathCount(Message m) {
        var deaths = (List<Map<String, ?>>) m.getMessageProperties().getHeaders().get("x-death");
        return deaths == null ? 0 : ((Long) deaths.get(0).get("count")).intValue();
    }
}
Why this beats a retry tableBackoff, attempt counting and parking are broker configuration, not application state. No scheduler to run, no column to migrate, and the retry ladder keeps working even while your service is being redeployed.

Sync vs async in Spring Boot Architecture

Four mechanisms, four different meanings of "async". Interviewers check whether you can tell them apart.

MechanismWhat is actually asyncCaller getsSurvives a restart?Use for
RestClient / JDBCNothing — blockingThe resultn/aYou need the answer now
@Async + CompletableFutureA thread handoff inside one JVMA futureNo — the work is lostParallel fan-out within a request
Virtual threads / WebFluxNon-blocking I/O; no thread parkedResult / MonoNoHigh-concurrency I/O-bound work
Kafka / RabbitMQOwnership of the work moves to a brokerAn ack that it's queuedYes — durableAnything that must eventually happen
The distinction that catches people out@Async is not asynchronous architecture — it's a thread pool. Kill the pod mid-task and that email is gone with no trace and no retry. A broker persists the message first, which is why "fire an @Async email" and "publish an email event" are fundamentally different designs.
CheckoutService.javasync for the decision, async for the consequences
@Service
public class CheckoutService {

    private final PaymentClient payment;      // SYNC — the user cannot proceed without it
    private final OrderRepository orders;
    private final OutboxRepository outbox;

    @Transactional
    public OrderResponse checkout(CheckoutRequest req) {

        // ── 1. SYNCHRONOUS: the answer changes what the user sees next ───────────
        var auth = payment.authorize(req.card(), req.amount());     // ~120 ms, blocking
        if (!auth.approved()) throw new PaymentDeclinedException(auth.reason());

        var order = orders.save(Order.confirmed(req, auth.id()));

        // ── 2. ASYNCHRONOUS: must happen, but not before the response ────────────
        // Same transaction as the order ⇒ no dual-write problem.
        outbox.save(new OutboxEvent("order.placed", order.id(), json(OrderPlaced.from(order))));

        return OrderResponse.confirmed(order);      // ~160 ms end to end
    }
}

@Component
class OutboxRelay {

    private final OutboxRepository outbox;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafka;

    /** Commit and publish are now decoupled — at-least-once, never lost. */
    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
    @Transactional
    public void publishPending() {
        for (OutboxEvent e : outbox.lockNextBatch(100)) {
            kafka.send(e.topic(), e.aggregateId(), e.payload())
                 .thenRun(() -> outbox.markPublished(e.id()));
        }
    }
}
Closing line"I keep the decision synchronous and make the consequences asynchronous. The decision needs consistency and an immediate answer; the consequences need durability and retries. The transactional outbox is what joins the two without a dual-write."

Config recap · one line each

ConceptDependencyThe switch that turns it on
IP / TCP / UDP—Timeouts, pool sizes, forward-headers-strategy. No code.
Connection handlingstarter-webthreads.max, accept-count, keep-alive-timeout, virtual threads
Frame processing—Nothing to configure — but it explains every framing bug you'll debug
HTTP/2starter-web + TLSserver.http2.enabled: true and an h2-capable client
HTTP/3edge proxyAlt-Svc: h3=":443" + 425 guard for 0-RTT

WebSocketstarter-websocket@EnableWebSocketMessageBroker + STOMP broker relay
gRPCgrpc-*-spring-boot-starter@GrpcService, @GrpcClient, deadlines
Kafkaspring-kafkaKafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener, acks=all, manual ack
RabbitMQstarter-amqp@RabbitListener, DLX + TTL retry queues
If you remember five things 1. TCP gives you ordered bytes with no boundaries — everything above it invents framing.   2. Handshakes are round trips; pooling and keep-alive are how you stop paying them.   3. threads.max is your concurrency ceiling until virtual threads remove it.   4. HTTP/2 fixed application HOL blocking; HTTP/3 fixed the transport-level kind.   5. Sync the decision, async the consequence — with an outbox in between.
