01Service Decomposition 02Database per Service 03API Gateway 04Service Discovery 05Circuit Breaker 06Saga Pattern 07Event-Driven Communication 08Transactional Outbox 09Logging & Tracing 10Containers & Kubernetes 11SQL vs NoSQL 12Caching (Redis) 13CQRS 14Idempotency 15Strangler Fig

Why companies leave monoliths behind, one bottleneck at a time

Every pattern here exists because a monolith hit a specific wall in production. For each of the 15 concepts: the real problem monoliths run into, why the monolith architecture structurally can't fix it, how splitting into services solves it, how Amazon/Flipkart/Uber/Netflix/Tinder/Google actually did it, and the exact tech (Kafka, Redis, Kubernetes...) with the reason it was chosen for that job.

Java 17Spring Boot 3KafkaResilience4jKubernetesRedisMongoDBCassandra

The one mental model behind all 15 patterns

A monolith is one codebase, one build, one deploy, one database, one runtime. That's fantastic on day one — one repo to clone, one place to debug, transactions just work. The problem was never the code quality. The problem is that one of everything means every axis — scaling, deploying, failing, hiring — is shared across the entire business, whether it wants to be or not.

Microservices don't fix bugs or add features. They exist to give each business capability its own axis: its own deploy schedule, its own scaling knob, its own failure boundary, its own team, its own database engine. Every pattern below is really the same move applied to a different axis — that repetition is the mental model.

One honest catch: splitting the monolith isn't free. It trades old bottlenecks for new problems — services now need a way to find each other, which is what an API Gateway and Service Discovery solve. One sick service (say, a slow bank integration) shouldn't be able to freeze every other service waiting on it — that's what a Circuit Breaker prevents. Data that used to live in one database now has to stay consistent across several — that's what the Saga Pattern and Transactional Outbox solve. And a request that now hops across 6 services needs a way to be followed end to end — that's Distributed Tracing. Most of this guide, after the first couple of ideas, is really the set of answers to the problems splitting itself creates.

Every concept below is this same split, applied to deploys, scaling, failure, data, or ownership.
01

Service Decomposition

Design

Break one application into small services, each owning one business capability — its own code, its own team, its own deploy. This is the root decision every other pattern in this guide builds on.

🏚️ The Monolith Reality
A typical growth story: an e-commerce app starts as one Spring Boot WAR — UserController, OrderController, PaymentController, InventoryController, all in one repo, one build, one running process. Eighteen months and 40 engineers later, a junior dev fixes a one-line typo in the refund email template. To ship it, the entire application has to rebuild, redeploy, and restart — because that's the only unit of deployment that exists.
🚧 Why the Monolith Can't Fix This
It's not a process problem — it's structural. A monolith is one build artifact, one running process, one shared heap:
  • Deploy is all-or-nothing: there's no way to ship only the email-template fix — the deploy pipeline doesn't know your change was 3 lines out of 400,000.
  • Scale is all-or-nothing: Search gets 10× the load Payments does on sale day, but they run in the same process — you scale the whole monolith just to give Search more headroom.
  • Failure is shared: a memory leak in the Reviews module eventually OOMs the whole JVM — and Ordering, which has nothing to do with Reviews, goes down with it.
  • Ownership is shared: 40 engineers committing to one repo means merge conflicts, one team's bad migration blocking everyone's release train, and nobody able to say "this is fully mine."
🔀 How Microservices Solve It
Split by business capability, not technical layer. Order Service, Payment Service, and Inventory Service become separate deployable units — separate repos or at least separate build/deploy pipelines, separate runtimes, separate teams. The Search team now ships 5 times a day without asking Payments. A memory leak in Reviews takes down only Reviews. Scaling decisions become per-service knobs instead of one global one.
One shared process becomes three independent ones — each with its own deploy, scale, and blast radius.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Amazon ran one large C++ monolith through the late 1990s. Order volume grew, and the same story repeated: unrelated teams blocked each other's releases, and one bad change could take down checkout. Amazon's leadership eventually mandated that all teams expose their functionality only through well-defined APIs, effectively forcing the monolith apart into service-owning teams — the origin of the "you build it, you run it" culture that's now industry-wide.
  • Uber started as a single Python monolith dispatching rides in one city. As they expanded city by city, one city's edge-case code (say, surge pricing rules unique to São Paulo) risked breaking rides in Chicago on every deploy. They decomposed into services by capability — pricing, dispatch, maps, payments — specifically so a bug in one domain couldn't take down rides globally.
💻 Complete Code
OrderController.java — lives in its own Spring Boot app (order-service)
// order-service — a complete, small Spring Boot app. Nothing else lives here.
@SpringBootApplication
public class OrderServiceApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(OrderServiceApplication.class, args);
    }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/orders")
public class OrderController {

    private final OrderService orderService;

    public OrderController(OrderService orderService) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
    }

    @PostMapping
    public ResponseEntity<OrderResponse> placeOrder(@RequestBody OrderRequest request) {
        // This service ONLY knows about orders.
        // To charge money, it CALLS payment-service over HTTP or Kafka —
        // it does not contain payment code in the same process.
        return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED)
                             .body(orderService.placeOrder(request));
    }
}
🧰 Why Split Along These Boundaries
RuleMeaning in simple words
By business capabilityOne service = one thing the business does (orders, payments, shipping). Not "controller service" and "database service".
Single responsibilityIf you can't describe the service in one sentence, it's too big.
Team ownershipOne small team should be able to own, build, and deploy it end to end.
Don't start too small200 tiny services is worse than 8 sensible ones. Split more only when the monolith's pain actually shows up.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "We decompose by business capability, not technical layer — each service owns one job, its own data, and its own deployment lifecycle, because that's the only way to make deploy, scale, and failure independent axes instead of one shared one."
02

Database per Service

Data

Each service gets its own database that nobody else touches. Other services never run SQL on your tables — they ask through your API or listen to your events.

🏚️ The Monolith Reality
One database, every team's fingerprints on it: the monolith has a single PostgreSQL instance. The Analytics team runs a heavy end-of-day report query Friday at 6 PM — it takes table locks, and suddenly login slows down for the entire platform, even though login has nothing to do with analytics. Meanwhile, the User team wants to rename one column, but three other teams' queries touch that table, so it takes a scheduling meeting and a migration window at 2 AM.
🚧 Why the Monolith Can't Fix This
One shared schema means one shared blast radius and one shared bottleneck, structurally:
  • Lock contention is shared: any heavy query — a report, a backfill, a bad index — can degrade every other feature reading the same tables, because they're the same physical database.
  • Schema changes require cross-team consensus: you can't evolve your table's shape without checking every other team's queries against it first.
  • One storage engine has to fit every access pattern: a strict relational DB is right for orders and payments, but wrong for a fast-growing photo feed or a session store — yet the monolith forces everyone onto the same engine.
🔀 How Microservices Solve It
Give each service its own database, and let it pick the engine that fits its job. A report query in Analytics's own database can never lock User Service's login table — they're physically different systems. Schema changes become a one-team decision. And each service can choose Postgres, Cassandra, MongoDB, or Redis based on its actual read/write shape, not a company-wide default.
Each service picks the database that fits its job — and hides it from everyone else.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Instagram-scale photo apps split exactly this way: User Service on PostgreSQL (strict uniqueness rules, ACID for account changes), Post Service on Cassandra (100M+ photo writes/day, simple reads-by-ID), Feed Service on Redis (precomputed timelines, sub-millisecond reads). One shared database could never serve all three access patterns well at once.
  • Netflix stores viewing history — billions of "user watched X at time Y" events per day — in Cassandra specifically because it accepts nonstop writes across hundreds of nodes and keeps working when some nodes fail; that write volume would choke a single relational instance shared with, say, billing.
  • Flipkart's product catalog spans wildly different product types — a phone has RAM and screen size, a saree has fabric and length — which is exactly the flexible-schema problem a document store like MongoDB solves; forcing it into the same relational schema as Orders (which genuinely needs strict transactions) would mean dozens of mostly-empty columns and constant migrations.
💻 Complete Code
application.yml — user-service vs post-service (two different apps)
# ---------- user-service/src/main/resources/application.yml ----------
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://user-db:5432/users   # its OWN Postgres
    username: user_svc
  jpa:
    hibernate:
      ddl-auto: validate

# ---------- post-service/src/main/resources/application.yml ----------
spring:
  cassandra:                                    # its OWN Cassandra
    contact-points: post-db-1,post-db-2
    keyspace-name: posts
    local-datacenter: dc1

# post-service has NO credentials for user-db.
# If it needs a username, it calls:  GET http://user-service/api/users/{id}
🎯 Interview one-liner: "Database per service removes the shared lock contention and shared schema of a monolith, and lets each service pick the storage engine that matches its access pattern — the trade-off is no cross-service joins and eventual consistency, handled with events."
03

API Gateway

Traffic

One single front door for all clients. The gateway routes each request to the right internal service and handles cross-cutting work — auth, rate limiting, SSL — once, instead of in every service.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: your system is now Order Service, Product Service, and User Service, each independently deployed on its own host and port. The mobile app needs data from all three to render a single screen — say, an order confirmation page showing order details, product info, and the buyer's name. The obvious first approach: the app calls all three services directly, each with its own hostname. It works at first, but as you add Shipping Service, Review Service, and Recommendation Service, the app is now juggling six hostnames, and each of those six services has independently implemented its own JWT-checking and rate-limiting logic — some more carefully than others.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
Calling services directly from the client seems simple, but it creates real structural problems as the service count grows:
  • Clients become coupled to internal topology: rename, split, or merge a service, and every client — mobile, web, partner integrations — has to be updated and re-released.
  • Cross-cutting logic gets duplicated N times: auth, rate limiting, and request logging get implemented separately in every one of 15+ services, and they drift out of sync as each team patches its own copy differently.
  • There's no single choke point for abuse: without one front door, there's nowhere to enforce "this IP gets 100 requests/min" across the whole API surface — a client hammering one service slips past any protection another service has in place.
✅ The Solution
Put one API Gateway in front of every service. Clients only ever know one hostname — the gateway's. The gateway verifies the JWT once, enforces rate limits once, and routes each request by path to the right internal service. Internally, services can be renamed, split, or merged freely, because the gateway is the only thing clients ever talk to; none of that internal reshuffling is visible to them.
Clients see one URL. The gateway checks, limits, and routes — internal topology stays hidden.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Swiggy/Zomato-style food delivery apps: the app calls one address, e.g. api.swiggy.com. The gateway checks the JWT, rejects bots hammering the menu endpoint, and routes /orders/**, /track/**, and /restaurants/** internally — the phone never learns this internal map. Launching a new "Dine-out" feature is one new gateway route; 50 million installed apps don't change.
  • Uber runs thousands of internal services (pricing, dispatch, maps, payments) behind a small number of edge gateway layers — the rider and driver apps only ever talk to Uber's public edge, never to internal service hostnames, which is what lets Uber refactor internal services constantly without ever shipping an app update for it.
💻 Complete Code
application.yml — gateway-service (Spring Cloud Gateway)
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: order-route
          uri: lb://order-service        # "lb" = pick a healthy instance via discovery
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/orders/**
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter   # protect order-service from abuse
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 100
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 200

        - id: product-route
          uri: lb://product-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/products/**
JwtAuthFilter.java — check the token once, at the front door
@Component
public class JwtAuthFilter implements GlobalFilter {

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, GatewayFilterChain chain) {
        String authHeader = exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().getFirst("Authorization");

        if (authHeader == null || !isValidJwt(authHeader.replace("Bearer ", ""))) {
            // Stop bad requests HERE. Order/Product services never even see them.
            exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
            return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
        }
        return chain.filter(exchange);
    }
}
🧰 Why This Tech Stack
OptionWhen to pick it
Spring Cloud Gateway Java-friendlyA Spring shop wanting routes as code/config it fully controls.
AWS API GatewayAlready on AWS, want a managed gateway (pay per request, zero servers to run).
Kong / NGINXPolyglot company, very high traffic, gateway owned by a dedicated platform team.
Netflix Zuul 1 legacyOld blocking gateway — mention as history; replaced by Spring Cloud Gateway.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "The gateway is the single entry point that centralizes cross-cutting concerns so individual services stay simple — it replaces the coupling clients would otherwise have to N internal hostnames with coupling to one stable public contract."
04

Service Discovery

Traffic

Services find each other by name, not by IP address. Instances come and go constantly — a registry keeps a live list: "order-service is currently at these 3 addresses."

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: Order Service needs to call Payment Service to charge a customer's card. A first cut hard-codes Payment Service's IP address — 10.0.1.5 — into Order Service's config. It works fine in a small test environment. Then it goes to production on auto-scaling cloud infrastructure: a sale event triggers Payment Service to scale from 3 pods to 30 within two minutes, a routine deploy replaces every one of those pods with fresh instances at fresh addresses, and one pod crashes under load and gets rescheduled onto a different machine entirely. Order Service's hard-coded IP is now stale within hours of going live.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
The whole benefit of running services on elastic, auto-scaling infrastructure is that instance counts and locations change constantly — which is exactly what breaks static addressing:
  • Auto-scaling changes IPs constantly: a sale event might add 27 new Payment pods in two minutes — 27 addresses that didn't exist a moment ago.
  • Deploys change IPs on every release: a rolling deploy replaces every pod with a fresh one at a fresh address, potentially several times a day.
  • Crashes must be invisible to callers: if a pod dies, every caller with its IP hard-coded keeps sending requests into a black hole until someone manually intervenes.
✅ The Solution
Instances register themselves with a registry on startup and send heartbeats. Callers ask the registry for "payment-service" by name and get back only the currently healthy addresses — scale-ups, deploys, and crashes are all absorbed by the registry, invisible to every caller.
Instances register themselves; callers ask the registry, never hard-code IPs.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Tinder famously migrated its backend from a few hundred VMs running a large service footprint into hundreds of microservices on Kubernetes, as documented in Kubernetes' own public case study. The move only worked because Kubernetes gives every service a stable DNS name backed by live, auto-updated endpoints — matching pods appear and disappear behind that name constantly (deploys, autoscaling, node failures) without any service needing to track individual pod IPs.
  • Uber's dispatch system geo-shards services by city/region and scales each shard independently as demand shifts through the day — this only works because services resolve each other by name through a discovery layer; the actual instance count and placement changes continuously as Uber scales regions up and down.
💻 Complete Code
Order service — registering & calling payment-service by name
// 1. Each service registers itself (spring-cloud-starter-netflix-eureka-client)
// application.yml:
//   spring.application.name: order-service
//   eureka.client.service-url.defaultZone: http://eureka:8761/eureka

@Configuration
public class RestClientConfig {

    @Bean
    @LoadBalanced   // ← resolves service NAMES via the registry
    public RestTemplate restTemplate() {
        return new RestTemplate();
    }
}

@Service
public class PaymentClient {

    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;

    public PaymentClient(RestTemplate restTemplate) {
        this.restTemplate = restTemplate;
    }

    public PaymentResponse charge(PaymentRequest request) {
        // "payment-service" is a NAME, not a host.
        // Spring asks Eureka for live instances and load-balances between them.
        return restTemplate.postForObject(
                "http://payment-service/api/payments",
                request,
                PaymentResponse.class);
    }
}
🧰 Why This Tech Stack
OptionWhen to pick it
Kubernetes DNS default todayRunning on K8s? Discovery is free: http://payment-service just works via Services. This is what Tinder's migration relies on.
Netflix EurekaClassic Spring Cloud setup, especially outside Kubernetes (VMs, EC2).
HashiCorp ConsulPolyglot stack needing health checks + key-value config + multi-datacenter.
ZooKeeperMostly seen holding up older Kafka clusters; rarely chosen fresh for discovery.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "Instances register with a registry and heartbeat; callers resolve by logical name and load-balance across healthy instances — on Kubernetes the platform's DNS and Services give us this for free, which is exactly what let companies like Tinder run hundreds of constantly-scaling services without any hard-coded addressing."
05

Circuit Breaker

Resilience

When a downstream service keeps failing, stop calling it and fail fast. Otherwise every request waits for a timeout, threads pile up stuck waiting, and your service dies too — a single sick dependency cascades into a platform-wide outage.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: Payment Service calls an external bank API to authorize a charge. One evening, the bank's API starts hanging — each call now takes 30 seconds to time out instead of returning instantly. Payment Service has a finite thread pool (say, 200 threads); within a couple of minutes, every one of those threads is sitting blocked, waiting on the bank. New requests to Payment Service — even ones that have nothing to do with the bank — start queuing because there are no free threads left to handle them. Order Service, which calls Payment Service for every checkout, now finds Payment Service unresponsive too, and its own threads start blocking in turn.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
Every network call between services is a new opportunity for one dependency's problem to become everyone's problem:
  • Thread pools are finite: if the bank's API hangs for 30 seconds per call, every Payment Service thread eventually sits blocked waiting on it.
  • The blockage propagates upstream: Order Service calls the now-frozen Payment Service and its own threads block too — one dependency's outage climbs the call chain.
  • Nothing in a plain HTTP client stops this on its own: without an explicit breaker, retries and timeouts alone can even make it worse by piling more load onto an already-struggling dependency.
✅ The Solution
Wrap inter-service calls in a circuit breaker. After a threshold of failures, the circuit trips OPEN and new calls fail in milliseconds via a fallback — instead of hanging — freeing threads immediately. Periodic test calls (HALF-OPEN) check if the dependency has recovered before fully trusting it again.
CLOSED = healthy. OPEN = tripped, fail fast. HALF-OPEN = careful probing.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Netflix is where this pattern was proven at scale: after their move to AWS exposed just how easily one degraded backend service could cascade into wider outages, Netflix built and open-sourced Hystrix — the circuit breaker library that established this exact CLOSED → OPEN → HALF-OPEN model as the industry standard (Resilience4j is its modern successor).
  • Flipkart, during Big Billion Days-scale sale traffic, depends on external bank/UPI switches for payment authorization that can slow down under the load every bank sees during a national sale. A circuit breaker around those calls is what lets checkout degrade gracefully (queue the payment, offer Cash on Delivery) instead of every Payment Service thread hanging and taking browsing and cart down with it.
💻 Complete Code
BankClient.java — @CircuitBreaker with a fallback
// dependency: io.github.resilience4j:resilience4j-spring-boot3
@Service
public class BankClient {

    private final RestTemplate restTemplate;

    public BankClient(RestTemplate restTemplate) {
        this.restTemplate = restTemplate;
    }

    @CircuitBreaker(name = "bankApi", fallbackMethod = "chargeFallback")
    public PaymentResult charge(PaymentRequest request) {
        return restTemplate.postForObject(
                "https://bank.example.com/charge", request, PaymentResult.class);
    }

    // Called automatically when the circuit is OPEN or the call fails.
    private PaymentResult chargeFallback(PaymentRequest request, Throwable t) {
        return PaymentResult.pending("Bank is busy. Payment queued, will retry.");
    }
}
application.yml — tuning the breaker
resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      bankApi:
        sliding-window-size: 20
        failure-rate-threshold: 50               # >50% failed → OPEN the circuit
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 3
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 50
🧰 Why This Tech Stack
OptionWhen to pick it
Resilience4j recommendedToday's Spring Boot standard. Lightweight, annotation-based; also gives Retry, RateLimiter, Bulkhead, TimeLimiter.
Netflix Hystrix deprecatedThe pioneer that proved the pattern at Netflix's scale, now in maintenance mode — know the history, don't use it in new code.
Istio / Envoy (service mesh)Breaker lives in the infrastructure sidecar, zero code changes — good for polyglot teams on Kubernetes.
Alibaba SentinelPopular at very high traffic; adds flow control and adaptive protection.
⚠️ Common interview trap: "Circuit breaker vs retry?" These solve different problems, and the real answer combines all three of the following instead of picking just one:
  • Retry with backoff handles a brief, one-off glitch — a single dropped packet, a momentary blip that clears up in a second.
  • Wrap the call in a circuit breaker for sustained failure — this stops retries from continuing to hammer a dependency that's genuinely down, which is important because blind retries against a dying service just triple its load and make things worse.
  • Put a timeout on every call — so a hanging dependency can never block a thread indefinitely, breaker or not.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "A circuit breaker fails fast when a dependency is unhealthy, preventing the thread-pool exhaustion and cascading failure that network calls between services introduce — I use Resilience4j with a fallback that degrades gracefully."
06

Saga Pattern

Data

One business action often touches many services, each with its own database — so a single ACID transaction is impossible. A saga runs the action as a sequence of local steps, each with a compensating action to undo it if a later step fails.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: placing an order needs three things to happen: create the order (Order Service), charge the customer's card (Payment Service), and reserve stock (Inventory Service) — each owned by a different service, each with its own database. The order is created, the card is successfully charged, and then Inventory Service discovers the last unit of that product sold to someone else a second earlier. The charge already happened. The order already exists. There's no single database transaction spanning all three services that could simply roll back — because there's no single database at all.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
Two-phase commit (2PC) sounds like the obvious fix for spanning multiple databases, but it fails for structural reasons:
  • It requires every participant to lock resources and wait for a coordinator — under real traffic, that's slow and blocks other transactions.
  • Most modern data stores don't support it: Kafka, Cassandra, DynamoDB, and most NoSQL stores have no 2PC protocol to join.
  • A coordinator crash mid-commit can leave participants locked indefinitely — trading one failure mode for a worse one.
✅ The Solution
Replace one distributed transaction with a chain of local transactions plus compensations. Order Service commits locally, Payment Service commits locally, Inventory Service commits locally — if the last step fails, previously completed steps are undone in reverse order by explicit compensating calls (refund, cancel), not a database rollback.
Step 3 fails → refund payment → cancel order. Every step ships with its undo.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Uber books a ride as exactly this kind of chain: assign a driver → authorize payment → start the trip. Each step is a separate service with its own database, and each has an explicit undo — if payment authorization fails after a driver is assigned, that assignment is released (compensated) rather than left dangling. There is no single database transaction spanning driver-matching and billing at Uber's scale; there can't be.
  • Flipkart-style e-commerce checkout during a sale runs the same order → payment → inventory chain — the specific failure mode of "last unit sold to someone else a second earlier" is a saga compensation in action: refund the charge, cancel the order, show "just sold out" instead of silently losing track of the customer's money.
💻 Complete Code
OrderSagaOrchestrator.java — orchestration style (one brain directs the steps)
@Service
public class OrderSagaOrchestrator {

    private final OrderService orderService;
    private final PaymentClient paymentClient;
    private final InventoryClient inventoryClient;

    public OrderSagaOrchestrator(OrderService orderService,
                                 PaymentClient paymentClient,
                                 InventoryClient inventoryClient) {
        this.orderService = orderService;
        this.paymentClient = paymentClient;
        this.inventoryClient = inventoryClient;
    }

    public OrderResult placeOrder(OrderRequest request) {
        Order order = orderService.createPending(request);        // local txn 1

        PaymentResult payment;
        try {
            payment = paymentClient.charge(order);                // local txn 2
        } catch (Exception e) {
            orderService.markCancelled(order.getId());            // undo 1
            return OrderResult.failed("Payment failed");
        }

        try {
            inventoryClient.reserve(order);                       // local txn 3
        } catch (Exception e) {
            paymentClient.refund(payment.getTxnId());              // undo 2
            orderService.markCancelled(order.getId());             // undo 1
            return OrderResult.failed("Out of stock — amount refunded");
        }

        orderService.markConfirmed(order.getId());
        return OrderResult.success(order.getId());
    }
}
// In production these steps usually run via Kafka commands/events (async),
// and saga state is persisted so it survives a crash mid-way.
🧰 Why This Tech Stack
FlavorHow it works
Orchestration easier to reason aboutOne central conductor tells each service what to do next and triggers undo steps. Tools: Temporal, Camunda, Axon, or a custom Spring service + Kafka.
ChoreographyNo conductor — each service reacts to the previous event. Simple for 2–3 steps, hard to follow for many.
⚠️ Common interview trap: "Why not just use a distributed transaction (2PC)?" A few concrete reasons, each one enough on its own:
  • It's slow. Every participant has to lock its resources and wait for a central coordinator before anything can commit.
  • It blocks under failure. If the coordinator crashes mid-commit, participants can be left holding locks indefinitely, with no one to tell them to release.
  • Most modern data stores don't support it. Kafka, Cassandra, DynamoDB, and most NoSQL stores have no 2PC protocol to join at all.
Sagas trade instant consistency for availability instead: the system is briefly "in between" while compensations run, but it always ends up correct.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "A saga replaces the one impossible cross-database transaction that database-per-service creates with a sequence of local transactions plus compensating actions — I prefer orchestration for complex flows because the whole state machine lives in one visible place."
07

Event-Driven Communication

Messaging

Instead of Service A directly calling B, C, and D, it announces "this happened" on a broker like Kafka. Whoever cares, listens — A never knows or cares who's subscribed.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: a user posts a photo. Post Service saves it, then needs Feed Service to add it to followers' timelines, Notification Service to alert close friends, and Analytics Service to record the event. The straightforward implementation has Post Service call each of those three services synchronously, one after another, before it finally responds to the user with "Posted." Notification Service is having a slow day — its calls now take 2 extra seconds — and posting a photo, an action that should feel instant, now takes 2+ seconds too, for a reason the user has nothing to do with.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
Chaining synchronous calls across services couples them in time and in knowledge, in ways that get worse as more services need to react to the same event:
  • The slowest call in the chain holds everything hostage: if Notification Service is slow, the user's "post" spinner waits for it too, even though notifications aren't essential to posting.
  • Any one failing fails the whole action: Analytics Service being briefly down shouldn't mean photos can't be posted — but with a synchronous chain, it does.
  • Adding a new consumer means editing the producer: plugging in a new ML tagging service means Post Service's code and deploy have to change, coupling teams that shouldn't need to coordinate.
✅ The Solution
Publish one event and let interested services subscribe independently. Post Service saves the post, publishes PostCreated to Kafka, and responds to the user in milliseconds — Feed, Notification, Analytics, and any future consumer process it in parallel, on their own time, with zero code changes required upstream.
One event, many independent listeners. Adding a listener costs the publisher nothing.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Instagram-style apps: tapping Share triggers one PostCreated event. Feed Service pushes it into followers' timelines, Notification Service pings close friends, Media Service generates thumbnails, and Analytics counts it — five teams, zero synchronous coordination, and any one being briefly down never blocks the upload.
  • Google Maps' live traffic layer is a huge-scale version of the same idea in reverse: millions of phones stream anonymized location pings continuously. Maps doesn't process each ping with a synchronous call back to the sending phone — it ingests them as a firehose of events into a streaming pipeline that aggregates speed and congestion per road segment. A synchronous request/response model could never absorb that volume; publish-and-forget streaming is the only shape that fits.
💻 Complete Code
Producer (order-service) and Consumer (notification-service)
// ---------- order-service: publish and move on ----------
@Service
public class OrderEventPublisher {

    private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlacedEvent> kafkaTemplate;

    public OrderEventPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlacedEvent> kafkaTemplate) {
        this.kafkaTemplate = kafkaTemplate;
    }

    public void publishOrderPlaced(Order order) {
        OrderPlacedEvent event = new OrderPlacedEvent(
                order.getId(), order.getUserId(), order.getTotalAmount());
        // key = orderId → all events of one order land in the same partition, in order
        kafkaTemplate.send("order-events", order.getId().toString(), event);
    }
}

// ---------- notification-service: a completely separate app ----------
@Component
public class OrderEventsListener {

    @KafkaListener(topics = "order-events", groupId = "notification-service")
    public void onOrderPlaced(OrderPlacedEvent event) {
        // Order Service has no idea this class exists. That's the point.
        emailService.sendOrderConfirmation(event.userId(), event.orderId());
    }
}
🧰 Sync Call vs Event — When to Use Which
Use a direct REST call when…Use an event when…
You need the answer NOW to continue (e.g., "is this card valid?").It's a side effect that can happen a moment later (email, feed update, analytics).
The caller must know if it failed.Many services care about the same fact.
Simple request/response between two services.You want to add listeners later without touching the publisher.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "Events decouple producers from consumers in both time and knowledge — the publisher survives consumer outages, and new consumers attach with zero upstream changes. I use Kafka with the entity ID as the partition key to keep per-entity ordering."
08

Transactional Outbox

Messaging

The dual-write problem: saving to your database AND publishing to Kafka are two separate systems, so one can succeed while the other fails. Fix: write the event into an outbox table in the same DB transaction as your data; a separate process reliably ships it to Kafka.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: Wallet Service processes a transfer — it needs to debit one account in its database and publish a MoneyTransferred event to Kafka so Notification Service and Ledger Service can react. The straightforward code is two lines: db.save(debit), then kafka.send(event). A pod gets killed by an out-of-memory error right between those two lines. The database now shows the account debited — the money genuinely left — but the event was never sent. Ledger Service never records it, the recipient is never notified, and nothing in the system knows anything went wrong until a customer complains.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
The database and Kafka are two independent systems with no shared transaction — this "dual-write problem" is unavoidable without a specific fix:
  • A crash between the two writes loses the event silently — the database change is real, but nothing downstream ever hears about it.
  • Reordering the writes doesn't help: publish-then-save risks the opposite failure — an event about something that never actually got persisted.
  • At real transaction volumes, even a 0.01% loss rate means hundreds of silently broken records a day, each needing manual reconciliation.
✅ The Solution
Write the event into an outbox table, in the same local database transaction as the actual data change. A poller (or Debezium reading the DB's transaction log) picks up outbox rows afterward and publishes them to Kafka, marking them sent only after a successful publish — so the event can never be lost, only occasionally duplicated — and a consumer designed to safely ignore a duplicate message (the Idempotency pattern, later in this guide) makes that harmless.
Data + event committed atomically in one DB; a poller ships events to Kafka afterwards.
🌍 Proven at Scale
"At-least-once delivery plus idempotent consumers" — exactly what the outbox pattern gives you — is how real payment infrastructure (Stripe, PayPal, UPI switches) guarantees an event is never lost. A duplicate notification is a minor annoyance; a wallet debit that Ledger never heard about is a support escalation and, at scale, a compliance problem. This is why banking-grade systems treat the outbox as non-negotiable the moment money crosses a service boundary — not just a nice-to-have.
💻 Complete Code
OrderService.java + OutboxPublisher.java
@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final OrderRepository orderRepository;
    private final OutboxRepository outboxRepository;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    // ONE local ACID transaction — both rows, or none. No dual-write problem.
    @Transactional
    public Order placeOrder(OrderRequest request) throws JsonProcessingException {
        Order order = orderRepository.save(Order.confirmed(request));

        OutboxEvent event = new OutboxEvent(
                "Order", order.getId().toString(), "OrderPlaced",
                objectMapper.writeValueAsString(order));
        outboxRepository.save(event);                      // same DB, same txn

        return order;
    }
}

@Component
public class OutboxPublisher {

    private final OutboxRepository outboxRepository;
    private final KafkaTemplate<String, String> kafkaTemplate;

    @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 2000)
    public void publishPendingEvents() {
        List<OutboxEvent> pending = outboxRepository.findTop100ByStatusOrderByCreatedAt("PENDING");

        for (OutboxEvent event : pending) {
            kafkaTemplate.send("order-events", event.getAggregateId(), event.getPayload())
                         .whenComplete((result, ex) -> {
                             if (ex == null) {
                                 event.setStatus("SENT");   // mark done only after Kafka ack
                                 outboxRepository.save(event);
                             }
                             // on failure: stays PENDING → retried next cycle
                         });
        }
    }
}
🧰 Why This Tech Stack
OptionWhen to pick it
Polling publisher simplestA @Scheduled job like above. Easy, works everywhere. Small delay and some DB load.
CDC with DebeziumTails the DB's transaction log (WAL/binlog) and streams outbox rows to Kafka — near real-time, no polling queries, the production-grade choice.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "The outbox pattern solves the dual-write problem that database-per-service plus events creates: the state change and the event commit atomically in one local transaction, and a poller or Debezium CDC relays events with at-least-once delivery."
09

Centralized Logging & Distributed Tracing

Observability

One user click can now travel through 6 services. Tracing gives every request a trace ID that follows it everywhere; centralized logging puts all logs in one searchable place, tagged with that ID.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: a customer reports "checkout was slow around 3 PM." A single checkout request now passes through the API Gateway, Order Service, Payment Service, and an external bank integration — four separate log files on four separate machines, each with its own local timestamp and no shared field connecting the lines that belong to that one customer's request. Payment Service alone logs 40,000 "payment processed" lines an hour; nothing marks which one belongs to the slow request the customer is asking about.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
A request that fans out across several services leaves its story scattered across several disconnected log files:
  • No shared identifier means no way to reassemble the story: which of the 40,000 "payment processed" lines in Payment Service's log corresponds to the specific slow checkout a customer reported?
  • SSH-and-grep doesn't scale past a handful of services: at 4-6 services it's painful; at Netflix or Uber's hundreds of services, it's simply impossible by hand.
  • Slowness is now a distributed question: "which of the 4 hops actually took the extra time?" has no answer without visibility into every hop's timing, together.
✅ The Solution
Attach one trace ID to a request at the gateway and propagate it through every hop (HTTP headers, Kafka message headers). Every service tags its log lines with that ID and ships them to one central store; a tracing backend renders the whole journey as a waterfall, showing exactly which hop was slow.
Same trace ID at every hop → a waterfall view shows exactly where time went.
🌍 Proven at Scale
At Netflix or Uber scale — hundreds of services, millions of requests per minute — SSH-and-grep debugging isn't a slower option, it's not an option at all. Both companies (and most large microservice operators) rely on exactly this trace-ID-plus-central-logging model: an engineer filters traces by duration and service in a tracing UI, jumps straight to the slow hop, then pivots to that hop's logs using the same trace ID — turning what used to be hours of cross-team investigation into minutes, without ever SSH-ing into a single box.
💻 Complete Code
pom.xml deps — IDs propagate automatically
<!-- Spring Boot 3: Micrometer Tracing bridges to OpenTelemetry -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId>
  <artifactId>opentelemetry-exporter-otlp</artifactId>
</dependency>
application.yml + what a correlated log line looks like
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0            # dev: trace everything; prod: often 0.1 (10%)
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces

logging:
  pattern:
    level: "%5p [${spring.application.name},%X{traceId:-},%X{spanId:-}]"

# INFO [payment-service,7f3ab21c9e0d4f11,4c1d22aa] Charging order #8812 via bank API
# RestTemplate/WebClient/Kafka headers carry the traceId automatically —
# that's how the story stays connected across hops.
🧰 Why This Tech Stack
ConcernPopular tools
Tracing backendJaeger common OSS pick, Zipkin, Grafana Tempo, New Relic / Datadog (managed)
Log aggregationELK stack (Elasticsearch + Logstash + Kibana), Grafana Loki, CloudWatch Logs
Instrumentation standardOpenTelemetry (OTel) — vendor-neutral; instrument once, export anywhere
Metrics (3rd pillar)Micrometer → Prometheus + Grafana dashboards & alerts
🎯 Interview one-liner: "Observability rests on logs, metrics, and traces correlated by a trace ID propagated via HTTP/Kafka headers — with Micrometer + OpenTelemetry, propagation and log correlation are automatic, and Jaeger's waterfall pinpoints the slow hop in seconds instead of an SSH scavenger hunt."
10

Containerization & Orchestration

Infra

A container (Docker) packs a service + runtime + config into one standard box that runs the same everywhere. An orchestrator (Kubernetes) manages hundreds of these boxes: starts them, restarts crashed ones, and scales each one independently.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: a system of 15 independently-deployable services — each with its own runtime version, its own dependency set, its own scaling profile — needs to run reliably in production. One ops engineer is manually provisioning VMs for each service, making sure the right JDK patch version is installed everywhere, and watching dashboards to catch crashed instances. A flash sale is announced for Friday: Order Service needs to go from 3 instances to 30 within minutes of the sale opening, and back down afterward, without anyone staying up all night to do it by hand.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
Managing many independently-deployable services by hand doesn't scale with the number of services or the speed traffic can change:
  • "Works on my machine" multiplies by N services: each service can drift onto a slightly different JDK patch or OS library version across environments.
  • Manual scaling can't react in minutes: a flash sale needs Order Service to go from 3 to 30 instances in two minutes — no human can provision VMs that fast, repeatedly, every day.
  • Nobody's watching 15+ services' health at 2 AM: a crashed instance needs to be detected and replaced automatically, or someone's phone rings every night.
✅ The Solution
Package every service identically as a container image, and let Kubernetes manage the fleet. The image runs the same in dev, staging, and production. Kubernetes' autoscaler watches metrics and adjusts replica counts per service; liveness/readiness probes detect and replace crashed instances automatically — no human paged for a routine pod crash.
K8s heals crashed pods and scales the hot service automatically.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Flipkart's Big Billion Days sale is a public, well-documented case of exactly this: traffic and order volume jump to many multiples of a normal day within minutes of the sale opening. Manually provisioning enough VMs in advance for peak while not paying for that capacity the other 360 days a year isn't practical — Kubernetes-style autoscaling lets Order and Search services scale up right as the sale opens and back down after, while catalog-browsing services barely move.
  • Netflix runs thousands of services on a container-orchestrated fleet for exactly the same reason: streaming demand varies enormously by time zone and by evening peak, and no team wants to hand-manage instance counts for hundreds of services around the clock.
💻 Complete Code
Dockerfile — the standard box for a Spring Boot service
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-17 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:17-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/order-service.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
deployment.yaml — tell K8s the desired state, it keeps it true
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: order-service }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: order-service }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: myregistry/order-service:1.4.2
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi" }
            limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "1Gi" }
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: order-service-hpa
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: order-service
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 30
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 }
🧰 The Vocabulary Map
TermIn simple words
ImageThe recipe + packed box (built once, immutable).
Container / PodA running copy of the image. Pod = K8s wrapper around container(s).
Deployment"Keep N copies of this image running, roll out new versions safely."
Service (K8s)Stable name + load balancer in front of the pods — this is what gives you Service Discovery for free, without running Eureka or Consul yourself.
HPAAuto-scaler: watches CPU/memory/custom metrics, adjusts replica count.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "Docker gives every service an identical, portable runtime; Kubernetes turns 'desired state' YAML into reality — self-healing via probes and HPA-driven per-service autoscaling, which is the operational payoff of decomposing in the first place."
11

SQL vs NoSQL — Picking the Right Database

Data

There's no "best" database — each type is shaped for a different data shape and access pattern. Since giving each service its own database lets every service choose independently, a healthy microservices system usually runs several database types at once — polyglot persistence.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: a product catalog needs flexible per-category attributes — a TV needs screen size and refresh rate, a shirt needs fabric and size, and a new category launches almost every quarter. A cart/session store needs the opposite: pure "give me the value for this one key," at very high volume, with no need for complex queries. A viewing-history log needs to absorb billions of write events a day. If all three are forced onto the same relational database because that's the only database the team runs, the catalog team fights constant schema migrations, the session store pays for query planning it never needed, and the write-heavy log outpaces what one primary database node can absorb.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
Forcing every access pattern onto one engine means every workload except the one the schema was designed for suffers:
  • Flexible-schema data becomes dozens of nullable columns: a TV needs screen size, a shirt needs fabric — one relational table for "products" ends up mostly empty per row, or needs a schema migration every time a new category launches.
  • Grab-by-key workloads pay for query planning they don't need: a session lookup is always "give me THE cart for user X" — running that through a full SQL query planner is wasted overhead at millions of requests per minute.
  • Firehose write volume doesn't fit a single-writer relational instance: billions of "user viewed X" events a day will outpace what one primary database node can absorb, no matter how well-indexed it is.
✅ The Solution
Let each service pick the storage engine that matches its actual queries — strict relational for money and rules, key-value for grab-by-key, document for flexible schemas, wide-column for massive partitioned writes, graph for relationship traversal. Giving each service its own database is what makes mixing all five safely possible in one system.
Five questions, five shapes, five different databases — all in one system.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Amazon's DynamoDB was born directly from this bottleneck: their shopping cart service hit relational database scaling limits during peak Christmas traffic in the early 2000s, which pushed Amazon to build a key-value store purpose-built for "grab-by-key, millions of times a minute" — a workload a relational engine handles poorly at that volume.
  • Netflix writes viewing-history events into Cassandra specifically because the write volume (billions of events/day, always reads-by-user-ID) needs a store that spreads writes across hundreds of machines and tolerates node failures without blocking writes.
  • LinkedIn-style "People you may know" style features are the classic case for a graph database (Neo4j): "friends of friends" is a natural relationship walk in a graph, but a self-join nightmare in SQL.
💻 Complete Code
Same company: JPA entity vs Mongo document vs Redis key-value
// ---------- order-service: money → JPA + PostgreSQL (strict, ACID) ----------
@Entity
@Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {
    @Id @GeneratedValue
    private Long id;
    private Long userId;
    private BigDecimal totalAmount;   // money → SQL + transactions. Non-negotiable.
    private String status;
}

// ---------- product-service: catalog → MongoDB (flexible documents) ----------
@Document(collection = "products")
public class Product {
    @Id
    private String id;
    private String name;
    private Map<String, Object> attributes;  // TV: screenSize; shirt: fabric.
}

// ---------- cart-service: grab-by-key → Redis ----------
@Service
public class CartService {

    private final RedisTemplate<String, Cart> redis;

    public CartService(RedisTemplate<String, Cart> redis) { this.redis = redis; }

    public Cart getCart(String userId) {
        return redis.opsForValue().get("cart:" + userId);        // one lookup, <1ms
    }

    public void saveCart(String userId, Cart cart) {
        redis.opsForValue().set("cart:" + userId, cart, Duration.ofDays(7));
    }
}
🧰 Cheat Sheet
TypeAsk yourselfReal user at scale
SQL (Postgres, MySQL)"Do I need strict correctness and joins?"Every bank ledger; order systems everywhere
Key-Value (Redis, DynamoDB)"Is it always fetch-by-one-key?"Amazon cart, session stores
Document (MongoDB)"Does every record have different fields?"Product catalogs, content/CMS data
Wide-column (Cassandra)"Huge nonstop writes, reads by partition key?"Netflix viewing history, Instagram feed storage
Graph (Neo4j)"Are relationships the whole point?"LinkedIn "People you may know", fraud rings
⚠️ Common interview trap: "NoSQL is faster than SQL, right?" No — you give up joins and cross-row transactions to gain scale for one specific access pattern. In NoSQL you model around your queries, not your entities.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "I pick storage per access pattern — ACID and joins → relational; grab-by-key → key-value; flexible schema → document; massive partitioned writes → wide-column; relationship traversal → graph. Database-per-service is what makes mixing them safe."
12

Caching with Redis

Performance

Keep frequently-read data in memory, right next to the service, so most reads never touch the database. RAM answers in under a millisecond and, just as important, shields the database from millions of identical queries.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: Profile Service, which handles fetching user profile data, suddenly needs to serve millions of reads for the exact same row — a celebrity just posted, and everyone is opening their profile within minutes. Profile Service queries its database directly on every request, the way it always has. At normal traffic this is fine; at 5 million nearly-identical queries in 10 minutes, the database's connection pool is exhausted, and every other feature that shares that database — not just Profile Service — starts slowing down too.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
A popularity spike concentrates enormous read load onto one specific service and, through it, one specific database:
  • Popularity creates self-inflicted load spikes: 5 million people opening the same profile in 10 minutes means 5 million nearly-identical queries hitting the same rows.
  • The database's connection pool is finite: enough concurrent identical queries exhausts connections, and every other feature sharing that database slows down too.
  • Read replicas only buy you a multiple, not headroom: at true viral scale, even replicated reads eventually saturate — the problem is query volume, not just where the data lives.
✅ The Solution
Cache-aside with Redis: check the cache first; on a miss, read the database once and populate the cache with a TTL. The database ends up seeing roughly one query per key per TTL window instead of millions — regardless of how popular that key becomes.
Check cache → on miss, read DB once → store with TTL. The DB sees ~1 query per key per minute.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Instagram-scale apps: when a celebrity posts, millions of identical profile-page requests hit within minutes. Without a cache, that's millions of identical SQL queries — enough to exhaust the database's connections and slow down every unrelated feature on the platform. Cache-aside turns that into one DB read per 60-second TTL window.
  • Tinder's swipe deck — the batch of nearby candidate profiles served to a user — is a natural fit for the same pattern: recomputing "who's nearby and swipeable" from scratch on every single swipe would hammer the database at Tinder's request volume, so a precomputed deck is cached and served from memory, refreshed periodically rather than on every swipe.
💻 Complete Code
ProductService.java — @Cacheable + @CacheEvict
@Service
public class ProductService {

    private final ProductRepository productRepository;

    public ProductService(ProductRepository productRepository) {
        this.productRepository = productRepository;
    }

    @Cacheable(cacheNames = "products", key = "#productId")
    public Product getProduct(long productId) {
        return productRepository.findById(productId)
                .orElseThrow(() -> new ProductNotFoundException(productId));
    }

    @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "products", key = "#product.getId()")
    public Product updateProduct(Product product) {
        return productRepository.save(product);
    }
}
application.yml — Redis as the cache store, with TTL
spring:
  cache:
    type: redis
    redis:
      time-to-live: 60s
  data:
    redis:
      host: redis
      port: 6379
🧰 Why This Tech Stack
OptionWhen to pick it
Redis default choiceShared cache all service instances see; rich data types; also does locks, counters, queues.
Caffeine (in-process)Ultra-hot data cached inside the JVM itself (L1), often layered in front of Redis (L2).
MemcachedDead-simple string cache; Redis does more and is the ecosystem standard now.
CDN (CloudFront)Caching for images/static files at the network edge — a cache too, just geographic.
⚠️ Common interview trap: "What's hard about caching?" The honest answer is invalidation — knowing when a cached value has gone stale and needs refreshing. A few simple rules keep it manageable:
  • Always set a TTL (time-to-live). Every cached value should expire on its own after some time. That way, even if you forget to update it somewhere, it can never stay wrong forever.
  • On update, delete the key — don't try to update it in place. When the real data changes, just remove the old cached copy. The next read will miss, fetch the fresh value from the database once, and re-cache it. That's simpler and safer than trying to patch the cached value directly.
  • Never cache data where staleness costs money. A wallet balance or a live stock count should never be served from a slightly-old cache — the tiny speed gain isn't worth the risk of showing the wrong number.
One more term worth knowing: a cache stampede is when a very popular key expires and thousands of requests hit the database at the exact same moment. It's usually fixed with a short lock around the refresh, or by adding a small random jitter to each key's TTL so they don't all expire together.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "Cache-aside with TTL turns millions of identical reads into one DB query per TTL window — the cheapest high-leverage fix once decomposition concentrates hot reads onto a single service."
13

CQRS — Separate Read & Write Models

Architecture

Writes (Commands) go into a strict, normalized model. Reads (Queries) are served from a separate, pre-flattened model kept up to date by events — useful when reads and writes have very different shapes or scale.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: the "My Orders" page needs to show order details, the product's name and image, and the current delivery status — three pieces of information owned by Order Service, Product Service, and Shipping Service respectively, each with its own database. The direct approach: the page calls all three services live, every time it loads, and stitches the results together. At low traffic this is fine. At millions of page views an hour, that's three network calls per view instead of one query, and if Product Service is having a slow afternoon, the entire order history page becomes unreadable — even though nothing is actually wrong with the customer's orders.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
Calling every owning service live, on every page view, reintroduces real coupling and fragility at scale:
  • Three network calls per page view, at millions of views per hour, multiplies load and latency compared to one query.
  • Any one dependency being down breaks the whole page: Product Service having a bad day shouldn't mean your order history is unreadable.
  • Stitching results client-side or in a thin aggregator duplicates logic every page that needs this view has to repeat.
✅ The Solution
Build a separate, purpose-shaped read model. A small projector listens to events from Order, Product, and Shipping services and maintains one flattened "order history" document per order in a fast read store. The page becomes a single, cheap query — no runtime joins, no dependency on three services being up simultaneously.
Writes stay strict on the left; events build a ready-to-show view; reads hit only the view.
🌍 Proven at Scale
Amazon's "Your Orders" page is the textbook version of this pattern: order details, product name/image, and live delivery status come from separate systems, but the page renders as one fast, flattened view rather than live cross-service joins. Instagram's feed — built the same way, via events published whenever someone posts — is the same idea at more extreme scale — write the post once, precompute the read side for every follower — because computing a personalized feed live, per page-load, at that traffic volume isn't feasible.
💻 Complete Code
OrderHistoryProjector.java + OrderHistoryController.java
// ---------- read-side builder: listens to events, flattens data ----------
@Component
public class OrderHistoryProjector {

    private final OrderHistoryViewRepository viewRepository;

    public OrderHistoryProjector(OrderHistoryViewRepository viewRepository) {
        this.viewRepository = viewRepository;
    }

    @KafkaListener(topics = {"order-events", "shipping-events"},
                   groupId = "order-history-projector")
    public void on(OrderEvent event) {
        OrderHistoryView view = viewRepository.findByOrderId(event.orderId())
                                              .orElseGet(OrderHistoryView::new);
        view.apply(event);
        viewRepository.save(view);
    }
}

// ---------- read side: one cheap query. No joins. No service calls. ----------
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/order-history")
public class OrderHistoryController {

    private final OrderHistoryViewRepository viewRepository;

    public OrderHistoryController(OrderHistoryViewRepository viewRepository) {
        this.viewRepository = viewRepository;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{userId}")
    public List<OrderHistoryView> history(@PathVariable String userId) {
        return viewRepository.findByUserIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(userId);  // ~10ms
    }
}
⚠️ Common interview trap: "Why not use CQRS everywhere?" It's a complexity tax: two models, a projector, and eventual consistency. For simple CRUD it's over-engineering — reach for it when reads and writes differ wildly in shape or scale.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "CQRS keeps the write model strict and builds purpose-shaped read models from events, replacing the cross-service joins that database-per-service makes illegal with one cheap query, at the cost of eventual consistency on the view."
14

Idempotency — Safe Retries

Resilience

An operation is idempotent if doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. Timeouts, retries, and at-least-once delivery — the guarantee a Transactional Outbox gives you — mean duplicates will happen — idempotency is what makes them harmless.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: a customer taps "Pay ₹999." Payment Service receives the request, calls the bank, and the bank successfully charges the card — but the network blips right as the response is coming back, and the client only sees a timeout. The customer doesn't know if they were charged. The client app, doing the reasonable thing, automatically retries the exact same payment request. If Payment Service has no way to recognize this as a repeat of the same attempt, the bank charges the card a second time.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
Once a call crosses the network, "did it work?" stops being a question the client can answer with certainty:
  • A timeout doesn't mean failure — the server may have completed the operation and only the response was lost.
  • Don't retry, and money may never move — the customer thinks they paid; nothing was actually charged.
  • Retry blindly, and money may move twice — exactly the failure mode a naive retry-on-timeout policy introduces.
✅ The Solution
Every state-changing endpoint takes a client-generated idempotency key. The server atomically claims the key (e.g. Redis SETNX) before doing the real work; a duplicate request with the same key gets the stored result replayed instead of a second charge.
Same key twice → second attempt gets the saved answer, not a second charge.
🌍 Proven at Scale
This is literally how Stripe's public payment API works — every POST accepts an Idempotency-Key header, for exactly the reason above: "should I retry a payment timeout?" has no safe answer without one. On the Kafka side, where a Transactional Outbox guarantees at-least-once delivery, consumers record processed event IDs and silently skip repeats — the same principle, applied to event processing instead of HTTP retries.
💻 Complete Code
PaymentService.java — claim the key, charge once, replay duplicates
@Service
public class PaymentService {

    private final StringRedisTemplate redis;

    public PaymentService(StringRedisTemplate redis) { this.redis = redis; }

    public PaymentResponse pay(String idempotencyKey, PaymentRequest request) {

        Boolean firstTime = redis.opsForValue()
                .setIfAbsent("idem:" + idempotencyKey, "IN_PROGRESS", Duration.ofHours(24));

        if (Boolean.FALSE.equals(firstTime)) {
            String saved = redis.opsForValue().get("result:" + idempotencyKey);
            return PaymentResponse.fromJson(saved);   // duplicate → replay, no re-charge
        }

        PaymentResponse response = chargeBank(request);   // happens exactly once
        redis.opsForValue().set("result:" + idempotencyKey,
                                response.toJson(), Duration.ofHours(24));
        return response;
    }
}
// Belt-and-braces: also a UNIQUE constraint on payments.idempotency_key in the DB.
🧰 Why This Tech Stack
StrategyWhere it fits
Naturally idempotent verbsPUT/DELETE are safe to repeat by design. POST is not.
Idempotency-Key header for POSTsClient generates a UUID per action; server stores key → response (Stripe's model).
DB unique constraintUnique index on the idempotency key — the database itself rejects duplicates.
Consumer dedup tableKafka listeners insert eventId first; duplicate insert fails → skip.
⚠️ Common interview trap: "Can't Kafka just give exactly-once?" Across system boundaries, exactly-once delivery is practically a myth. Real systems do at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing — which from the outside looks exactly-once.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "Network calls between services turn 'did it work?' into an uncertain question — so every money-moving endpoint takes an idempotency key, claims it atomically, and replays the stored response for repeats."
15

Strangler Fig — Monolith to Microservices, Safely

Architecture

You almost never rewrite a monolith in one go. Put a gateway in front, carve out one capability at a time into a new service, route just that traffic to it, and repeat — until the monolith is an empty shell you switch off.

🧩 The Problem in Practice
Concrete scenario: a company has a large existing legacy application handling its entire business, and needs to move it to a microservices architecture without stopping feature delivery or risking an outage. The tempting option is a full rewrite: build the new architecture from scratch, then cut over on a single day. An 18-month rewrite means 18 months of no new user-facing value shipping, while the legacy system keeps getting bug fixes and feature changes in the meantime — the target you're rewriting against keeps moving, and the entire risk of the migration is concentrated into one all-or-nothing cutover day.
🔍 Why This Is Genuinely Hard
A full rewrite concentrates every risk of a migration into a single moment instead of spreading it out:
  • One giant cutover day instead of many small, reversible ones — if it fails, everything fails at once.
  • The business doesn't pause for you: the legacy system keeps getting feature changes and bug fixes during the rewrite, so the target keeps moving.
  • No incremental validation: you don't find out the new architecture has a problem until the very end, at maximum cost to fix it.
✅ The Solution
Strangler fig migration: put an API gateway in front of the legacy system first (changes nothing else). Then carve out one capability, route just its traffic to the new service, and validate before moving to the next. Rollback is always one gateway route flip away. The legacy system shrinks like the host tree inside a strangler fig, until one day it's switched off entirely.
The gateway peels traffic away route by route; the monolith shrinks until it's gone.
🌍 Proven at Scale
  • Amazon famously did not rewrite its early monolith overnight — the internal API mandate — forcing every team to expose functionality only through APIs, the same root idea behind splitting into services in the first place — forced capabilities apart gradually, capability by capability, over years, while the business kept shipping.
  • Netflix spent roughly the better part of a decade migrating from its data-center monolith to cloud-based microservices, carving out services piece by piece and running old and new side by side during the transition rather than attempting a single cutover.
  • The graveyard of "we'll rewrite everything from scratch in 18 months" projects across the industry is far larger than the list of companies that pulled it off — which is exactly why the strangler fig approach is the default recommendation, not the rewrite.
💻 Complete Code
application.yml — carved-out route, canary weights, monolith default
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        # --- Payments: canary in progress — 10% new service, 90% monolith ---
        - id: payments-new
          uri: lb://payment-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/payments/**
            - Weight=payments, 10
        - id: payments-legacy
          uri: http://legacy-monolith:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/payments/**
            - Weight=payments, 90        # dial 10 → 50 → 100 as confidence grows

        # --- Notifications: fully carved out already ---
        - id: notifications
          uri: lb://notification-service
          predicates:
            - Path=/api/notifications/**

        # --- Everything not yet migrated falls through to the monolith ---
        - id: legacy-default
          uri: http://legacy-monolith:8080
          predicates:
            - Path=/**
🧰 Big-Bang Rewrite vs Strangler Fig
Big-bang rewriteStrangler fig
18+ months of building with zero user value shipped.Value ships continuously; migration and features run in parallel.
One giant, terrifying cutover day.Dozens of tiny, boring cutovers — each reversible in seconds.
The old system keeps changing while you rewrite it.Each carved-out piece is frozen, moved, verified, done.
Risk concentrated: if it fails, everything fails.Risk sliced per capability; a failed carve-out affects one route.
🎯 Interview one-liner: "Strangler fig: own the front door with a gateway, carve out one capability at a time behind a route flip, canary the risky ones, and keep rollback one config line away — the monolith shrinks in production, safely, while the business keeps shipping."
Monolith → Microservices · Java 17 + Spring Boot 3 · Read one concept a day, connect it back to the monolith problem it solves. 🎤

SPRING BOOT · CORE COMPONENTS

Every core Spring Boot component, taught through the apps you use daily

19 chapters. Each one explains a component in plain English, then shows the exact business problem it solves inside Amazon, Instagram, YouTube, or WhatsApp — followed by runnable Spring Boot code for that scenario.

🛒 Amazon — orders, inventory, payments
📸 Instagram — posts, follows, feed
▶️ YouTube — uploads, views, streaming
💬 WhatsApp — messages, delivery, presence

🎯 What this covers

The components that actually come up in day-to-day Spring Boot work and in interviews: DI, auto-config, MVC, JPA, AOP, transactions, caching, async, security, actuator, and more.

🧩 Why 4 apps, not 1

Some components fit an e-commerce mental model best (transactions, inventory), others fit social feeds (caching a feed) or messaging (events, async). Each chapter uses whichever app makes the concept click fastest.

▶️ How to read a chapter

Plain-English definition → the real app scenario → runnable code for that exact scenario → a pitfall and a tip. Skim the first two if you already know the concept; read the code either way.

1Plain-English idea
→
2Real app scenario
→
3Runnable code
→
4Pitfall + tip
Part 1 — Foundations
01
Spring Boot vs the Spring Framework

Same engine, but Boot removes the assembly required to start it.

Spring Framework gives you all the building blocks (DI, MVC, data access) but you wire everything yourself in XML or Java config. Spring Boot is Spring plus sane defaults — an embedded server, auto-configured beans, and one dependency ("starter") per feature — so you get a running app in minutes instead of days.
Amazon — checkout service

Before Boot, a team standing up Amazon's checkout service had to hand-configure a DispatcherServlet, deploy a WAR to a Tomcat server, wire a DataSource bean, and set up a view resolver — all before writing a single line of checkout logic.

With Spring Boot, the same team runs mvn spring-boot:run and gets an embedded Tomcat, JSON serialization, and a connection pool out of the box. They spend day one writing the CheckoutController, not XML.

// This ONE class is a complete, runnable web application in Spring Boot.
// No web.xml, no external Tomcat install, no manually registered servlets.

@SpringBootApplication   // = @Configuration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan
public class AmazonCheckoutApplication {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        SpringApplication.run(AmazonCheckoutApplication.class, args);
        // Embedded Tomcat starts on :8080 automatically.
    }
}
💡
TipSpring Boot is not a replacement for Spring — every @Service, @Autowired, and ApplicationContext you use is still plain Spring. Boot only automates the setup.
Part 1 — Foundations
02
IoC Container & Dependency Injection

Classes declare what they need; Spring hands them a ready-made instance.

Instead of a class creating its own dependencies with new, it just declares what it needs in its constructor. Spring's IoC (Inversion of Control) container builds every bean once at startup and injects the right instances wherever they're needed. You get loose coupling and classes that are trivial to test.
Amazon — placing an order

OrderService needs to charge a card and reduce stock. It doesn't know or care how PaymentService talks to the payment gateway, or how InventoryService talks to the warehouse database — it just asks for both in its constructor, and Spring supplies them.

@Service
public class PaymentService {
    public void charge(String orderId, BigDecimal amount) {
        // talks to the payment gateway
    }
}

@Service
public class InventoryService {
    public void reserveStock(String sku, int qty) {
        // decrements warehouse stock
    }
}

@Service
public class OrderService {

    private final PaymentService paymentService;
    private final InventoryService inventoryService;

    // Constructor injection: Spring sees this constructor, finds a
    // PaymentService bean and an InventoryService bean, and passes them in.
    // No "new PaymentService()" anywhere in this class.
    public OrderService(PaymentService paymentService,
                         InventoryService inventoryService) {
        this.paymentService = paymentService;
        this.inventoryService = inventoryService;
    }

    public void placeOrder(String orderId, String sku, int qty, BigDecimal amount) {
        inventoryService.reserveStock(sku, qty);
        paymentService.charge(orderId, amount);
    }
}
⚠️
PitfallField injection (@Autowired directly on a field) works but hides a class's real dependencies and makes it hard to unit test without Spring. Constructor injection — as above — makes dependencies explicit and lets you build the class in a plain JUnit test with new OrderService(mockPayment, mockInventory).
Part 1 — Foundations
03
Auto-Configuration & Starters

Adding one dependency wires up an entire feature for you.

A "starter" is a bundle of dependencies for one feature (data access, security, web). Auto-configuration is Spring Boot inspecting what's on your classpath at startup and registering the beans that feature needs — only if you haven't already configured them yourself.
Instagram — adding database support

A backend engineer wants Instagram's post service to save posts to MySQL. They add one line to pom.xml: spring-boot-starter-data-jpa. On startup, Boot detects a JPA implementation (Hibernate) and a JDBC driver on the classpath, and auto-configures a DataSource, an EntityManagerFactory, and a PlatformTransactionManager — nobody wrote that configuration by hand.

<!-- pom.xml — this single starter pulls in Hibernate, HikariCP connection
     pool, and Spring's JPA support, and triggers their auto-configuration -->
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-data-jpa</artifactId>
</dependency>
// A simplified version of what Spring Boot auto-configures behind the
// scenes once it sees spring-boot-starter-data-jpa + a MySQL driver.
// You never write this class yourself — @ConditionalOnClass triggers it.

@Configuration
