Chapter 8's profiles solve per-environment config for one service — but with 40 services each carrying their own application.yml, shared settings drift and every change means a rebuild-and-redeploy. Spring Cloud Config centralizes it: a Config Server serves configuration out of a Git repository, each service fetches its own settings (by app name + profile) at startup, and beans marked @RefreshScope can pick up changes live — no restart. Git as the backing store is the quiet superpower: every config change is a commit, with an author, a diff, a review, and an instant git revert when a change goes wrong.
Instagram — feature flag on the new feed ranking

The team ships a new feed-ranking algorithm dark — deployed but disabled behind a flag. Enabling it for a small slice of users must be instant, and disabling it must be even faster if engagement metrics dip. Redeploying 200 feed-service instances to flip a boolean would take twenty minutes each way — an eternity when the feed is misbehaving in production.

With central config, the flag lives in one Git file. Enabling: commit rollout-percent: 5, trigger a refresh, and all 200 instances flip within seconds. When metrics look wrong at 2 AM, rollback is git revert + refresh — feed back to the old algorithm in under a minute, full audit trail of who changed what and when included for free.

# In the CONFIG GIT REPO: feed-service.yml -- one file governs all instances
feed:
  new-ranking-algorithm:
    enabled: true
    rollout-percent: 5

# In feed-service itself: just one line pointing at the Config Server
# application.yml:
#   spring.config.import: configserver:http://config-server:8888
@RefreshScope   // re-reads its @Value fields on refresh -- no restart needed
@Component
public class FeedRankingConfig {

    @Value("${feed.new-ranking-algorithm.enabled:false}")
    private boolean newRankingEnabled;

    @Value("${feed.new-ranking-algorithm.rollout-percent:0}")
    private int rolloutPercent;

    public boolean useNewRanking(Long userId) {
        return newRankingEnabled && (userId % 100) < rolloutPercent;
    }
}
💡
TipRefreshing 200 instances one by one via /actuator/refresh doesn't scale — pair the Config Server with Spring Cloud Bus (backed by Kafka or RabbitMQ) so a single refresh event fans out to every instance at once.
Part 10 — Microservices & Cloud
38
Declarative REST Clients — OpenFeign

Call another service like a local method — no manual HTTP plumbing.

Every hand-rolled RestTemplate call repeats the same ceremony: build the URL, set headers, serialize the body, deserialize the response, translate errors. Feign inverts it — you write only an interface describing the remote API in the same annotations you'd use on a controller (@PostMapping, @RequestBody), and Feign generates the entire HTTP client implementation at startup. Point it at a Eureka logical name and load balancing comes along free; wire in Resilience4j and the circuit breakers from Chapter 27 wrap every call. The calling code reads like it's calling a local service — which is exactly the point.
Amazon — checkout's clients, before and after

Checkout-service calls inventory, payment, and shipping. As RestTemplate code, that's three families of URL-building, header-setting, error-mapping boilerplate — subtly inconsistent with each other, each drifting as the remote APIs evolve, none of it business logic.

As Feign clients, each remote API is one small interface that reads like documentation: method, path, request, response. CheckoutService injects them like any local bean and calls inventoryClient.reserveStock(...) — the fact that a network hop, service discovery lookup, load-balancing decision, and JSON round-trip happen behind that line is entirely Feign's business.

// The ENTIRE client. No implementation class exists anywhere -- Feign
// generates it at startup from these annotations.
@FeignClient(name = "inventory-service")   // logical name -> Eureka + load balancing
public interface InventoryClient {

    @PostMapping("/api/reserve")
    boolean reserveStock(@RequestBody ReserveRequest request);

    @GetMapping("/api/stock/{sku}")
    StockLevel getStock(@PathVariable("sku") String sku);
}

@Service
public class CheckoutService {

    private final InventoryClient inventoryClient;   // injected like any local bean

    public CheckoutService(InventoryClient inventoryClient) {
        this.inventoryClient = inventoryClient;
    }

    public void checkout(String sku, int qty) {
        // Reads like a local call; is actually discovery + LB + HTTP + JSON.
        if (!inventoryClient.reserveStock(new ReserveRequest(sku, qty))) {
            throw new OutOfStockException(sku);
        }
    }
}
// Requires @EnableFeignClients on a configuration class.
⚠️
PitfallThe convenience is also the danger: a Feign call looks local but can be slow, can fail, and crosses a network. Never call it in a tight loop (that's N network round trips), and always pair Feign with the timeouts and circuit breakers from Part 8 — an unprotected Feign client inherits every failure mode of Chapter 27's opening scenario.
Part 11 — Observability
39
Distributed Tracing

Follow one request as it hops across every microservice it touches.

In a monolith, one stack trace tells the whole story of a slow request. Split the work across six services and that story shatters into six unconnected log files. Tracing reconnects it: when a request first enters the system, it's assigned a trace ID, and that ID rides along in a header through every HTTP call and Kafka message the request triggers. Each unit of work (a controller handling, a client call, a DB query) records a span — its name, duration, and parent — and a backend like Zipkin or Jaeger assembles all spans sharing a trace ID into one waterfall diagram of the request's entire journey. Micrometer Tracing does the propagation automatically for Spring's HTTP clients, Kafka, and logging; you mostly just add the dependency.
YouTube — "uploads are slow," but where?

Users report uploads taking 6 seconds. The request path: gateway → upload-service → transcoding-service → storage-service, plus a metadata write. Without tracing, diagnosis is archaeology — four teams grepping four log systems, trying to match timestamps, each concluding "our part looks fine."

With tracing, an engineer pulls up one slow trace in Zipkin and reads the waterfall: gateway 3ms, upload-service 40ms, transcoding submit 25ms... and there it is — storage-service's span shows 5.4 seconds, and its child span reveals why: an internal retry loop hitting a misconfigured bucket region three times before succeeding. Diagnosis in minutes, the right team paged, and the trace ID printed in every log line means the matching logs across all four services are one search away.

// build.gradle -- this pair is most of the work:
// implementation 'io.micrometer:micrometer-tracing-bridge-brave'   // creates/propagates traces
// implementation 'io.zipkin.reporter2:zipkin-reporter-brave'       // ships them to Zipkin

@RestController
public class UploadController {

    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(UploadController.class);

    @PostMapping("/api/videos/upload")
    public UploadResponse upload(@RequestBody UploadRequest request) {
        // This log line automatically includes [app,traceId,spanId] --
        // the SAME traceId appears in transcoding-service's and
        // storage-service's logs for this request. Correlation for free.
        log.info("starting upload for {}", request.title());

        return transcodingClient.submit(request);
        // The outgoing call carries the trace ID in headers automatically --
        // no manual propagation code anywhere.
    }
}
💡
TipProduction systems sample — tracing every request at high volume is costly, so typically ~10% of traces are kept (plus, ideally, everything that errored). Set it via management.tracing.sampling.probability: 0.1. For debugging a specific issue, you can temporarily raise it.
Part 11 — Observability
40
Metrics & Dashboards

Turn app behavior into numbers a dashboard can graph and alert on.

Tracing explains one request; metrics summarize all of them — request rates, error percentages, latency percentiles, queue depths — as cheap numeric time series you can graph and, crucially, alert on. The pipeline: Micrometer is the metrics API inside your app (think "SLF4J, but for metrics"), Actuator exposes everything at /actuator/prometheus, Prometheus scrapes that endpoint every few seconds and stores the history, Grafana graphs it, and Alertmanager pages a human when a threshold breaks. Spring Boot auto-instruments a lot (every HTTP endpoint's rate and latency, JVM memory, connection pools) — the skill is adding the business metrics that generic instrumentation can't know about.
Amazon — catching a silent checkout failure

A bad deploy at 14:00 makes one payment provider integration start failing — but only for that provider, roughly 8% of checkouts. No exception storm, servers healthy, HTTP dashboards green: the failures return well-formed error responses. Generic infrastructure metrics literally cannot see this problem.

The business metric can. checkout.failures, tagged by failure reason and provider, jumps from ~2/minute to 40/minute at 14:01. The Grafana alert fires by 14:03, the on-call engineer sees the spike is isolated to one provider tag, correlates it with the 14:00 deploy, and rolls back — total customer impact, a few minutes. Without that one counter, the first signal would have been angry customers hours later.

@Service
public class CheckoutService {

    private final MeterRegistry registry;

    public CheckoutService(MeterRegistry registry) {
        this.registry = registry;
    }

    public void checkout(Order order) {
        // Timer: counts calls AND tracks latency percentiles (p95, p99)
        Timer.Sample sample = Timer.start(registry);
        try {
            processCheckout(order);
        } catch (PaymentException ex) {
            // Tags turn one counter into a sliceable dashboard dimension:
            // failures BY reason, BY provider -- that's what located the bug.
            registry.counter("checkout.failures",
                    "reason", ex.getReason(),
                    "provider", order.getPaymentProvider()).increment();
            throw ex;
        } finally {
            sample.stop(registry.timer("checkout.duration"));
        }
    }
}
⚠️
PitfallNever use an unbounded value (user ID, order ID) as a tag — each distinct tag value creates a separate time series, and a million users means a million series: a "cardinality explosion" that takes down Prometheus itself. Tag with small, fixed sets: reason, provider, region, status.
Part 12 — Security Extras
41
OAuth2 / JWT Authentication

Stateless login: the token itself proves who you are.

Session-based auth stores login state on the server and hands the browser a cookie pointing at it — fine for one server, awkward for twenty microservices that would all need access to a shared session store. A JWT (JSON Web Token) flips the model: after login, the auth server issues a token containing the user's identity and claims (ID, roles, expiry), cryptographically signed. The client sends it as a bearer header on every request, and any service can verify the signature with the auth server's public key and trust the claims — no session store, no call back to the auth server, no shared state. That self-contained verification is what makes JWTs the default currency of microservice authentication. OAuth2 is the surrounding protocol standardizing how tokens are issued and refreshed (and how "Log in with Google" works).
Instagram — one login, twenty services

You log in once on your phone. Over the next hour, the app talks to the feed service, profile service, DM service, notification service — separate deployments, separate teams, separate databases. With sessions, every one of them would need to check a shared session store on every request: a bottleneck and a single point of failure touched by all traffic.

With JWT, login returns a signed token asserting "user 8271, expires in 15 minutes." Each service verifies the signature locally — a fast cryptographic check, no network call — and proceeds. The DM service never asks the auth service "is this session valid?"; the token's signature already answers it. A refresh token quietly obtains new access tokens so the user isn't re-prompted every 15 minutes.

// AUTH SERVICE: verify credentials, issue the signed token.
@RestController
public class AuthController {

    @PostMapping("/api/auth/login")
    public TokenResponse login(@RequestBody LoginRequest request) {
        User user = authService.authenticate(request);   // check password
        String jwt = jwtService.generateToken(user.getId(), user.getRoles(),
                                              Duration.ofMinutes(15));
        return new TokenResponse(jwt);
    }
}

// EVERY OTHER SERVICE: three lines of config = "verify JWTs, trust their claims."
@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    public SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
                .requestMatchers("/api/auth/**").permitAll()
                .anyRequest().authenticated())
            .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth2 -> oauth2.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));
        return http.build();
        // Signature verified locally against the auth server's public key
        // (fetched once from its JWKS endpoint). No per-request network call.
    }
}
⚠️
PitfallA JWT can't be un-issued — it stays valid until expiry even if the user logs out or is banned. That's why access tokens are kept short-lived (minutes), with refresh tokens (which can be revoked server-side) obtaining new ones. Long-lived access tokens turn one leaked header into a long-term compromise.
Part 12 — Security Extras
42
CORS Configuration

Tell browsers exactly which other origins may call your API.

Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: JavaScript on site-a.com can't read responses from api.site-b.com unless site-b explicitly allows it. This isn't the browser being difficult — it's what stops a malicious page you accidentally opened from silently calling your bank's API with your logged-in cookies. CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is the server's allowlist: response headers declaring which origins, methods, and headers are permitted. For non-trivial requests the browser first sends a preflight — an OPTIONS request asking permission — and only proceeds if the server's CORS headers approve. The critical mental model: the error appears in the frontend console, but the fix is always on the backend.
Amazon — seller dashboard blocked by the browser

The seller dashboard is a React app on seller.amazon.com; the product API lives on api.amazon.com — different subdomains, therefore different origins. The frontend team deploys, opens the dashboard, and every API call fails with the console error every developer eventually meets: "blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header." Confusingly, the same API works perfectly from Postman — because Postman isn't a browser and enforces no same-origin policy.

The fix is one backend config class: allow origin https://seller.amazon.com, the needed methods, and the Authorization header (the dashboard sends JWTs from Chapter 41). Preflights now succeed, and — importantly — a malicious evil-shop.com still gets blocked, because it's not on the allowlist. CORS didn't get disabled; it got configured.

@Configuration
public class CorsConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {

    @Override
    public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry registry) {
        registry.addMapping("/api/**")
                .allowedOrigins("https://seller.amazon.com")   // exact allowlist -- not "*"
                .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE")
                .allowedHeaders("Authorization", "Content-Type")
                .maxAge(3600);   // cache the preflight verdict for an hour
    }
}
⚠️
PitfallallowedOrigins("*") is the tempting "make the error go away" fix — and it invites any website on the internet to call your API from its users' browsers. Worse, wildcard + credentials is forbidden by the spec entirely. List your real origins explicitly; in Spring Security setups, also ensure CORS is enabled in the filter chain or preflights get rejected before your config is consulted.
Part 13 — Batch & Files
43
Spring Batch

Process millions of records reliably, with restart-from-failure built in.

A naive "loop over all rows" job has three famous failure modes: it loads too much into memory, a crash at record 4.7 million loses all progress, and rerunning it double-processes everything before the crash. Spring Batch is the framework answer. Work is structured as a Job of Steps, each step a read → process → write loop over chunks — read 1,000 items, process them, write them, commit, repeat — so memory stays flat and progress commits incrementally. The JobRepository persists execution state in database tables: which job ran, with which parameters, how far each step got. That's the superpower — a failed job restarts from the last committed chunk, not from zero.
Amazon — nightly seller payouts, crash included

Every night, a job aggregates the day's millions of order rows into payout records for hundreds of thousands of sellers — money, so correctness is non-negotiable: no seller skipped, none paid twice. At 2:47 AM, four million records in, the database fails over and the job dies.

With Spring Batch, the night shift's response is one command: restart the job. The JobRepository knows exactly which chunks committed, the step resumes from chunk 4,000, and the already-written payouts are neither redone nor duplicated. The 8 AM payout deadline is met. A hand-rolled loop would have meant a very different morning: forensic SQL to figure out who was already paid, and a hand-edited rerun script — with real money riding on getting it right.

@Bean
public Job payoutReportJob(JobRepository jobRepository, Step calculatePayoutsStep) {
    return new JobBuilder("payoutReportJob", jobRepository)
            .start(calculatePayoutsStep)      // real jobs chain multiple steps
            .build();
}

@Bean
public Step calculatePayoutsStep(JobRepository jobRepository,
                                  PlatformTransactionManager tx,
                                  ItemReader<Order> orderReader,          // pages from the DB
                                  ItemProcessor<Order, Payout> processor, // order -> payout
                                  ItemWriter<Payout> payoutWriter) {      // bulk insert
    return new StepBuilder("calculatePayoutsStep", jobRepository)
            .<Order, Payout>chunk(1000, tx)   // read/process/write, commit every 1000
            .reader(orderReader)               // <- restart resumes from the last
            .processor(processor)              //    committed chunk, automatically
            .writer(payoutWriter)
            .build();
}
💡
TipJob parameters (like the run date) identify a job instance — rerunning with the same parameters means "resume that instance," a new date means "new run." Trigger nightly execution with Chapter 15's @Scheduled, passing today's date as the parameter: scheduling starts the job, Batch guarantees its integrity.
Part 13 — Batch & Files
44
File Upload Handling

Accepting large binary files without loading them entirely into memory.

HTTP sends files as multipart/form-data — the request body carries one or more file "parts" alongside regular form fields. Spring's MultipartFile hands each part to your controller, and its most important method is getInputStream(): it lets you stream the bytes onward (to disk, to S3) without ever materializing the whole file in heap memory. The other essential is centrally-configured size limits, enforced by the framework before your code runs — the difference between "a too-large upload gets a clean 413 response" and "a too-large upload takes down the JVM."
YouTube — a 4 GB video meets a 2 GB heap

A creator uploads a 4 GB video to a service instance running with a 2 GB heap. If the handler naively calls file.getBytes() — the whole file as one byte array — the math doesn't work: OutOfMemoryError, instance dead, and every other creator's in-flight upload on that instance dies with it. Two concurrent large uploads would kill it even faster.

The streaming version never holds more than a small buffer: bytes flow from the network socket through the input stream into object storage in chunks, heap usage flat regardless of file size — ten simultaneous 4 GB uploads are fine. The 5 GB configured cap rejects oversized requests up front with a clean error, and the controller returns quickly by kicking off transcoding asynchronously (Chapter 14's @Async) instead of making the creator's browser wait on processing.

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/videos")
public class VideoUploadController {

    private final StorageService storageService;
    private final TranscodingService transcodingService;

    public VideoUploadController(StorageService storageService,
                                  TranscodingService transcodingService) {
        this.storageService = storageService;
        this.transcodingService = transcodingService;
    }

    @PostMapping("/upload")
    public ResponseEntity<UploadResponse> upload(@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file)
            throws IOException {
        if (file.isEmpty()) {
            return ResponseEntity.badRequest().build();
        }

        // STREAM to storage -- never file.getBytes() for large files.
        // Heap holds only a small buffer, whatever the file size.
        String storedPath = storageService.store(
                file.getInputStream(), file.getOriginalFilename(), file.getSize());

        transcodingService.transcodeAsync(storedPath);   // @Async -- don't block the upload

        return ResponseEntity.ok(new UploadResponse(storedPath));
    }
}
# Enforced by the framework BEFORE your controller runs --
# an oversized request gets a clean 413, not an OutOfMemoryError.
spring:
  servlet:
    multipart:
      max-file-size: 5GB
      max-request-size: 5GB
💡
TipAt real scale, big files often skip your server entirely: the API returns a pre-signed URL and the client uploads straight to S3/GCS, so your service handles metadata while the storage provider handles the bytes. Know both patterns — "when would you use pre-signed URLs?" is a favorite interview follow-up.
Part 14 — API Docs
45
OpenAPI / Swagger

Interactive, always-up-to-date API documentation generated from your code.

Hand-written API docs share a destiny: they drift. Someone renames a field, adds a parameter, changes a status code — the wiki page doesn't hear about it, and consumers integrate against documentation that's quietly wrong. OpenAPI fixes the incentive problem by generating the spec from the code itself: springdoc scans your controllers, request/response types, and validation annotations at runtime and produces a machine-readable spec plus Swagger UI — a browsable page where every endpoint can be tried live, right from the browser. The spec being machine-readable is the second win: consumers can generate typed client SDKs from it instead of hand-writing HTTP calls against prose.
Amazon — the Marketplace API and ten thousand sellers

External sellers and tool vendors integrate against Amazon's Marketplace API. At that scale, documentation quality is support-ticket volume: every ambiguity — "is this field required?", "what does a 409 mean here?" — turns into thousands of identical questions. And a hand-maintained doc for hundreds of evolving endpoints would be permanently, somewhere, wrong.

Generated docs can't drift: when a developer adds a fulfillmentType parameter, the spec updates the moment the code deploys, because the code is the source. A seller's developer opens Swagger UI, reads the endpoint, tries a real call against sandbox with their token, sees the exact response shape — and then generates a typed Java or Python client from the spec instead of hand-rolling requests. The @Operation annotations layer human explanation on top of the auto-detected structure.

// build.gradle: implementation 'org.springdoc:springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui:2.x'
// That single dependency = /v3/api-docs (the spec) + /swagger-ui.html (the UI).

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/products")
@Tag(name = "Products", description = "Marketplace product catalog operations")
public class ProductController {

    @Operation(
        summary = "Get a single product by ID",
        description = "Returns full product details. Requires the catalog:read scope."
    )
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", description = "Product found")
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "No product with this ID")
    @GetMapping("/{id}")
    public ResponseEntity<ProductResponse> getProduct(@PathVariable String id) {
        return productService.findById(id)
                .map(p -> ResponseEntity.ok(ProductResponse.from(p)))
                .orElse(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
    }
    // Validation annotations from Chapter 9 (@NotBlank, @Size) show up in the
    // generated schema automatically -- consumers see the real constraints.
}
⚠️
PitfallSwagger UI on a production, internet-facing service is a free map of your entire attack surface. Expose it freely in dev and staging; in production, disable it (springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled: false) or lock it behind authentication — publish the spec to partners through a proper developer portal instead.
Spring Boot Core Components — a study guide built with real scenarios from Amazon, Instagram, YouTube & WhatsApp.
A learning journey · beginner → advanced · one e-commerce platform throughout

Docker & Kubernetes, explained by shipping a real store

You run ShopKart, an e-commerce platform built as Spring Boot 4 microservices: product-service, cart-service, order-service, and payment-service. This guide follows those four services from "works on my laptop" all the way to a production Kubernetes cluster — every concept introduced by the real problem it solves for this store, with diagrams and copy-paste code at every step.

Java 25Spring Boot 4Docker · Kubernetes · Helm26 chapters
1 · Why Docker 2 · Images & Dockerfile 3 · Containers 4 · Networking 5 · Volumes 6 · Registries 7 · Docker Compose
Docker 1 · The problem before the tool

"Works on my machine" — the bug that isn't in the code

Scenario: order-service runs on your laptop, crashes on the server
The ShopKart scenario

Your order-service works perfectly on your laptop. You copy the JAR to the staging server and it crashes: the server has Java 21, you built on Java 25. You fix that; now a font library is missing. Then an environment variable differs. Three hours gone — and nothing was wrong with your code. The environment was the bug.

Why this problem exists

An application is never just your code. It's code + runtime (JDK 25) + system libraries + config + OS assumptions. Traditionally only the code travels between machines, and the rest is rebuilt by hand on every machine — imperfectly. Every difference is a potential crash.

How Docker solves it

Docker packages the application and its entire environment into one sealed box called an image. Think of a shipping container: the goods inside never change whether the container sits on a truck, a ship, or a crane — because nobody repacks it. Your laptop, the staging server, and production all run the same image, so "works on my machine" becomes "works on every machine."

Real world · Netflix

Netflix runs thousands of microservices, and its container platform Titus launches hundreds of thousands of containers every day. That pace is only safe because each container is the same sealed box everywhere — the laptop, the test rig, and production run identical images, so what passed in test behaves identically for 200M+ subscribers.

Containers vs virtual machines — why containers are light

A VM ships a whole guest operating system (gigabytes, minutes to boot). A container shares the host's Linux kernel and isolates just your process using kernel features (namespaces & cgroups — Docker 3). Result: megabytes instead of gigabytes, milliseconds instead of minutes, and dozens of containers per machine. That efficiency is why microservices and containers grew up together.

Docker 2 · Images

The Dockerfile — a recipe that builds the sealed box

Scenario: packaging order-service (Java 25, Spring Boot 4) as an image
The ShopKart scenario

You want the sealed box from chapter 1 for order-service. You need to describe exactly what goes inside: which Java, which JAR, what command starts it. That description is the Dockerfile — a recipe anyone (or any CI server) can run to produce the identical image.

How images work internally — layers

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer — a read-only snapshot of the change it made. Layers are cached and shared: if only your JAR changes, Docker rebuilds only that top layer and reuses the JDK layer beneath. That's why the order of instructions matters — put the things that change least (base image, dependencies) first, and the things that change most (your code) last.

The production Dockerfile — multi-stage build

Stage 1 builds the JAR with the full JDK + Maven; stage 2 copies only the JAR into a slim runtime image. The build tools never ship to production — smaller image, smaller attack surface.

# Dockerfile — order-service (Java 25, Spring Boot 4)
# ---- Stage 1: build ----
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-25 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline          # cached layer: deps change rarely
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests            # only this layer rebuilds when code changes

# ---- Stage 2: run ----
FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre            # slim: JRE only, no Maven, no compiler
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/order-service.jar app.jar
EXPOSE 8080
USER 1001                              # never run as root (best practice)
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
# build the image, tag it, run it
docker build -t shopkart/order-service:1.0 .
docker run -p 8080:8080 shopkart/order-service:1.0
Best practices
  • Multi-stage builds: build tools in stage 1, only the JAR + JRE in the final image.
  • Order instructions least-changing → most-changing to maximize layer-cache hits.
  • Pin exact base-image versions (temurin:25-jre, not latest) — "latest" breaks reproducibility.
  • Run as a non-root user; add a .dockerignore (target/, .git) to keep the build context small.
Docker 3 · Containers

A running box — and what "isolated" really means

Scenario: order-service and payment-service on one machine, unable to hurt each other
The ShopKart scenario

You run order-service and payment-service on the same machine. One day a memory leak in order-service eats all the RAM — and payment-service dies with it. Two apps on one OS share everything: memory, CPU, ports, files. You need walls between them without paying for two machines.

How a container works internally

A container is just a normal Linux process wearing two kernel features:

Namespaces = private views. Each container gets its own process list, network interfaces, hostname, and filesystem view — it genuinely cannot see the other container. cgroups = resource fences. The kernel caps how much CPU and memory the process may use — order-service's leak hits its own 512MB ceiling and gets killed, while payment-service never notices.

In practice — lifecycle and limits 
# run with resource fences (cgroups in action)
docker run -d --name order --memory=512m --cpus=1.0 -p 8080:8080 shopkart/order-service:1.0
docker run -d --name payment --memory=512m --cpus=1.0 -p 8081:8080 shopkart/payment-service:1.0

docker ps                        # both running, isolated
docker logs -f order             # stream order-service logs
docker exec -it order sh         # shell INSIDE the container's world
docker stats                     # live CPU/memory per container
docker stop order && docker rm order
Key mental model: image = the frozen recipe result (read-only); container = a running instance of it (with a thin writable layer on top). One image, many containers — exactly like one class, many objects.
Docker 4 · Networking

How order-service calls payment-service by name

Scenario: containers need to talk to each other and be reached from outside
The ShopKart scenario

When a customer checks out, order-service must call payment-service. But each container has its own private network world (namespaces!). Hardcoding container IPs breaks every restart — IPs change. You need stable, name-based connectivity.

How Docker solves it — user-defined bridge networks

Put both containers on the same bridge network, and Docker runs a built-in DNS: each container can reach the other by container name. IPs may change; names don't. Port mapping (-p 8080:8080) opens a chosen door from the host into a container for outside traffic.

docker network create shopkart-net

docker run -d --name payment --network shopkart-net shopkart/payment-service:1.0
docker run -d --name order   --network shopkart-net -p 8080:8080 shopkart/order-service:1.0
# order-service application.yml — call payment BY NAME, not IP
payment:
  base-url: http://payment:8080     # "payment" resolves via Docker's DNS
Docker 5 · Volumes

The database that survives its container

Scenario: MySQL for orders must not lose data when the container restarts
The ShopKart scenario

You run MySQL in a container for order data. One day you recreate the container to upgrade MySQL — and every order is gone. A container's writable layer dies with the container. Order data must outlive any single container.

Why containers forget

Containers are designed to be disposable — the writable layer on top of the image is temporary by design. That's a feature for stateless apps (order-service itself keeps no data). It's fatal for databases. The fix: store data outside the container, on the host, and mount it in.

How Docker solves it — volumes

A volume is a Docker-managed folder on the host, mounted into the container at a path. The container writes to /var/lib/mysql as usual — but the bytes land in the volume. Kill the container, start a new one with the same volume, and every order is still there.

docker volume create orders-data

docker run -d --name orders-db \
  -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=secret \
  -e MYSQL_DATABASE=orders \
  -v orders-data:/var/lib/mysql \      # volume → container path
  mysql:8.4

# upgrade later: new container, SAME volume → zero data loss
docker stop orders-db && docker rm orders-db
docker run -d --name orders-db -v orders-data:/var/lib/mysql mysql:8.5
Best practices
  • Named volumes for databases; bind mounts (-v $(pwd)/src:/app/src) for live-reload during development.
  • Keep application containers stateless — state lives in databases, caches, and object storage, never in the app container.
Docker 6 · Registries

Shipping the box — where images live between machines

Scenario: your CI builds the image; the production server must fetch it
The ShopKart scenario

The image builds on your CI server, but production runs elsewhere. You need a warehouse both sides can reach: CI pushes the image; production pulls it. That warehouse is a registry — Docker Hub, AWS ECR, GitHub Container Registry.

# tag with the registry address + version, then push
docker tag shopkart/order-service:1.0  123456.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/order-service:1.0
docker push 123456.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/order-service:1.0

# production (or Kubernetes) pulls the exact same sealed box
docker pull 123456.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/order-service:1.0
Best practices
  • Tag with real versions (1.0.3, or the git SHA) — never deploy latest to production; you can't tell what's actually running or roll back precisely.
  • Scan images for vulnerabilities in CI (Trivy, ECR scanning) before they ship.
Docker 7 · Docker Compose

The whole store on one laptop — with one command

Scenario: 4 services + MySQL + Redis, started together for local development
The ShopKart scenario

A new developer joins. To run ShopKart locally they need product, cart, order, payment, MySQL, and Redis — six docker run commands with networks, ports, volumes, and env vars in the right order. Day one becomes a copy-paste nightmare. You want: docker compose up, done.

How Compose solves it

One YAML file declares every service, network, and volume. Compose creates a shared network automatically (so services talk by name), starts things in dependency order, and tears it all down with one command. It's the whole store as a single, versioned file in your repo.

# docker-compose.yml — the entire ShopKart dev stack
services:
  mysql:
    image: mysql:8.4
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: secret
      MYSQL_DATABASE: shopkart
    volumes: [db-data:/var/lib/mysql]

  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine          # cart storage

  product-service:
    build: ./product-service
    ports: ["8081:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/shopkart
    depends_on: [mysql]

  cart-service:
    build: ./cart-service
    ports: ["8082:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST: redis   # by name — same network
    depends_on: [redis]

  order-service:
    build: ./order-service
    ports: ["8083:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/shopkart
      PAYMENT_BASE_URL: http://payment-service:8080
    depends_on: [mysql, payment-service]

  payment-service:
    build: ./payment-service
    ports: ["8084:8080"]

volumes:
  db-data:
docker compose up -d      # the whole store, one command
docker compose logs -f order-service
docker compose down       # stop everything (add -v to wipe volumes)
Where Compose ends: it's perfect for one machine — local dev and small setups. It cannot spread services across many machines, restart them on another host when one dies, or autoscale under Diwali-sale traffic. Those are orchestration problems — and exactly where Kubernetes begins. Switch to the ☸️ tab.

Kubernetes 1 · The orchestration problem

3 AM: a server dies, and nobody restarts your containers

Scenario: ShopKart grows beyond one machine — and beyond manual care
The ShopKart scenario

ShopKart now runs 20 containers across 5 machines. At 3 AM, machine 2 dies — taking two order-service containers with it. Nobody notices until customers complain. Next week the Diwali sale needs 10× more cart-service containers for exactly 6 hours. Who starts them? Who spreads them across machines? Who moves them when a machine dies? Doing this by hand doesn't scale past a handful of containers.

How Kubernetes solves it — desired state

Kubernetes is an orchestrator: you declare the state you want — "6 replicas of order-service, always" — and it works non-stop to make reality match. Machine dies at 3 AM? K8s notices within seconds and starts replacements on healthy machines. You never say how; you only say what. This "declare, then reconcile" loop is the single most important idea in Kubernetes — every feature in the next 15 chapters is that loop applied to a different problem.

Analogy: Docker gave you shipping containers. Kubernetes is the automated port: cranes, scheduling, replacements, traffic routing — run by a control room that never sleeps.
Real world · Google & YouTube

Kubernetes is the open-source child of Google's internal orchestrator Borg — the system that has run YouTube, Search, and Gmail for over a decade. Every YouTube video is served by containers that Borg placed, restarted, and moved exactly this way: declare desired state, reconcile forever. Google published the idea; Kubernetes gave it to everyone.

Kubernetes 2 · Architecture

The control room and the workers

Scenario: what actually runs where when you deploy order-service
The pieces, in one pass

Control plane (the control room): the API server is the single front door — kubectl, dashboards, and all components talk only to it. etcd is the cluster's memory — every declared object lives there. The scheduler picks which machine each new Pod should run on. Controllers run the reconcile loops ("desired 6, actual 5 → start 1").

Worker nodes (the machines doing real work): each runs a kubelet (the local agent that starts/stops containers as told), a container runtime (what actually runs them), and kube-proxy (network plumbing for Services — K5).

Kubernetes 3 · Pods

The smallest deployable thing is not a container

Scenario: running one copy of order-service in the cluster
Why Pods exist

Sometimes two processes must live and die together, sharing localhost and files — an app plus a tiny log-shipping sidecar, for example. Kubernetes therefore wraps containers in a Pod: one or more containers that share an IP and always land on the same node. 95% of your Pods (all four ShopKart services) hold exactly one container — but the wrapper makes the sidecar pattern possible.

# pod.yaml — one order-service Pod (learning only — see K4 for real deployments)
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: order-service
  labels:
    app: order-service        # labels = sticky notes; Services find Pods by them
spec:
  containers:
    - name: order-service
      image: shopkart/order-service:1.0
      ports:
        - containerPort: 8080
kubectl apply -f pod.yaml
kubectl get pods -o wide          # its IP + which node it landed on
kubectl logs order-service
kubectl exec -it order-service -- sh
But here's the thing: a bare Pod is mortal — if its node dies, nobody recreates it. You almost never create Pods directly. You create Deployments, which manage Pods for you. That's the next chapter, and it's the one you'll use every day.
Kubernetes 4 · Deployments & ReplicaSets

"Always 6 order-services" — and zero-downtime releases

Scenario: self-healing replicas + rolling out v1.1 during business hours
The ShopKart scenario

You need 6 copies of order-service running at all times — including at 3 AM when a node dies. And when you release v1.1, you can't take the store offline: old Pods must drain out while new Pods roll in, gradually, with an instant undo button.

How it works — two layers of reconcile

A Deployment manages ReplicaSets; a ReplicaSet keeps N identical Pods alive (its loop: "desired 6, actual 5 → start 1"). On an image update, the Deployment creates a new ReplicaSet for v1.1 and scales it up while scaling v1.0's down, a few Pods at a time — a rolling update. Rollback = scale the old ReplicaSet back up. You never touch Pods by hand.

# order-deployment.yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: order-service
spec:
  replicas: 6                          # the promise K8s keeps, 24/7
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: order-service }
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 1                # at most 1 Pod down during rollout
      maxSurge: 2                      # at most 2 extra Pods during rollout
  template:                            # the Pod recipe (as in K3)
    metadata:
      labels: { app: order-service }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: order-service
          image: shopkart/order-service:1.0
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" }   # for the scheduler (K10)
            limits:   { cpu: "1",    memory: "1Gi" }
kubectl apply -f order-deployment.yaml
kubectl scale deployment order-service --replicas=10        # sale coming

# release v1.1 with zero downtime, watch it roll, and the undo button:
kubectl set image deployment/order-service order-service=shopkart/order-service:1.1
kubectl rollout status deployment/order-service
kubectl rollout undo deployment/order-service               # instant rollback
Best practices
  • Deployments are the default for every stateless service — all four ShopKart services.
  • Always set resource requests/limits; the scheduler and autoscaler depend on them.
  • Rolling updates only protect you if probes are set (K8) — otherwise traffic hits Pods that aren't ready.
Real world · Amazon

Amazon deploys to production thousands of times per day. That's only possible because every release is a rolling replacement of containers behind load balancers — the same maxSurge / maxUnavailable dance shown above — plus automatic rollback when a metric dips. Nobody "installs" software on a machine; machines are just places where containers land.

Kubernetes 5 · Services

Pods come and go — the Service address stays

Scenario: order-service must reach payment-service even as its Pods churn
The ShopKart scenario

Order-service calls payment-service — but payment Pods are replaced constantly (rollouts, node failures, scaling). Every new Pod = new IP. Which address does order-service call?

How Services solve it

A Service is a stable virtual address + built-in load balancer in front of a set of Pods, selected by labels. DNS gives it a permanent name: http://payment-service. Pods behind it churn freely; the name and traffic-spreading never change. Three main types: ClusterIP (internal-only — service-to-service, the default), NodePort (opens a port on every node — dev/testing), LoadBalancer (provisions a cloud load balancer — real external traffic, usually via Ingress, K6).

# payment-service.yaml — internal stable address
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: payment-service            # becomes the DNS name
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: payment-service           # matches Pod labels → they become backends
  ports:
    - port: 8080                   # the Service's port
      targetPort: 8080             # the container's port
# order-service application.yml — same trick as Docker DNS, cluster-wide now
payment:
  base-url: http://payment-service:8080
Mental model: a Service is a restaurant's front desk phone number. Waiters (Pods) change shifts all day; the number on the card never does, and the desk routes each call to whoever's free.
Kubernetes 6 · Ingress

One front door for shopkart.com — routed by path

Scenario: /products, /cart, /orders must reach different services via one domain
The ShopKart scenario

Customers hit shopkart.com/products, /cart, /orders. One LoadBalancer per service would mean four cloud load balancers — four bills, four DNS entries. You want ONE entrance that reads the URL and routes to the right internal Service, plus HTTPS in one place.

How Ingress solves it

An Ingress is an HTTP routing rulebook: host/path → Service. An Ingress Controller (NGINX, Traefik, or a cloud one) is the actual gateway Pod that enforces it. One external load balancer, all routing and TLS handled at the door.

# shopkart-ingress.yaml
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shopkart
  annotations:
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rewrite-target: /
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: [shopkart.com]
      secretName: shopkart-tls          # HTTPS terminated at the door (cert in a Secret, K7)
  rules:
    - host: shopkart.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /products
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: product-service, port: { number: 8080 } } }
          - path: /cart
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: cart-service, port: { number: 8080 } } }
          - path: /orders
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: order-service, port: { number: 8080 } } }
Kubernetes 7 · ConfigMaps & Secrets

Same image everywhere — different settings per environment

Scenario: staging vs production DB URLs, and the payment API key
The ShopKart scenario

The Docker chapter taught: one sealed image for all environments. But staging talks to a staging DB and production to the real one — and the payment gateway API key absolutely cannot be baked into an image anyone can pull. Config must live outside the image and be injected at runtime.

How K8s solves it

ConfigMap = plain settings (URLs, feature flags). Secret = sensitive values (API keys, passwords), stored separately with tighter access (RBAC, K13) and encryption-at-rest options. Both are injected as env vars or mounted files — Spring Boot picks them up like any environment variable.

apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata: { name: order-config }
data:
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:mysql://mysql:3306/shopkart
  PAYMENT_BASE_URL: http://payment-service:8080
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata: { name: order-secrets }
type: Opaque
stringData:                             # plain here; stored base64 + protected by RBAC
  SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: prod-db-pass
  PAYMENT_API_KEY: pk_live_xxx
# in the Deployment's container spec — inject both
envFrom:
  - configMapRef: { name: order-config }
  - secretRef:    { name: order-secrets }
Best practices
  • Never bake config or secrets into images; never commit real secrets to git (use External Secrets / Vault / cloud secret managers feeding K8s Secrets).
  • Restrict who can get secrets with RBAC (K13) — a Secret readable by everyone is not a secret.
Kubernetes 8 · Probes

Don't send customers to a Pod that isn't ready

Scenario: Spring Boot takes 20s to start; a deadlocked Pod looks "running"
The ShopKart scenario

Two incidents. (1) During a rollout, traffic hit a brand-new order-service Pod while Spring was still starting — customers saw errors for 20 seconds. (2) A Pod deadlocked: the process was alive, so K8s thought all was well, but it answered nothing for an hour. "Container running" ≠ "application healthy." K8s needs a way to ask the app how it feels.

The three probes
  • Startup probe — "has it finished booting?" Protects slow-starting apps from the other probes during launch.
  • Readiness probe — "can it take traffic right now?" Fails → Pod is removed from the Service's rotation (not killed). This is what makes rolling updates truly zero-downtime.
  • Liveness probe — "is it alive at all?" Fails repeatedly → K8s restarts the container. This kills the deadlocked Pod automatically.

Spring Boot 4 ships these endpoints ready-made via Actuator: /actuator/health/readiness and /actuator/health/liveness.

# in the order-service container spec
startupProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  failureThreshold: 30          # up to 30×2s = 60s to boot before probes count
  periodSeconds: 2
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 5
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3           # 3 misses → restart the container
Best practices
  • Readiness should check dependencies the request path needs (DB reachable); liveness should NOT (a dead DB shouldn't restart-loop every Pod).
  • No probes = rolling updates silently send traffic to unready Pods. Probes are not optional in production.
Real world · Instagram (Meta)

Meta — Instagram, WhatsApp — runs a Kubernetes-like platform called Twine across millions of machines. At that scale hardware fails constantly, whole racks a day, and nobody gets paged for a dead machine: health checks mark workloads unhealthy and the reconcile loop reschedules them elsewhere, exactly like these probes. Humans investigate patterns of failure; machines handle failures.

Kubernetes 9 · HPA & autoscaling

The Diwali sale — scale out at noon, scale in at midnight, automatically

Scenario: cart-service needs 4 Pods normally, 40 during the sale
The ShopKart scenario

Sale traffic is 10× normal for a few hours. Keeping 40 cart Pods all year wastes money; keeping 4 during the sale melts the site. A human watching dashboards and running kubectl scale is slow and error-prone at noon and asleep at midnight.

How the HPA solves it

The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler watches live metrics (CPU by default, custom metrics like requests/sec if you feed them) and adjusts replicas between a floor and a ceiling. Traffic rises → CPU crosses the target → more Pods; traffic falls → scale in gradually. Pairs with the Cluster Autoscaler, which adds/removes whole nodes when Pods no longer fit — Pods scale on machines, machines scale under Pods.

apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata: { name: cart-hpa }
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: cart-service
  minReplicas: 4                 # normal days
  maxReplicas: 40                # sale ceiling
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 }  # of the Pod's REQUEST (K4)
Note the dependency chain: HPA math is based on resource requests — no requests (K4), no sane autoscaling. And new Pods only help if readiness probes (K8) gate them into traffic when actually ready. Kubernetes features compose.
Real world · Flipkart

Flipkart's Big Billion Day multiplies traffic within minutes of midnight. Surviving it takes more than one HPA: pre-scaled floors, custom-metric scaling, and a queue in front of checkout. The full playbook is chapter 18 — ★ the Big Billion Day case study.

Kubernetes 10 · Scheduling

Which machine gets which Pod — and how to influence it

Scenario: spread order-service across zones; give payment-service dedicated nodes
The ShopKart scenario

Three needs: (1) order-service replicas must not all land on one node — one node death shouldn't take all six. (2) payment-service must run on the PCI-hardened node group only. (3) Nothing else should sneak onto those payment nodes.

The scheduler's dials
  • Requests (K4) — the scheduler only places a Pod where the requested CPU/memory fits.
  • Pod anti-affinity / topology spread — "keep my replicas apart" (per node, per zone) → solves (1).
  • Node affinity — "run me only on nodes labeled X" → payment on hardened nodes, solves (2).
  • Taints & tolerations — a taint on a node repels all Pods except those that explicitly tolerate it → keeps everyone else off, solves (3). Affinity attracts; taints repel — use both for dedicated nodes.
# spread order-service across zones (in the Pod template)
topologySpreadConstraints:
  - maxSkew: 1
    topologyKey: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
    whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway
    labelSelector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }

# payment-service → hardened nodes only, and tolerate their taint
affinity:
  nodeAffinity:
    requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
      nodeSelectorTerms:
        - matchExpressions:
            - { key: node-pool, operator: In, values: [pci-hardened] }
tolerations:
  - { key: "dedicated", operator: "Equal", value: "payments", effect: "NoSchedule" }
# and taint the hardened nodes so ONLY tolerating Pods may land there
kubectl taint nodes payment-node-1 dedicated=payments:NoSchedule
Kubernetes 11 · StatefulSets · DaemonSets · Jobs · CronJobs

Not everything is a stateless web service

Scenario: MySQL, a log agent on every node, a one-off migration, a nightly reconciliation
The ShopKart scenario

Four workloads that a Deployment handles badly: (1) MySQL — replicas are NOT interchangeable; the primary and its replicas each need a stable identity and their own disk. (2) A log agent that must run on every node, exactly once per node. (3) A database migration that must run once to completion, then stop. (4) The nightly payment reconciliation (remember: webhooks are optimisation, reconciliation is the guarantee) that must run at 2 AM every day.

Four controllers for four shapes of work
  • StatefulSet — Pods get stable names (mysql-0, mysql-1) and each keeps its own persistent disk across restarts. For databases, Kafka, anything where identity matters.
  • DaemonSet — exactly one Pod per node, automatically added on new nodes. For log shippers, node monitoring agents.
  • Job — run to completion N times, with retries. For migrations, batch imports.
  • CronJob — a Job on a schedule. For the nightly reconciliation.
# StatefulSet — MySQL with stable identity + its own disk per replica
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata: { name: mysql }
spec:
  serviceName: mysql
  replicas: 2
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: mysql } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: mysql } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: mysql
          image: mysql:8.4
          volumeMounts: [{ name: data, mountPath: /var/lib/mysql }]
  volumeClaimTemplates:            # each Pod gets ITS OWN PersistentVolumeClaim (K12)
    - metadata: { name: data }
      spec:
        accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]
        resources: { requests: { storage: 50Gi } }
# Job — one-off schema migration          # CronJob — nightly reconciliation
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata: { name: orders-migration }
spec:
  backoffLimit: 3                  # retry up to 3 times on failure
  template:
    spec:
      restartPolicy: Never
      containers:
        - name: migrate
          image: shopkart/db-migrator:1.0
---
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: CronJob
metadata: { name: payment-reconciliation }
spec:
  schedule: "0 2 * * *"           # 2 AM daily — compare gateway vs orders DB
  jobTemplate:
    spec:
      template:
        spec:
          restartPolicy: OnFailure
          containers:
            - name: reconcile
              image: shopkart/reconciler:1.0
Rule of thumb: stateless service → Deployment. Identity + own disk → StatefulSet. One per node → DaemonSet. Run once → Job. Run on schedule → CronJob. (In production, many teams run databases on managed services like RDS and keep only stateless things in the cluster — a perfectly good choice.)
Kubernetes 12 · Storage

PV, PVC, StorageClass — disks on demand

Scenario: where MySQL's 50Gi actually comes from
Why three objects instead of one

Kubernetes separates asking for storage from providing it — same philosophy as the rest of K8s. The app says what it needs; the cluster figures out how. That separation is what makes the same YAML work on AWS, GCP, or on-prem.

The three pieces
  • PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) — the request: "I need 50Gi, read-write" (what MySQL's volumeClaimTemplates created in K11).
  • PersistentVolume (PV) — an actual disk known to the cluster (an EBS volume, a GCP disk).
  • StorageClass — the vending machine: when a PVC appears, it provisions a matching PV automatically (dynamic provisioning). Nobody creates disks by hand.
apiVersion: storage.k8s.io/v1
kind: StorageClass
metadata: { name: fast-ssd }
provisioner: ebs.csi.aws.com          # AWS EBS driver creates real disks
parameters: { type: gp3 }
reclaimPolicy: Retain                 # keep the disk even if the claim is deleted
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata: { name: reports-data }
spec:
  storageClassName: fast-ssd
  accessModes: [ReadWriteOnce]      # one node at a time (typical block disk)
  resources: { requests: { storage: 50Gi } }
Best practices
  • reclaimPolicy: Retain for anything you can't lose — deleting a PVC shouldn't delete order data.
  • Volumes ≠ backups. A disk that survives Pod restarts can still die with its zone; run real backups.
Kubernetes 13 · Namespaces & RBAC

Dev can't touch prod — walls and keys inside one cluster

Scenario: dev/staging/prod separation; an intern deletes the wrong deployment
The ShopKart scenario

Everything lives in one cluster. An intern practicing kubectl deletes... the production order-service deployment. Nothing separated environments, and everyone had cluster-admin. You need rooms (so names and resources don't collide) and door keys (so people can only act where allowed).

Rooms and keys

Namespaces = rooms: dev, staging, prod. Same deployment names can exist in each; quotas and policies apply per room. RBAC = keys: a Role lists allowed verbs on resources within a namespace; a RoleBinding hands that key to a person or a ServiceAccount (an identity for Pods/CI, not humans). Cluster-wide versions exist (ClusterRole/ClusterRoleBinding) for admins.

kubectl create namespace prod
kubectl create namespace dev
# Role: read-only in prod        # Binding: give that key to the intern
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: Role
metadata: { name: prod-viewer, namespace: prod }
rules:
  - apiGroups: ["", "apps"]
    resources: ["pods", "deployments", "services"]
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch"]        # no delete, no update
---
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: RoleBinding
metadata: { name: intern-view-prod, namespace: prod }
subjects: [{ kind: User, name: intern@shopkart.com }]
roleRef: { kind: Role, name: prod-viewer, apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io }
Best practices
  • Least privilege: start read-only, add verbs when a real need appears. Nobody uses cluster-admin day-to-day.
  • Give CI/CD its own ServiceAccount that can deploy to exactly one namespace.
  • Pair namespaces with ResourceQuotas so dev experiments can't starve prod.
Kubernetes 14 · Network policies & security

Only order-service may call payment-service

Scenario: a compromised product-service must not reach the payment network
The ShopKart scenario

By default, every Pod can talk to every Pod. If an attacker compromises product-service (the biggest, most exposed surface), they can call payment-service directly from inside the cluster. Business rule: only order-service has any reason to call payment-service — the network should enforce that, not just convention.

How NetworkPolicies solve it

A NetworkPolicy is a Pod-level firewall rule matched by labels: who may talk to whom, on which ports. Best practice is default-deny per namespace, then allow only the flows the architecture actually needs.

# 1) default deny all ingress in prod          # 2) allow ONLY order → payment :8080
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: default-deny-ingress, namespace: prod }
spec:
  podSelector: {}                    # all Pods in prod
  policyTypes: [Ingress]
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata: { name: allow-order-to-payment, namespace: prod }
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels: { app: payment-service }      # protecting payment
  ingress:
    - from:
        - podSelector:
            matchLabels: { app: order-service } # only order may enter
      ports: [{ protocol: TCP, port: 8080 }]
Pod & supply-chain hardening (the rest of the security story)
  • Pod securityContext: runAsNonRoot: true, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, allowPrivilegeEscalation: false — matches the USER 1001 from Docker 2.
  • Scan images in CI (Trivy); pull only from your own registry; pin versions.
  • Secrets via RBAC-restricted K8s Secrets or an external manager (K7, K13).
Kubernetes 15 · Helm · GitOps · CI/CD · Observability · Service mesh

Running it like a team, not a hero

Scenario: 4 services × 3 environments, deployed and observed without midnight kubectl
The ShopKart scenario

You now have ~15 YAML files per service × 3 environments — copy-pasted with tiny differences, drifting apart. Deploys are one engineer running kubectl from a laptop at midnight. When checkout is slow, you grep logs across 40 Pods. The cluster works; operating it doesn't.

Helm — the package manager (kills copy-paste)

A chart = your YAML as templates + a values.yaml of the differences. One chart for all ShopKart services; one small values file per environment.

# values-prod.yaml (only the differences live here)
image: { repository: 123456.dkr.ecr.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/order-service, tag: "1.4.2" }
replicas: 6
resources: { requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi } }
helm upgrade --install order-service ./charts/spring-service \
     -n prod -f values-prod.yaml          # same chart, dev/staging/prod values
GitOps + CI/CD — git is the only door to prod

CI (GitHub Actions): test → build image → push to ECR → bump the tag in the config repo. GitOps (ArgoCD): an agent in the cluster continuously syncs the cluster to that repo — reconcile-loop thinking applied to deployment itself. Rollback = git revert; the audit log = git history; no laptop kubectl to prod.

# .github/workflows/deploy.yml (essence)
- run: mvn -B verify
- run: docker build -t $ECR/order-service:${{ github.sha }} . && docker push $ECR/order-service:${{ github.sha }}
- run: |          # bump tag in config repo → ArgoCD does the rest
    yq -i '.image.tag = "${{ github.sha }}"' envs/prod/values.yaml
    git commit -am "deploy order-service ${{ github.sha }}" && git push
Observability — Prometheus, Grafana, tracing

Prometheus scrapes metrics (Spring Boot exposes them at /actuator/prometheus via Micrometer); Grafana dashboards + alerts ("checkout p99 > 800ms → page on-call"); Loki/ELK centralizes logs; tracing (OpenTelemetry + Jaeger/Tempo) follows one checkout across cart → order → payment to show exactly which hop is slow.

Service mesh & Operators — the advanced tier

A mesh (Istio/Linkerd) adds a sidecar proxy to every Pod, giving mTLS between all services, automatic retries/timeouts, and canary traffic-splitting (send 5% of checkouts to order-service v2) — all without touching Java code. Adopt when service-to-service security and traffic control become real requirements; it's operational weight, not a starter kit. Operators package human runbooks as custom controllers with CRDs — e.g. a Kafka operator that handles failover; you write kind: Kafka, it does the surgery.

Kubernetes 16 · System design on AWS

From a phone in Pune to a Pod — the full request path

Scenario: Load Balancer + API Gateway + EKS, the interview-whiteboard view
The ShopKart scenario

A customer taps "Buy" on her phone. Between her thumb and your order-service Pod sit half a dozen systems. In a system design interview — and in production — you must know exactly what each one does: who resolves the name, who terminates TLS, who balances, who authenticates, who routes to which Pod.

The problem

Kubernetes Services (K5) balance inside the cluster. The internet can't see a ClusterIP. And cross-cutting edge concerns — TLS, authentication, rate limiting per user, request routing — shouldn't be re-implemented inside every one of the four services.

The layered answer
  1. Route 53 (DNS) resolves shopkart.com to the load balancer.
  2. ALB — Application Load Balancer (Layer 7): understands HTTP — paths, headers, TLS termination. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller watches your Ingress (K6) and provisions the ALB automatically; with target-type: ip it sends traffic straight to Pod IPs, skipping extra hops. (NLB is its Layer-4 sibling: raw TCP, millions of connections, static IPs — for non-HTTP or extreme throughput.)
  3. API Gateway (Spring Cloud Gateway Pods): the smart front desk — validates JWTs once, rate-limits per user, then forwards to internal Services. Services stay clean.
  4. Service → Pods: ClusterIP spreads requests across ready Pods in all AZs (multi-pod routing, gated by readiness probes).
  5. EKS: AWS runs the control plane (API server + etcd) across 3 availability zones for you; you manage only node groups — pair with the Cluster Autoscaler (K9).
Implementation — ALB Ingress + Spring Cloud Gateway (Boot 4, Java 25) 
# Ingress → the AWS Load Balancer Controller builds the ALB from this
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: shopkart
  annotations:
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/scheme: internet-facing
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/target-type: ip        # route straight to Pod IPs
    alb.ingress.kubernetes.io/healthcheck-path: /actuator/health/readiness
spec:
  ingressClassName: alb
  rules:
    - host: shopkart.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
            backend: { service: { name: gateway, port: { number: 8080 } } }
# gateway application.yml — Spring Cloud Gateway routes + per-user rate limit
spring:
  cloud:
    gateway:
      routes:
        - id: orders
          uri: http://order-service:8080       # K5 Service names
          predicates: [Path=/orders/**]
          filters:
            - name: RequestRateLimiter
              args:
                redis-rate-limiter.replenishRate: 20   # 20 req/s per user
                redis-rate-limiter.burstCapacity: 40
        - id: cart
          uri: http://cart-service:8080
          predicates: [Path=/cart/**]
Interview one-liners
  • ALB = Layer 7 (HTTP smart), NLB = Layer 4 (TCP fast). E-commerce APIs → ALB; game servers / MQTT / static-IP needs → NLB.
  • Ingress is the wish; the controller (NGINX in-cluster, or ALB controller on AWS) is the machine that grants it.
  • Edge concerns live once at the gateway — never copied into every microservice.
Kubernetes 17 · High availability & self-healing

A node dies mid-sale — and customers never notice

Scenario: node failure, an AZ outage, and deploying during peak — without downtime
The ShopKart scenario

Peak hour. A worker node running two order-service Pods dies. Separately, cloud maintenance wants to drain a node while you're mid-rollout. High availability isn't one feature — it's several small guarantees stacked so that no single failure, and no deploy, is visible to a customer.

The self-healing timeline (what actually happens)

Node stops reporting → control plane marks it NotReady (~40s) → its Pods are marked for eviction → the ReplicaSet sees "desired 6, actual 4" and creates 2 replacements → the scheduler places them on healthy nodes in other zones (topology spread, K10) → readiness probes gate them into the Service → traffic rebalances. Total: a couple of minutes, zero human involvement — and because the remaining 4 Pods in other AZs kept serving, customers saw nothing.

The HA stack — and safe deploys under load
  • Replicas spread across AZs (K4 + K10) — surviving a node or a whole zone.
  • PodDisruptionBudget — a floor for voluntary disruptions (drains, upgrades): "never fewer than 5 order Pods, even during maintenance."
  • Graceful shutdown — the subtle one: when a Pod is terminated, endpoint removal and SIGTERM race. Spring Boot must finish in-flight checkouts before exiting, and a small preStop pause lets load balancers catch up.
  • EKS control plane + multi-AZ ALB are HA by default — your job is the data plane.
# PodDisruptionBudget — maintenance can never dip below 5
apiVersion: policy/v1
kind: PodDisruptionBudget
metadata: { name: order-pdb }
spec:
  minAvailable: 5
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
# Spring Boot 4 (application.yml) — finish in-flight requests on SIGTERM
server:
  shutdown: graceful
spring:
  lifecycle:
    timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s

# Pod spec — pause so the LB stops sending first, then allow 30s to drain
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec: { command: ["sh", "-c", "sleep 5"] }
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30
Kubernetes 18 · ★ Case study

Big Billion Day — surviving a million concurrent shoppers

Scenario: a Flipkart-style sale, minute by minute, with the actual math
The ShopKart scenario

ShopKart announces its own Big Billion Day. Normal load: ~50K concurrent users. At midnight, flash deals go live and within 10 minutes load hits 1M+ concurrent users — a 20× spike. Last year's attempt without preparation: carts timed out, the payment gateway choked, and the site fell over 4 minutes into the sale. This time, Kubernetes runs the playbook.

First, the capacity math (do this before any YAML)

1M concurrent users browsing ≈ 1 request every 5s each → ~200K RPS hitting product-service. ~10% actively carting → ~20K RPS on cart-service. ~3% checking out → ~6K RPS on order-service. A load test says one cart Pod handles 400 RPS at 70% CPU → you need 50 cart Pods + headroom. The payment gateway's contract caps you at 8K TPS — no amount of Pods fixes that, so checkout must be queued, not parallel-blasted.

Why "just add an HPA" fails

Three timing traps. (1) CPU-based HPA reacts after Pods are already melting, and new nodes take 2–3 minutes to join — the sale is lost in those minutes. (2) The database and the payment gateway don't autoscale with your Pods. (3) At midnight the spike is near-vertical: reactive scaling alone starts from too far behind.

The playbook — pre-scale what you can predict, auto-scale the rest, queue the bottleneck
  1. T-7 days: load test → capacity math above. Raise cloud quotas. Pre-pull images onto nodes (a DaemonSet trick) so new Pods start in seconds, not minutes.
  2. T-1 hour — pre-scale the floors: raise HPA minReplicas: cart 4→60, product 6→120, order 6→30. Add warm node headroom so the first wave needs no new machines. Warm Redis caches; add DB read replicas.
  3. Midnight — autoscale on the right signal: HPA on requests-per-second (custom metric via Prometheus adapter) instead of CPU — it reacts to traffic itself, ~15–30s, while the Cluster Autoscaler adds nodes behind it.
  4. Protect the bottleneck: gateway rate-limits per user (K16); checkout becomes accept → queue (Kafka) → process at 8K TPS. Customers get instant "order placed ✓"; workers drain the queue at the gateway's pace. Inventory uses row-locking (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED) so flash-deal stock never oversells.
  5. Priorities: a PriorityClass makes checkout Pods preempt recommendation Pods if capacity runs short — revenue before suggestions.
  6. T+6h — scale in slowly: HPA scale-down stabilization avoids flapping while traffic decays.
Implementation — the three key manifests + the intake endpoint 
# HPA on requests-per-second, fast up / slow down (autoscaling/v2)
metrics:
  - type: Pods
    pods:
      metric: { name: http_server_requests_per_second }   # via Prometheus adapter
      target: { type: AverageValue, averageValue: "300" } # scale before saturation (cap 400)
behavior:
  scaleUp:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 0
    policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 100, periodSeconds: 15 }]  # may double every 15s
  scaleDown:
    stabilizationWindowSeconds: 300
    policies: [{ type: Percent, value: 10, periodSeconds: 60 }]   # decay gently after
# checkout preempts nice-to-haves if capacity runs short
apiVersion: scheduling.k8s.io/v1
kind: PriorityClass
metadata: { name: checkout-critical }
value: 1000000
# order/payment Pod spec: priorityClassName: checkout-critical
// order-service (Java 25, Boot 4) — accept instantly, process at the queue's pace
@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/orders")
class OrderIntakeController {
  private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> kafka;   // constructor...

  @PostMapping
  ResponseEntity<OrderAck> place(@RequestBody OrderRequest req) {
    var event = OrderPlaced.from(req);
    kafka.send("orders.placed", event.orderId(), event);  // ~5ms — the buffer takes the burst
    return ResponseEntity.accepted()                       // 202: "order placed ✓"
        .body(new OrderAck(event.orderId(), "CONFIRMED_PENDING_PAYMENT"));
  }
}
// a consumer drains the topic at ≤8K TPS toward the payment gateway — flat, safe, steady
The five lessons of sale day
  • Autoscaling reacts; capacity math predicts. Pre-scale floors for what you know is coming.
  • Scale on traffic signals (RPS, queue depth), not CPU, for spiky events.
  • Your slowest fixed dependency (payment, DB writes) sets the ceiling — queue in front of it.
  • Scale up violently, scale down gently.
  • Everything here composed from earlier chapters: HPA (K9) + probes (K8) + spread (K10) + PDB (K17) + gateway (K16). Sale day is just the final exam.
Kubernetes 19 · Production checklist

ShopKart's go-live checklist — every chapter, one line each

Print this. It is the whole guide compressed.
AreaThe ruleChapter
ImagesMulti-stage, pinned versions, non-root, scanned, pushed with real tagsD2 D6
WorkloadsDeployments for stateless; StatefulSet/Job/CronJob for the rest; never bare PodsK4 K11
ResourcesRequests + limits on every container — scheduler and HPA depend on themK4 K10
HealthStartup + readiness + liveness probes on every service (Actuator)K8
TrafficClusterIP inside, one Ingress with TLS outsideK5 K6
ConfigConfigMaps + Secrets injected at runtime; nothing baked into images or gitK7
ScalingHPA per hot service (floor/ceiling) + cluster autoscaler; spread across zonesK9 K10
DataStorageClass + Retain; volumes ≠ backups; consider managed DBsK12 K11
AccessNamespaces per env; least-privilege RBAC; CI has its own ServiceAccountK13
NetworkDefault-deny NetworkPolicy; allow only architectural flows (order → payment)K14
OperateHelm charts + GitOps deploys; Prometheus/Grafana + alerts + tracingK15
EdgeRoute 53 → ALB Ingress → gateway; multi-AZ everything; PDB + graceful shutdownK16 K17
Sale daysPre-scale floors, custom-metric HPA, queue the checkout burst, priority classesK18
The one idea to keep: everything in Kubernetes is the same move — declare the state you want, let a controller reconcile reality toward it. Replicas (K4), autoscaling (K9), storage (K12), even deployment itself under GitOps (K15). Master that loop and every new K8s feature is just "what state does this one reconcile?"
ShopKart · Docker & Kubernetes from first problem to production · Java 25 · Spring Boot 4
A learning journey · beginner → advanced · one food-delivery app throughout

AWS for backend engineers, explained by shipping a real Swiggy-scale app

Picture yourself as a backend engineer scaling Zomato — customers search restaurants, order, pay, and track riders live, millions of times a day. This guide walks through the AWS services a platform at that scale actually leans on, from a single EC2 instance to a full multi-AZ architecture — each service introduced by the real problem it solves, illustrated with how Zomato, Amazon, Instagram, Uber, and other real systems use it, plus a Spring Boot 4 / Java 25 implementation for each. The AWS Services tab covers concepts, architecture, and best practices; the Spring Boot tab is the working code, deployment, and pitfalls.

Note: architectural details attributed to Zomato below are illustrative of how a platform at that scale is commonly built on AWS, not a disclosure of Zomato's actual internal systems.

Java 25Spring Boot 4AWS SDK v2~18 services covered
Compute EC2ECS/FargateEKSLambda Storage S3EBS/EFS Databases RDSDynamoDBElastiCache Network VPCALB/NLBCloudFrontRoute 53 Messaging SQSSNSKinesisMSK Security IAMKMSSecrets Manager Observability CloudWatchX-Ray DevOps Code* / CI-CD The whole picture ★ Zomato architecture
Compute · 1 · EC2

Virtual servers you rent by the hour

Scenario: standing up Zomato's very first server
The problem

You need a server to host Zomato's Spring Boot API. Buying a physical server means weeks of procurement, upfront capital, and — worst — you're stuck with whatever size you bought, whether you get 100 orders/day or 100,000.

The AWS answer — EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)

EC2 rents you a virtual machine in minutes: pick an instance type (t3.medium for dev, m6i.large for prod), pick a region, and it's running in 60 seconds. Pay per second while it's on. Instance types come in families — t (burstable, cheap), m (balanced), c (CPU-heavy), r (memory-heavy), g (GPU) — pick the one matching your workload.

Why use it

Full OS control (SSH in, install anything), Auto Scaling Groups add/remove instances automatically as traffic grows, and multiple pricing modes: On-Demand (flexible, expensive), Reserved (1-3 year commit, 40-70% cheaper — for your always-on baseline), Spot (AWS's unused capacity, up to 90% off, can be terminated with 2 min warning — great for stateless/batch work).

Real world — Netflix

Netflix runs the majority of its streaming platform on EC2, using Auto Scaling Groups to add thousands of instances every evening when viewership peaks and remove them at 3 AM when it drops.

Best practices
