  • Never SSH into individual instances to fix things — bake changes into a new AMI or the container image, replace instances. Treat servers as cattle, not pets.
  • Cost optimization: Reserved / Savings Plans for the baseline, Spot for stateless/batch workers, On-Demand only for the spiky top.
  • Security: instances in private subnets (VPC), only the load balancer in public. No public IPs on app servers.
  • Spread ASG across multiple Availability Zones — one AZ outage shouldn't take down Zomato.
Compute · 2 · ECS & Fargate

Run containers without managing servers

Scenario: shipping Zomato as Docker containers
The problem

You've containerized order-service. Running containers on raw EC2 means you're now managing the OS and Docker and the container lifecycle. You want to just say "run 6 copies of this image" and stop caring about the servers.

The AWS answer — ECS with Fargate

ECS is AWS's container orchestrator. Fargate is its serverless launch mode: you specify CPU, memory, and image; AWS runs the containers on infrastructure you never see. No EC2 to patch, no Docker to install, no cluster to size. You pay per second of container runtime.

Why use it vs EKS (K8s)

ECS/Fargate is simpler — you learn 3 concepts (Task Definition, Service, Cluster) instead of Kubernetes' 30. Perfect when you don't need K8s-specific features. For Zomato's early days: ECS. Once you outgrow it — many namespaces, custom operators, cross-cloud portability — move to EKS.

Real world — Uber Eats (early platform)

Delivery-tech teams often start on ECS/Fargate for microservices because it gives container orchestration without the K8s learning curve — engineers focus on the app, not the platform.

Best practices
  • One service per container image — don't cram order + payment into one task.
  • Right-size CPU/memory using CloudWatch data; over-provisioning wastes money at Fargate's per-second billing.
  • Use ECS Service Auto Scaling (target-tracking on CPU or request count) — same idea as EC2 ASGs but for containers.
  • Store container images in ECR (Elastic Container Registry) — pinned tags, never latest.
Compute · 3 · EKS

Managed Kubernetes for teams that need K8s

Scenario: Zomato outgrows ECS — 15 services, custom operators, GitOps
The problem

You've decided you need Kubernetes (multi-team namespaces, Helm charts, ArgoCD, service mesh). But running the K8s control plane yourself — etcd, API server, scheduler across 3 zones — is a full-time job for a platform team.

The AWS answer — EKS

AWS runs the K8s control plane for you across 3 AZs. You bring worker nodes (EC2 node groups, or Fargate for serverless pods). The AWS Load Balancer Controller reads your Ingress objects and provisions ALBs automatically; the Cluster Autoscaler pairs with your ASGs. Everything from Chapter 16 of your Docker/K8s guide, but AWS-native.

Best practices
  • Use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) so each pod gets exactly the AWS permissions it needs — no shared node roles.
  • Multi-AZ node groups, PodDisruptionBudgets, and topology spread constraints — one AZ down, Zomato keeps serving.
  • Managed node groups over self-managed for OS patching; Fargate profiles for spiky workloads that shouldn't wait for a node to scale.
Compute · 4 · Lambda

Run a function; forget servers exist

Scenario: generating a thumbnail every time a restaurant uploads a menu photo
The problem

Zomato restaurants upload menu photos. Each photo needs to be resized into 3 thumbnails. Running an always-on EC2 instance for a job that fires 200 times a day is silly — most of the day it's idle.

The AWS answer — Lambda

Write a function. AWS runs it in response to triggers (S3 upload, API Gateway request, SQS message, EventBridge schedule). You pay per invocation + per ms of runtime. Idle costs = zero. Scales from 0 to thousands of parallel invocations automatically.

When Lambda fits — and when it doesn't

Great fit: event-driven glue code, image processing, scheduled jobs, low-traffic APIs. Poor fit: long-running requests (15 min hard limit), latency-sensitive traffic where cold starts matter (100ms-3s startup, especially for JVM), high sustained throughput (ECS/EC2 is cheaper past a threshold). Use SnapStart or GraalVM native for Java to cut cold starts.

Real world — Coca-Cola vending & iRobot

Coca-Cola processes vending machine telemetry via Lambda — each machine ping triggers a function, so idle machines cost zero. iRobot processes Roomba fleet events the same way — millions of devices, but the compute bill only reflects actual events.

Best practices
  • Keep functions small and single-purpose — one Lambda per event type.
  • For Java, enable Lambda SnapStart or use GraalVM native-image to fight cold starts.
  • Set reserved concurrency to protect downstream services (a Lambda flood can hammer your DB).
  • Always set a DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) for async invocations — failed events must go somewhere.
Storage · 5 · S3

Infinite object storage, pay per GB

Scenario: storing restaurant photos, user profile pics, invoices
The problem

Storing millions of restaurant photos in your database is a terrible idea — bloats backups, slows queries, and 5 MB blobs don't belong in a relational table. You need cheap, effectively unlimited storage for binary files, served fast to users worldwide.

The AWS answer — S3

An object store: you PUT a file into a bucket with a key (the path), and GET it back later. 11 nines of durability (99.999999999%). Serves petabytes. Storage classes let you match cost to access frequency: Standard for hot data, Standard-IA for occasionally accessed, Glacier for archives (retrievable in minutes to hours).

Why use it

Cheap ($0.023/GB/month Standard), directly serveable via CloudFront CDN, event-driven (S3 → Lambda on upload triggers thumbnailing), lifecycle policies auto-move old objects to cheaper tiers, versioning protects against accidental deletes.

Real world — Netflix & Airbnb

Netflix stores every source video, every encoded variant, and every image on S3 — exabytes of it. Airbnb keeps all listing photos and user uploads on S3, served through CloudFront for global speed.

Best practices
  • Block all public access by default; serve user-facing files via CloudFront with signed URLs.
  • Enable versioning + MFA delete on critical buckets — accidental deletion is otherwise permanent.
  • Lifecycle rules: after 30 days move to Standard-IA, after 90 to Glacier — massive cost savings.
  • Server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) on every bucket. Non-negotiable.
Storage · 6 · EBS & EFS

Block storage (a virtual hard drive) and shared file storage

Scenario: MySQL needs a fast disk; multiple containers need a shared folder
The problem

Your MySQL EC2 instance needs a fast, persistent disk that survives instance restarts. Separately, 5 containers producing PDF invoices need to share one folder.

The AWS answer — EBS and EFS

EBS = a virtual hard drive attached to one EC2 instance at a time. Fast (gp3 for most, io2 for extreme IOPS). Used by databases, boot volumes. EFS = a shared filesystem multiple instances/containers can mount at once (NFS). Slower per-op than EBS but shareable.

Best practices
  • Take EBS snapshots regularly (automated via Data Lifecycle Manager) — free backups.
  • Encrypt every volume with KMS. Default encryption on at the account level.
  • Prefer S3 for anything shareable — EFS is more expensive and only needed for POSIX-file-semantics workloads.
Databases · 7 · RDS & Aurora

Managed relational databases — MySQL/Postgres without the ops

Scenario: Zomato's orders, users, restaurants — the core relational data
The problem

Running MySQL yourself means handling backups, replicas, failover, version upgrades, patching, and monitoring — a full-time DBA role. Get any of it wrong once, and you lose data.

The AWS answer — RDS (and Aurora)

RDS runs MySQL/PostgreSQL/MariaDB/Oracle/SQL Server for you: automated backups, point-in-time recovery, one-click read replicas, Multi-AZ failover in ~60 seconds. Aurora is AWS's own MySQL/Postgres-compatible engine — up to 5× faster, storage auto-grows to 128 TB, 6-way replicated across 3 AZs.

Multi-AZ vs read replicas

Multi-AZ = a hot standby in another AZ for HA — synchronous replication, invisible failover on primary failure. Costs 2×. Read replicas = extra async copies you send read traffic to — cuts primary load. Zomato production needs both.

Real world — Amazon.com & Robinhood

Amazon migrated its own retail transaction data off Oracle onto Aurora. Robinhood runs its trading platform's critical relational data on Aurora for the automatic multi-AZ replication and instant failover.

Best practices
  • Always Multi-AZ for production. Automated backups + 30-day retention.
  • Read replicas for read-heavy workloads (restaurant catalog reads far outnumber writes).
  • Store DB credentials in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation, never in application config.
  • Enable Performance Insights — you'll actually be able to debug slow queries in production.
Databases · 8 · DynamoDB

Managed NoSQL — single-digit-ms at any scale

Scenario: session tokens, cart items, live delivery tracking pings
The problem

Zomato's rider apps ping location every 3 seconds. Across 50,000 active riders that's ~17,000 writes/second — sustained. RDS chokes; you need a database that scales writes horizontally without pain.

The AWS answer — DynamoDB

Key-value/document store that scales writes and reads independently. You pick a partition key (e.g. rider_id); DynamoDB shards data across many partitions automatically. On-demand mode auto-scales, provisioned mode is cheaper if load is predictable. Single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale.

When to reach for it

Sessions, feature flags, shopping carts, IoT/location streams, anything with a natural key-based access pattern and predictable query shape. Not for ad-hoc reporting (no JOINs, no GROUP BY) — that stays on RDS or a data warehouse.

Real world — Amazon.com carts, Lyft rides, Disney+

Every Amazon.com shopping cart is a DynamoDB item. Lyft tracks every active ride on DynamoDB. Disney+ stores user session state and per-user watch progress on DynamoDB across regions.

Best practices
  • Design the partition key to spread writes evenly — a single "hot" partition kills throughput.
  • Enable DAX (in-memory cache) for read-heavy items (session lookups).
  • TTL attribute on items that expire (sessions, tracking pings older than 24h) — auto-deletes, no cron job.
  • Global Tables for multi-region active-active — same table replicated to Mumbai + Singapore.
Databases · 9 · ElastiCache

Managed Redis / Memcached — a distributed cache in one click

Scenario: restaurant listings and menus cached in front of RDS
The problem

Every home-page load hits the DB for the same top-100 restaurants. That's millions of identical queries hitting RDS for data that changes hourly. You need Redis in front — but running Redis yourself means clustering, failover, and patching.

The AWS answer — ElastiCache

Managed Redis or Memcached. Multi-AZ with automatic failover, backups, patching handled. Cluster mode enabled → sharded across many nodes for huge datasets. Pair it with @Cacheable in Spring Boot (Ch 13 of your Spring Boot guide) and RDS load drops 90%.

Best practices
  • Always set TTLs — a cache that never expires eventually holds stale data.
  • Use Redis (not Memcached) unless you know you need pure key-value only — Redis has lists, sorted sets, pub/sub, all useful for rate limiting and leaderboards.
  • Encryption in transit + at rest, in a private subnet. Never expose ElastiCache to the internet.
Network · 10 · VPC

Your own private network in the cloud

Scenario: keeping the database off the public internet
The problem

If your MySQL is on a public IP, the entire internet is knocking on port 3306 within minutes. You need network-level isolation — only the app tier reaches the database; the database is invisible to everyone else.

The AWS answer — VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)

A private network you define with a CIDR (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16), split into subnets per AZ. Public subnets (for the ALB) route to the internet via an Internet Gateway; private subnets (for app + DB) can only be reached from within. Security groups = per-instance firewalls: "port 3306 only from the app-tier security group."

Best practices
  • 3 tiers × 3 AZs = 9 subnets. Minimum for HA.
  • Default-deny security groups — start with nothing open, add exactly what's needed.
  • VPC Flow Logs on — you'll need them the first time something looks off.
  • Use VPC endpoints for S3/DynamoDB — traffic stays inside AWS, no NAT gateway cost.
Network · 11 · ALB & NLB

Load balancing — Layer 7 HTTP and Layer 4 TCP

Scenario: routing zomato.com to the right microservice
The AWS answer

ALB (Application LB, Layer 7) understands HTTP — path/host routing, TLS termination, WebSocket, HTTP/2. This is the default for web APIs. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller provisions ALBs from Ingress objects. NLB (Network LB, Layer 4) is raw TCP/UDP — millions of connections/sec, static IPs, ultra-low latency. Reach for it for gRPC-heavy backends, gaming, non-HTTP protocols.

Best practices
  • Terminate TLS at the ALB using ACM (free public certificates), not at the app.
  • Health checks hit /actuator/health/readiness (Spring Boot). Match the timing to your app's real startup.
  • WAF (Web Application Firewall) in front of the ALB — SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting built in.
Network · 12 · CloudFront

CDN — cache content at 400+ edge locations

Scenario: restaurant photos loading fast for a user in Bengaluru
The problem

Zomato's photos live on S3 in Mumbai. A user in Kolkata waits 100+ ms per image on every load. Multiply by 30 images per home screen and it feels sluggish. And your S3 bill grows with every miss.

The AWS answer — CloudFront

A global CDN. Users hit the nearest edge location; CloudFront serves cached content or fetches once from S3/ALB. TLS + HTTP/2 + Brotli compression at the edge. Can also cache dynamic API responses briefly (5-30s) to shed massive load off ALB during traffic spikes.

Real world — Hotstar (Disney+) IPL live streams

Disney+ Hotstar serves cricket to 25M+ concurrent viewers via CloudFront — the origin never sees most requests, they hit edge caches close to viewers.

Best practices
  • Signed URLs / signed cookies for private content (invoices, user documents).
  • Cache-Control headers on origin — CloudFront respects them; long TTLs for photos, short for API data.
  • Invalidate carefully (paths, not /*) — invalidations cost money past the free tier.
Network · 13 · Route 53

DNS with health checks and routing policies

Scenario: zomato.com pointing to the right region + failover
The AWS answer

DNS service, but with policies: Latency-based (send Mumbai users to Mumbai region, Singapore to Singapore), Weighted (10% canary), Failover (health check the primary; on failure, DNS starts returning the secondary automatically), Geolocation. Also registers domain names.

Best practices
  • Set sensible TTLs — too high delays failover; too low means clients hammer DNS.
  • Health checks + failover policy are your first-line disaster recovery for multi-region.
  • Use alias records (not CNAMEs) for ALB/CloudFront — no extra hop, no cost.
Messaging · 14 · SQS

A managed queue between services

Scenario: order placement doesn't wait for payment to finish
The problem

When a Zomato order is placed, the API needs to (1) save the order, (2) charge the payment gateway, (3) notify the restaurant, (4) push mobile notifications, (5) update analytics. Doing all this synchronously means the customer waits 4-5 seconds and sees an error if any single step fails.

The AWS answer — SQS (Simple Queue Service)

Order-service does step 1 and puts a message on an SQS queue. Payment/notification/analytics workers read from the queue independently, retry on failure, and don't block the customer response. Standard queues = high throughput, at-least-once (rare duplicates). FIFO queues = strict order, exactly-once, lower throughput (300 msg/s per shard).

Real world — Amazon.com order pipeline

Every Amazon.com order flows through SQS between order intake, warehouse, shipping, billing. If warehouse is down, orders queue up safely and process when it recovers — customers never see the outage.

Best practices
  • Always configure a Dead Letter Queue after N retries — bad messages stop poisoning the queue.
  • Long polling (WaitTimeSeconds=20) — cuts empty receive costs by 20×.
  • Make consumers idempotent (see Ch 2 patterns) — Standard queues can deliver twice.
Messaging · 15 · SNS

Pub/sub — one event to many subscribers

Scenario: "order delivered" fans out to email, SMS, analytics, loyalty
The AWS answer — SNS

Publisher sends one message to a topic. SNS fans it out to every subscriber — SQS queues, Lambda, HTTPS endpoints, email, SMS. Perfect for "one thing happened, many parts of the system should know." The standard pattern for a resilient event fan-out is SNS → SQS per subscriber: each consumer has its own retry buffer.

Best practices
  • Message filtering — subscribers can filter by attributes so they don't get everything.
  • Every subscriber should be its own SQS queue, not a direct Lambda subscription, for retries and back-pressure.
  • Encrypt topics with KMS; verify signatures on HTTP subscribers.
Streaming · 16 · Kinesis

Streaming for high-volume telemetry and analytics

Scenario: rider location pings, clickstream, real-time dashboards
The AWS answer — Kinesis Data Streams

An ordered, partitioned event stream (think Kafka, managed). Producers write records with a partition key; multiple consumers read at their own pace. Data is retained 24 hours to 365 days. Perfect for millions of writes/sec (rider location, clickstream) feeding real-time analytics and long-term storage.

SQS vs Kinesis

SQS = work queue: a message is consumed by one worker, then gone. Kinesis = event log: same records read by many independent consumers, replayable. Use SQS for tasks, Kinesis for events/telemetry with multiple downstream needs.

Real world — Netflix & Lyft

Netflix pipes viewing telemetry through Kinesis to power recommendations, quality-of-experience alerts, and billing — all consuming the same stream independently. Lyft's Amazon Location + trip telemetry runs through Kinesis for fraud detection and dispatch analytics.

Streaming · 17 · MSK

Managed Apache Kafka

Scenario: you already use Kafka and want AWS to run it
The AWS answer — MSK (Managed Streaming for Kafka)

Real Apache Kafka, AWS-operated. Multi-AZ brokers, patching, monitoring — you own the topics and clients. Choose MSK over Kinesis when you already have Kafka expertise/ecosystem (Kafka Connect, KStreams, Debezium) or need Kafka's exact semantics.

Security · 18 · IAM

Who can do what on AWS

Scenario: order-service can read S3 photos but not delete them
The problem

By default, nothing on AWS can do anything. Every access is denied until an explicit permission grants it. But if you grant "everything to everyone" (which people do out of frustration), a single compromised credential owns your entire account.

The AWS answer — IAM

Users = humans. Roles = temporary credentials for services (EC2, Lambda, containers). Policies = JSON documents listing "on which resources, what actions, allowed/denied." Attach a role to an EC2 instance and its code gets AWS credentials automatically — no hardcoded keys anywhere.

Best practices — this section matters more than any other
  • Least privilege. Grant the exact actions on the exact resources needed, nothing more.
  • Never use the root account after initial setup. Never create long-lived access keys for a service — always use roles.
  • MFA on every human user. Federate to Google/Okta via IAM Identity Center (SSO) instead of managing users.
  • For EKS: IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts). For ECS: task roles. Each pod/task gets exactly its own permissions.
Security · 19 · KMS

Managed encryption keys

Scenario: encrypting the database, S3, and logs — with a key AWS can't read either
The AWS answer — KMS

Managed keys used by RDS, S3, EBS, Secrets Manager, and your app code. Envelope encryption: KMS holds the master key; your data is encrypted by a per-object data key which is itself encrypted by KMS. You never see the raw key. Every use is logged in CloudTrail — full audit trail.

Best practices
  • Customer-managed keys (CMKs) over AWS-managed ones — you control rotation and access.
  • Enable annual automatic rotation on symmetric keys.
  • Restrict who can use vs manage each key with separate policies.
Security · 20 · Secrets Manager

Store, rotate, and fetch secrets — no more secrets in git

Scenario: the RDS password rotates every 30 days without a deployment
The AWS answer

Store secrets (DB passwords, API keys, JWT signing keys), retrieve at runtime with an IAM-controlled API call, and set automatic rotation for supported types (RDS, DocumentDB) with zero code changes. Alternative: Systems Manager Parameter Store (cheaper, simpler, no rotation) for non-critical config.

Best practices
  • Every secret rotates automatically, on a schedule — no manual rotations.
  • App fetches on startup + refresh; don't cache forever.
  • Never commit secrets to git — CI/CD reads them from Secrets Manager at deploy time.
Observability · 21 · CloudWatch

Logs, metrics, alarms — the AWS monitoring hub

Scenario: knowing when order latency spikes at 2 AM
The AWS answer

Logs = every log line from EC2/ECS/Lambda, searchable with Logs Insights. Metrics = CPU, memory, request count, custom app metrics (Micrometer publishes them). Alarms = "if p99 checkout latency > 800 ms for 3 mins, page on-call." Dashboards = single-pane view of the whole stack.

Best practices
  • Structured JSON logs (not plain text) — Logs Insights queries them in seconds.
  • Log retention policies — don't pay to keep every DEBUG line for 5 years.
  • Alarms on SLIs (p99 latency, error rate) — not on infrastructure metrics like CPU. Users don't care about CPU; they care about slow orders.
Observability · 22 · X-Ray

Distributed tracing across microservices

Scenario: which of the 6 services made this checkout take 4 seconds?
The AWS answer — X-Ray

Traces a single request across every service it touches — order → payment → notification. Shows a flame graph with the exact time spent in each hop and each downstream call (RDS, DynamoDB, external HTTP). Instantly reveals which service is the bottleneck. Add OpenTelemetry SDK to your Spring Boot app; X-Ray receives the traces.

Best practices
  • Sample intelligently — 100% traces on Black Friday will bankrupt you; 5% of normal + 100% of errors is a good default.
  • Add custom subsegments for the DB queries and external calls that matter — they show up in the flame graph.
DevOps · 23 · CodePipeline / CodeBuild / CodeDeploy

Automated build and deploy on every git push

Scenario: order-service goes from commit to production in 15 minutes, safely
The AWS answer

CodePipeline = orchestrator. CodeBuild = Maven/Gradle build + tests + Docker build. CodeDeploy = deploy strategies including blue/green (spin up new fleet, switch ALB, keep old for rollback) and canary. ECR for images. CDK or Terraform for infrastructure as code. Many teams also use GitHub Actions for the CI part and just use Code* for AWS-side deployment.

Best practices
  • Every environment defined in code (CDK/Terraform) — no console clicks in production.
  • Blue/green for stateless services; rolling for containers with orchestration (K8s handles it).
  • Automated rollback on health check / alarm failure — humans shouldn't be in the hot path at 3 AM.
  • Never deploy Fridays. Really.
★ The whole picture

Zomato's complete production architecture

Every service you've read about, wired together for a real food-delivery app
The scenario, end to end

A customer opens Zomato, sees restaurants, orders a biryani, pays, tracks the rider live, and rates the meal. Behind that one hour, roughly a dozen AWS services quietly cooperate. Here's the full map.

Feature-by-feature: which services do what

FeatureServices involvedWhy
AuthenticationCognito, API Gateway, Secrets ManagerManaged user pools + JWT verification at the gateway; secrets never in code.
Restaurant searchOpenSearch, ElastiCache, CloudFrontFull-text + geo-distance queries on OpenSearch; hot results cached; static images edge-cached.
Place orderALB → order-service (EKS) → Aurora → SQSSync save + async fan-out; customer response in ~200 ms.
Paymentpayment-service, SQS, KMS, Secrets ManagerAsync worker consumes SQS; gateway key held in Secrets Manager, rotated; TLS + audit log.
Live trackingRider app → Kinesis → tracking-service → DynamoDB17K writes/s of location pings; DynamoDB partition key = rider_id; TTL clears old pings.
NotificationsSNS → SQS → notification-service → mobile push / SMSOne "order placed" event fans out to every channel independently.
RecommendationsKinesis stream → S3 → SageMaker (offline train) → DynamoDB (serve)Batch train, serve pre-computed lists via key-value lookup for low latency.
AnalyticsKinesis → S3 (data lake) → Athena / RedshiftSame stream, different consumers — order funnel, restaurant reports, city dashboards.
MonitoringCloudWatch (logs + metrics + alarms), X-Ray (traces)SLI-based alarms (p99 latency, error rate) page on-call; X-Ray shows which hop is slow.
CI/CDGitHub → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR → EKS (blue/green)Push to main triggers build, scan, deploy with automatic rollback on health failure.
SecurityWAF, Shield, GuardDuty, IAM, KMSWAF filters SQLi/XSS at the edge; GuardDuty flags anomalous API activity; IAM least-privilege everywhere.
HA / DRMulti-AZ everything + Route 53 failover + cross-region replication (S3, DynamoDB Global Tables, Aurora Global Database)AZ failure = invisible; region failure = ~1 min DNS failover to secondary region.

The three operational rules that hold it all together

Rule 1 · Multi-AZ from day one
  • Every stateful service (RDS, ElastiCache, MSK) in Multi-AZ mode. Stateless services spread across 3 AZs via ASG/EKS topology spread.
  • Cost is ~2× vs single-AZ; the alternative is total downtime whenever AWS has an AZ incident (they do, occasionally).
Rule 2 · Async everything the customer doesn't wait for
  • Customer sees "order placed ✓" within 200 ms; payment, notifications, analytics all happen behind SQS/SNS/Kinesis.
  • If any consumer is down, messages queue safely. Customers never see it.
Rule 3 · Every piece runs in code (IaC + CI/CD)
  • CDK or Terraform describes every resource. Pipelines deploy from git. Nobody makes changes in the console.
  • Recovering from disaster = terraform apply in the DR region + restore backups. Tested quarterly.
Setup Base setup Storage S3 uploads Databases RDS/AuroraDynamoDBElastiCache Messaging SQSSNS Security Secrets ManagerCognito / JWT Ops CloudWatch metrics Deploy Local → AWS
Boot · Base setup

Dependencies, credentials, and the AWS SDK v2

The setup that everything else builds on

Every Zomato microservice uses AWS SDK v2 (async-first, modular per service). Credentials come from an IAM role — never hardcoded. Local dev uses LocalStack so you don't hit real AWS on every run.

<!-- pom.xml — depend only on the SDK modules you use -->
<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId>
      <artifactId>bom</artifactId>
      <version>2.28.0</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>

<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency><groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId><artifactId>s3</artifactId></dependency>
  <dependency><groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId><artifactId>sqs</artifactId></dependency>
  <dependency><groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId><artifactId>dynamodb-enhanced</artifactId></dependency>
  <dependency><groupId>software.amazon.awssdk</groupId><artifactId>secretsmanager</artifactId></dependency>
</dependencies>
# application.yml — region + LocalStack override for dev only
aws:
  region: ap-south-1          # Mumbai

spring:
  profiles:
    active: ${SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE:local}

---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: local
aws:
  endpoint-override: http://localhost:4566   # LocalStack
// AwsConfig.java — one place to build every AWS client
@Configuration
public class AwsConfig {

  @Value("${aws.region}") private String region;
  @Value("${aws.endpoint-override:}") private String endpointOverride;   // empty in prod

  private <B extends AwsClientBuilder<B,?>> B configure(B builder) {
    builder.region(Region.of(region))
           .credentialsProvider(DefaultCredentialsProvider.create());   // picks up IAM role in prod
    if (!endpointOverride.isBlank()) builder.endpointOverride(URI.create(endpointOverride));
    return builder;
  }

  @Bean S3Client s3Client()                 { return configure(S3Client.builder()).build(); }
  @Bean SqsClient sqsClient()               { return configure(SqsClient.builder()).build(); }
  @Bean DynamoDbClient dynamoDbClient()     { return configure(DynamoDbClient.builder()).build(); }
  @Bean SecretsManagerClient smClient()     { return configure(SecretsManagerClient.builder()).build(); }
}
The rules
  • Use DefaultCredentialsProvider — it picks up IAM role in prod, env vars locally, in that order. Never inject access keys.
  • One @Bean per client, singletons — clients are thread-safe and expensive to build.
  • Every dependency pinned via BOM. Never upgrade one SDK module by itself.
Boot · S3

Restaurant photo uploads — pre-signed URL flow

The pattern

Never route file bytes through your Spring app — it wastes bandwidth, memory, and time. The customer uploads directly to S3; your backend only issues a short-lived pre-signed URL.

@Service
public class PhotoUploadService {

  private final S3Presigner presigner;
  @Value("${zomato.photos.bucket}") private String bucket;

  public PhotoUploadService(S3Presigner presigner) { this.presigner = presigner; }

  public UploadTicket issueUploadTicket(String restaurantId, String contentType) {
    String key = "restaurants/" + restaurantId + "/" + UUID.randomUUID() + ".jpg";

    PutObjectRequest put = PutObjectRequest.builder()
        .bucket(bucket).key(key).contentType(contentType)
        .serverSideEncryption(ServerSideEncryption.AWS_KMS)   // KMS-encrypted at rest
        .build();

    PresignedPutObjectRequest signed = presigner.presignPutObject(
        r -> r.signatureDuration(Duration.ofMinutes(5)).putObjectRequest(put));

    return new UploadTicket(signed.url().toString(), key);   // customer PUTs directly to this URL
  }
}
public record UploadTicket(String uploadUrl, String finalKey) {}
@RestController @RequestMapping("/api/restaurants/{id}/photos")
public class PhotoController {
  private final PhotoUploadService uploads;

  @PostMapping("/upload-url")
  public UploadTicket getUploadUrl(@PathVariable String id) {
    return uploads.issueUploadTicket(id, "image/jpeg");   // mobile app receives this, PUTs the bytes
  }
}
Pitfalls to avoid
  • Never stream file bytes through the Spring app for uploads — use pre-signed URLs.
  • An S3 upload triggers a Lambda that produces thumbnails — don't do resizing in the API.
  • Bucket is private + block-all-public — serve reads via CloudFront with signed URLs.
Boot · RDS / Aurora

Just Spring Data JPA — with the DB password from Secrets Manager

spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://${DB_HOST}:3306/zomato
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}                # populated from Secrets Manager, see below
    hikari:
      maximum-pool-size: 20                 # right-size for your Aurora tier
      connection-timeout: 3000
  jpa:
    open-in-view: false                       # classic hidden N+1 source — off
Practical points
  • Point spring.datasource.url at the Aurora cluster endpoint for writes; the reader endpoint (or a separate @Qualifier-tagged DataSource) for read replicas.
  • Enable HikariCP metrics; expose via Micrometer to CloudWatch. Pool exhaustion is the #1 cause of "slow API" tickets.
  • Use IAM DB Auth for extra security, or Secrets Manager for the password with rotation.
Boot · DynamoDB

Live rider tracking — Enhanced Client

@DynamoDbBean
public class RiderLocation {
  private String riderId;
  private Long timestamp;
  private Double lat, lng;
  private Long ttl;   // item expires; DynamoDB deletes it automatically

  @DynamoDbPartitionKey public String getRiderId() { return riderId; }
  @DynamoDbSortKey     public Long   getTimestamp() { return timestamp; }
  // other getters/setters/attribute names omitted
}

@Configuration
public class DynamoConfig {
  @Bean DynamoDbEnhancedClient enhanced(DynamoDbClient c) {
    return DynamoDbEnhancedClient.builder().dynamoDbClient(c).build();
  }
  @Bean DynamoDbTable<RiderLocation> riderLocationTable(DynamoDbEnhancedClient e) {
    return e.table("rider-locations", TableSchema.fromBean(RiderLocation.class));
  }
}

@Service
public class TrackingService {
  private final DynamoDbTable<RiderLocation> table;

  public void recordPing(String riderId, double lat, double lng) {
    RiderLocation r = new RiderLocation();
    r.setRiderId(riderId);
    r.setTimestamp(Instant.now().toEpochMilli());
    r.setLat(lat); r.setLng(lng);
    r.setTtl(Instant.now().plus(24, ChronoUnit.HOURS).getEpochSecond());
    table.putItem(r);   // ~5 ms latency, scales to 17K writes/s effortlessly
  }

  public List<RiderLocation> recentPings(String riderId, int minutes) {
    QueryConditional q = QueryConditional.sortGreaterThan(
        Key.builder().partitionValue(riderId)
                     .sortValue(Instant.now().minus(minutes, ChronoUnit.MINUTES).toEpochMilli())
                     .build());
    return table.query(q).items().stream().toList();
  }
}
Pitfalls
  • Design the partition key first — a hot rider partition kills throughput.
  • Enable TTL on tracking pings — no cleanup cron needed.
  • Enhanced Client is worth it — hand-mapped AttributeValue code is a bug factory.
Boot · ElastiCache Redis

Spring Boot @Cacheable, backed by ElastiCache

# application.yml
spring:
  data:
    redis:
      host: ${REDIS_HOST}          # ElastiCache primary endpoint
      port: 6379
      ssl:
        enabled: true              # in-transit encryption on
  cache:
    type: redis
    redis:
      time-to-live: 300000        # 5 minutes default TTL
@SpringBootApplication @EnableCaching
public class SearchServiceApplication {}

@Service
public class RestaurantMenuService {
  private final RestaurantRepository repo;

  @Cacheable(value = "menus", key = "#restaurantId")
  public Menu getMenu(String restaurantId) {
    return repo.findMenuFor(restaurantId);   // hits Aurora once; subsequent calls skip the DB
  }

  @CacheEvict(value = "menus", key = "#restaurantId")
  public void onMenuChanged(String restaurantId) {}   // called when restaurant updates prices
}
Boot · SQS

Order pipeline — publish + consume

@Service
public class OrderPipeline {
  private final SqsClient sqs;
  @Value("${zomato.queues.order-placed}") private String queueUrl;
  private final ObjectMapper json;

  @Transactional
  public void place(Order order) {
    orderRepo.save(order);                              // 1) commit to Aurora
    sqs.sendMessage(m -> m
        .queueUrl(queueUrl)
        .messageBody(json.writeValueAsString(new OrderPlacedEvent(order)))
        .messageAttributes(Map.of("orderId", StringAttr.of(order.getId()))));
    // 2) customer sees "order placed ✓" now; payment/notification/analytics happen async
  }
}

// A worker in another Spring Boot service (or the same one, different profile)
@Component
public class PaymentWorker {
  private final SqsClient sqs;
  private final PaymentGateway gateway;
  @Value("${zomato.queues.order-placed}") private String queueUrl;

  @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 100)
  public void pollAndProcess() {
    ReceiveMessageResponse resp = sqs.receiveMessage(r -> r
        .queueUrl(queueUrl).maxNumberOfMessages(10).waitTimeSeconds(20));   // long-poll

    for (Message msg : resp.messages()) {
      try {
        OrderPlacedEvent e = json.readValue(msg.body(), OrderPlacedEvent.class);
        gateway.charge(e.orderId(), e.amount());                       // idempotent!
        sqs.deleteMessage(d -> d.queueUrl(queueUrl).receiptHandle(msg.receiptHandle()));
      } catch (Exception ex) {
        log.error("payment worker failure — msg goes back to queue → DLQ after N tries", ex);
        // don't delete; SQS re-delivers automatically. Configure a Dead Letter Queue after 5 tries.
      }
    }
  }
}
Rules
  • Consumers MUST be idempotent — SQS Standard delivers twice occasionally.
  • Always attach a DLQ to production queues. Bad payloads must go somewhere.
  • Consider Spring Cloud AWS (@SqsListener) for a cleaner listener API than manual polling.
Boot · SNS

Fan out "order delivered" to email, push, analytics

@Service
public class OrderEvents {
  private final SnsClient sns;
  @Value("${zomato.topics.order-delivered}") private String topicArn;

  public void publishDelivered(Order order) {
    sns.publish(p -> p
        .topicArn(topicArn)
        .message(json.writeValueAsString(new OrderDeliveredEvent(order)))
        .messageAttributes(Map.of(
            "eventType", MessageAttributeValue.builder().dataType("String").stringValue("DELIVERED").build())));
  }
}
// SNS fans out to 3 subscribers (each its own SQS queue): email-worker, analytics-worker, loyalty-worker.
// Each queue is a Spring Boot consumer exactly like the SQS example above.
Boot · Secrets Manager

DB password from Secrets Manager on startup

@Component
public class DbSecretsInitializer implements EnvironmentPostProcessor {

  @Override
  public void postProcessEnvironment(ConfigurableEnvironment env, SpringApplication app) {
    try (SecretsManagerClient sm = SecretsManagerClient.create()) {
      String value = sm.getSecretValue(r -> r.secretId("zomato/prod/db")).secretString();
      Map<String,String> parsed = new ObjectMapper().readValue(value, new TypeReference<>() {});
      env.getPropertySources().addFirst(new MapPropertySource("aws-secrets",
          Map.of("DB_USER", parsed.get("username"),
                 "DB_PASSWORD", parsed.get("password"))));
    }
  }
}
// Register in src/main/resources/META-INF/spring.factories:
// org.springframework.boot.env.EnvironmentPostProcessor=com.zomato.DbSecretsInitializer
Rules
  • Enable automatic rotation on the RDS secret (Secrets Manager handles it).
  • App reads once at startup; if the rotation strategy is multi-user, no restart needed. Otherwise, a rolling restart on rotation.
  • The IAM role attached to the pod/task must have secretsmanager:GetSecretValue for exactly this ARN. Least privilege.
Boot · Cognito & JWT

Verify Cognito-issued JWTs on every request

@Configuration @EnableWebSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

  @Bean SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
      .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
        .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
        .anyRequest().authenticated())
      .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));   // verifies Cognito JWT
    return http.build();
  }
}

# application.yml — Spring Security auto-configures a JwtDecoder from this issuer
spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        jwt:
          issuer-uri: https://cognito-idp.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/${COGNITO_USER_POOL_ID}
Notes
  • Most JWT verification happens at the API Gateway (edge). Services still verify defense-in-depth.
  • Cognito issues both ID and access tokens — use the access token for API calls, id for user info.
Boot · CloudWatch

Micrometer → CloudWatch: metrics with zero code

<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-registry-cloudwatch2</artifactId>
</dependency>
management:
  metrics:
    export:
      cloudwatch:
        namespace: zomato/order-service
        step: 1m                     # push every minute
    tags:
      application: order-service
      environment: ${SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE}
@RestController
public class OrderController {
  private final Counter orderCounter;

  public OrderController(MeterRegistry registry) {
    this.orderCounter = registry.counter("orders.placed", "channel", "mobile");
  }

  @PostMapping("/api/orders")
  public OrderResponse place(@RequestBody OrderRequest r) {
    OrderResponse resp = orderService.place(r);
    orderCounter.increment();   // shows up in CloudWatch as a metric you can alarm on
    return resp;
  }
}
// Latency percentiles come free from Spring MVC's http.server.requests metric.
Rules
  • Structured JSON logs (Logback with logstash-encoder) — Logs Insights becomes a real query tool.
  • Alarm on p99 latency and error rate — not on CPU.
  • Enable X-Ray tracing (add aws-otel-java agent) — costs almost nothing, invaluable when debugging.
Boot · Local → AWS

From mvn spring-boot:run to production EKS

# 1) Local dev with LocalStack — no AWS credentials needed
docker run -d -p 4566:4566 localstack/localstack
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=local mvn spring-boot:run
# 2) Dockerfile — multi-stage, non-root, pinned JRE (from your Docker/K8s guide, Ch D2)
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-25 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:25-jre
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /app/target/order-service.jar app.jar
USER 1001
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
# 3) Push to ECR, deploy to EKS
aws ecr get-login-password | docker login --username AWS --password-stdin $ECR
docker build -t $ECR/order-service:$SHA .
docker push $ECR/order-service:$SHA

# EKS Deployment updated by CI/CD; ALB Ingress Controller provisions the ALB from Ingress YAML.
kubectl set image deployment/order-service order-service=$ECR/order-service:$SHA -n prod
Production release checklist
  • Image scan passes (Trivy or ECR scanning) — no HIGH/CRITICAL CVEs.
  • Health check (/actuator/health/readiness) reflects real dependencies (DB up, SQS reachable).
  • Graceful shutdown enabled (server.shutdown=graceful) — in-flight orders complete on rollout.
  • Alarms configured; runbook link in the alarm description; on-call knows the drill.
Zomato · A complete AWS journey · Java 25 · Spring Boot 4
A learning journey · beginner → advanced · one food-delivery app throughout

AWS for backend engineers, explained by shipping a real Swiggy-scale app

Picture yourself as a backend engineer scaling Zomato — customers search restaurants, order, pay, and track riders live, millions of times a day. This guide walks through the AWS services a platform at that scale actually leans on, from a single EC2 instance to a full multi-AZ architecture — each service introduced by the real problem it solves, illustrated with how Zomato, Amazon, Instagram, Uber, and other real systems use it, plus a Spring Boot 4 / Java 25 implementation for each. The AWS Services tab covers concepts, architecture, and best practices; the Spring Boot tab is the working code, deployment, and pitfalls.

Note: architectural details attributed to Zomato below are illustrative of how a platform at that scale is commonly built on AWS, not a disclosure of Zomato's actual internal systems.

Java 25Spring Boot 4AWS SDK v2~18 services covered
Compute EC2ECS/FargateEKSLambda Storage S3EBS/EFS Databases RDSDynamoDBElastiCache Network VPCALB/NLBCloudFrontRoute 53 Messaging SQSSNSKinesisMSK Security IAMKMSSecrets Manager Observability CloudWatchX-Ray DevOps Code* / CI-CD The whole picture ★ Zomato architecture
Compute · 1 · EC2

Virtual servers you rent by the hour

Scenario: standing up Zomato's very first server
The problem

You need a server to host Zomato's Spring Boot API. Buying a physical server means weeks of procurement, upfront capital, and — worst — you're stuck with whatever size you bought, whether you get 100 orders/day or 100,000.

The AWS answer — EC2 (Elastic Compute Cloud)

EC2 rents you a virtual machine in minutes: pick an instance type (t3.medium for dev, m6i.large for prod), pick a region, and it's running in 60 seconds. Pay per second while it's on. Instance types come in families — t (burstable, cheap), m (balanced), c (CPU-heavy), r (memory-heavy), g (GPU) — pick the one matching your workload.

Why use it

Full OS control (SSH in, install anything), Auto Scaling Groups add/remove instances automatically as traffic grows, and multiple pricing modes: On-Demand (flexible, expensive), Reserved (1-3 year commit, 40-70% cheaper — for your always-on baseline), Spot (AWS's unused capacity, up to 90% off, can be terminated with 2 min warning — great for stateless/batch work).

Real world — Netflix

Netflix runs the majority of its streaming platform on EC2, using Auto Scaling Groups to add thousands of instances every evening when viewership peaks and remove them at 3 AM when it drops.

Best practices
  • Never SSH into individual instances to fix things — bake changes into a new AMI or the container image, replace instances. Treat servers as cattle, not pets.
  • Cost optimization: Reserved / Savings Plans for the baseline, Spot for stateless/batch workers, On-Demand only for the spiky top.
  • Security: instances in private subnets (VPC), only the load balancer in public. No public IPs on app servers.
  • Spread ASG across multiple Availability Zones — one AZ outage shouldn't take down Zomato.
Compute · 2 · ECS & Fargate

Run containers without managing servers

Scenario: shipping Zomato as Docker containers
The problem

You've containerized order-service. Running containers on raw EC2 means you're now managing the OS and Docker and the container lifecycle. You want to just say "run 6 copies of this image" and stop caring about the servers.

The AWS answer — ECS with Fargate

ECS is AWS's container orchestrator. Fargate is its serverless launch mode: you specify CPU, memory, and image; AWS runs the containers on infrastructure you never see. No EC2 to patch, no Docker to install, no cluster to size. You pay per second of container runtime.

Why use it vs EKS (K8s)

ECS/Fargate is simpler — you learn 3 concepts (Task Definition, Service, Cluster) instead of Kubernetes' 30. Perfect when you don't need K8s-specific features. For Zomato's early days: ECS. Once you outgrow it — many namespaces, custom operators, cross-cloud portability — move to EKS.

Real world — Uber Eats (early platform)

Delivery-tech teams often start on ECS/Fargate for microservices because it gives container orchestration without the K8s learning curve — engineers focus on the app, not the platform.

Best practices
  • One service per container image — don't cram order + payment into one task.
  • Right-size CPU/memory using CloudWatch data; over-provisioning wastes money at Fargate's per-second billing.
  • Use ECS Service Auto Scaling (target-tracking on CPU or request count) — same idea as EC2 ASGs but for containers.
  • Store container images in ECR (Elastic Container Registry) — pinned tags, never latest.
Compute · 3 · EKS

Managed Kubernetes for teams that need K8s

Scenario: Zomato outgrows ECS — 15 services, custom operators, GitOps
The problem

You've decided you need Kubernetes (multi-team namespaces, Helm charts, ArgoCD, service mesh). But running the K8s control plane yourself — etcd, API server, scheduler across 3 zones — is a full-time job for a platform team.

The AWS answer — EKS

AWS runs the K8s control plane for you across 3 AZs. You bring worker nodes (EC2 node groups, or Fargate for serverless pods). The AWS Load Balancer Controller reads your Ingress objects and provisions ALBs automatically; the Cluster Autoscaler pairs with your ASGs. Everything from Chapter 16 of your Docker/K8s guide, but AWS-native.

Best practices
  • Use IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts) so each pod gets exactly the AWS permissions it needs — no shared node roles.
  • Multi-AZ node groups, PodDisruptionBudgets, and topology spread constraints — one AZ down, Zomato keeps serving.
  • Managed node groups over self-managed for OS patching; Fargate profiles for spiky workloads that shouldn't wait for a node to scale.
Compute · 4 · Lambda

Run a function; forget servers exist

Scenario: generating a thumbnail every time a restaurant uploads a menu photo
The problem

Zomato restaurants upload menu photos. Each photo needs to be resized into 3 thumbnails. Running an always-on EC2 instance for a job that fires 200 times a day is silly — most of the day it's idle.

The AWS answer — Lambda

Write a function. AWS runs it in response to triggers (S3 upload, API Gateway request, SQS message, EventBridge schedule). You pay per invocation + per ms of runtime. Idle costs = zero. Scales from 0 to thousands of parallel invocations automatically.

When Lambda fits — and when it doesn't

Great fit: event-driven glue code, image processing, scheduled jobs, low-traffic APIs. Poor fit: long-running requests (15 min hard limit), latency-sensitive traffic where cold starts matter (100ms-3s startup, especially for JVM), high sustained throughput (ECS/EC2 is cheaper past a threshold). Use SnapStart or GraalVM native for Java to cut cold starts.

Real world — Coca-Cola vending & iRobot

Coca-Cola processes vending machine telemetry via Lambda — each machine ping triggers a function, so idle machines cost zero. iRobot processes Roomba fleet events the same way — millions of devices, but the compute bill only reflects actual events.

Best practices
  • Keep functions small and single-purpose — one Lambda per event type.
  • For Java, enable Lambda SnapStart or use GraalVM native-image to fight cold starts.
  • Set reserved concurrency to protect downstream services (a Lambda flood can hammer your DB).
  • Always set a DLQ (Dead Letter Queue) for async invocations — failed events must go somewhere.
Storage · 5 · S3

Infinite object storage, pay per GB

Scenario: storing restaurant photos, user profile pics, invoices
The problem

Storing millions of restaurant photos in your database is a terrible idea — bloats backups, slows queries, and 5 MB blobs don't belong in a relational table. You need cheap, effectively unlimited storage for binary files, served fast to users worldwide.

The AWS answer — S3

An object store: you PUT a file into a bucket with a key (the path), and GET it back later. 11 nines of durability (99.999999999%). Serves petabytes. Storage classes let you match cost to access frequency: Standard for hot data, Standard-IA for occasionally accessed, Glacier for archives (retrievable in minutes to hours).

Why use it

Cheap ($0.023/GB/month Standard), directly serveable via CloudFront CDN, event-driven (S3 → Lambda on upload triggers thumbnailing), lifecycle policies auto-move old objects to cheaper tiers, versioning protects against accidental deletes.

Real world — Netflix & Airbnb

Netflix stores every source video, every encoded variant, and every image on S3 — exabytes of it. Airbnb keeps all listing photos and user uploads on S3, served through CloudFront for global speed.

Best practices
  • Block all public access by default; serve user-facing files via CloudFront with signed URLs.
  • Enable versioning + MFA delete on critical buckets — accidental deletion is otherwise permanent.
  • Lifecycle rules: after 30 days move to Standard-IA, after 90 to Glacier — massive cost savings.
  • Server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) on every bucket. Non-negotiable.
Storage · 6 · EBS & EFS

Block storage (a virtual hard drive) and shared file storage

Scenario: MySQL needs a fast disk; multiple containers need a shared folder
The problem

Your MySQL EC2 instance needs a fast, persistent disk that survives instance restarts. Separately, 5 containers producing PDF invoices need to share one folder.

The AWS answer — EBS and EFS

EBS = a virtual hard drive attached to one EC2 instance at a time. Fast (gp3 for most, io2 for extreme IOPS). Used by databases, boot volumes. EFS = a shared filesystem multiple instances/containers can mount at once (NFS). Slower per-op than EBS but shareable.

Best practices
  • Take EBS snapshots regularly (automated via Data Lifecycle Manager) — free backups.
  • Encrypt every volume with KMS. Default encryption on at the account level.
  • Prefer S3 for anything shareable — EFS is more expensive and only needed for POSIX-file-semantics workloads.
Databases · 7 · RDS & Aurora

Managed relational databases — MySQL/Postgres without the ops

Scenario: Zomato's orders, users, restaurants — the core relational data
The problem

Running MySQL yourself means handling backups, replicas, failover, version upgrades, patching, and monitoring — a full-time DBA role. Get any of it wrong once, and you lose data.

The AWS answer — RDS (and Aurora)

RDS runs MySQL/PostgreSQL/MariaDB/Oracle/SQL Server for you: automated backups, point-in-time recovery, one-click read replicas, Multi-AZ failover in ~60 seconds. Aurora is AWS's own MySQL/Postgres-compatible engine — up to 5× faster, storage auto-grows to 128 TB, 6-way replicated across 3 AZs.

Multi-AZ vs read replicas

Multi-AZ = a hot standby in another AZ for HA — synchronous replication, invisible failover on primary failure. Costs 2×. Read replicas = extra async copies you send read traffic to — cuts primary load. Zomato production needs both.

Real world — Amazon.com & Robinhood

Amazon migrated its own retail transaction data off Oracle onto Aurora. Robinhood runs its trading platform's critical relational data on Aurora for the automatic multi-AZ replication and instant failover.

Best practices
  • Always Multi-AZ for production. Automated backups + 30-day retention.
  • Read replicas for read-heavy workloads (restaurant catalog reads far outnumber writes).
  • Store DB credentials in Secrets Manager with automatic rotation, never in application config.
  • Enable Performance Insights — you'll actually be able to debug slow queries in production.
Databases · 8 · DynamoDB

Managed NoSQL — single-digit-ms at any scale

Scenario: session tokens, cart items, live delivery tracking pings
The problem

Zomato's rider apps ping location every 3 seconds. Across 50,000 active riders that's ~17,000 writes/second — sustained. RDS chokes; you need a database that scales writes horizontally without pain.

The AWS answer — DynamoDB

Key-value/document store that scales writes and reads independently. You pick a partition key (e.g. rider_id); DynamoDB shards data across many partitions automatically. On-demand mode auto-scales, provisioned mode is cheaper if load is predictable. Single-digit-millisecond latency at any scale.

When to reach for it

Sessions, feature flags, shopping carts, IoT/location streams, anything with a natural key-based access pattern and predictable query shape. Not for ad-hoc reporting (no JOINs, no GROUP BY) — that stays on RDS or a data warehouse.

Real world — Amazon.com carts, Lyft rides, Disney+

Every Amazon.com shopping cart is a DynamoDB item. Lyft tracks every active ride on DynamoDB. Disney+ stores user session state and per-user watch progress on DynamoDB across regions.

Best practices
  • Design the partition key to spread writes evenly — a single "hot" partition kills throughput.
  • Enable DAX (in-memory cache) for read-heavy items (session lookups).
  • TTL attribute on items that expire (sessions, tracking pings older than 24h) — auto-deletes, no cron job.
  • Global Tables for multi-region active-active — same table replicated to Mumbai + Singapore.
Databases · 9 · ElastiCache

Managed Redis / Memcached — a distributed cache in one click

Scenario: restaurant listings and menus cached in front of RDS
The problem

Every home-page load hits the DB for the same top-100 restaurants. That's millions of identical queries hitting RDS for data that changes hourly. You need Redis in front — but running Redis yourself means clustering, failover, and patching.

The AWS answer — ElastiCache

Managed Redis or Memcached. Multi-AZ with automatic failover, backups, patching handled. Cluster mode enabled → sharded across many nodes for huge datasets. Pair it with @Cacheable in Spring Boot (Ch 13 of your Spring Boot guide) and RDS load drops 90%.

Best practices
  • Always set TTLs — a cache that never expires eventually holds stale data.
  • Use Redis (not Memcached) unless you know you need pure key-value only — Redis has lists, sorted sets, pub/sub, all useful for rate limiting and leaderboards.
  • Encryption in transit + at rest, in a private subnet. Never expose ElastiCache to the internet.
Network · 10 · VPC

Your own private network in the cloud

Scenario: keeping the database off the public internet
The problem

If your MySQL is on a public IP, the entire internet is knocking on port 3306 within minutes. You need network-level isolation — only the app tier reaches the database; the database is invisible to everyone else.

The AWS answer — VPC (Virtual Private Cloud)

A private network you define with a CIDR (e.g. 10.0.0.0/16), split into subnets per AZ. Public subnets (for the ALB) route to the internet via an Internet Gateway; private subnets (for app + DB) can only be reached from within. Security groups = per-instance firewalls: "port 3306 only from the app-tier security group."

Best practices
  • 3 tiers × 3 AZs = 9 subnets. Minimum for HA.
  • Default-deny security groups — start with nothing open, add exactly what's needed.
  • VPC Flow Logs on — you'll need them the first time something looks off.
  • Use VPC endpoints for S3/DynamoDB — traffic stays inside AWS, no NAT gateway cost.
Network · 11 · ALB & NLB

Load balancing — Layer 7 HTTP and Layer 4 TCP

Scenario: routing zomato.com to the right microservice
The AWS answer

ALB (Application LB, Layer 7) understands HTTP — path/host routing, TLS termination, WebSocket, HTTP/2. This is the default for web APIs. On EKS, the AWS Load Balancer Controller provisions ALBs from Ingress objects. NLB (Network LB, Layer 4) is raw TCP/UDP — millions of connections/sec, static IPs, ultra-low latency. Reach for it for gRPC-heavy backends, gaming, non-HTTP protocols.

Best practices
  • Terminate TLS at the ALB using ACM (free public certificates), not at the app.
  • Health checks hit /actuator/health/readiness (Spring Boot). Match the timing to your app's real startup.
  • WAF (Web Application Firewall) in front of the ALB — SQL injection, XSS, rate limiting built in.
Network · 12 · CloudFront

CDN — cache content at 400+ edge locations

Scenario: restaurant photos loading fast for a user in Bengaluru
The problem

Zomato's photos live on S3 in Mumbai. A user in Kolkata waits 100+ ms per image on every load. Multiply by 30 images per home screen and it feels sluggish. And your S3 bill grows with every miss.

The AWS answer — CloudFront

A global CDN. Users hit the nearest edge location; CloudFront serves cached content or fetches once from S3/ALB. TLS + HTTP/2 + Brotli compression at the edge. Can also cache dynamic API responses briefly (5-30s) to shed massive load off ALB during traffic spikes.

Real world — Hotstar (Disney+) IPL live streams

Disney+ Hotstar serves cricket to 25M+ concurrent viewers via CloudFront — the origin never sees most requests, they hit edge caches close to viewers.

Best practices
  • Signed URLs / signed cookies for private content (invoices, user documents).
  • Cache-Control headers on origin — CloudFront respects them; long TTLs for photos, short for API data.
  • Invalidate carefully (paths, not /*) — invalidations cost money past the free tier.
Network · 13 · Route 53

DNS with health checks and routing policies

Scenario: zomato.com pointing to the right region + failover
The AWS answer

DNS service, but with policies: Latency-based (send Mumbai users to Mumbai region, Singapore to Singapore), Weighted (10% canary), Failover (health check the primary; on failure, DNS starts returning the secondary automatically), Geolocation. Also registers domain names.

Best practices
  • Set sensible TTLs — too high delays failover; too low means clients hammer DNS.
  • Health checks + failover policy are your first-line disaster recovery for multi-region.
  • Use alias records (not CNAMEs) for ALB/CloudFront — no extra hop, no cost.
Messaging · 14 · SQS

A managed queue between services

Scenario: order placement doesn't wait for payment to finish
The problem

When a Zomato order is placed, the API needs to (1) save the order, (2) charge the payment gateway, (3) notify the restaurant, (4) push mobile notifications, (5) update analytics. Doing all this synchronously means the customer waits 4-5 seconds and sees an error if any single step fails.

The AWS answer — SQS (Simple Queue Service)

Order-service does step 1 and puts a message on an SQS queue. Payment/notification/analytics workers read from the queue independently, retry on failure, and don't block the customer response. Standard queues = high throughput, at-least-once (rare duplicates). FIFO queues = strict order, exactly-once, lower throughput (300 msg/s per shard).

Real world — Amazon.com order pipeline

Every Amazon.com order flows through SQS between order intake, warehouse, shipping, billing. If warehouse is down, orders queue up safely and process when it recovers — customers never see the outage.

Best practices
  • Always configure a Dead Letter Queue after N retries — bad messages stop poisoning the queue.
  • Long polling (WaitTimeSeconds=20) — cuts empty receive costs by 20×.
  • Make consumers idempotent (see Ch 2 patterns) — Standard queues can deliver twice.
Messaging · 15 · SNS

Pub/sub — one event to many subscribers

Scenario: "order delivered" fans out to email, SMS, analytics, loyalty
The AWS answer — SNS

Publisher sends one message to a topic. SNS fans it out to every subscriber — SQS queues, Lambda, HTTPS endpoints, email, SMS. Perfect for "one thing happened, many parts of the system should know." The standard pattern for a resilient event fan-out is SNS → SQS per subscriber: each consumer has its own retry buffer.

Best practices
  • Message filtering — subscribers can filter by attributes so they don't get everything.
  • Every subscriber should be its own SQS queue, not a direct Lambda subscription, for retries and back-pressure.
  • Encrypt topics with KMS; verify signatures on HTTP subscribers.
Streaming · 16 · Kinesis

Streaming for high-volume telemetry and analytics

Scenario: rider location pings, clickstream, real-time dashboards
The AWS answer — Kinesis Data Streams

An ordered, partitioned event stream (think Kafka, managed). Producers write records with a partition key; multiple consumers read at their own pace. Data is retained 24 hours to 365 days. Perfect for millions of writes/sec (rider location, clickstream) feeding real-time analytics and long-term storage.

SQS vs Kinesis

SQS = work queue: a message is consumed by one worker, then gone. Kinesis = event log: same records read by many independent consumers, replayable. Use SQS for tasks, Kinesis for events/telemetry with multiple downstream needs.

Real world — Netflix & Lyft

Netflix pipes viewing telemetry through Kinesis to power recommendations, quality-of-experience alerts, and billing — all consuming the same stream independently. Lyft's Amazon Location + trip telemetry runs through Kinesis for fraud detection and dispatch analytics.

Streaming · 17 · MSK

Managed Apache Kafka

Scenario: you already use Kafka and want AWS to run it
The AWS answer — MSK (Managed Streaming for Kafka)

Real Apache Kafka, AWS-operated. Multi-AZ brokers, patching, monitoring — you own the topics and clients. Choose MSK over Kinesis when you already have Kafka expertise/ecosystem (Kafka Connect, KStreams, Debezium) or need Kafka's exact semantics.

Security · 18 · IAM

Who can do what on AWS

Scenario: order-service can read S3 photos but not delete them
The problem

By default, nothing on AWS can do anything. Every access is denied until an explicit permission grants it. But if you grant "everything to everyone" (which people do out of frustration), a single compromised credential owns your entire account.

The AWS answer — IAM

Users = humans. Roles = temporary credentials for services (EC2, Lambda, containers). Policies = JSON documents listing "on which resources, what actions, allowed/denied." Attach a role to an EC2 instance and its code gets AWS credentials automatically — no hardcoded keys anywhere.

Best practices — this section matters more than any other
  • Least privilege. Grant the exact actions on the exact resources needed, nothing more.
  • Never use the root account after initial setup. Never create long-lived access keys for a service — always use roles.
  • MFA on every human user. Federate to Google/Okta via IAM Identity Center (SSO) instead of managing users.
  • For EKS: IRSA (IAM Roles for Service Accounts). For ECS: task roles. Each pod/task gets exactly its own permissions.
Security · 19 · KMS

Managed encryption keys

Scenario: encrypting the database, S3, and logs — with a key AWS can't read either
The AWS answer — KMS

Managed keys used by RDS, S3, EBS, Secrets Manager, and your app code. Envelope encryption: KMS holds the master key; your data is encrypted by a per-object data key which is itself encrypted by KMS. You never see the raw key. Every use is logged in CloudTrail — full audit trail.

Best practices
  • Customer-managed keys (CMKs) over AWS-managed ones — you control rotation and access.
  • Enable annual automatic rotation on symmetric keys.
  • Restrict who can use vs manage each key with separate policies.
Security · 20 · Secrets Manager

Store, rotate, and fetch secrets — no more secrets in git

Scenario: the RDS password rotates every 30 days without a deployment
The AWS answer

Store secrets (DB passwords, API keys, JWT signing keys), retrieve at runtime with an IAM-controlled API call, and set automatic rotation for supported types (RDS, DocumentDB) with zero code changes. Alternative: Systems Manager Parameter Store (cheaper, simpler, no rotation) for non-critical config.

Best practices
  • Every secret rotates automatically, on a schedule — no manual rotations.
  • App fetches on startup + refresh; don't cache forever.
  • Never commit secrets to git — CI/CD reads them from Secrets Manager at deploy time.
Observability · 21 · CloudWatch

Logs, metrics, alarms — the AWS monitoring hub

Scenario: knowing when order latency spikes at 2 AM
The AWS answer

Logs = every log line from EC2/ECS/Lambda, searchable with Logs Insights. Metrics = CPU, memory, request count, custom app metrics (Micrometer publishes them). Alarms = "if p99 checkout latency > 800 ms for 3 mins, page on-call." Dashboards = single-pane view of the whole stack.

Best practices
  • Structured JSON logs (not plain text) — Logs Insights queries them in seconds.
  • Log retention policies — don't pay to keep every DEBUG line for 5 years.
  • Alarms on SLIs (p99 latency, error rate) — not on infrastructure metrics like CPU. Users don't care about CPU; they care about slow orders.
Observability · 22 · X-Ray

Distributed tracing across microservices

Scenario: which of the 6 services made this checkout take 4 seconds?
The AWS answer — X-Ray

Traces a single request across every service it touches — order → payment → notification. Shows a flame graph with the exact time spent in each hop and each downstream call (RDS, DynamoDB, external HTTP). Instantly reveals which service is the bottleneck. Add OpenTelemetry SDK to your Spring Boot app; X-Ray receives the traces.

Best practices
  • Sample intelligently — 100% traces on Black Friday will bankrupt you; 5% of normal + 100% of errors is a good default.
  • Add custom subsegments for the DB queries and external calls that matter — they show up in the flame graph.
DevOps · 23 · CodePipeline / CodeBuild / CodeDeploy

Automated build and deploy on every git push

Scenario: order-service goes from commit to production in 15 minutes, safely
The AWS answer

CodePipeline = orchestrator. CodeBuild = Maven/Gradle build + tests + Docker build. CodeDeploy = deploy strategies including blue/green (spin up new fleet, switch ALB, keep old for rollback) and canary. ECR for images. CDK or Terraform for infrastructure as code. Many teams also use GitHub Actions for the CI part and just use Code* for AWS-side deployment.

Best practices
  • Every environment defined in code (CDK/Terraform) — no console clicks in production.
  • Blue/green for stateless services; rolling for containers with orchestration (K8s handles it).
  • Automated rollback on health check / alarm failure — humans shouldn't be in the hot path at 3 AM.
  • Never deploy Fridays. Really.
★ The whole picture

Zomato's complete production architecture

Every service you've read about, wired together for a real food-delivery app
The scenario, end to end

A customer opens Zomato, sees restaurants, orders a biryani, pays, tracks the rider live, and rates the meal. Behind that one hour, roughly a dozen AWS services quietly cooperate. Here's the full map.

Feature-by-feature: which services do what

FeatureServices involvedWhy
AuthenticationCognito, API Gateway, Secrets ManagerManaged user pools + JWT verification at the gateway; secrets never in code.
Restaurant searchOpenSearch, ElastiCache, CloudFrontFull-text + geo-distance queries on OpenSearch; hot results cached; static images edge-cached.
Place orderALB → order-service (EKS) → Aurora → SQSSync save + async fan-out; customer response in ~200 ms.
Paymentpayment-service, SQS, KMS, Secrets ManagerAsync worker consumes SQS; gateway key held in Secrets Manager, rotated; TLS + audit log.
Live trackingRider app → Kinesis → tracking-service → DynamoDB17K writes/s of location pings; DynamoDB partition key = rider_id; TTL clears old pings.
NotificationsSNS → SQS → notification-service → mobile push / SMSOne "order placed" event fans out to every channel independently.
RecommendationsKinesis stream → S3 → SageMaker (offline train) → DynamoDB (serve)Batch train, serve pre-computed lists via key-value lookup for low latency.
AnalyticsKinesis → S3 (data lake) → Athena / RedshiftSame stream, different consumers — order funnel, restaurant reports, city dashboards.
MonitoringCloudWatch (logs + metrics + alarms), X-Ray (traces)SLI-based alarms (p99 latency, error rate) page on-call; X-Ray shows which hop is slow.
CI/CDGitHub → CodePipeline → CodeBuild → ECR → EKS (blue/green)Push to main triggers build, scan, deploy with automatic rollback on health failure.
SecurityWAF, Shield, GuardDuty, IAM, KMSWAF filters SQLi/XSS at the edge; GuardDuty flags anomalous API activity; IAM least-privilege everywhere.
HA / DRMulti-AZ everything + Route 53 failover + cross-region replication (S3, DynamoDB Global Tables, Aurora Global Database)AZ failure = invisible; region failure = ~1 min DNS failover to secondary region.

The three operational rules that hold it all together

Rule 1 · Multi-AZ from day one
  • Every stateful service (RDS, ElastiCache, MSK) in Multi-AZ mode. Stateless services spread across 3 AZs via ASG/EKS topology spread.
  • Cost is ~2× vs single-AZ; the alternative is total downtime whenever AWS has an AZ incident (they do, occasionally).
Rule 2 · Async everything the customer doesn't wait for
  • Customer sees "order placed ✓" within 200 ms; payment, notifications, analytics all happen behind SQS/SNS/Kinesis.
  • If any consumer is down, messages queue safely. Customers never see it.
Rule 3 · Every piece runs in code (IaC + CI/CD)
  • CDK or Terraform describes every resource. Pipelines deploy from git. Nobody makes changes in the console.
  • Recovering from disaster = terraform apply in the DR region + restore backups. Tested quarterly.
